topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Can I add a second floppy drive to a Mac Plus?
a: Yes, an external 800K drive plugs into the floppy port on the back. Apple makes one, and third-party drives work too. It makes disk copying much easier.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Can I connect a hard drive to a Mac Plus?
a: Yes, through the SCSI port on the back. Drives from Rodime, Apple, Jasmine and others work. Turn the drive on before the Mac, and make sure the SCSI chain is terminated and IDs don't clash.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Can I use a Mac Plus keyboard on the SE?
a: Yes, they both use the ADB-style connection on later models, but the original Plus keyboard uses a telephone-style plug. The SE shipped with the Apple Keyboard using the ADB port, so use the right one for each.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Can I use a modem with the Mac Plus?
a: Yes, plug a Hayes-compatible modem into the modem port with a Mac modem cable. Programs like Red Ryder or MacTerminal handle the communications. 1200 or 2400 baud is common.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Can the Mac SE read MS-DOS disks?
a: Yes, if you have the SuperDrive and a utility like Apple File Exchange, which comes with the system disks. Older 800K drives can't read DOS disks at all. Apple File Exchange translates between Mac and DOS formats.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How can I tell how much memory my Mac has?
a: Choose About the Finder from the Apple menu while in the Finder. It lists total memory and the amount each open program is using.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I add RAM to a Mac SE?
a: Open the case, then replace the SIMMs on the logic board. The SE can take up to 4 MB in 1 MB SIMMs. Take proper static precautions and don't touch the CRT.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I adjust the brightness on a Mac SE?
a: Use the brightness knob on the lower front or side of the case, depending on the model. The Plus has a brightness dial on the right side of the back panel. Turn it until the picture looks right.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I back up my hard disk?
a: Use a program like Redux, DiskFit or Apple's Backup utility to copy changed files to floppies. Do it often, because hard drives can crash without warning.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I clean the mouse on my Mac?
a: Turn the retaining ring on the bottom counter clockwise, remove the ball, and wipe it with a soft cloth. Clean the rollers inside with a cotton swab and a little alcohol.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I copy a disk when I have just one drive?
a: Drag the disk icon onto another disk icon to copy everything, and the Mac will prompt you to swap disks. It takes many swaps, so use a hard disk or second drive if possible.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I eject a disk from my Mac Plus when it won't come out?
a: Straighten a paper clip and push it into the small hole to the right of the drive slot. That manually releases the disk. If it happens a lot, the drive may need cleaning or service.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I get more free space on my 800K floppy?
a: Delete unneeded files and empty the Trash. You can also move things to another disk. Compression programs like StuffIt or Compact Pro shrink files so more fit on a disk.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I get rid of the nVIR virus?
a: Run Disinfectant, which finds and removes nVIR and other known viruses. Then check any floppies you use. Lock your disks when you can to protect them.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I make a startup disk for my Mac?
a: Copy the System Folder onto a floppy using the Installer on your system disks, or just drag the System and Finder over. Keep it small so you have space for applications.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I print to an ImageWriter from my Mac SE?
a: Connect the ImageWriter to the printer port with the cable, open the Chooser, and click the ImageWriter icon and the port. Then use Print from your application's File menu.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I tell which SE I have, the old one or the SuperDrive one?
a: The SuperDrive models were released in 1989 and say FDHD on the front. Older SEs have only an 800K drive. Check About the Finder as well, since the SuperDrive needs System 6.0 or later.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How do I zap the PRAM on my Mac SE?
a: Hold down Command, Option and Shift while choosing Control Panel from the Apple menu, or on older systems pull the battery for a few minutes. The reset restores default settings like the clock and mouse speed.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: How much RAM can I put in a Mac Plus?
a: The Plus takes four 1 MB SIMMs for 4 MB total, and that is the maximum. It ships with 1 MB, so you need to swap in four 1 MB SIMMs to reach 4 MB.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Is it OK to leave my Mac on all the time?
a: On the Plus, the lack of a fan means it runs a bit warm, but it's okay. Turn the brightness down when you leave to avoid screen burn, or just shut it off for long periods.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Is it worth upgrading my Mac Plus to an SE?
a: Only if you need the expansion slot or an internal drive. Speed is nearly the same. For most people, adding an external SCSI hard disk and more RAM to the Plus is cheaper and does more good.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Is the Mac SE good for desktop publishing?
a: Yes, with PageMaker and a LaserWriter it works well. The small 9 inch screen is a pain though, and you will want a hard disk and at least 2 MB of RAM.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Is the Mac SE hard drive upgrade easy to do myself?
a: It's doable with the right tools. You need a Torx driver and a long-handled tool to crack the case, and the screen can hold a dangerous charge. If you're not comfortable, have a dealer do it.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What are fonts and how do I install them?
a: Fonts are typefaces. In System 6, use the Font/DA Mover to move them into your System file. In MultiFinder you may need to restart before the new fonts show up.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What baud rate should I use for my Mac modem?
a: Use the fastest that your modem and the other end support, typically 1200 or 2400 baud. Set 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit unless the system says otherwise.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What can I do about the tiny 9 inch screen?
a: You can add a larger monitor on an SE with a video card in its expansion slot. The Plus has no slot, so the options are limited. Some people use screen enlargers like Full Page Display.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What does 800K mean on my disk?
a: It means the double-sided 3.5 inch disk holds 800 kilobytes. The older single-sided disks hold 400K. The Plus and SE read both, but the 128K and 512K Macs can't read 800K.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What does ADB mean on the back of my SE?
a: ADB stands for Apple Desktop Bus. It is the port for the keyboard, mouse and other input devices, which can be chained together. The SE was the first compact Mac with it.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What does Command-Shift-3 do?
a: It takes a snapshot of the screen and saves it as a MacPaint file called Screen 0 on your startup disk. Open it in MacPaint to edit or print it.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What does rebuilding the desktop do and how do I do it?
a: It rebuilds the Desktop file, fixing wrong icons and cleaning out old info. Hold Command and Option while the Mac starts or a disk mounts, and click OK when it asks. It takes a minute on a big disk.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What does the Chooser do?
a: The Chooser lets you pick printers, file servers and other network devices. Open it from the Apple menu, click a driver icon, and then choose the specific device or zone.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What does the bomb icon with a number mean?
a: It's the system error dialog, usually after a crash. The ID number tells you the type, for example ID=1 is a bus error and ID=2 an address error. Restart and write the number down if it repeats.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is HyperCard and does it run on a Plus?
a: HyperCard is Apple's tool for building stacks of cards with text, graphics and scripts. It runs on a Plus with 1 MB, but 2 MB is better. It's bundled with new Macs.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is MultiFinder and should I use it on a Mac Plus?
a: MultiFinder lets you run several programs at once, available with System 5.0 and later. On a Plus with 1 MB it's cramped, but with 2 or 4 MB it works well.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is StuffIt and why do all the files on the nets end in .sit?
a: StuffIt is a shareware compression program by Raymond Lau. The .sit files are archives that hold one or more compressed files, so downloads are smaller. You need StuffIt or Unstuffit to open them.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is a LaserWriter and can my Plus use one?
a: It's Apple's PostScript laser printer, and yes, the Plus connects to it via AppleTalk with a LocalTalk connector. It costs a lot, but the output is much better than a dot matrix.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is a SCSI ID and how do I set it?
a: Each device on the SCSI chain needs a unique number from 0 to 7. The Mac uses 7, and an internal startup drive is usually 0. Set the ID on the drive with its switch or dial.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is a good price for a used Mac Plus?
a: In the last couple of years used Plus machines go for around $700 to $900 with a keyboard. Prices fall as newer Macs come out, so shop around and ask about drive condition.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is a good terminal program to call BBS systems?
a: Red Ryder is a popular shareware program and easy to use. MicroPhone and Versaterm are good commercial options. They all support XMODEM file transfers.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is a virus and should I worry about it on my Mac?
a: Mac viruses like nVIR and Scores exist and spread through shared disks and software. Use Disinfectant, a free utility from John Norstad, and be careful with software from unknown sources.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is the best word processor for a Mac Plus?
a: Microsoft Word 4.0 is popular and powerful, while MacWrite is simpler and cheaper. WriteNow is fast and fits well in limited memory. Pick based on how much formatting you need.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is the difference between System 6 and System 7?
a: System 6 is the current release for the Plus and SE, and works well with 1 MB or 2 MB. Features like virtual memory and file sharing are only rumors on this group, so stay with System 6.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: What is the difference between a Mac Plus and a Mac SE?
a: The SE has the same 8 MHz 68000 and screen, but adds an expansion slot, room for an internal hard drive, a built-in fan option, and a 1.44 MB-capable SuperDrive on later models. The Plus has SCSI on the back, which the SE also has.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Which is better for a first Mac, a Plus or an SE?
a: If the price difference is small, get the SE. The extra expansion slot and internal hard disk option give you room to grow. If you find a cheap Plus, it runs the same software.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Which spreadsheet should I buy for my Mac?
a: Excel is the best on the Mac right now and is easy to use. Microsoft Works is cheaper and includes a spreadsheet, word processor and database. Both run fine on a 1 MB machine.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Why does my Mac Plus show a flashing question mark disk at startup?
a: It can't find a usable System Folder on any disk. Insert a startup floppy, or check that your hard drive is powered on first and its SCSI ID isn't conflicting. Then restart.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Why does my Mac make a clicking sound and not start?
a: Usually a bad disk or drive. Try a different startup disk first. If the clicking persists with several disks, the drive is likely failing and needs service.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Why does my Mac run out of memory when I open a second program?
a: Each application takes a fixed chunk of RAM. With only 1 MB under MultiFinder there's little left. Either add RAM or turn MultiFinder off and run one program at a time.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Why does my external hard drive not show up on my Plus?
a: Check the power, cable and ID number first. Turn the drive on before the Mac and give it time to spin up. Also make sure the drive is formatted with a driver such as Apple HD SC Setup.

topic: the Mac Plus and Mac SE
q: Why is my Mac screen shrinking or getting dim?
a: Likely the analog board is aging, perhaps the flyback or a bad solder joint. Don't open the case yourself because of the high voltage on the CRT. Take it to a service center.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Are Mac II clones or compatible machines available?
a: Not legally. Apple does not license the Mac ROM, so there are no true clones. You can find accelerators, upgrade boards, and emulation cards that make PCs act like Macs, but they are slow.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Can I run a Mac II with a black and white monitor?
a: Sure, the Apple video card works with the Apple monochrome monitor and also the 13 inch RGB. You can pick the number of grays or colors in the Control Panel.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Can I use SIMMs from my PC clone in a Mac II?
a: Usually yes, the Mac II uses standard 30-pin 100 ns or faster SIMMs. They must be installed in banks of four, all the same size. Be sure they are not parity (9 bit) types if the board does not expect them.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Can I use an Apple IIGS monitor on a Mac?
a: No, the IIGS uses a different RGB interface. Mac II video cards want a 15-pin Apple RGB connector, so you need a Mac-compatible monitor or a proper adapter cable.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Can the Mac II run virtual memory?
a: Not under System 6. System 7 supports it on a Mac II with the 68851 PMMU installed, and on 68030 machines like the IIx and IIcx without any extras.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Do I need a video card to use a Mac II?
a: Yes, the Mac II has no built-in video. You need a NuBus card like the Apple Macintosh II Video Card, which does 4 or 8 bit color, plus a monitor to plug into it.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Does the Mac II have a power switch on the front?
a: Yes, the Mac II has a keyboard power key, which is the one on the Apple Extended Keyboard. The rear switch also works. A small switch is on the back, and the machine can shut down under software control.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Does the Mac II need the FDHD upgrade to read high density disks?
a: Yes, the original Mac II needs the FDHD upgrade, which gets you the SuperDrive and new ROMs. Then you can use 1.4 MB disks and read MS-DOS floppies with Apple File Exchange.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How do I add more memory to a Mac IIcx?
a: Open the case by unscrewing the back and sliding the lid off, then press the SIMMs into the banks, starting with bank A. Use 1 MB, 4 MB, or larger SIMMs, all the same in a bank of four.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How do I install a second monitor on a Mac II?
a: Put a second video card in another NuBus slot, plug in the monitor, and restart. Then open the Monitors section of the Control Panel and drag the little menu bar to the screen you want as primary.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How do I move the menu bar between screens?
a: Open the Monitors control panel, then drag the little white menu bar from one miniature screen onto the other. You will need to restart the Mac for the change to take effect.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How do I switch my Mac II to color from the Control Panel?
a: Open the Control Panel from the Apple menu, choose the Monitors icon, and click Colors, then pick 16 or 256 colors. Gray scale is offered there too. The change takes effect right away.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How do I zap the PRAM on my color Mac?
a: Hold down Command and Option while choosing the Control Panel, or on System 6 hold Command-Option-Shift and select Control Panel. It resets the settings battery-backed RAM, and you then reset the colors and time.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How many SCSI devices can I chain on a Mac II?
a: Seven devices plus the Mac itself, each with its own ID from 0 to 6. Keep the cable under about 20 feet total and terminate both ends of the chain, or you will get flaky behavior.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How many colors can the Mac II display?
a: With the standard Apple video card and 256K of VRAM you get 16 colors, or 256 with the extra VRAM added. The palette is 16.7 million colors, but only 256 can be on screen at once.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: How much RAM can a Mac II hold?
a: The original Mac II takes 8 MB on the motherboard using 1 MB SIMMs, and it ships with 1 MB. With the right ROM and 4 MB SIMMs you can go beyond that, but 8 MB is the practical limit for most people.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Is the Mac II good for programming in Pascal or C?
a: Yes, MPW from Apple, Think C, and Think Pascal all run well on it. A Mac II compiles much faster than a Plus, and the color screen is handy for testing your own color QuickDraw code.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Is the Mac IIfx worth the money?
a: The IIfx at 40 MHz is the fastest Mac you can buy, with special I/O processors and fast RAM. But it costs a lot, so unless you do heavy graphics or publishing the IIci is a better deal.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Is the Mac LC a real color Mac?
a: Yes, the LC from late 1990 has built-in color video, a 68020 at 16 MHz, and a cheap price aimed at schools. It has one LC slot instead of NuBus, and a 16-bit data bus that slows it down.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Is the Mac SE/30 a color Mac?
a: No, the SE/30 has a built-in 9 inch black and white screen. It has a 68030 and an SE/30 slot, and you can add a video card in that slot to drive an external color monitor.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What does 8-bit color mean on a Mac?
a: It means each pixel uses 8 bits, so you get 256 colors on screen at a time chosen from a palette of 16 million. Set it in the Monitors section of the Control Panel.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What does CLUT mean?
a: It stands for color lookup table. In 8 bit mode each pixel is an index into a table of 256 colors, and programs can change that table, which is how color cycling and palettes work.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What does the 640 by 480 on the 13 inch monitor mean?
a: It is the number of pixels, 640 across and 480 down. That is more than the 512 by 342 of the compact Macs, so you see more of a document at once.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What does the Mac IIci add over the IIcx?
a: The IIci runs the 68030 at 25 MHz, has built-in video on the motherboard, and has a cache card slot. You do not need a video card to run a color monitor, which saves a NuBus slot.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What happens if I put a 68881 in the Mac II?
a: The Mac II comes with a 68881 floating point chip, which speeds up math in programs that support it, such as Mathematica, Excel, and 3D renderers. Programs not written for it will not get any faster.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is 32-bit addressing and do I need it?
a: The Mac II ROM only handles 24-bit addresses, which limits you to 8 MB of RAM. Connectix MODE32 lets a Mac II or IIx use more memory. Without a clean 32-bit ROM or that INIT you cannot use more.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is A/UX?
a: A/UX is Apple's version of Unix for the Mac II. It follows System V and BSD and runs Mac programs too. You need a Mac II with the PMMU, at least 4 MB of RAM and a SCSI hard disk of 80 MB or more.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is Apple's 8-24 display card?
a: It is a NuBus card that does 8-bit color on its own, and with extra VRAM and the 24-bit upgrade supports 24-bit color on the 13 inch monitor. It was made for the Mac II family.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is Color QuickDraw?
a: It is the part of the Mac ROM that draws in color, introduced with the Mac II. It adds color pixmaps and palettes to the original QuickDraw. Programs must be written for it to use color.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is NuBus?
a: NuBus is the 32-bit expansion bus in the Mac II family. Cards configure themselves, so there are no jumpers or switches to set like on a PC. Just plug the card in and install the software.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is a 24-bit video card?
a: It gives each pixel 24 bits of color, so you see 16.7 million colors at once and photo images look smooth. Cards such as the RasterOps 24L or Apple's Display Card 8-24 work in NuBus slots.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is the PMMU and why does the Mac II need it?
a: The PMMU is the 68851 memory management chip, which allows virtual memory. The Mac II ships with a socket for it, and it is required for A/UX. Without it, System 7 virtual memory will not work.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is the best program for painting in color on a Mac II?
a: Studio/8 and SuperPaint are popular, and Photoshop is on its way from Adobe for the high end. Studio/32 from Electronic Arts handles 24-bit color if you have a 24-bit card.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is the best way to back up a Mac II hard disk?
a: Use a program like Retrospect or DiskFit to copy files to floppies or a tape drive. For a 40 MB disk, a SCSI tape drive is much easier than swapping 800K disks.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is the difference between System 6 and System 7 for color Macs?
a: System 7 adds virtual memory, 32-bit addressing on supported machines, TrueType fonts, and file sharing. It needs at least 2 MB of RAM and runs slowly on a Mac II without more memory.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is the difference between the Mac II and the Mac SE?
a: The Mac II is a modular box with a 68020, six NuBus slots, and a separate monitor, so it can drive color displays. The SE is an all-in-one with a 9 inch black and white screen and a single SE slot.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: What is the difference between the Mac IIcx and the IIx?
a: The IIcx is smaller with three NuBus slots instead of six and one fewer drive bay. It has the same 68030 and 16 MHz speed and costs less, so it is a good choice if you do not need many cards.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Which Mac should I pick for a school lab on a small budget?
a: The Mac LC is the cheapest color Mac and has an Apple IIe card option, so schools can reuse old software. If you need more speed, a Mac IIsi has a 68030, a NuBus slot, and built-in sound input.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Which Mac should a beginner buy for desktop publishing in color?
a: A Mac IIcx or IIci with a 13 inch color monitor and 5 MB of RAM is a good start, with PageMaker or Quark XPress. If money is tight, an SE/30 does fine for black and white layout.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Which is better for color work, the Mac II or the Mac IIx?
a: The IIx has a 68030 and a built-in FPU and is noticeably faster, especially at 16 MHz. For graphics and number crunching it is worth the extra money. For ordinary word processing you will barely notice.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Which monitor should I buy for my Mac II, the 12 inch RGB or the 13 inch?
a: The 13 inch Apple High-Resolution RGB is sharper and brighter, with 640 by 480 pixels, and is the one most people get. The 12 inch is a lower-priced 512 by 384 display that is fine for basic color.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Why do some games not work in color on my Mac II?
a: Many older games assume a 512 by 342 black and white screen. Set the monitor to black and white and 1 bit mode in the Control Panel before launching them, then they will usually behave.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Why does my Mac II say it has a bad battery?
a: The clock and PRAM are powered by a lithium battery on the logic board. If the time keeps resetting after you turn off the machine, replace it with a new 3.6 volt lithium cell.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Why does my Mac IIci run hot?
a: The IIci has a built-in video circuit that uses part of main RAM, and a small fan that vents the power supply. Make sure the vents are clear. Mild heat is normal.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Why does my Trinitron look better than the Apple RGB monitor?
a: The Sony Trinitron tube uses an aperture grille and gives a brighter, sharper image. Apple's own 13 inch uses a Sony tube too, so the picture quality is very close.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Why is my color Mac slower than before after I switched to 256 colors?
a: The CPU has to push more bits to the screen at 8 bit depth than at 1 bit. Drop to 4 bits or black and white in the Control Panel and scrolling will speed up, or buy an accelerated video card.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Why won't my Mac II boot with a new hard drive?
a: Check the SCSI ID and the termination first. The internal drive is normally ID 0 and the computer is 7. The disk also needs to be formatted with Apple HD SC Setup or a similar driver.

topic: the Mac II and color Macs
q: Will my old Mac Plus software run on the Mac II?
a: Most does, but programs that write directly to the screen or depend on the old ROM may crash. If something fails, check with the maker for an update, or try turning off color in the Control Panel.

q: Can I copy and paste between two programs in MultiFinder?
a: Yes, and that's one of the best reasons to use it. Copy in one program, switch using the Application menu, and Paste into the other. The Clipboard is shared, so text and pictures move across easily.

q: Can I get files back after emptying the Trash?
a: Not from the Finder, but if you haven't saved anything new on that disk, a utility like Norton Utilities for the Mac or Complete Undelete may recover the file. Stop using the disk straight away.

q: Can I run System 6 on a Mac Plus?
a: Yes, System 6.0.8 runs fine on a Plus with 1MB, though MultiFinder is a squeeze there. With 2 or 4MB it works well. An 800K floppy can hold a minimal System and Finder, but a hard disk is much nicer.

q: Can I see files in a folder sorted by date modified?
a: Yes. Open the folder, choose By Date from the View menu, and the newest files appear first. It's good for finding the file you saved last, especially on a hard disk with lots of documents.

q: Can I use a Mac SE with System 6 and a 20 meg hard drive?
a: Sure. A 20MB drive easily holds System 6 (about 1.5MB for the System Folder) plus a few programs. Make sure the drive is formatted with the driver that supports HFS, which Apple HD SC Setup does for Apple drives.

q: How can I change an icon in the Finder?
a: Copy a picture from ResEdit's ICN# editor or use a tool like Icon Maker, then select the file, choose Get Info, click the small icon and paste. Applications' icons are inside the file's resources, so ResEdit is the proper way.

q: How can I get more than 9 or so items in the Apple menu?
a: You can put aliases of things? No, those don't exist yet. In System 6 only desk accessories show up in the Apple menu, and the limit is about 15 of them. Use Apple Menu Options? Also not available. Try DA Handler or a similar utility.

q: How do I change how much memory a program uses in MultiFinder?
a: Quit the program, click its icon in the Finder, and choose Get Info from the File menu (Command-I). Type a new number into the Application Memory Size box. Don't go below the suggested minimum or it may crash.

q: How do I check how much space is left on a disk?
a: Open the disk window and look at the top. It shows how many items are in the disk, how much is used in K, and how much is available. Get Info on the disk icon gives the same information.

q: How do I copy a whole floppy disk?
a: Insert the source disk and drag its icon onto the destination disk's icon. The Finder will copy it and ask to replace the contents. With one drive it will swap disks several times, so use a hard disk as intermediary if you can.

q: How do I eject a disk that is stuck in the drive?
a: Try Command-Shift-1 for the internal drive or Command-Shift-2 for the external one at the Finder. If that fails, restart holding the mouse button down. As a last resort, straighten a paper clip and push it into the small hole beside the slot.

q: How do I empty the Trash and why does it say the file is in use?
a: Choose Empty Trash in the Special menu. If it says an item is in use, that program is still open under MultiFinder, so quit it first. A locked file also won't go until you unlock it in Get Info or hold Option when emptying.

q: How do I get the startup disk to boot from the external drive?
a: Open the Control Panel and use the Startup Device control, in the Control Panel, to select the disk. Or hold down the mouse button with the disk inserted. With SCSI drives, the Mac boots from the lowest-number device it finds first.

q: How do I install a desk accessory?
a: Run Font/DA Mover, click the Desk Accessory button, open the file containing the DA, and copy it into the System file. It then shows up in the Apple menu. Under MultiFinder you can only do this after quitting other programs.

q: How do I know if a floppy has a virus?
a: Run a program like Disinfectant, which is free from user groups and bulletin boards, or Virex or SAM. The nVIR and WDEF viruses are common, so don't use unknown disks without scanning them.

q: How do I make a folder named with a special symbol or a blank-looking name?
a: You can type Option-Space for a nonbreaking space as the name, which looks blank to the eye. Folders with names like that are handy for tricks, but some utilities and backups may get confused by them.

q: How do I print in the background with MultiFinder?
a: Turn on Background Printing in the Chooser after selecting a LaserWriter, and run MultiFinder. The PrintMonitor program handles the job while you keep working, though the Mac will slow down a bit during printing.

q: How do I rebuild the Desktop file?
a: Hold down Command and Option while the Mac starts up, or while you quit a program back to the Finder, and click OK when it asks if you want to rebuild. It fixes wrong icons but wipes out your Get Info comments.

q: How do I rename a file without it being slow?
a: Click on the file name once, wait a second, then type the new name and press Return. Or select the icon and just start typing a name. The limit is 31 characters, and you can't use a colon.

q: How do I see a list view with sizes and dates in the Finder?
a: Use the View menu and pick By Name, By Date, By Size, or By Kind. Small Icon is also handy. In list views you can click the small triangle? No, that's later; in System 6 you open each folder as a separate window.

q: How do I select several files at once?
a: Hold Shift and click each icon, or drag a selection rectangle around them from an empty part of the window. You can then drag them all together to a disk or to the Trash, or get information on them.

q: How do I take a screen picture on a Mac?
a: Press Command-Shift-3 and the Mac writes a MacPaint-format file called Picture 1 to the startup disk. Number 4 with Caps Lock down on some versions prints the screen to an ImageWriter. Open the saved files in MacPaint.

q: How do I turn on MultiFinder in System 6?
a: Open the Control Panel isn't needed. Just restart and hold down Command-Option at startup, or better, select the Finder file's Set Startup command in the Special menu and choose MultiFinder. With System 6.0.x you pick it from Set Startup, then restart.

q: How much RAM do I need to run MultiFinder?
a: One meg is really too tight. With 2MB you can run a couple of small programs, and 4MB is comfortable. MultiFinder and System 6 themselves eat about 400K to 600K before you launch anything.

q: Is MultiFinder stable enough to use every day?
a: Mostly yes, with 2MB or more. Older programs that write directly to memory or assume they're the only app may crash it, so check with the vendor. I run it all the time with Word and PageMaker.

q: Is it worth upgrading from System 4.1 to System 6?
a: Yes. System 6 is faster, fixes lots of Finder bugs, and gives you MultiFinder if you have the memory. Apple's upgrade kit is cheap through dealers and user groups, and the disks are often free to copy from a friend.

q: My Mac crashes with a bomb box and a number, what does that mean?
a: The bomb with an ID number means a system error. Common ones: ID=1 bus error, ID=2 address error, ID=28 stack ran into the heap. Press the Restart button in the box if it offers one, or hit the programmer's switch.

q: What are INITs and cdevs?
a: INITs are small programs that load into memory at startup from the System Folder, and cdevs are control panel devices that show up in the Control Panel. Together they add things like screen savers, but too many can cause crashes at startup.

q: What does Get Info show for a file?
a: It shows the kind, size, where it lives, creation and modification dates, and a Comments box you can type in. The Locked checkbox protects a file from being changed or thrown away. For applications you also see the memory size.

q: What does it mean when a program is not MultiFinder-friendly?
a: It means the program wasn't written to share the Mac with others, so it may grab too much memory or fail to give up time to other apps. Companies like Microsoft and Aldus mark their newer versions as MultiFinder compatible.

q: What does the Option key do when I open a folder?
a: If you hold Option while double-clicking a folder, the old window closes as the new one opens. It's useful to keep the desktop from getting cluttered with windows. The same trick works when you open a document from the Finder.

q: What does the Set Startup command do?
a: It lets you pick whether the Mac starts up with Finder or MultiFinder on the next restart. It also selects the startup application on a disk, so a particular program can launch itself every time you turn on the Mac.

q: What does the Special menu Clean Up Window do?
a: It lines up the icons in the active window on the invisible grid. Holding Option while choosing it, the command changes to Clean Up by Name, or Clean Up Selection if icons are selected. It doesn't change anything on the disk itself.

q: What does the little icon at the right of the menu bar do?
a: That is the Application menu in MultiFinder. It shows the icon of the active program, and clicking it gives you a list of everything running so you can switch. You can also hide the current application or all the others from there.

q: What is HFS and how is it different from MFS?
a: MFS, the Macintosh File System, was the original format on the 128K Mac and has no real folders. HFS, the Hierarchical File System, is what you want now. It has real nested folders and handles hard disks much better.

q: What is ResEdit and is it safe to use?
a: ResEdit is Apple's resource editor, free from user groups and online services. It lets you change icons, menus, and dialogs. Always work on a copy of the file because a mistake can wreck the program.

q: What is the Chooser for?
a: The Chooser, in the Apple menu, is where you pick your printer, such as an ImageWriter or LaserWriter, and the port or AppleTalk zone. It is also where you log onto file servers if your Mac is on a network.

q: What is the Desktop file and can I delete it?
a: It's an invisible file that stores icons and Get Info comments for each disk. Don't delete it by hand; rebuilding it with Command-Option at startup is the safe way, and the Finder recreates it anyway.

q: What is the Scrapbook and how do I use it?
a: It's a desk accessory in the Apple menu where you can store pictures, text, and sounds. Copy something, open the Scrapbook, and Paste. You can later copy it back out to any other program.

q: What is the Switch Launcher?
a: It's a Finder feature of 6.0 where you can choose to start up with a different application than the Finder, set with Set Startup in the Special menu. It's handy for dedicated machines running one program all day.

q: What is the WDEF virus and how do I get rid of it?
a: WDEF infects the Desktop file and spreads when you merely insert a disk. Run Disinfectant, which finds and removes it. Rebuilding the Desktop file by hand helps, but a scanner is the proper fix.

q: What is the difference between the Finder and MultiFinder?
a: The plain Finder runs one application at a time. MultiFinder lets you run several programs at once, switch between them from the menu at the right of the menu bar, and have background tasks like printing or file copying keep going.

q: Which is better, Font/DA Mover or just putting fonts in the System file?
a: In System 6 you still use Font/DA Mover to add fonts and desk accessories to the System file. Suitcases from Suitcase or Font/DA Juggler let you keep extra fonts outside the System. Too many fonts will slow your menus down.

q: Which is the best version of System 6?
a: 6.0.8 is generally considered the most stable and is what I would use on most Macs. 6.0.5 was the first one to work on all models including the IIci and SE/30, but 6.0.8 fixed several bugs.

q: Why can't I put a colon in a file name?
a: The colon is the separator in Mac pathnames, like HardDisk:Folder:File, so the file system uses it internally. Use a dash or a space instead. Every other character is okay, including slashes.

q: Why do my icons turn into generic blank documents?
a: Your Desktop file is probably damaged or too big. Rebuild it with Command-Option at startup. If it keeps happening on a hard disk, a utility like Complete Undelete or Disk First Aid can help check for deeper trouble.

q: Why does my Mac say there is not enough memory to open an application under MultiFinder?
a: Each program gets a fixed memory partition, and the free space left after the System and other open apps is smaller than that. Quit something, or select the app's icon, choose Get Info, and lower its Application Memory Size if it will still run.

q: Why does the Finder say a disk is unreadable and offer to initialize it?
a: Either the disk is new and unformatted, or its directory is damaged. If it has data you need, click Eject, don't initialize. Try another drive, or use Norton Utilities or Disk First Aid to attempt repairs.

q: Why does the Mac keep asking me to insert a disk that I already ejected?
a: Ejecting a disk with Command-E or from the menu removes the disk but leaves its icon dimmed so the Mac remembers it. Drag the icon to the Trash to unmount it completely, and the Mac stops asking for it.

q: Can HyperCard do color?
a: Not natively. The 1.x and 2.0 versions are strictly black and white. Some XCMDs like ColorizeHC and Adrian Fox's colorizing tools can show PICT color pictures, but it's an add-on and a bit fussy.

q: Can HyperCard play sounds?
a: Yes. Use the play command with a sound resource, like play "boing". Sounds are 'snd ' resources stored in the stack, and you can copy them in with ResEdit or a utility like SoundMover.

q: Can HyperCard print stacks?
a: Yes. Print Card prints the current card, and Print Report in 2.0 lets you do labels and lists. Under 1.x you can set up Print Stack to put several cards on a page, and the printing script can use open printing for full control.

q: Can HyperCard run on a Mac Plus with 1 meg of RAM?
a: Yes, but barely. HyperCard 1.x runs in 1 meg under the Finder, though you need MultiFinder off and you will have little room for big stacks. 2 megs is much more comfortable, and 2.0 prefers it.

q: Can HyperCard talk to a modem?
a: With an XCMD or the dial command, which lets you send touch tones through the Mac speaker to the phone. For real serial data, use an XCMD like Serial or Apple's Communications toolkit stack.

q: Can I read a text file into a field?
a: Yes. In a script use open file "name", read from file "name" until end, put it into field 1, and then close file. Under version 1.2 you need an XCMD, since file commands are 2.0 and later features.

q: How can I copy a button from one stack to another?
a: Select the button with the button tool, choose Copy Button from the Edit menu, go to the other stack and choose Paste Button. The script comes along too, but check any references to cards or other objects.

q: How can I make a stack visual transition between cards?
a: Use visual effect before go. For example: visual effect dissolve, then go next card. Others include wipe left, iris open, barn door open and checkerboard. You can add fast or slow, and to black or to white.

q: How do I add a sound to my stack?
a: Use ResEdit or a utility like Sound Mover to copy a snd resource into your stack file. Then in a script say play "yoursound". Digitized sounds eat space fast, so keep them short.

q: How do I change the font in a field?
a: Select the field with the field tool, double-click for the info box, and press the Font button. Pick a font, size and style. With the browse tool you can't change text style in a locked field.

q: How do I do a loop in HyperTalk?
a: Use repeat. For example, repeat 10 times, or repeat with i = 1 to 10, or repeat while, repeat until. End with end repeat. You can leave early with exit repeat.

q: How do I find all cards containing a word?
a: Press Command-F and type the word, then press Return. It finds the first card with a word beginning with that text. Press Command-G for the next match in 2.0. In scripts, use find "word" in field "Name".

q: How do I get HyperCard? Do I have to buy it?
a: Before the 2.0 release, Apple bundled it free with every new Mac. If you have an older Mac without it, user groups and dealers can copy it for you. HyperCard 2.0 and later are sold through dealers, and Claris handles it now.

q: How do I get the date and time in a script?
a: Use the date and time functions. the date gives like 4/12/90, the long date gives Thursday, April 12, 1990, and the time gives 3:15 PM. Also the seconds returns a number to use for timing.

q: How do I make a button that goes to the next card?
a: Choose New Button from the Objects menu, then double-click it to open the button info. Click Script and type: on mouseUp, go next card, end mouseUp. Or just use the LinkTo button in the info box and click the destination card.

q: How do I make a pop-up menu in HyperCard?
a: In 2.0 you make a field or button style Popup in the button info, and put the menu items in the contents. In 1.x you had to use a button that shows a list of choices or an XCMD like PopUpMenu.

q: How do I make a stack password protected?
a: Choose Protect Stack from the File menu and set a password, or make it private access. Be aware the password only stops casual users. Also be careful, if you forget it you can lose access to the stack's design.

q: How do I make a stack that runs from a floppy for a friend?
a: Copy the stack and use a HyperCard Player if your friend has no HyperCard. Apple allows the Player to be distributed with stacks. It only lets them browse and type, not edit, and your stack needs to be on the disk too.

q: How do I make my own icon for a button?
a: Use ResEdit or an icon editor stack to create an ICON resource and paste it into your stack. Then pick it from the Icon button in the button's info box. Many icon collections are in the user group libraries.

q: How do I open the message box?
a: Press Command-M, or choose Message from the Go menu. Type a HyperTalk command like go to card 5 and hit Return. You can also type an expression like 2+2 and the answer shows up right there.

q: How do I run a videodisc player from HyperCard?
a: You use an XCMD or the serial port with commands for your player. Many Pioneer players take serial commands, and Apple's Videodisc Toolkit stack has the scripts to get you started.

q: How do I use a scanner with HyperCard?
a: Scan the picture into MacPaint or a scanning program and save as a MacPaint or PICT file. Then import it in HyperCard with Import Paint from the File menu. HyperCard is 512 by 342 pixels so scale to that.

q: I messed up my Home stack. How do I fix it?
a: Copy a fresh Home from your original HyperCard disk or the install disk, and put it in the HyperCard folder. You'll lose your preferences and custom buttons, so back up Home before experimenting with it.

q: Is HyperCard worth it for a simple address book?
a: Sure, for a few hundred names it works fine. Apple's Address stack comes with it and the Find command is quick. For thousands of records or heavy sorting, a real database like FileMaker or 4th Dimension will serve you better.

q: Is it OK to share stacks on bulletin boards?
a: Yes, there are plenty of freeware and shareware stacks on CompuServe, GEnie, AppleLink and local BBSes. Compress with StuffIt or Compactor first, and give credit for clip art and sounds you didn't make.

q: Is there a way to get an animation going in HyperCard?
a: Yes. Make a series of cards with slightly different paint and flip through them quickly, or use a repeat loop that moves a button or uses show and hide. AddColor aside, you can do simple cartoons. Don't expect video speeds.

q: My stack got huge after I edited it. Why?
a: HyperCard doesn't reclaim deleted space until you compact it. Choose Compact Stack from the File menu and the size should drop back. Paint-heavy cards also use lots of space, so check how many cards you have.

q: What are good books to learn HyperTalk?
a: The Waite Group's HyperTalk Bible and Danny Goodman's Complete HyperCard Handbook are the popular ones. Goodman's book is big, readable, and covers 2.0 in the latest edition. Apple's own HyperTalk reference is also worthwhile.

q: What does 'Can't understand arguments' mean?
a: The script has a syntax error, HyperCard saw something it can't parse after a command. Check spelling, quote marks around text, and commas. Try the line in the message box to see exactly where it breaks.

q: What does 'idle' do and should I use it?
a: HyperCard sends idle to the current card when nothing else is happening, many times a second. It's good for clocks and checks, but a heavy idle script will slow everything, so keep it short.

q: What does 'on mouseUp' mean?
a: It's a message handler. HyperCard sends the mouseUp message to a button when you click and release on it, and the script between on mouseUp and end mouseUp runs. Other common ones are openCard, closeCard and idle.

q: What does Compact Stack do?
a: It cleans out free space left behind when you delete or change things, so the file gets smaller and works faster. Do it before you copy a stack onto a floppy, and run it regularly on stacks you edit a lot.

q: What does HyperTalk's 'put' command do?
a: It puts a value into a container, like put 5 into field "Count" or put it after line 3 of card field 1. Without a destination it puts the text into the message box, which is handy for testing expressions.

q: What does the 'it' variable do?
a: It's a special local variable that holds the result of commands like ask, answer, get and read. For example, ask "Name?" puts what the user typed into it. Copy it right away because the next command can overwrite it.

q: What does the User Level setting mean?
a: It's the Home stack's Preferences card. Browsing only lets you click, Typing lets you enter text, Painting adds paint tools, Authoring adds buttons and fields, and Scripting gives you everything including the script editor. Set it to 5 to write HyperTalk.

q: What exactly is HyperCard?
a: It's Apple's authoring program for the Mac, written by Bill Atkinson. You build stacks of cards that hold text, graphics, buttons and fields, and script them with HyperTalk. It's part database, part presentation tool, part toy programming language.

q: What is a stack?
a: A stack is a HyperCard document, a file made up of a series of cards. A stack can be an address book, a game, a tutorial or whatever you want. Each stack is a separate file with its own scripts and background.

q: What is an XCMD?
a: An external command, a code resource written in Pascal or C that you add to a stack or Home. It extends HyperTalk with things the language can't do, like serial port access or color. XFCNs are the same thing but return a value.

q: What is the 'Power Keys' feature?
a: It's keyboard shortcuts for paint tools. Turn it on with Power Keys in the Paint menu. After that single keys do things, like d for draw dither, f for flip, and so on. Press Escape or turn it off to type normally.

q: What is the Home stack?
a: It's the stack HyperCard opens by default. It holds your preferences, the Home card with buttons to your other stacks, and the Stack Names and Addresses cards. Its script catches messages that nobody else handled, so keep a backup.

q: What is the difference between a card and a background?
a: The background holds objects shared by many cards, like a form layout and fields. The card holds things unique to that one card. Put the field layout on the background so every card gets it, and the data goes in the fields.

q: What is the difference between a field and a text object painted on a card?
a: A field holds real text you can edit, search, and read with scripts. Painted text is just bitmap graphics, so HyperCard can't find or change it. Use fields for anything the user types or your script reads.

q: What is the message hierarchy?
a: Messages go first to the object clicked, then to the card, then the background, then the stack, then the Home stack, and finally HyperCard itself. If no handler catches it on the way up, nothing happens. Use pass to send it on.

q: What's new in HyperCard 2.0?
a: There's a built-in script editor, a much faster Find, multiple-line text styles, a debugger, the ability to open more than one stack per window group, and a lot of new commands and functions. It's a big upgrade from 1.2.

q: What's the biggest size a stack can be?
a: The old limit is around 16 megabytes for a stack, and in practice you get slow long before that. A stack with a few thousand cards works fine. Compact Stack from the File menu often shrinks it a lot.

q: Which is better for a beginner, HyperCard or SuperCard?
a: HyperCard is a fine place to start since it is free or cheap and has the most stacks and help around. SuperCard offers color, resizable windows and menus, but costs more. Learn HyperCard first.

q: Why can't I see the Objects menu?
a: Your user level is too low. Go to the Home stack, open Preferences, and set the user level to Authoring or Scripting. You can also hold Command and type a stack with the menu shown, but the Preferences card is the real fix.

q: Why does HyperCard run so slowly on my Mac 512KE?
a: It really needs at least 1 meg of RAM, and the 512KE with 512K can't run HyperCard at all unless you upgrade memory. Even on a Plus a hard disk helps a lot. Floppy-only stacks are painfully slow.

q: Why does my field not let me type anything?
a: The field is probably locked. Open the field info and uncheck Lock Text. Also check your user level, since at Browsing you can't type into any field.

q: Can I add a hard drive to my A500?
a: Yes, the A590 plugs into the side expansion port and holds a 20MB SCSI or XT-style drive, with a socket for extra RAM. Third parties like GVP also make A500 hard drive units.

q: Can I connect a printer to the Amiga?
a: Yes, use the parallel port with a standard Centronics cable. Run Preferences to choose a printer driver such as Epson or HP LaserJet. Most Epson-compatible dot matrix printers work fine.

q: Can I put a 68020 or 68030 accelerator in my A500?
a: Yes, boards like the GVP A500-HD8+ and Commodore's own A2630 for the A2000 exist. The A500 ones plug into the side expansion port or the CPU socket. Prices are high, so make sure you need the speed.

q: Can I run a Commodore 64 emulator on the Amiga?
a: Yes, there is a C64 emulator that works using a program like the Transformer's counterpart. It runs the C64 software, though slower than the real machine. For better results, you can attach a real C64 drive and use the serial port link.

q: Can I use a standard PC monitor with the Amiga?
a: Only a multi-sync, or one that takes analog RGB at 15kHz. A VGA monitor won't sync with it. Some multisync models work, but the standard digital RGB or CGA monitors are not a good match.

q: Can the Amiga read MS-DOS disks?
a: Yes, using CrossDOS or the MessyDOS program on the Fish disks. Standard 3.5 inch 720K disks work with the A500's drive, but the Amiga's drive can't read 1.44MB PC disks.

q: Do I need a virus checker?
a: Yes, boot block viruses like the SCA virus spread fast on pirated games disks. Use VirusX or Xcopy-style checkers to scan new disks. Write-protecting your disks and rebooting before inserting them helps too.

q: How can I make a bootable game disk copy of my own data disk?
a: Format with the INSTALL command: type INSTALL DF0: to write the boot block. Then copy a S directory with a startup-sequence file to the disk. That makes it bootable into the CLI or whatever program you run.

q: How do I back up my Workbench disk?
a: Use DiskCopy from the CLI: DISKCOPY FROM DF0: TO DF0: NAME Backup, then swap disks when asked. Or drag the disk icon onto another disk icon in Workbench. Always keep the original safe and run from the copy.

q: How do I boot my Amiga 500 from a floppy if I have no hard drive?
a: Just insert your Workbench disk when the screen shows the hand holding a disk, and it boots. For games, put the game disk in DF0: at the same prompt, or reset with Ctrl-Amiga-Amiga and insert it.

q: How do I change the screen colors in Workbench?
a: Run the Preferences program from the System disk and choose the palette screen. You can set the four colors and the screen resolution. In 2.0 you have more control and many more options.

q: How do I find out which Kickstart version I have?
a: Look at the screen at power up, or use the Version command from the CLI. Workbench 1.3 shows Kickstart 34.5 in the title info, while 1.2 is version 33. Typing VERSION in the CLI will print the numbers.

q: How do I format a blank floppy on Workbench?
a: Insert the disk, click its icon, then choose Initialize from the Disk menu. Give it a name and confirm. From the CLI you can type FORMAT DRIVE DF0: NAME MyDisk. Add NOICONS if you don't want a Trash icon.

q: How do I get a program to run from the CLI when I double-click it does nothing?
a: Some programs need to be run from the CLI because they need a stack size greater than the default 4000. Type STACK 20000 before the program, then run it. You can also set the Stack in the icon's Information window.

q: How do I get rid of the SCA virus?
a: Reboot with the power off for at least ten seconds, since the virus survives a warm reset. Then use VirusX or a similar checker to restore the boot block of each infected disk with INSTALL.

q: How do I get the date and time to stay set after turning off the Amiga?
a: You need a battery-backed clock. The A2000 has one built in, while the A500 needs a memory expansion with a clock chip. Then run SetClock SAVE in your startup-sequence and SetClock LOAD to read it.

q: How do I make music on the Amiga?
a: Use a tracker like Soundtracker or NoiseTracker, which play 4-channel sample modules. Others, like Sonix or Deluxe Music Construction Set, use MIDI or notation. A MIDI interface plugs into the serial port.

q: How do I run PC software on the Amiga?
a: On the A2000 you can install a Commodore Janus bridgeboard, an XT or AT card, which runs MS-DOS. On the A500, there is a software emulator called Transformer that runs slowly but gets some programs working.

q: How do I use the CLI in Workbench 1.3?
a: Open the System disk and double-click the Shell or CLI icon, or find it in the System drawer. Type commands like DIR, COPY, and DELETE. In 1.3 you can also use the Shell, which has command history.

q: How many colors can the Amiga show?
a: Palette is 4096 colors. In low-res you can have 32 on screen at once, or 64 with Extra Half-Brite, or 4096 in HAM. In high-res 640 mode you get 16 colors, and in interlace the same.

q: How many sound channels does the Amiga have?
a: Four channels of 8-bit sampled sound, two for left and two for right speakers. Samples are played from Chip RAM. You can combine channels or modulate one with another.

q: Is an Amiga 2000 good for desktop publishing?
a: It can be, with PageStream or Professional Page and a hard drive plus 2MB or more RAM. Add a PostScript-compatible printer driver for good output. A flicker fixer helps with the interlaced display.

q: Is it worth getting the 512K expansion for my A500?
a: Yes, definitely. Many programs and games want 1MB, and the extra RAM is cheap. Get one with a clock chip if you can, because Workbench 1.3 will then keep the correct date and time.

q: Is there a way to get more than 1MB into an A500?
a: Yes. Memory expansions on the side port, such as the A590 with 2MB, or others, take you to 8MB of Fast RAM. Some cards fit inside the trapdoor for 512K. For more serious needs there are accelerator boards for the A2000.

q: What does ARexx do?
a: ARexx is the Amiga's version of the REXX scripting language, which ships with Workbench 2.0. It lets programs send commands to each other, so you can script a paint program, a text editor, and a terminal at the same time.

q: What does Guru Meditation mean?
a: It's the Amiga's crash screen, a red or flashing box with an error code. The first number is the error type and the second is the address of the task. Usually you just have to reboot, and 0000000x errors often mean a bad program or memory problem.

q: What does Software Failure mean?
a: It's the error requester shown on Workbench 2.0 and later when a task crashes. The message includes an error number and task name. Press the left mouse button to reboot. Mind that it means the program tried something invalid.

q: What does the Amiga key do?
a: The right Amiga key works like the Command key on a Mac. Combined with other keys it gives you menu shortcuts, such as Right-Amiga-N for new drawer. Ctrl and both Amiga keys together reset the machine.

q: What does the Copper do?
a: The Copper is a simple coprocessor that executes instructions synchronized to the video beam. It can change colors or registers on certain scan lines, which is how you get a screen with more than 32 colors, or split screens.

q: What is HAM mode?
a: Hold-And-Modify lets the Amiga display 4096 colors on screen at once at low res. Each pixel either picks a palette color or modifies one color component of the pixel to its left. It gives photo-like pictures, but with some color fringing.

q: What is Workbench 2.0 and when can I get it?
a: Workbench and Kickstart 2.0 is a major update with a new look, new Shell, ARexx, and better handling of the hardware. It is available with the A3000 and as an upgrade, though the ROM can be hard to find for the A500.

q: What is a good terminal program for calling BBSs?
a: VT100 by Dave Wecker comes on a Fish disk and works well, as does Online! or A-Talk III. For file transfers it supports Xmodem and Zmodem. A Hayes-compatible modem on the serial port is what you need.

q: What is the Fish disk collection?
a: Fred Fish collects public domain and freely distributable software and releases it on numbered disks. There are hundreds of them now, and each has a handful of programs with source. You can get them from user groups or by mail order.

q: What is the best game for the Amiga so far?
a: It depends on your taste, but Defender of the Crown, Shadow of the Beast, and Speedball are popular. For strategy, try Populous. Lemmings is also quite good, and Sim City works well here too.

q: What is the best word processor for the Amiga?
a: ProWrite and Scribble! are popular and easy. Wordperfect is also available, and Final Copy is nice for outline fonts. For desktop publishing, PageSetter and Professional Page are the main choices.

q: What is the blitter?
a: It is a custom chip part of Agnus that moves blocks of memory very fast. It copies, fills, and draws lines, so the CPU does not have to. Games use it for sprites and moving objects.

q: What is the difference between Chip RAM and Fast RAM?
a: Chip RAM is shared with the custom chips, so graphics and sound can access it, but the 68000 gets slowed when they compete. Fast RAM is only for the CPU, so it runs without that contention. Programs run faster with Fast RAM.

q: What is the difference between Kickstart 1.2 and 1.3?
a: Kickstart 1.3 adds autobooting from a hard drive and a faster file system option called FFS support on the hard disk side. It also fixes a number of bugs. If you have a 1.2 machine, a ROM upgrade is worth it, especially with an A590.

q: What is the difference between OCS and ECS?
a: OCS is the original chip set, while ECS is the Enhanced Chip Set found in newer machines. ECS Agnus can address 2MB of Chip RAM, and the new Denise adds productivity modes. The A500 Plus has it.

q: What is the startup-sequence?
a: It's a script file in the S: directory on your boot disk that runs automatically at boot. It sets up assigns, loads the Workbench, and so on. You can edit it with ED or any text editor, and it's the place for your own startup commands.

q: What modem should I buy for my Amiga?
a: Any Hayes-compatible modem works on the serial port with a standard RS-232 cable, but the Amiga uses a 25-pin plug. A 2400 baud modem is a good buy now, such as the Supra, and the 9600 baud ones cost a lot.

q: What monitor should I buy for the A500?
a: The Commodore 1084 is the standard choice. It takes RGB and gives a sharp picture in both low and high resolution. A TV via the RF modulator works but text in interlace mode is very hard to read.

q: What video work can I do with the A2000?
a: With a Video Toaster, no wait, that's coming for the Amiga 2000 only for NTSC. With a genlock such as the Amiga A2300 or Rendale you can overlay Amiga graphics on a video signal and record onto tape.

q: Which is better, the A500 or the A2000?
a: The A2000 has Zorro II expansion slots, a built-in 3.5 inch drive bay for a hard disk, and room for a PC bridgeboard. If you only want games and light use, the A500 is cheaper and fine. For video or serious work get the 2000.

q: Which paint program is best, Deluxe Paint or something else?
a: Deluxe Paint III is the one most people use. It has animation, color cycling, and good brushes, and supports HAM mode. Photon Paint is the alternative if you want HAM painting with more features.

q: Why does my Amiga click when there is no disk in the drive?
a: That's the drive checking for a disk, which Kickstart does every few seconds. It's normal on the A500 and harmless, though it can be annoying. Some utilities on Fish disks will stop the clicking.

q: Why does my Amiga say Please insert volume in any drive?
a: A program or Workbench is looking for a disk that is not mounted, such as a volume it was told to use through an assign. Insert the named disk or cancel it. It often happens if you remove a disk while it is open.

q: Why does my screen flicker in high-res mode?
a: The 640x400 interlaced mode draws alternating fields, so thin horizontal lines flicker on a normal monitor. A long-persistence monitor helps. Use 640x200 non-interlaced if you can, or buy a flicker fixer on an A2000.

q: Will my old games work with Kickstart 2.0?
a: Many do, but some that bang the hardware directly or rely on old system bugs fail. Games that boot from their own disks usually work fine. Lots of programs have been patched, and some will need a 1.3 ROM switch.

q: Can I connect an Amiga to a TV?
a: Yes, with an RF modulator on the A500, or via the composite video out on the back. For a cleaner image, use a monitor like the Commodore 1084. A TV will make interlace text flicker badly.

q: Can I multitask on 512K?
a: Yes, multitasking is built in and works fine in 512K for small programs, like a terminal and a clock. Big programs such as DeluxePaint III or a word processor take most of the RAM, so be careful.

q: Can I run Workbench 1.3 programs on a Kickstart 2.0 machine?
a: Most will, but some that poke at system structures or use hardware directly will crash. Games that boot from their own disk are the worst. Check whether you can use a 1.3 Kickstart in a ROM switcher or boot from disk.

q: Can I use an IBM PC floppy on my Amiga?
a: Not with the stock drive. You need CrossDOS or a tool like Dos-2-Dos, which reads 720K MS-DOS disks. The Amiga drive can't read the 360K disks from older PCs reliably, and 1.44 meg disks need a different drive.

q: Can I use the Amiga as a workstation with UNIX?
a: Yes, Commodore sells the Amiga 3000UX with System V Release 4. Otherwise you can use a terminal program to log into a Unix machine, or a port of programs like the Fish disk uucp tools.

q: How can I speed up my floppy-based system?
a: Copy the commands you use to a RAM disk, with COPY C:DIR RAM: and use PATH RAM: to find them. Add more memory so you can use a larger RAM disk. A hard drive is the real fix.

q: How do I change the Workbench screen colors?
a: Open the Preferences tool on your Workbench disk and click Pointer or Colors. Change the sliders, then save. In Workbench 1.3 it's the Palette gadget. The settings are saved in the system-configuration file in the Devs directory.

q: How do I copy a whole disk?
a: Use DISKCOPY FROM DF0: TO DF1: if you have two drives, or just DF0: to DF0: and swap disks when asked. It copies every track exactly, including the boot block. Don't use it on disks with different formats.

q: How do I find a file on a disk?
a: Use DIR with the ALL option, or the WHICH command for commands in the path. The best option is a program like Find in the Fish disks. Under 2.0, Search in the CLI checks text inside files.

q: How do I format a blank floppy from the CLI?
a: Use FORMAT DRIVE DF0: NAME MyDisk. Add NOICONS if you don't want a Trashcan icon. Make sure the disk isn't your Workbench disk, and double check the drive name before pressing Return, because it wipes everything.

q: How do I get more than 512K on my A500?
a: Plug in a trapdoor expansion under the machine. The A501 gives you 512K more and a clock, and third parties sell larger ones. That gives you 1 meg of Chip RAM, or slow memory depending on the board.

q: How do I get my printer to work with the Amiga?
a: Open Preferences, choose a printer driver such as Epson Q or HP LaserJet, and set the port to parallel or serial. Save it. Then DeluxePaint and others print using that driver. Check your cable.

q: How do I install a program on my hard drive?
a: Make a drawer with MAKEDIR, then COPY the files across, including the .info files. Add any assigns or libraries it needs to your Startup-Sequence. Many programs come with an Installer script.

q: How do I make a RAM disk survive a reboot?
a: With Kickstart 1.3 you can use RAD: which is a recoverable RAM disk, and it survives a warm reboot. Use MOUNT RAD: from the Devs/DOSDrivers or a mountlist, and copy your files there.

q: How do I make a disk bootable?
a: Run INSTALL DF0: from the CLI on a formatted disk. That writes the boot block. Then put a C directory with the commands you need, an S directory with Startup-Sequence, and a Libs and Devs directory as required.

q: How do I read a text file page by page?
a: Use MORE filename if your Workbench has it, or TYPE filename with Ctrl-S to pause. Under 2.0 there's MORE in C. Press space for the next page. Fish disks also have programs like PowerView.

q: How do I rename a file in the CLI?
a: Type RENAME oldname newname. You can also use RENAME FROM oldname TO newname. The same command moves a file to another directory if you give a path, as long as it's on the same volume.

q: How do I run a program in the background?
a: Type RUN programname in the CLI. The prompt returns and the program runs as a separate process. If it needs input, you can use RUN >NIL: programname to detach it from the window.

q: How do I set the date and time?
a: Type DATE 12-Mar-90 14:30 in the CLI, or use the Preferences tool on Workbench 1.3 or the Time editor in 2.0. Without a battery-backed clock, you must set it every boot. Add DATE to your startup if you like.

q: How do I stop a runaway program from a CLI window?
a: Press Ctrl-C in the CLI where it was started to send a break. If you started it with RUN, use the STATUS command to find the process number, then BREAK number C. If that fails, you must reboot.

q: How do I upgrade an A500 to Kickstart 2.0?
a: Buy the 2.0 ROM kit from Commodore dealers, open the case, and replace the Kickstart chip. Or get a ROM switcher board. Boot with the older ROM when a game doesn't work with 2.0.

q: How much RAM do I need for DeluxePaint III?
a: One meg is the practical minimum, and the manual says that. With 512K you can only use small low-color screens. If you want larger pictures or animation, 2 meg or more is far better.

q: Is the A590 hard drive worth it for an A500?
a: Yes, if you do anything serious. It plugs into the side expansion port, gives you a 20 meg hard disk with autoboot on Kickstart 1.3, and has a socket for up to 2 meg of RAM. Loading from floppies gets old fast.

q: What does 'Disk is full' mean when I know there is space?
a: You may have run out of free blocks on the volume, or the directory is too crowded. Use INFO to see used and free blocks. A floppy has only about 880K and loses some to the file system.

q: What does 'Unknown command' mean?
a: AmigaDOS couldn't find the command in the current directory, the path, or C:. Check the spelling, or use PATH to add the right directory. If it's a program on another disk, give the full path.

q: What does ASSIGN do?
a: It gives a logical name to a directory or a disk, such as ASSIGN FONTS: DF1:Fonts. Programs can then ask for FONTS: without knowing where it is. Type ASSIGN alone to see the list.

q: What does Workbench 2.0 add over 1.3?
a: A much better look with 3D gadgets, a new Shell, ARexx, a proper Preferences set, public screens and new file system options. It needs Kickstart 2.0, so older machines need a ROM swap.

q: What does the Guru Meditation message with 00000004 mean?
a: Error 00000004 is usually a bad address error, often caused by a program writing through a bad pointer. The second number gives the task or the subsystem. Reboot and try the program with less stuff running.

q: What does the Please insert volume in any drive requester mean?
a: A program or script is looking for a disk named in an assign or path. Insert that volume, or fix the assign. Often it's a missing disk like Fonts: or LIBS: not found because it's not on your boot disk.

q: What does the Protect command do?
a: It sets the file's flags. PROTECT myfile +s makes it a script, +p makes it pure and residentable, +r +w +e +d set read, write, execute, and delete. A script needs the s flag set to run by name.

q: What does the number after a program name in the Workbench title bar mean?
a: The title bar shows free Chip and Fast memory, like 480000 free memory. In 1.3 it shows graphics and other memory figures. Watch it to see if you're running low before starting a big program.

q: What is ARexx and is it worth learning?
a: ARexx is the Amiga version of the REXX scripting language, standard with Workbench 2.0. It lets programs send commands to each other, so it's good for automating things like a text editor or terminal program.

q: What is a .info file?
a: It's the icon file for a program, disk, drawer, or project, and holds the picture and tooltype information. Copying a file in the CLI won't copy its icon unless you copy file.info too.

q: What is a Fish disk?
a: Fred Fish compiles freely distributable Amiga software onto numbered disks, now past number 400. They have utilities, games, and source code. User groups and BBSs sell them cheap, and you can find them on Usenet FTP sites.

q: What is interlace and why does it flicker?
a: Interlace gives you 400 lines in NTSC or 512 in PAL by drawing two fields. Thin horizontal lines blink at 30 or 25 times a second. A long-persistence monitor or a flicker fixer helps.

q: What is the Fast File System?
a: FFS arrived with Workbench 2.0. It stores data more efficiently and is around two to four times faster than the old file system. You use it on hard drives and can format floppies with FFS.

q: What is the Kickstart?
a: It's the operating system core in ROM: Exec, Intuition, Graphics, and AmigaDOS. Kickstart 1.2 and 1.3 are on the A500 and A2000 while 2.0 is newer. Workbench is the disk-based part, loaded after Kickstart.

q: What is the best Amiga paint program?
a: Most people say DeluxePaint III from Electronic Arts, with animation and good color cycling. For 24-bit work and HAM, look at Digi-Paint or Photon Paint. DPaint is the one most artists use.

q: What is the best way to back up my hard drive?
a: Use a backup program like Quarterback or the Fish disk utility HDBackup, writing to floppies. Back up the whole partition every month, and key files each week. Floppies fail, so keep two sets.

q: What is the difference between a soft reset and a hard reset?
a: A soft reset is Ctrl-Amiga-Amiga, which restarts the machine but may leave memory intact. Switching the power off and on is a hard reset. If something is locked up, use the soft reset first.

q: What is the difference between the CLI and the Shell?
a: The CLI is the original command window. The Shell, new in 1.3 and 2.0, adds command line editing and history, a few extra commands, and works better in a resizable window. Most commands are the same.

q: Which is better for a first Amiga, the A500 or the A2000?
a: The A500 is cheaper and does almost everything. The A2000 costs more but has expansion slots, so you can add a hard drive controller, accelerator or bridgeboard. If you won't expand, get the A500.

q: Which is better for terminal work, Term or VT100?
a: Term by Sebastiano Vigna is faster, has more protocols like XModem, YModem and Kermit, and is still being improved. VT100 by Dave Wecker is simpler and works for basic login. Try both, as they're free.

q: Why does my A500 show a blank screen with a color after boot?
a: Usually it's a diagnostics color. A grey screen often means a bad Kickstart or hardware fault, and red points to a ROM problem. A flashing screen with a disk icon just wants a disk inserted.

q: Why does my Amiga click when there's no disk?
a: That's the drive polling to see if a disk is inserted. It's normal. You can stop the clicking in games with a utility, or just insert a disk. The click can also mean a bad disk.

q: Why does my Amiga not boot with the external drive connected?
a: Probably the disk in DF1: is confusing the boot, or the drive is faulty. The A500 boots from DF0: first. Try disconnecting it and check the cable. A bad drive can hang the whole bus.

q: Why does my disk say Not a DOS disk?
a: The disk is either unformatted, a game disk with its own format, damaged, or from another system. Try another drive. If it was your own disk, you may need DiskDoctor or a tool like DiskSalv for recovery.

q: Can I connect two STs together?
a: Yes, link them through the MIDI ports or serial ports with a null modem cable. People use the serial link for file transfer and sometimes for two-player games like MIDI Maze. Terminal software on both ends handles file transfers.

q: Can I put a 3.5 inch drive on the ST as a second drive?
a: Yes, you can plug an external drive into the floppy port on the back. The Atari SF314 is a double-sided one, and many third-party ones exist. It shows up as drive B on the desktop.

q: Can I run Mac software on my ST?
a: Not directly, but the Spectre 128 emulator lets you run Mac software on the ST if you have Mac 128K ROMs. You need to supply those ROMs yourself, and it runs about as fast as a real Mac. It works with most older Mac programs.

q: Can I use a joystick on my ST?
a: Yes, the ST has two ports for Atari-style joysticks. The mouse uses port 0 and a joystick can go in port 0 or 1, but some games want port 1. Most standard Atari 2600 style joysticks work fine.

q: Can I use my ST with a regular color TV?
a: Yes, with an RF modulator on the early 520ST models, but the picture is fuzzy and text is hard to read in medium resolution. A color monitor like the SC1224 looks much better. For serious text work get the SM124 monochrome monitor.

q: Can the ST read IBM PC disks?
a: Yes, the ST uses standard MS-DOS format 720K disks, so it can read and write 3.5 inch double-sided PC disks. The catch is that the PC must also be able to read 720K, and high density 1.44M disks won't work.

q: Can the ST run MS-DOS programs?
a: Yes, with the PC Ditto software emulator, which works with plenty of text-based programs but is fairly slow. Hardware options like the Supercharger add a real 8088 processor and run much faster. Neither handles every program.

q: How do I clean the drive heads on my ST floppy drive?
a: Use a 3.5 inch head cleaning disk with a few drops of cleaning fluid, and run it for around 30 seconds. Don't do it too often because it wears the head. Do it if you start getting read errors on known good disks.

q: How do I connect a hard drive to my ST?
a: Use the DMA port on the back. The Atari SH204 is a 20 meg drive made for it, and there are third-party ones from Supra and others. You plug it in, and partition it with the HDX software or the driver that comes with it.

q: How do I copy a disk with one drive?
a: Drag the drive A icon onto itself, and the desktop will ask you to swap source and destination disks at the prompts. It's slow and you may swap a few times on a 520ST. A RAM disk or a second drive makes it far easier.

q: How do I format a double-sided disk on my Atari ST?
a: Click the disk icon on the desktop, pick Format from the Special menu, and choose double sided. It takes about a minute and gives you roughly 720K per disk. Back up anything on the disk first because formatting wipes it.

q: How do I get my ST to talk to a modem?
a: Plug a Hayes-compatible modem into the RS-232 serial port with a standard cable. Run a terminal program like Flash or ST Talk, set the baud rate to 1200 or 2400, and use the Hayes ATDT command to dial.

q: How do I get the Rainbow TOS ROMs for my ST?
a: The newer TOS 1.4 is only in a ROM chip set, which you buy from a dealer and install in the sockets inside the machine. It fixes lots of bugs, speeds up the desktop, and supports hard disk partitions. Some ST models already ship with it.

q: How do I make a RAM disk on my ST?
a: Use a desk accessory or AUTO program like VDISK or the one that comes with your disk utility. It sets aside part of memory as a fast pseudo-drive. Remember that anything in it vanishes when you reset or turn off the machine.

q: How do I save my desktop settings so they load every time?
a: Set up your windows and preferences the way you want, then choose Save Desktop from the Options menu. It writes a DESKTOP.INF file to the disk. Make sure the disk is not write protected when you do it.

q: How do I set the date and time on the ST?
a: Open the Control Panel desk accessory and set them with the date and time controls. Only the Mega ST has a battery-backed clock, so on other models you have to set it each boot. Some programs in the AUTO folder do this for you.

q: How does the ST compare to the Amiga 500?
