a: The Amiga has better sound and graphics with more colors and custom chips, while the ST has a faster-feeling desktop, built-in MIDI, and a sharp mono monitor. The ST is usually a bit cheaper. Pick the Amiga for games and video, the ST for music and work.

q: How many colors can the ST show at once?
a: The ST has a palette of 512 colors, but you can only show 16 at once in low res, 4 in medium res, and 2 in high res. Some programs use tricks like raster interrupts to display more on the screen.

q: How many desk accessories can I load?
a: The ST can only handle six desk accessories at a time. Extra ones will not load. They go in the root directory of your boot disk with the extension ACC, and you can rename them to .AC_ to disable them.

q: Is Calamus better than Pagestream for desktop publishing?
a: Calamus is faster and has precise vector-based layout tools, but is pricey. Pagestream works with more fonts and outputs well to PostScript printers. For a plain newsletter either is fine, so try demos if you can.

q: Is GFA BASIC better than ST BASIC?
a: Yes, by a lot. GFA BASIC is much faster, has structured programming, and good access to GEM. ST BASIC from Atari is slow and limited. GFA BASIC is the choice for most people writing their own programs.

q: Is it worth upgrading my 520ST to 1 meg?
a: Yes, if you do anything serious. Many programs like Degas Elite with big pictures, or desktop publishing, are cramped in 512K. Upgrade kits run about $100 to $200, and some need soldering, so be careful or have a dealer do it.

q: Is the Supra 20 meg hard drive any good?
a: Supra drives are popular and generally good value, usually around $500 to $600. They're quick for the price and come with decent partitioning software. Make sure you get one with a battery-free clock option if you care about the date.

q: Is there a good magazine for the ST?
a: Antic's STart magazine comes with a disk and is good. ST-Log is also popular, and Atari Explorer is more of an Atari company publication. For news and reviews, look at the British mags ST Format and ST User too.

q: What does TOS stand for on the ST?
a: TOS means Tramiel Operating System, named after Jack Tramiel. It is the operating system that includes GEM, the desktop with windows and icons. The ST originally loaded it from disk and later versions came in ROM.

q: What does the Control-Alternate-Delete do on the ST?
a: That key combination does a warm reset on the ST, much like on a PC. It doesn't clear all memory, so some programs can survive it. For a complete reset, switch the machine off for about ten seconds and then back on.

q: What does the Mega ST offer over the 1040ST?
a: The Mega ST comes in 1, 2, or 4 megabyte versions, in a separate case with a detachable keyboard. It adds a blitter, a battery-backed clock, and an expansion bus. It's built to be a more serious professional machine.

q: What does the ST use for a CPU?
a: A Motorola 68000 running at 8 MHz. It is a 16/32-bit chip, which is why Atari called the ST a 16/32-bit machine. It's the same processor that the original Macintosh and Amiga use.

q: What does the blitter chip do?
a: The blitter is a chip that moves blocks of graphics memory faster than the 68000 can. It speeds up scrolling and window redraws. The Mega STs have one built in, but the 520 and 1040 need an add-on, and TOS 1.2 or later is needed to use it.

q: What is Degas Elite?
a: Degas Elite is a popular paint program for the ST by Tom Hudson. It supports all three resolutions, has color cycling, and has several drawing tools. It's the standard for ST art, and many games use its picture format.

q: What is GEM?
a: GEM stands for Graphics Environment Manager and was written by Digital Research. It gives the ST its windows, menus, icons, and mouse control. The PC also had a version, but the ST uses it as its main desktop.

q: What is MIDI and why does the ST have it built in?
a: MIDI is a standard for connecting synthesizers, drum machines, and computers. The ST has MIDI in and out ports built in, so you can plug in keyboards without extra hardware. That is why it's so popular with musicians.

q: What is a good first game for the ST?
a: Dungeon Master from FTL is the great one and is a must-have if you like role-playing. For quick action try Xenon or Carrier Command. If you like puzzles, Tetris and Rainbow Islands are also well regarded.

q: What is a good source of free ST software?
a: Public domain disk libraries advertise in the magazines, and you can download programs from bulletin boards and CompuServe's Atari forums. The ST Xformer and Mark Williams programs are often there. Check your local user group, many have a big disk collection.

q: What is a good word processor for the ST?
a: 1st Word comes with many STs and is simple and quick. For more features try WordPerfect, Word Writer ST, or Microsoft Write. First Word Plus is a nice upgrade with better layout and mail merge features.

q: What is the 40 folder limit I keep hearing about?
a: The early TOS in disk and ROM could only handle about 40 folders open at once for disk access. After that you get disk errors or lost files. Put FOLDR100.PRG in your AUTO folder to raise the limit to 100.

q: What is the AUTO folder for?
a: Programs placed in the AUTO folder on your boot disk run automatically at startup, before the desktop loads. People use it for RAM disks, print spoolers, and fixes like FOLDR100 that deal with the 40 folder limit.

q: What is the best MIDI sequencer for the ST?
a: Cubase and Steinberg Pro-24 are the most widely used, with Dr. T's KCS also popular. Notator from C-Lab is great for notation and sequencing, and Pro-24 is a good choice if you're on a budget.

q: What is the best terminal program for the ST?
a: Flash by Antic is very popular and has scripting and good file transfers. Interlink is also well liked. Both support XMODEM, and most also have YMODEM and Kermit for downloading from BBSs.

q: What is the best way to back up my software?
a: Use a disk copier like the one on the desktop or a utility like FCOPY, which copies disks and files fast. Keep backups of important disks only, and store disks away from monitors and magnets. Also check that backup disks work.

q: What is the difference between a desk accessory and a program?
a: A desk accessory loads at boot, sits in memory, and appears in the Desk menu so you can open it inside any program. Programs run on their own and take up memory only when active. Accessories use RAM all the time, so don't load too many.

q: What is the difference between the 520ST and the 1040ST?
a: The 520ST has 512K of RAM and the 1040ST has 1 megabyte. The 1040 also has a built-in double-sided drive and a built-in power supply. Early 520s needed an external drive and a separate supply.

q: What programming languages are available for the ST?
a: You can get Atari BASIC, GFA BASIC, Personal Pascal, Megamax C, Lattice C, and Alcyon C from the Atari Developer's kit. GFA BASIC is fast and very popular. For assembly, Devpac from HiSoft is a great choice.

q: What resolutions does the Atari ST support?
a: Low is 320x200 with 16 colors, medium is 640x200 with 4 colors, and high is 640x400 monochrome. High needs the mono monitor. You switch resolutions from the Set Preferences option on the Options menu.

q: Which is better for the ST, the SM124 mono monitor or a color monitor?
a: The SM124 gives a sharp 640x400 picture that is very easy on the eyes and is great for word processing, DTP, and MIDI software. Color gives you games and paint programs but only 640x200 in medium res. Many people end up with both.

q: Which printer should I get for my ST?
a: For dot matrix, an Epson FX-80 or compatible works with nearly everything. For good output, the Atari SLM804 laser is great but expensive at around $1500. The HP LaserJet works with some software via drivers, but check compatibility first.

q: Why does my ST show bombs on the screen?
a: The bombs mean the 68000 hit an error it couldn't handle, such as a bad address or a program bug. The number of bombs tells you the exception type. Two bombs is a bus error and three is an address error. Reboot and check for a bad program or an incompatible desktop accessory.

q: Why does my disk drive make a clicking noise at boot?
a: It's usually the drive head hunting for track zero when no disk is in it, or a disk with bad sectors. Try a different disk first. If it persists with every disk, the head may be dirty or misaligned.

q: Why does my mouse pointer jump around or not move smoothly?
a: The mouse ball and rollers are probably dirty. Take the ball out and clean the rollers with a cotton swab and rubbing alcohol. Also check that the mouse is plugged into port 0 on the right side of the machine.

q: Why won't my old 520ST work with a hard drive when I add the ROMs?
a: The DMA port supports hard drives on all models, but you need the right TOS version. The early disk-loaded TOS lacks proper hard drive support. Get the ROM TOS upgrade, and use the drive's software to set up partitions.

q: Can I connect my C64 to a modem and call BBSes?
a: Yes. The Commodore 1650 and 1670 modems plug into the user port, and Hayes-compatible ones like the Westridge work with an interface. Terminal programs like Novaterm or STRATUM are good choices, and 300 or 1200 baud is typical.

q: Can I use a C64 with a hard drive?
a: Yes, third party ones exist, such as the Lt. Kernal from Xetec and the Fiscal 20 meg. They are costly, but they work great with GEOS and BBS software. Most connect via a cartridge slot.

q: Can I use a regular cassette recorder with the 64?
a: No, you need the Commodore Datasette or a compatible one that uses the special port. A regular recorder will not connect to the cassette port, though some interfaces exist for that.

q: How can I print on my Epson printer from my C64?
a: The 64 needs a Commodore serial printer or an interface like the Cardco or Xetec that translates the serial bus. Then OPEN 4,4 and PRINT#4 sends text out. Without an interface, a standard Centronics printer won't work.

q: How can I read the disk error message from BASIC?
a: Type OPEN 15,8,15 then INPUT#15,A,B$,C,D followed by PRINT A;B$;C;D. On some systems the DOS Wedge lets you just type @ and see it. Remember to CLOSE 15.

q: How do I back up my disks?
a: Use a copy program such as Fast Hack'em, Maverick, or Disk Mate. Plain file copying will not work on protected disks, and copying commercial software to share is illegal. A backup for your own safety is another matter.

q: How do I change the screen and border colors on the 64?
a: POKE 53280,X sets the border and POKE 53281,X sets the background, where X is 0 to 15. For example POKE 53281,0 gives a black background.

q: How do I draw a circle in BASIC 7.0 on the 128?
a: First use GRAPHIC 1,1 to open the hi-res screen, then CIRCLE 1,160,100,50,50 to draw one in the middle. The 128 has built in graphics commands like BOX, DRAW, PAINT, and CHAR, which the 64 lacks.

q: How do I format a new disk on a 1541?
a: Type OPEN 15,8,15,"N0:DISKNAME,ID" then CLOSE 15. The two character ID is any two characters you like. This erases the disk entirely, so check you have the right one.

q: How do I get my C64 to display on a monitor instead of a TV?
a: Use the 8 pin DIN video port to connect a Commodore 1702 or similar. That gives a sharper picture than the RF output. The composite video and separate luma/chroma signals are both there.

q: How do I get the 80 column display on my 128?
a: You need an RGB or composite monitor like the 1901 or 1902 connected to the 80 column video port. Set the 40/80 key down before power on, or press Escape then X to switch screens. A regular TV can't show it legibly.

q: How do I load a program from disk without wiping out my BASIC program in memory?
a: Use LOAD "NAME",8 from inside a program to chain, or MERGE-style tricks aren't built in on the 64. Easiest is to save your work first, then LOAD "NAME",8. Loading always replaces the program in memory.

q: How do I make a sprite appear on the screen in BASIC?
a: Point the sprite pointer at 2040 to your data block, POKE 53269 to turn the sprite on, then set its position with 53248 and 53249. The data goes in a 64 byte block, and you POKE it from DATA statements.

q: How do I stop a program from being listed?
a: There's no real protection, but people poke tricks into the program to confuse LIST or disable the RUN/STOP key. Anyone determined can get around it, so don't count on it.

q: How fast is the 1571 compared to the 1541?
a: In native 128 mode the 1571 is several times faster than the 1541, because it uses a burst mode on the serial bus. It also reads both sides of a disk. In 64 mode it behaves like a 1541.

q: How much RAM does the 1700 and 1750 expansion add?
a: The 1700 adds 128K to a C128, and the 1750 adds 512K. The 1764 gives 256K for the C64. All are used mainly with GEOS as a fast RAM disk.

q: Is it OK to flip a 5 1/4 disk and use the back side?
a: You can, if you punch a notch in the jacket on the opposite side for the write protect, since the 1541 only reads one side. Many people do this with a disk notcher. Use good quality disks if you do.

q: Is it a good idea to buy a used C64 today?
a: Yes if the price is right. They are tough, and games and software are cheap and plentiful. Test the keyboard, the video, and the sound, and make sure the power supply works, since they tend to run hot.

q: Is the Commodore 128 really compatible with C64 software?
a: Mostly yes. Hold down the Commodore key while powering on, or type GO64, and you get a C64 mode. A few games that poke at odd hardware or use certain fast loaders fail, but the vast majority run fine.

q: Is the Epyx Fast Load cartridge worth it?
a: Absolutely, it's cheap and speeds up 1541 loading by about five times. It only helps with programs that load normally via the DOS, and copy protected games may not benefit.

q: Is there a way to add graphics commands to BASIC 2.0 on the 64?
a: Yes, cartridges such as Simons' BASIC add hundreds of commands, including graphics and structured programming. Other options are Super Expander 64 and a machine language library you load yourself.

q: What are the best word processors for the 64?
a: Paperclip, Word Writer, and Pocket Writer get good reviews. Paperclip is liked for its power, and Pocket Writer has good 80 column support on the 128. Add a printer interface if you plan to print.

q: What does ?FILE NOT FOUND ERROR mean?
a: The 1541 can't find a file with that exact name on the disk. Check the spelling with LOAD "$",8, and remember that spaces and shifted characters in names count. Wildcards like * can help.

q: What does ?OUT OF MEMORY ERROR mean when I only have a small program?
a: BASIC has about 38K free on a 64. You may have a big array DIMmed, or too many strings, or a cartridge or loaded machine code taking space. Try CLR and reduce your DIM sizes.

q: What does FAST do in BASIC 7.0?
a: The FAST command switches the 128 to 2 MHz, doubling speed in 80 column mode. The 40 column screen blanks while FAST is on, so it is mostly useful with the 80 column display.

q: What does LOAD "$",8 do?
a: It loads the disk directory into BASIC memory as if it were a program. Type LIST to see it. It does overwrite whatever program you had in memory, so save first.

q: What does POKE 56334,PEEK(56334) AND 254 do?
a: It turns off the keyboard scan interrupt on CIA 1, which is needed when you're reading or changing certain I/O areas. You must turn it back on by setting that bit again, or the keyboard stops working.

q: What does SYS 64738 do?
a: It jumps to the C64's reset routine, which acts like switching the machine off and on again. It clears memory and restarts the screen, though it won't always wipe a cartridge or a resident program.

q: What does a 1351 mouse work with?
a: The 1351 plugs into joystick port 1 and works with GEOS and software that supports it. In proportional mode it's smooth, but it won't do anything in programs that only read a joystick.

q: What does the 6510 CPU run at in the C64?
a: It runs at about 1 MHz, specifically 1.023 MHz on NTSC machines and 0.985 MHz on PAL. It is a 6502 variant with a built in I/O port that handles memory banking.

q: What does the Commodore key plus shift do?
a: It toggles between the uppercase graphics character set and the lowercase and uppercase text set. You can disable it with PRINT CHR$(8) in a program, and re-enable it with CHR$(9).

q: What does the red LED blinking on my 1541 mean?
a: A steady red light means the drive is working. A blinking red LED means there's an error, like a bad disk or file not found. Read the error channel with OPEN 15,8,15 and INPUT#15 to see what.

q: What is CP/M on the 128 good for?
a: It runs business software like WordStar, dBase II, and Turbo Pascal using the Z80 chip. Disks are slow, and the 1571 is the better drive for it. The library is old and not very exciting for games.

q: What is GEOS and is it worth buying?
a: GEOS from Berkeley Softworks is a graphical desktop with icons, menus, geoWrite and geoPaint for the 64 and 128. It's worth it if you have a 1541 and a joystick or mouse, though it's slow without a RAM expansion.

q: What is a SID chip?
a: The 6581 Sound Interface Device is the C64's sound chip. It has three voices, four waveforms, adjustable ADSR envelopes, and a programmable filter. It's why the 64 sounds so much better than most home computers.

q: What is an assembler good for on the 64?
a: It lets you write machine code for the 6510 that runs far faster than BASIC. Popular ones are Merlin 64, PAL, and Commodore's own assembler. A monitor like Supermon is handy too.

q: What is the DOS Wedge?
a: It is a small program on the 1541 Test/Demo disk that adds shortcut commands. For example, @$ shows the directory, and /NAME loads a file. It saves a lot of typing, although it takes up some memory.

q: What is the RUN/STOP RESTORE key combination for?
a: It resets the screen, colors, and I/O vectors without erasing your BASIC program. If you've locked up the screen in strange colors or characters, it often rescues you.

q: What is the best terminal program for the 64?
a: Novaterm is widely liked for its speed and features, with XMODEM and Punter support. Color Term and STRATUM are also good. Many people use the Swiftlink cartridge for 2400 baud and above.

q: What is the difference between LOAD "NAME",8 and LOAD "NAME",8,1?
a: Without the ,1 the program loads to the start of BASIC memory at $0801. With ,1 it loads to the address stored in the file's first two bytes. Machine language programs and graphics usually need the ,1.

q: What is the difference between the old C64 and the new C64C?
a: The 64C has a restyled case and newer chips, including the 8580 SID, which sounds slightly different. Software is identical, though a few music programs are tuned to the old 6581.

q: Where do I learn 6502 machine language for the 64?
a: Try Jim Butterfield's Machine Language for the Commodore 64 and Programmer's Reference Guide from Commodore. Compute! Books also published several good ones. Start by reading small examples and tracing them with a monitor.

q: Which is better for a first purchase, a C64 or a 128?
a: If you mainly want games, the 64C is cheaper and has the biggest software library. The 128 gives you 128K, a better BASIC 7.0, and CP/M, so it makes sense if you want to do word processing or programming.

q: Which joystick is the best for games on the 64?
a: The Competition Pro is very popular for its microswitches and feel. The Atari-style sticks, such as the Quickshot II, are cheaper and work fine. Anything with a 9 pin Atari plug works.

q: Why does my 1541 take forever to load anything?
a: The 1541 sends data over the serial bus one bit at a time, which is very slow, about 300 bytes per second. A fast loader cartridge like Action Replay or Fast Load can speed it up several times.

q: Why does my 64 say ?SYNTAX ERROR when I type a line that looks right?
a: Usually a typo, a missing quote, or a colon in the wrong place. The 64 only tells you the line, not the spot. Also check that you didn't type letter O for zero or lowercase L for one.

q: Why does my screen go black and the border flash when I load a program?
a: The 64 blanks the screen during tape loading and does the border flash for visual feedback. On disk it is usually the fast loader. It's normal and nothing is wrong.

q: Why is my 1541 head knocking loudly when I format or hit an error?
a: That's the head hitting the end stop while it searches for track 1, which is normal on a bad or unformatted disk. If it happens on a good disk, the head may be out of alignment and need adjusting.

q: Can I add slots to my Apple IIc?
a: No, not really. The IIc has a closed design with only serial ports, a mouse and joystick port, and a memory expansion connector. Some cards like the Z-Ram add memory, but nothing adds true slots.

q: Can I connect my Apple II to a modem and call BBSes?
a: Absolutely. Get a Hayes-compatible modem, an Apple Super Serial Card or a IIgs modem port, and a terminal program like ProTerm or Z-Link. 1200 baud is the sweet spot for price, and 2400 is nice.

q: Can I use a Macintosh 3.5 inch disk in my IIgs?
a: Yes, with GS/OS and the HFS file system translator you can read 800K Mac disks, and also 1.4MB disks if you have a SuperDrive. You can then copy files, though Mac programs won't run.

q: Can I use a hard drive with my Apple IIGS?
a: Sure. SCSI cards from Apple or Western Digital-style controllers work, and the Apple High-Speed SCSI card is the usual choice. Chinook and Sider drives are popular options as well. Format it under ProDOS 16 and GS/OS.

q: Can I use a regular cassette recorder with my Apple II?
a: Yes, the II, II+ and IIe have a cassette in and out jack, and LOAD and SAVE work from BASIC. It's slow and flaky, though, so a disk drive is a much better buy.

q: Can the Apple IIe run Apple IIgs software?
a: No. IIgs programs need the 65816 processor and the GS toolbox, so they won't run on an 8-bit IIe. Going the other way, the IIgs runs most IIe software.

q: How can I copy a disk on my Apple II?
a: Under ProDOS, use the COPY II PLUS or the Filer on the System Utilities disk for whole disks. For DOS 3.3 disks, use the FID program on the System Master to copy files, or COPYA for the whole disk.

q: How do I back up a copy-protected game?
a: Many are protected on purpose, so it's hit or miss. Programs like Copy II Plus bit copiers or Locksmith can sometimes make a copy for your own backup. Some new games can't be copied, and just need the original disk.

q: How do I boot a ProDOS disk on my Apple IIe?
a: Put the disk in drive 1, close the door, and turn the machine on, or press Control-Open Apple-Reset to reboot. If you're already at BASIC, type PR#6 and hit Return to boot slot 6.

q: How do I clear the screen in Applesoft BASIC?
a: Type HOME and press Return. In a program, use HOME on its own line. In graphics mode, use HGR or GR for the screen, or TEXT to go back to text mode.

q: How do I format a disk in ProDOS?
a: Run the Filer on the ProDOS User's Disk, choose Volume commands, then Format a Volume, pick the slot and drive, and enter a volume name. In BASIC with DOS 3.3, use INIT HELLO.

q: How do I get a printer working with my IIe?
a: You need an interface card in a slot, like the Grappler+ for parallel printers or the Apple Super Serial Card for serial ones. Then type PR#1 for slot 1, and Control-I with an option code to set it up.

q: How do I get into the Control Panel on a IIgs?
a: Press Control-Open Apple-Escape. It brings up the Desk Accessory menu, where you pick Control Panel to change slots, RAM disk size, display, clock, and sound settings.

q: How do I get the Apple II to run faster?
a: Add an accelerator like the TransWarp or Zip Chip, or on the GS, set the speed to Fast in the Control Panel. Using a RAM disk for programs also gives a big boost over floppy drives.

q: How do I list a BASIC program to the printer?
a: Type PR#1 (or whichever slot holds your printer card), then LIST, and when it's done type PR#0 to get output back on the screen.

q: How do I run my old DOS 3.3 disks on a IIgs?
a: Just boot them. The IIgs is compatible with DOS 3.3, and if the program is picky, set Speed to Normal in the Control Panel. The 3.5 inch drives won't read 5.25 disks, so you need a 5.25 drive on the disk port.

q: How do I use a mouse on my Apple IIe?
a: You need the Apple Mouse Card in slot 4, and software that supports it, such as MousePaint or AppleWorks 3.0. On the IIgs, the mouse plugs in the back and works with the desktop.

q: How many colors can the Apple IIe show?
a: Low-res graphics offer 16 colors at 40x48, and high-res graphics offer 6 colors at 280x192, with plenty of restrictions on which colors can be next to each other. Double hi-res on the extended IIe gives 16 colors at 140x192.

q: How much memory can a IIgs hold?
a: The original has 256K on the board, and the later ROM 01 model came with 1MB. With a memory expansion card like the Apple GS RAM card you can reach 8MB, and third-party cards go further.

q: Is it worth upgrading my Apple IIe to an enhanced IIe?
a: Yes, it's cheap. You swap two ROM chips and the 6502 for a 65C02, and you get MouseText and better 80-column support. Most new software like AppleWorks 3.0 expects it.

q: Is the Apple IIgs a dead end?
a: Apple is still selling it and adding to the system software, and new software is still coming from companies like Activision and Sierra. But Apple is pushing Macs, so expect fewer new products over time.

q: Is the ImageWriter II a good printer for a IIgs?
a: Yes, it's what most people buy. It prints 250 cps draft, handles color with a ribbon, and plugs into the serial port with no extra card on the GS. Text quality in the best mode is decent.

q: What do I need to run AppleWorks 3.0?
a: You need an enhanced IIe, IIc, or IIgs with at least 128K, and ProDOS. More memory gives you a bigger desktop, with up to 1MB on a IIgs using a card. It supports 80 columns and has a spell checker.

q: What do the numbers in PR#6 and IN#1 mean?
a: They refer to slot numbers. PR#6 sends output to slot 6, which transfers control to the disk controller card and boots it. IN#1 takes input from slot 1, usually a serial card.

q: What does 'I/O error' mean when I read a disk?
a: The drive couldn't read the disk. Usually it's a bad or unformatted disk, a dirty head, or a disk made on a drive that's misaligned. Try another disk, and clean the head with a cleaning disk.

q: What does 'Out of memory' mean in Applesoft?
a: Your program and variables have used all the memory available to BASIC. Try cutting back on big arrays, removing REMs, and using fewer strings, or use a RAM-based tool like the ProDOS BASIC.SYSTEM to free some memory.

q: What does 'Syntax error' mean in Applesoft?
a: You typed something Applesoft doesn't understand, like a misspelled command, a missing quotation mark, or a wrong punctuation mark. Check the line you just LISTed carefully, because the error number won't tell you which part.

q: What does 80-column card do for me?
a: It gives you 80 characters per line instead of 40 on screen, which you need for word processing and CP/M. On the IIe the Extended 80-Column Card also adds 64K of memory, which AppleWorks uses for desktop space.

q: What does BinSCII do?
a: It converts binary files to text so you can send them through email or Usenet. Run it to decode the posted pieces and you get the original file back. It's needed because mail only carries 7-bit text.

q: What does the 'Open Apple' key do?
a: It's the key on the left of the space bar, wired to the first game port button. Programs like AppleWorks use it as a command key, and Control-Open Apple-Reset forces a full reboot or self-test.

q: What is GS/OS?
a: It's the new operating system for the IIgs, replacing ProDOS 16. It uses file system translators for ProDOS, HFS, and others, and it comes with the Finder and desktop. Version 4.0 or 5.0 are current.

q: What is ShrinkIt?
a: It's the standard Apple II compression program by Andy Nicholas for ProDOS files, and it produces .SHK files. You'll see it a lot on BBSes and GEnie. Get NuLib or ShrinkIt to unpack them.

q: What is a Applesoft PEEK and POKE?
a: PEEK reads a byte from a memory address, and POKE writes one. For example, POKE 49168,0 clears the keyboard strobe, and PEEK(-16384) reads the last key pressed. They're how BASIC programs reach the hardware.

q: What is a RAM disk and how do I set one up?
a: It's memory used like a very fast disk drive, and ProDOS makes /RAM on a 128K IIe automatically. On a IIgs, set the RAM disk size in the Control Panel. Remember that it's wiped when you turn the power off.

q: What is a Z-80 card and do I need one?
a: It's a card like the Microsoft SoftCard that puts a Z-80 CPU in a slot so your Apple can run CP/M software such as WordStar and dBase II. You need it only if you want that software.

q: What is the Apple IIc and how is it different from the IIe?
a: The IIc is a compact portable-ish IIe with built-in 5.25 drive, 128K, serial ports, and 80 columns, but it has no expansion slots. The IIc Plus runs at 4 MHz and has a 3.5 inch drive built in.

q: What is the Ensoniq chip in the IIgs?
a: It's the 5503 Digital Oscillator Chip, giving the GS 32 oscillators that can be paired into 15 voices, with its own 64K of sound RAM. That's why GS music sounds far better than the old speaker click.

q: What is the Zip Chip?
a: It's a small accelerator that replaces the 6502 on your IIe or II+, running at up to 8 MHz with onboard cache. It's cheaper than the TransWarp and works with most hardware, but some copy-protected games fail.

q: What is the best word processor for the IIgs?
a: Most people like AppleWorks GS or Publish It! For plain text, AppleWorks Classic with 1.5MB is still hard to beat. For desktop publishing, Springboard Publisher and Medley are options, but they are rather slow.

q: What is the difference between DOS 3.3 and ProDOS?
a: ProDOS supports subdirectories, 32MB volumes, and hard drives, and it's faster at reading and writing. DOS 3.3 is limited to 140K floppies with a flat catalog. ProDOS also uses 512-byte blocks instead of tracks and sectors.

q: What is the difference between the IIgs and the Mac?
a: The IIgs has a 65816 running at 2.8 MHz, 4096 colors, and a 15-voice Ensoniq synthesizer, and it runs most old Apple II software. The Mac has a 68000 and a much bigger software library for business, but only black and white on most models.

q: What's the best Apple II game right now?
a: Prince of Persia is gorgeous, and Ultima V and Wizardry are great role-playing. The IIgs has good stuff like Dungeon Master and Defender of the Crown. Sierra's King's Quest series is also popular.

q: What's the difference between Integer BASIC and Applesoft?
a: Integer BASIC handles whole numbers only and is built into the original Apple II ROM. Applesoft supports floating point, and is standard on II+ and later machines. Applesoft is slower on integers, but far more useful.

q: Which is better for a first computer, an Apple IIgs or an Atari ST?
a: The ST is faster, with a 68000 at 8 MHz and a lower price. But the IIgs runs the huge Apple II library and educational software, and has strong sound. For schools or old software, get the IIgs.

q: Which is better, AppleWorks or Bank Street Writer?
a: AppleWorks, no contest, if you have 128K. It combines word processor, database, and spreadsheet and moves data between them. Bank Street Writer is easier for kids, but it's much more limited.

q: Why does my 3.5 inch drive not work with the IIe?
a: The IIe needs a controller card, such as the Apple 3.5 Drive card, to run UniDisk 3.5 drives. The Apple 3.5 Drive works in slot 5 normally, and you need ProDOS 1.1.1 or later.

q: Why does my Apple II beep when I turn it on and then do nothing?
a: One beep is normal at startup. If the screen shows garbage or nothing, a chip could be bad, or a card is loose. Pull all cards from the slots, then put them back one by one.

q: Why does my IIgs say 'Check startup device'?
a: It can't find a bootable disk. Check that the disk is in the right drive, and look at the Control Panel's Slots setting to make sure Startup Slot points to the right place, or set it to Scan.

q: Why is my IIgs display so blurry on the composite monitor?
a: Composite color blends adjacent pixels, so text looks fuzzy. Get an Apple RGB monitor for the IIgs, which is much sharper. A green monochrome monitor also works well for text and the 80-column display.

q: Will a Transwarp accelerator card speed up my IIe?
a: Yes, the Applied Engineering TransWarp runs at 3.6 MHz, which is about 3.5 times faster than stock 1 MHz. It works with most software, but some copy-protected games and disk drives are unhappy with it.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Can I put a hard disk in my original IBM PC?
a: Yes, but the stock power supply is marginal. Most people buy a hard card or an add-on controller kit from Seagate or Western Digital, usually with its own supply. A 20 meg ST-225 with a controller is the common choice.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Can I run 1.2 meg floppies on an XT?
a: Not really. The 1.2 meg drive needs the AT controller and BIOS support, and an XT can't use it directly. Stick with 360K drives, or look at a third-party controller if you must have high density.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Can I run Lotus 1-2-3 on a two-floppy PC?
a: Yes, 1-2-3 Release 2 runs on 256K and two floppy drives, but you will swap disks a lot and spreadsheets will be small. A hard disk and 640K make it a lot happier.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Can I run Windows on an XT?
a: Windows 2.0 will run on an XT in real mode, but it is very slow and cramped. You really want a 286 with a megabyte or more of memory and EGA or VGA. Most people will be happier with a DOS program.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Can I use my IBM PC with a modem?
a: Sure. Get a Hayes-compatible modem, either an internal card or an external one on the serial port, plus a program like Procomm or Crosstalk. 1200 baud is common and 2400 is affordable now. Set the COM port correctly.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How can I tell how much memory is free?
a: Type CHKDSK and look at the last line, which shows bytes free in memory. It also reports disk space and any lost clusters. If it finds lost chains, run CHKDSK /F to fix them.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I add more memory to my AT?
a: Many AT boards hold 512K on the motherboard, and you can add a memory card like an AST SixPak or Intel Above Board. Set it as extended memory above 1 meg, or as EMS if your software needs it. Run SETUP afterward so the AT knows the new size.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I format a floppy disk in my IBM PC?
a: Put your DOS disk in drive A, type FORMAT B: with a blank disk in B, and follow the prompts. With one drive, use FORMAT A: and swap disks when asked. Formatting erases everything on the disk, so double-check the drive letter.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I get rid of a file I deleted by mistake?
a: Stop writing to the disk right away. DOS only marks the first letter of the filename as erased, so the Norton Utilities UNERASE or PC Tools can often recover it. DOS 5 will have no help here, so use a third-party tool.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I install a second floppy drive in my PC?
a: Attach it to the middle connector on the floppy cable, since the end connector is used for drive A. Check the jumper or drive-select setting, since the cable has a twist for drive A. The PC DIP switches must also say two drives.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I make my computer boot straight into a program?
a: Make an AUTOEXEC.BAT file in the root directory of the boot disk. Put the commands you want on separate lines, such as the date, your PATH and the name of your program. DOS runs it automatically at boot.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I partition a hard disk bigger than 32 meg?
a: Before DOS 4.0, DOS can't handle a partition over 32 meg. Use FDISK to make several partitions, such as C: and D:, or use a third-party driver like Disk Manager or SpeedStor that gets around the limit.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I print the screen to my printer?
a: Press Shift-PrtSc on the PC and XT, or PrtSc on the AT's keyboard. The printer needs to be on-line, and it prints text only. For graphics, load GRAPHICS.COM first, which works with Epson-compatible printers.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I set the date and time on my XT?
a: Type DATE and TIME at the prompt and enter the new values, like 10-16-88 and 14:30. The XT has no clock battery, so unless you add a clock card with a battery, you must enter them every boot, or put them in AUTOEXEC.BAT.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I set up a RAM disk?
a: Add DEVICE=VDISK.SYS to CONFIG.SYS if you have DOS 3.x, or use the driver that came with your memory board. It shows up as a new drive letter, such as D:. Copy programs to it for speed, but remember it vanishes when you turn off power.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I speed up my hard disk?
a: Add a disk cache with SMARTDRV or a program like PC-Cache, and set BUFFERS in CONFIG.SYS to a good number. Check the interleave and defragment the disk. A faster controller helps most on an AT.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I switch my PC between color and monochrome monitors?
a: Use the DIP switches on the motherboard for the primary display, and the MODE command such as MODE CO80 or MODE MONO to select the adapter. If you have both a monochrome and a color card installed, they can work together in some programs.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: How do I tell if my floppy is double-sided?
a: Look at the label on the box, which says DS/DD for double-sided, double-density, which is 360K. Single-sided disks are 180K. An AT's 1.2 meg drive needs high density disks marked HD, and they cost a lot more.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Is a 286 AT worth it over an XT clone?
a: Yes, if you can afford it. A 286 at 8 to 12 MHz runs several times faster than an XT, has a real 16-bit bus, and can use extended memory. Prices are down, so an XT clone is only a smart buy on a tight budget.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Is it safe to move my hard disk computer around?
a: Mostly yes with modern drives, but run a head parking program like SHIP or PARK first on older ones such as the ST-225. Many newer drives park the heads automatically when power is turned off. Don't bump it while it's spinning.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Is it worth upgrading my XT to a turbo board or an AT clone?
a: If money is tight, a V20 chip swap is cheap and gives roughly 10 to 20 percent. A turbo motherboard is better, but a 286 clone has gotten cheap enough that I'd buy that instead of sinking more money into an XT.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does 640K mean and why can't I use more?
a: DOS on the 8088 can address only 1 meg, and IBM reserved the upper 384K for video, ROM and adapter cards. That leaves 640K for programs. Expanded memory boards using LIM EMS get around it for programs that support them.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does Abort, Retry, Ignore, Fail mean?
a: DOS had trouble reading or writing a device, such as an open drive door or an unformatted disk. Fix the problem and press R to retry. A for abort cancels the program, and I ignores the error, which is risky.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does CONFIG.SYS do?
a: DOS reads it at boot to set things like FILES, BUFFERS and device drivers. A typical one has FILES=20 and BUFFERS=20, plus drivers like ANSI.SYS or a RAM disk. Put it in the root directory of your boot disk.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does interleave mean on a hard disk?
a: It's how sectors are numbered around the track. On an XT, the controller is slow, so 1:6 or 1:5 is common, while an AT usually uses 1:3. The wrong value makes the disk much slower, and a program like SpinRite can test it.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does the A> prompt mean?
a: It's the DOS command prompt, and A is the current drive. Type B: to change to drive B, or C: for the hard disk. Without the PROMPT command you won't see the directory path, so try PROMPT $P$G.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does the ANSI.SYS driver do?
a: It lets programs and batch files use escape sequences to move the cursor, set colors and redefine keys. Add DEVICE=ANSI.SYS to CONFIG.SYS. Many BBS door programs and some games need it, and you can use it to color your prompt.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does the BREAK ON command do?
a: It makes DOS check for Ctrl-Break more often, not only during keyboard and screen I/O but also during disk operations. That lets you stop a runaway program sooner. Put BREAK=ON in CONFIG.SYS if you want it permanently.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What does the FILES= line in CONFIG.SYS mean?
a: It sets how many files DOS lets programs have open at once. The default is just 8, which is too few for dBase, Lotus or many compilers. Use FILES=20 or higher, and BUFFERS=20 too, if programs complain.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is a 3.5 inch drive and can I put one in my PC?
a: It is the compact 720K floppy, or 1.44 meg on newer machines. You can put one in a PC or XT with a mounting kit and DOS 3.2 or later, and the DRIVER.SYS file helps if your BIOS doesn't support it.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is a TSR program?
a: It is a Terminate and Stay Resident program, which stays in memory after you start it and pops up with a hotkey. Sidekick is the best known. Several of them together can use up memory and sometimes crash each other.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is a clone and are they compatible?
a: A clone is a PC-compatible built by another company. The good ones from Compaq, Dell or AST run nearly all software, while cheap ones may have trouble with some programs. Flight Simulator is the classic compatibility test.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is a math coprocessor and do I need one?
a: It's an 8087 for the PC and XT, or an 80287 for the AT, that speeds up floating point math. You need one only if your software uses it, like AutoCAD or Lotus 1-2-3 recalculation. For word processing it does nothing.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the AT's battery for?
a: It keeps the clock and the setup information in CMOS memory alive when the power is off. If the AT forgets the date or gives a configuration error at boot, the battery is probably dead and needs replacing.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the best word processor for the IBM PC?
a: WordPerfect 5.0 is the most popular for serious work right now, and WordStar is still liked by many. Microsoft Word is good if you like a mouse. For a cheap one, PC-Write is shareware and works fine.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the difference between CGA, EGA and Hercules?
a: CGA gives 4 colors at 320x200 and a fuzzy text display. EGA gives 16 colors at 640x350 and is sharp. Hercules is monochrome only, but at 720x348 with crisp text, and it's cheap. VGA from the PS/2 line now beats them all.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the difference between COM1 and COM2?
a: They are the two serial ports, using IRQ4 and IRQ3. If your mouse and modem both sit on the same port number or have the same interrupt, they will fight. Set one card's jumpers to COM2.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the difference between DOS 3.2 and 3.3?
a: DOS 3.3 came with the PS/2 and adds support for 1.44 meg 3.5 inch disks, extended partitions over 32 meg, and a few new commands like APPEND and FASTOPEN. If you have a big hard disk, it is well worth getting.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the difference between a .COM and an .EXE file?
a: A .COM file is a simple memory image limited to 64K, and loads quickly. An .EXE file can be larger and has a header that tells DOS how to relocate it. Both are run by typing their names.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the difference between expanded and extended memory?
a: Extended memory is the RAM above 1 meg on 286 and 386 machines, and DOS programs can't use it directly. Expanded memory follows the Lotus-Intel-Microsoft spec and swaps 16K pages into a window in the upper memory area. It works on any PC.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: What is the difference between the PC, XT and AT?
a: The PC has an 8088 and two floppies, the XT adds a 10 or 20 meg hard disk and more slots, and the AT uses the 80286 with a 16-bit bus and 1.2 meg floppies. The AT is a good deal faster than both.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Which is better, a 20 meg hard disk or two floppies?
a: The hard disk, without question. It is much faster and you stop swapping disks. Just make regular backups to floppy with the BACKUP command, because hard disks do crash eventually.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Which printer should I buy for my PC, dot matrix or daisy wheel?
a: Get a dot matrix such as an Epson FX-85 or an Okidata if you want graphics and speed. A daisy wheel gives better letters but is slow and noisy and can't print graphics. A 24-pin printer such as the NEC P6 looks nearly as good as a daisy wheel.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Why do I get Bad command or file name?
a: DOS can't find the program you typed. Check the spelling, make sure you're in the right directory, or add the directory to your PATH. Only .COM, .EXE and .BAT files will run by name.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Why does my AT say 201 error at boot?
a: That is a memory error. A chip or a board is bad, or a DIP switch or jumper is set wrong. Reseat the memory chips, check the setting for the amount of memory, and see if the error goes away with a board removed.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Why does my PC lock up when I load Sidekick?
a: Probably a conflict with another resident program or your video card. Try loading Sidekick last, or first, and see if that helps. Also check that your keyboard enhancer or print spooler is not grabbing the same hotkey.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Why does my hard disk get slower over time?
a: Files get fragmented as you create and delete them, so the heads jump around. Back up the whole disk, reformat, and restore, or use a utility like the Norton Utilities or PC Tools to compact it. Try changing the interleave too.

topic: the IBM PC, XT and AT
q: Why is my keyboard beeping at me?
a: The keyboard buffer is full, usually because the program is busy and not reading keys. A continuous beep at boot can mean a stuck key or a loose keyboard connector. Turn it off and check the cable.

q: Can DOS 4.0 handle big disks like 100MB?
a: Yes, 4.0 uses 32-bit sector numbers, so partitions can be larger than 32MB, up to 2 gigabytes. One 100MB partition is no problem. Make sure your controller and BIOS support the drive too.

q: Can I run DOS 4.0 on my XT?
a: Yes, it runs on an 8088, but it needs a lot more RAM than 3.3. Plan on at least 512K, and 640K is better. On a floppy-only XT it will feel slow and tight, so I'd stay with 3.3.

q: Can I run two programs at once under DOS?
a: Not really. DOS is single-tasking. TSRs and print spoolers give a limited form of background work. For real multitasking you'd need DESQview on a 286 or 386, or Microsoft Windows 2.x or OS/2, and you need lots of RAM.

q: Can I use a 3.5 inch drive with DOS 3.3?
a: Yes, DOS 3.3 supports 720K 3.5 inch drives, and 3.2 did too. The 1.44MB high density drives need 3.3 or later with the proper BIOS support. 3.3 is the version I'd use with them.

q: How can I copy a whole floppy disk?
a: Use DISKCOPY A: B: if you have two matching drives, or DISKCOPY A: A: with one and swap disks when asked. It formats the target and makes an exact copy. It only works on disks of the same size and type.

q: How can I print the screen to a printer?
a: Press Shift-PrtSc on the original keyboard, or just PrtSc on the AT-style one. It sends the text on screen to LPT1. For graphics screens, run GRAPHICS first, and your printer must be on-line.

q: How do I back up my hard disk to floppies?
a: Use BACKUP C:\*.* A: /S to include subdirectories. You'll need plenty of formatted floppies, and you restore with RESTORE A: C:\*.* /S. A tape drive is easier if you have a lot of data.

q: How do I change the prompt to show the current directory?
a: Type PROMPT $P$G. That shows the drive and path followed by a greater-than sign, like C:\DOS>. Put the line in AUTOEXEC.BAT so you get it every time you boot.

q: How do I check how much memory is free?
a: Run CHKDSK and read the last line, which gives bytes free in memory. In DOS 4.0, MEM isn't included in all versions, but CHKDSK works everywhere. A fully loaded system should show around 550K or more free.

q: How do I get a directory listing sorted by name?
a: DOS 3.3 DIR doesn't sort, but you can pipe it: DIR | SORT. For sorting by size or date, use SORT /+14 for the size column. Or use a utility like Norton's DS or PC Tools to sort the directory on disk.

q: How do I get rid of a directory that has files in it?
a: DOS 3.3 has no single command for that. Delete the files with DEL dirname\*.*, remove any subdirectories first, then use RD dirname. RD only works on empty directories, and you can't remove the one you're in.

q: How do I make a batch file that takes parameters?
a: Use %1 through %9 inside the batch file. If you run GO FOO BAR, then %1 is FOO and %2 is BAR. Use SHIFT to get at more than nine. %0 is the name of the batch file itself.

q: How do I make a bootable floppy in DOS 3.3?
a: Put a blank disk in A: and type FORMAT A: /S. That formats it and copies the system files (IO.SYS, MSDOS.SYS, COMMAND.COM). Then copy over any utilities you want on it, plus a CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT if needed.

q: How do I redirect the output of DIR to a file?
a: Use the greater-than sign: DIR > LIST.TXT. Use >> to append to an existing file instead. You can also pipe, like DIR | SORT, or DIR | MORE to page through a long listing.

q: How do I rename a directory?
a: DOS 3.3 has no command for it, and REN only works on files. DOS 4.0 doesn't either. Make a new directory, copy the files with XCOPY, then delete the old one. Some utilities like Norton's FR or PC Tools can do it directly.

q: How do I set the date and time on my machine?
a: Type DATE and then TIME at the prompt and enter new values, such as 10-15-88 and 14:30. On an AT the setup program also changes the battery clock. XTs without a clock card ask you every boot.

q: How do I stop DOS from asking Abort, Retry, Fail on an empty drive?
a: You can't turn the message off, but pressing A or F gets you back to the prompt. Close the drive latch or insert a disk and press R to retry. Some programs let you skip it by handling the error themselves.

q: How do I use EXPAND or extended memory with DOS 4.0?
a: DOS 4.0 includes XMSMMGR and EMM, plus the new FASTOPEN and VDISK. Honestly, for expanded memory you'll want an EMS board and its driver, then use the EMS option on programs like Lotus 1-2-3 release 2.

q: How many FILES and BUFFERS should I set?
a: For most programs FILES=20 is plenty, though databases and some compilers want 30 or more. BUFFERS=20 is a decent value for a hard disk. Each buffer costs about 528 bytes of memory, so don't go wild.

q: Is DOS 4.0 worth upgrading to from 3.3?
a: Depends. 4.0 gives you DOS Shell and partitions over 32MB, but it eats more memory and some people report bugs and incompatibilities. If your disk is under 32MB and you're happy, stay on 3.3 for now.

q: Is it safe to use ANSI.SYS?
a: Yes, add DEVICE=ANSI.SYS to CONFIG.SYS. It lets you use escape sequences to set colors and remap keys via PROMPT or batch files. It slows screen output slightly, and some programs that write directly to the screen ignore it.

q: Is there a way to undelete a file in DOS 3.3?
a: Not in DOS itself. If you haven't written to the disk since, Norton Utilities or PC Tools can usually recover it. The sooner you try, the better the chance, because new files overwrite the freed clusters.

q: What does "Bad command or file name" mean?
a: DOS can't find what you typed. Either you misspelled it, or the program isn't in the current directory or on your PATH. Check the spelling, then try the full path or add its directory to PATH in AUTOEXEC.BAT.

q: What does LASTDRIVE do in CONFIG.SYS?
a: It sets the highest drive letter DOS will allow. The default is E, and you need to raise it for SUBST or network drives. Each extra letter uses a bit of memory, so don't set it to Z unless you must.

q: What does SUBST do?
a: SUBST makes a directory act like a drive letter, such as SUBST E: C:\WORK\DATA. Handy for programs that can't handle long paths. You need LASTDRIVE=E or higher in CONFIG.SYS for the letter to be available.

q: What does the APPEND command do?
a: APPEND, added in DOS 3.2, sets a search path for data files, much like PATH does for programs. Handy for old programs that look for files in the current directory only. It can confuse some software, so test it first.

q: What does the ASSIGN command do?
a: ASSIGN redirects requests for one drive letter to another, like ASSIGN A=B. It's meant for old programs that only work from drive A. Be careful, since it confuses commands like FORMAT and DISKCOPY while active.

q: What does the COMP command do?
a: COMP compares the contents of two files byte by byte and prints the differences. FC is more flexible, since it compares text files line by line or binary files, and is the one I'd use for source code.

q: What does the ECHO OFF command do in a batch file?
a: It stops DOS from displaying each command as it runs. Put @ECHO OFF at the top of a batch file in DOS 3.3 and later; the @ hides the ECHO OFF line itself, which older versions could not do. Use ECHO. to print a blank line.

q: What does the MODE command do?
a: MODE sets up devices. MODE COM1:9600,N,8,1 configures a serial port, MODE LPT1:132,6 sets printer width and lines, and MODE CON RATE=31 DELAY=1 speeds up keyboard repeat on newer machines. It also does display mode switches.

q: What does the PATH command do?
a: It tells DOS which directories to search for programs when you type a command that isn't in the current directory. Something like PATH C:\DOS;C:\UTIL in your AUTOEXEC.BAT lets you run those programs from anywhere.

q: What does the VER command show?
a: It prints the DOS version you're running, for example MS-DOS Version 3.30. It's useful for checking that you really booted the version you meant to, especially if you have several boot floppies.

q: What does the ^Z character mean at the end of a text file?
a: Control-Z, ASCII 26, is the end-of-file marker for text files. COPY with /A stops at it, and TYPE does too. If a file seems to stop short, there may be a stray Ctrl-Z in it.

q: What is AUTOEXEC.BAT and what should I put in it?
a: It's a batch file DOS runs automatically at boot from the root of the boot drive. Typical contents are PATH, PROMPT $P$G, SET commands, and loading TSR programs like a print spooler or mouse driver.

q: What is CONFIG.SYS for?
a: It's read at boot time and sets up the system. You use it for things like FILES=20, BUFFERS=20, and DEVICE= lines to load drivers such as ANSI.SYS or a mouse driver. Changes only take effect after a reboot.

q: What is a RAM disk and is it worth it?
a: It's a chunk of memory made to act like a disk drive. Add DEVICE=VDISK.SYS to CONFIG.SYS, and drive D: or similar appears. It's very fast for compilers and temp files, but contents vanish at power off.

q: What is a TSR?
a: A terminate and stay resident program. It loads into memory, returns to the DOS prompt, and stays there until a hotkey or interrupt calls it up. SideKick is the best known example. Too many can crash your system or use up your RAM.

q: What is the 640K limit and can I get past it?
a: DOS programs can address 640K of conventional memory because of the 8088's 1MB address space. On an AT or 386 you can use extended memory with a RAM disk, or expanded memory (LIM EMS 4.0) boards for programs that support it.

q: What is the DOS Shell in 4.0?
a: It's a menu and file manager front end that comes with DOS 4.0. You can pick programs from a list, copy and delete files by selecting them, and use a mouse in graphics mode. It's handy for beginners but takes up memory.

q: What is the best way to speed up my hard disk under DOS?
a: Increase BUFFERS, use FASTOPEN in DOS 3.3 or 4.0, and run a defragmenter like Norton Speed Disk or PC Tools Compress. Reformatting at a better interleave, using SpinRite or Disk Manager, often helps the most.

q: What is the difference between COPY and XCOPY?
a: XCOPY came with DOS 3.2 and later. Unlike COPY it can copy whole directory trees with /S, copies only changed files with /M, and reads many files into memory at once, so it's faster for lots of small files.

q: What is the difference between DOS 3.3 and Compaq DOS or PC-DOS?
a: PC-DOS is IBM's version of the same Microsoft code, and OEM versions like Compaq's are tailored to their hardware. They're nearly identical for applications. Small differences exist in utilities, like IBM's DOS having ADVANCED DISKCOPY options and BASICA instead of GW-BASIC.

q: What is the difference between FORMAT and FDISK?
a: FDISK creates and sets up partitions on a hard disk, which is done once. FORMAT then prepares each partition or floppy with a file system. A new hard disk needs FDISK first, then FORMAT C: /S to make it bootable.

q: What is the interleave and why does it matter?
a: It's the number of sectors skipped between logically consecutive sectors, so the controller can keep up. A 1:6 interleave on an XT is typical, 1:3 on an AT. Wrong values slow transfers a lot, and low-level format utilities can find the best one.

q: Why can't I make a hard disk partition bigger than 32MB under DOS 3.3?
a: DOS 3.3 uses 16-bit sector numbers with 512-byte sectors, which caps a partition at 32MB. You can split the disk into several partitions with FDISK, up to the extended DOS partition with logical drives. DOS 4.0 lifts the limit.

q: Why does CHKDSK report lost clusters?
a: Usually a program crashed or the machine was turned off while files were open, leaving allocated clusters with no directory entry. Run CHKDSK /F to turn them into FILEnnnn.CHK files. Look through them, then delete what you don't need.

q: Why does DIR show file sizes but my disk still says it's full?
a: DOS allocates space in clusters, so even a tiny file takes a whole cluster, 2K on an AT hard disk and 4K on some larger ones. Lots of small files waste space. CHKDSK shows you the allocation unit size.

q: Why does my computer say "Non-System disk or disk error" at boot?
a: There's a disk in drive A that isn't bootable. Remove it and press a key, and the machine will boot from the hard disk. If it happens with no floppy in, your hard disk's system files may be damaged.

q: Why does my old program say "Incorrect DOS version"?
a: The program checks the version number and refuses to run on a different one. Some DOS versions have SETVER, which lets you tell DOS to report an older version. DOS 4.0 includes it in some versions; otherwise you may need an update from the vendor.

q: Why does the system hang when I load two TSRs?
a: They probably hook the same interrupt or hotkey, or one of them isn't expecting the other. Try loading them in a different order in AUTOEXEC.BAT, and change one hotkey. Remove them one at a time until you find the culprit.

q: Why is DOS 4.0 using so much more memory than 3.3?
a: The resident kernel is bigger, around 10K more, and the new file system code, FASTOPEN, and shell add more. Using the /X option in the INSTALL line or leaving out the shell can win some of it back.

q: Can I multitask DOS programs in standard mode?
a: No. In standard mode a DOS program takes over the whole screen and the others are suspended while it runs. You need a 386 in enhanced mode to run DOS programs in the background.

q: Can I run Windows 3.0 on a 8088 machine?
a: Only in real mode, and it will crawl. You need at least 640K and a hard disk. It will run, but most Windows 3.0 programs are designed for 286 and 386 machines and won't be pleasant.

q: Can I use Adobe Type Manager with Windows 3.0?
a: Yes, ATM works with Windows 3.0 and gives you smooth scalable Type 1 fonts on screen and on dot matrix and laser printers. Install it with its own setup and it adds the fonts through its control panel.

q: Can Windows 3.0 read Macintosh disks?
a: No, not directly. A Mac 3.5 inch floppy uses a different format. You'd need a utility like Apple File Exchange on the Mac side with a PC-format disk, or transfer files over a serial cable or modem.

q: Do I need EMM386 to run Windows 3.0?
a: No. Windows 3.0 in 386 enhanced mode provides its own expanded memory for DOS programs. Running EMM386 isn't needed and can clash with it, so leave it out unless you need EMS outside Windows.

q: Do I need a mouse for Windows?
a: You can get by with the keyboard, since Alt opens menus and Alt+Tab or Alt+Esc switches tasks. It's a lot more awkward, though. Programs like Paintbrush are nearly useless without a mouse.

q: How can I change my wallpaper?
a: Open Control Panel, choose Desktop, and pick a file from the Wallpaper list. It uses BMP files you can make with Paintbrush. Tile or center it as you like, but wallpaper eats memory on small machines.

q: How can I run a DOS program from Windows 3.0?
a: Use File Run in Program Manager, or make a program item for it. You can also find the .EXE or .COM in File Manager and double click. A PIF file can tune memory and display settings for it.

q: How do I exit Windows 3.0 properly?
a: Choose Exit Windows from the Program Manager File menu, or press Alt+F4 with Program Manager active. Don't just reset the machine, since that can leave lost clusters on the disk.

q: How do I get Windows to start a program when it loads?
a: Put the program name on the load= or run= line in WIN.INI, or drag a program item into the StartUp group... actually in 3.0 the easiest way is the run= line, with the load= line for minimized programs.

q: How do I install Windows 3.0 on a hard disk?
a: Put Disk 1 in the floppy drive, type A:SETUP at the prompt, and follow the screens. It will ask for a directory, default C:\WINDOWS, and detect your display, mouse and printer. Have a few formatted floppies on hand just in case.

q: How do I install a printer in Windows 3.0?
a: Open Control Panel and choose Printers. Click Add Printer, pick yours from the list or install a driver from the maker's disk, then connect it to LPT1 or COM1 and make it the default.

q: How do I make a new program group in Program Manager?
a: Choose New from the File menu, pick Program Group, and type a description. You can then drag program icons from other groups or use File New again for Program Item to add your own DOS and Windows programs.

q: How do I set up a permanent swap file?
a: In 386 enhanced mode, open the 386 Enhanced icon in Control Panel and choose Virtual Memory. Click Change, pick Permanent, and set a size. It needs contiguous free space, so defragment first.

q: How do I start Windows 3.0 from the DOS prompt?
a: Just type WIN at the C:\ prompt, assuming the Windows directory is in your PATH. If it isn't, cd to C:\WINDOWS first. Windows 3.0 will pick the best mode for your machine automatically.

q: How do I switch between full screen and a window for a DOS program in 386 enhanced mode?
a: Press Alt+Enter. That toggles the DOS program between full screen and a window. It only works in 386 enhanced mode, and graphics programs may only run full screen.

q: How do I use a modem with Windows Terminal?
a: Open Terminal in Accessories, set the port and baud rate under Settings, then Communications. Enter a number in Phone Number, and Terminal will dial using Hayes style commands. Make sure your modem is on the same COM port.

q: How much RAM do I really need to run Windows 3.0?
a: Officially 1MB for standard mode and 2MB for 386 enhanced, but that's miserable. 2MB is the practical minimum on a 286 and 4MB is much happier on a 386, especially with a disk cache.

q: Is Excel for Windows better than Lotus 1-2-3?
a: Excel has a nicer interface, charts, and macros, and it runs on Windows 3.0, though it wants at least 2MB. Lotus 1-2-3 is faster on plain DOS machines and has the bigger user base. Try both if you can.

q: Is Windows 2.03 worth using on my XT?
a: Honestly, not really. It runs on an XT but it's slow and there is very little software for it beyond Excel, PageMaker and a few others. Unless you need one of those, stay with DOS and a menu shell.

q: What are the three modes in Windows 3.0?
a: Real, standard, and 386 enhanced. Real mode runs on 8086 class machines and is limited to 640K. Standard needs a 286 or better with extended memory. 386 enhanced needs a 386 with 2MB or more and gives you virtual memory and multitasking of DOS programs.

q: What does DDE mean?
a: Dynamic Data Exchange. It lets Windows programs share data live, so a number changed in an Excel sheet can update a link in a Word for Windows document. Both programs have to support it.

q: What does HIMEM.SYS do?
a: It's the extended memory manager that comes with Windows 3.0. It manages memory above 1MB and the HMA, the first 64K above 1MB. You need DEVICE=HIMEM.SYS in CONFIG.SYS for standard or enhanced mode.

q: What does a General Protection Fault mean?
a: It's what the 286 and 386 CPU raises when a program touches memory it isn't allowed to use. In Windows 3.0 standard or enhanced mode it usually shows up as an Unrecoverable Application Error. Look for a misbehaving program or driver.

q: What happened to the MS-DOS Executive?
a: That was the file-and-program window used in Windows 1.x and 2.x. In 3.0 it was replaced by the Program Manager for launching programs and File Manager for working with files and directories.

q: What is File Manager?
a: The Windows 3.0 tool for copying, moving, deleting, renaming and finding files and directories. It shows a directory tree on the left and files on the right. Drag and drop with the mouse to copy files between drives.

q: What is Print Manager?
a: It spools print jobs to disk so your program can return quickly while the printing continues in the background. You can pause or delete jobs from its window. It can be turned off in Control Panel if it causes trouble.

q: What is SMARTDRV and should I use it?
a: SMARTDRV.SYS is the disk cache that comes with Windows 3.0. Yes, use it. Add DEVICE=C:\WINDOWS\SMARTDRV.SYS 2048 to CONFIG.SYS if you have extended memory to spare, and disk access speeds up noticeably.

q: What is Windows Write?
a: It's the simple word processor that comes with Windows 3.0, replacing Windows Write from earlier versions. It does fonts, bold, italics, tabs and can embed pictures. It reads and writes Word files, which is handy.

q: What is a .INI file?
a: A plain text configuration file that Windows and its programs read at startup. WIN.INI holds your settings and fonts, and SYSTEM.INI holds hardware and driver settings. You can edit them with Notepad, but back them up first.

q: What is a PIF file?
a: A Program Information File. It tells Windows how a DOS application should run: how much memory it needs, whether it runs in a window or full screen, and what it may do with the keyboard and ports. You edit them with the PIF Editor.

q: What is a TrueType font?
a: I haven't seen anything by that name for Windows 3.0. What you can do is use Adobe Type Manager, which scales PostScript Type 1 fonts on screen and to non-PostScript printers, or the bitmap fonts that come with Windows.

q: What is the Alt+Tab key for?
a: It switches between running programs. Hold Alt and tap Tab to cycle through the names, then let go to land on the one you want. Alt+Esc also cycles but doesn't show names.

q: What is the Clipboard?
a: It's the holding area for cut, copy and paste between programs. Cut or copy something with Ctrl+Ins style commands in the Edit menu and paste in another application. Use the Clipboard Viewer to see what's in there.

q: What is the HMA?
a: The High Memory Area is the first 64K of extended memory, just above 1MB, that a 286 or 386 can address from real mode. DOS 5 style loading isn't here yet, but HIMEM.SYS lets some programs use it to free conventional memory.

q: What is the Program Manager?
a: It's the main shell in Windows 3.0 that replaced the old MS-DOS Executive. It holds your programs as icons grouped in windows, like Main, Accessories and Games. Double click an icon to launch the program.

q: What is the best mouse to use with Windows 3.0?
a: The Microsoft mouse is the safe choice, and Logitech and Mouse Systems also work well. Most Microsoft compatibles work with the standard driver. A serial mouse on COM1 or COM2 is fine, just don't let it share an IRQ with a modem.

q: What is the difference between Windows 3.0 and OS/2 1.2?
a: OS/2 is a full multitasking operating system with HPFS and Presentation Manager, but it needs more RAM and has fewer programs. Windows 3.0 sits on top of DOS, runs all your DOS programs, and has far more software coming.

q: What is the difference between Windows/286 and Windows/386?
a: Windows/286 is the regular version that can use the HMA on a 286 and above. Windows/386 version 2.01 uses the 386 virtual 8086 mode to run several DOS programs in their own windows with preemptive multitasking. Windows 3.0 combines both.

q: What's the difference between expanded and extended memory?
a: Extended memory is RAM above 1MB that 286 and 386 CPUs can address directly, and Windows 3.0 uses it. Expanded memory (EMS) is bank-switched through a 64K window in upper memory and is used by older programs like Lotus 1-2-3 version 2.

q: Which video card should I buy for Windows 3.0?
a: VGA is the sweet spot now, giving 640x480 in 16 colors. Super VGA cards at 800x600 are nice if you have a good monitor, but you'll need a driver from the card maker. EGA works but is cramped.

q: Which word processor is best for Windows 3.0?
a: Word for Windows is the big one, and Ami Professional from Samna is also well liked. Windows Write comes free and is fine for letters. WordPerfect has a Windows version coming but check before you buy.

q: Why do I get Out of Memory errors with plenty of RAM?
a: Windows has limited system resources, small heaps for things like windows and icons, in Windows 3.0 and they can run out regardless of RAM. Close programs, reduce icons, and use fewer fonts.

q: Why does Windows 3.0 give me an Unrecoverable Application Error?
a: That's the UAE, and it means a program broke the rules, usually by writing into memory it doesn't own. Often it's a buggy app or a bad driver. Save often, and try updating your video driver and removing TSRs.

q: Why does my mouse not work in a DOS box?
a: Standard DOS programs need their own mouse driver loaded before Windows, such as MOUSE.COM, unless Windows provides mouse support in enhanced mode windows. In 386 enhanced mode, mouse works in DOS windows with the Windows drivers.

q: Why is my Windows 3.0 so slow?
a: Most likely not enough RAM or no disk cache. Run SMARTDrive with a 1 or 2MB cache from CONFIG.SYS, set a permanent swap file if you have a 386, and try a plain solid color wallpaper instead of a bitmap.

q: Why won't my printer print from Windows?
a: Check that the right port is selected in Control Panel under Printers, and that the cable and online light are good. Also make sure the Print Manager isn't holding the job, and try turning it off.

q: Will my old Windows 2 programs run on Windows 3.0?
a: Most will, though some need to be run in real mode. Applications written properly for Windows 2.x generally run, but ones that peek at memory directly may not. Check with the vendor for an update.

q: Can DOS read an HPFS partition?
a: No. Native DOS can't see HPFS at all. Programs in the OS/2 DOS box can use the files though, with names shortened to 8.3 form, but if you boot real DOS the drive is invisible.

q: Can I run OS/2 and DOS on the same machine?
a: Yes. You can put each on its own partition with FDISK, or use FAT and share one partition. Then choose which to boot with the dual-boot option that came with OS/2 1.2.

q: Can I run Windows programs under OS/2?
a: Not in 1.x. OS/2 can run only DOS and OS/2 programs. Windows programs need Windows, so you'd have to boot DOS and run it there.

q: Can I use Turbo Pascal or Turbo C on OS/2?
a: Only as DOS programs in the compatibility box. Borland hasn't shipped a compiler that makes OS/2 programs, so for real OS/2 apps you'll want Microsoft C or a similar compiler.

q: Can OS/2 run my old DOS programs?
a: Yes, in the DOS compatibility box, which gives one DOS session of about 640K. Most well-behaved programs work fine, but anything that bangs directly on the hardware may fail.

q: Can OS/2 run on an XT or an 8088 machine?
a: No. OS/2 needs the protected mode of the 80286 or better, and an 8088 doesn't have it. If you're stuck with an XT, stay with DOS.

q: Can OS/2 use more than 16MB of memory?
a: No. The 286's address space tops out at 16MB, and OS/2 1.x is built around that limit. Few people have anywhere near that much, so it doesn't matter yet.

q: Do I need OS/2 to run a LAN Manager server?
a: Yes, the server software runs on OS/2 and uses its multitasking and HPFS386-style performance features. Clients can be plain DOS machines.

q: Does OS/2 1.0 have a graphical interface like the Mac?
a: No, 1.0 is text mode only, with a command prompt and a simple full-screen program selector. The graphical Presentation Manager didn't arrive until version 1.1 in late 1988.

q: Does OS/2 use the 386's 32-bit features?
a: Not yet. Version 1.x is written for the 286 and uses 16-bit code, so a 386 just runs it faster. Don't expect it to use 32-bit addressing.

q: How big does the swap file get?
a: It grows and shrinks as needed, and you can set a minimum free-space figure in SWAPPATH so it doesn't fill your disk. With a lot of programs open it can reach several megabytes.

q: How do I get a DOS prompt in OS/2 1.1?
a: In Presentation Manager's Start Programs window, choose the DOS Command Prompt. It starts the compatibility box, and you can run it full screen with Alt+Home.

q: How do I get an OS/2 command prompt?
a: Pick OS/2 Command Prompt from the Start Programs list. It runs CMD.EXE, which handles long commands, pipes and redirection a bit better than COMMAND.COM does.

q: How do I print from a DOS program in the OS/2 DOS box?
a: It prints through the OS/2 spooler to LPT1 as usual. Make sure the printer is set up in the Print Manager first, or the job will sit in the queue.

q: How do I reboot OS/2 without losing my disk?
a: Don't just hit the reset switch. Use Shutdown from the Desktop Manager menu in 1.1, wait for the message that it's safe, then press Ctrl+Alt+Del. Otherwise the file system may be left dirty.

q: How do I switch between programs in OS/2 1.1?
a: Press Alt+Esc to cycle through the open windows, or Ctrl+Esc to bring up the Task List and pick one. In a full-screen text session you can use those same keys.

q: How many hard disk partitions can OS/2 use?
a: You can make a primary partition and extended partitions with logical drives, same as DOS, using OS/2's FDISK. Partitions go up to 2GB with HPFS, but FAT stays limited by the old DOS rules.

q: Is OS/2 worth it for a single-user home PC?
a: Probably not yet. It needs a lot of memory, the software choice is thin, and most people will be better off with DOS and Windows 3.0. It's worth it if you do heavy multitasking or write OS/2 programs.

q: Is it better to buy a 286 or a 386 for OS/2?
a: A 386 is better. OS/2 1.x is still 286 code, but the 386 is faster and gives a more reliable DOS box on some machines. Whatever you buy, put in at least 4MB.

q: Is it worth switching to HPFS from FAT?
a: If you have a disk over 100MB or lots of files in each directory, yes, it's noticeably faster. On a small drive or if you boot DOS often, just stay with FAT.

q: What are named pipes?
a: A way for OS/2 programs to talk to each other, either on the same machine or across a LAN Manager network. They work like files you can read from and write to.

q: What are the minimum hardware requirements for OS/2 1.1?
a: On paper you need a 286, about 2MB of RAM and a 20MB hard disk. In practice get 3 or 4MB, because with 2MB it swaps constantly and crawls.

q: What are threads in OS/2?
a: A thread is a separate path of execution inside one program. A program can start several, for example one to handle the display and another to print or read the disk, and OS/2 schedules them preemptively.

q: What compiler should I use to write OS/2 programs?
a: Microsoft C 5.1 or later with the OS/2 toolkit is the usual choice, and Microsoft C 6.0 supports it as well. You also need the Programmer's Toolkit from IBM or Microsoft for headers, libraries and docs.

q: What does LIBPATH do in CONFIG.SYS?
a: It's the list of directories where OS/2 looks for dynamic link libraries (DLLs). If a program says it can't find a DLL, the directory with that file probably isn't on your LIBPATH.

q: What does MEMMAN=SWAP,MOVE mean in CONFIG.SYS?
a: It turns on the memory manager so OS/2 can swap segments out to disk and move them around in RAM. That's how you can run more than physical memory would allow.

q: What does the Print Manager do?
a: It's the print spooler in Presentation Manager. It takes print jobs from your programs, queues them and sends them to the printer so you can keep working.

q: What does the START command do?
a: START launches a program in its own new session from the command line, so your prompt comes back right away. For example, START EDLIN.EXE opens a new session for it.

q: What is CONFIG.SYS used for in OS/2?
a: Same idea as in DOS. It's read at boot and sets buffers, device drivers, the swap file, memory manager options and the shell. But the OS/2 one has its own commands like LIBPATH and PROTSHELL.

q: What is Dynamic Data Exchange?
a: DDE lets programs in Presentation Manager pass data to each other, like a spreadsheet updating a number in a word processor document. Both programs have to support it.

q: What is HPFS?
a: The High Performance File System, new with OS/2 1.2 in 1989. It allows file names up to 254 characters, partitions up to 2GB, and is much faster than FAT on big disks.

q: What is LAN Manager?
a: Microsoft's network server software, built on OS/2, with 3Com and others selling versions of it. The server runs OS/2, and DOS and OS/2 workstations can connect to it.

q: What is OS/2?
a: It's the multitasking operating system IBM and Microsoft built for 286 and 386 machines, announced with the PS/2 line in 1987. It runs in protected mode, so it can use up to 16MB of RAM and run several programs at once.

q: What is Presentation Manager?
a: It's the windowed graphical shell for OS/2, new in 1.1. It looks a lot like Windows, with overlapping windows and a mouse, and it follows IBM's SAA/CUA interface rules.

q: What is a DLL?
a: A dynamic link library is a file of code that programs link to when they run rather than when they're built. Several programs share one copy in memory, and OS/2 itself is mostly DLLs.

q: What is preemptive multitasking?
a: It means the operating system decides when each program gets the CPU and can interrupt it at any time. In Windows 3.0 programs have to give up control themselves, so one program that hangs can stall everything.

q: What is the DETACH command for?
