a: DETACH runs a background OS/2 program with no screen or keyboard, such as a server or a long copy. Anything detached must not need user input.

q: What is the Family API?
a: A subset of OS/2 calls that you can use to build a program that will run in both OS/2 and DOS. You link it with a special tool and get a single executable that works on both.

q: What is the difference between CMD.EXE and COMMAND.COM?
a: CMD.EXE is the OS/2 command processor, which runs OS/2 programs and also supports many DOS-style commands. COMMAND.COM is for the DOS box and only runs DOS programs.

q: What is the difference between OS/2 Standard Edition and Extended Edition?
a: Extended Edition is IBM's version with built-in Database Manager (an SQL database) and Communications Manager for host connections and 3270 emulation. Standard Edition is just the base system, which is what most people want.

q: Where does OS/2 put its swap file?
a: It's SWAPPER.DAT, and it lives in the directory named by the SWAPPATH line in CONFIG.SYS. Put it on your fastest drive with plenty of free space.

q: Which is better, OS/2 or Windows 3.0?
a: Windows 3.0 runs on less hardware and has much more software available. OS/2 has real preemptive multitasking and better protection, so one bad program doesn't take everything down, but you pay for it in RAM and software prices.

q: Which printers work under OS/2?
a: It comes with drivers for IBM, Epson and HP LaserJet printers, plus PostScript. If yours isn't listed, try emulating one of those, since a lot of printers can.

q: Which video cards does OS/2 support?
a: VGA and 8514/A work well, and EGA also works at lower resolution. Super VGA modes depend on the card maker supplying an OS/2 driver, so check with the manufacturer first.

q: Why can't I run more than one DOS program at a time under OS/2 1.x?
a: The compatibility box is a single real-mode session, and the 286 can't make more than one. You can run many OS/2 programs at once but only one DOS program, and it stops in the background.

q: Why does OS/2 need so much memory?
a: It's a full multitasking system with a graphical shell, a file system, and DOS emulation all loaded together, and the kernel and Presentation Manager use a good chunk of RAM. Extra memory helps more than a faster CPU.

q: Why does OS/2 run CHKDSK when I boot?
a: It means the disk wasn't shut down cleanly, so the system checks for lost clusters. With HPFS it can also run a lengthy recovery, so always do a proper Shutdown.

q: Why does my DOS program stop when I switch to another window?
a: The DOS box doesn't get CPU time while it's in the background on 1.x. It freezes until you switch back, so long jobs like a compile or a modem transfer need to be run as OS/2 programs.

q: Why is my hard disk so busy when I switch between programs?
a: That's the swapper working. OS/2 pushes inactive segments out to disk to make room, so when you go back to a program it reads them back. More RAM is the cure.

q: Will OS/2 Extended Edition run on non-IBM clones?
a: It's aimed at IBM PS/2s and often fussy about other hardware. Standard Edition from Microsoft's OEM versions is easier on clones, so check your maker's compatibility list before buying.

q: Will my Hercules or CGA card work with OS/2?
a: Text mode works on almost any card, but Presentation Manager in 1.1 needs EGA at the least. For the best experience get a VGA card.

q: Can DOS use more than 640K on a 386?
a: Not directly, but with a memory manager like QEMM-386 or 386MAX you can load drivers and TSRs into the upper memory blocks between 640K and 1MB. That frees up conventional memory for your programs.

q: Can I load DOS high on my 286?
a: With DOS 5.0 you can put DOS into the HMA with DOS=HIGH in CONFIG.SYS, as long as you have extended memory and HIMEM.SYS loaded. Loading drivers into upper memory blocks needs a 386, though.

q: Can I put a 287 in my 386 motherboard?
a: Generally no. The 386 wants a 387, and the 287 is made for the 286 sockets. Some early 386 boards actually had a 287 socket and a Weitek option, so check your manual before buying anything.

q: Can I run OS/2 on a 286?
a: Yes, OS/2 1.x was written for the 286 and runs fine in about 3MB of RAM or more. But it can't run multiple DOS boxes safely, and 1.x only has a single DOS compatibility box, so many people think the 386 is better.

q: Can I run Windows 3.0 on a 386SX with 2MB?
a: Yes, it will run in 386 enhanced mode, but 2MB is tight. Plan on 4MB for a comfortable setup, and set up a permanent swap file if you want to run several DOS programs and Windows apps together.

q: Can I swap the CPU on my 286 to a 386 myself?
a: Usually not, because the pinouts and the board logic differ. You need a replacement chip adapter, such as a 386SX upgrade module, and even then you must have a socketed CPU. A new motherboard is often easier.

q: Do I need a math coprocessor with my 386?
a: Only if your software uses it, like AutoCAD, Lotus 1-2-3 recalcs, or some compilers and CAD programs. Word processors and games ignore it. For a 386DX you want the 80387, and for the SX you want the 387SX.

q: Does the 486 have a built-in math coprocessor?
a: Yes, the 486DX has a floating point unit on the chip, so you don't buy a separate one. It's much faster than a 387 for the same clock speed, which is great for CAD and spreadsheets.

q: How do I tell what speed my CPU is really running at?
a: Run a utility like Norton SI or Checkit, which time the CPU and report a relative speed to the original PC. Some BIOS setups show the clock, and the crystal on the board is marked with twice the CPU speed.

q: How do I turn extended memory into expanded on my 386?
a: Use a 386 memory manager like QEMM-386, 386MAX, or Compaq's CEMM, and load it in CONFIG.SYS with a DEVICE= line. It emulates EMS 4.0 using the paging hardware on the 386, so you don't need a separate EMS board.

q: How fast is a 386DX 33 compared to a 25?
a: About 30 percent faster on CPU-bound work like compiles or spreadsheets. Disk-heavy stuff doesn't gain as much, and boards at 33MHz often need cache memory and fast RAM to really show it.

q: How much RAM should I put in a 386 machine?
a: 4MB is a sensible starting point for Windows 3.0 and a RAM disk or disk cache. 2MB works for DOS apps, but you'll run short with Windows or Unix. SIMMs are cheap, so go with 4 if your budget allows.

q: Is Micro Channel any good on a PS/2 Model 80?
a: The Model 80 has a 386DX at 16 or 20MHz and a fast 32-bit bus, and the MCA cards are good, but they cost a lot more and your old ISA cards will not fit. Clones are cheaper and run the same software.

q: Is an AMD 286 as good as an Intel 286?
a: Yes, the AMD 80286 runs fine and is rated up to 16 or 20MHz, a little faster than Intel's standard parts. It's a licensed second source for the Intel design, so software can't tell the difference.

q: Is it worth buying a 386 instead of a 286 right now?
a: If you can afford it, yes. A 386SX costs only a bit more than a fast 286 and runs Windows 3.0 in 386 enhanced mode and software like DESQview 386. A 286 is fine if all you run is DOS word processing and spreadsheets.

q: Is the 386 backwards compatible with 8088 programs?
a: Yes, it runs all real mode 8086 and 8088 code, and it also has virtual 8086 mode, which lets multiple DOS sessions run each in its own 1MB space. Windows 386 enhanced mode and DESQview 386 use that.

q: Is the 486 worth the money right now?
a: For most people, not yet. A 486 system costs roughly twice what a 386-33 does. If you run CAD, Unix compiles, or a file server it pays off, but for word processing and Windows a fast 386 is plenty.

q: Is the Cyrix coprocessor really compatible with Intel's 387?
a: The Cyrix FasMath is pin compatible with the 387 and runs about 20 to 50 percent faster on many tests, and costs less. It's not quite 100 percent, so check that your program doesn't depend on something odd.

q: Should I buy a 486 board that has an EISA bus or ISA?
a: If it's a file server with lots of disk and network traffic, EISA is nice since the cards can do bus mastering. For a desktop you will probably never need it, and ISA cards are much cheaper.

q: What are SIMMs and do they work on any 386 board?
a: SIMMs are small memory modules, 30-pin ones in 256K and 1MB sizes, that plug into sockets on the board. Check the manual for the speed rating, like 80ns, and whether it needs them installed in banks of two or four.

q: What does 32-bit mean on a 386?
a: It means the registers are 32 bits wide, and it handles 32-bit numbers and addresses in one go. Programs have to be written for it though. Plain DOS software still runs 16-bit code, so you see little gain from that alone.

q: What does 80ns on my RAM chips mean?
a: It's the access time, 80 billionths of a second. Lower is faster, so 70ns and 60ns parts are quicker. A 16MHz machine runs fine on 100ns, but 25 and 33MHz boards usually want 70ns or better.

q: What does the SX in 386SX mean?
a: The SX is Intel's cheaper 386 with a 16-bit external data bus and 24 address lines, so 16MB max. It runs the same 32-bit code as the 386DX but moves data slower, roughly 286-board prices with 386 features.

q: What does wait state mean?
a: A wait state is a clock cycle where the CPU sits idle waiting for slower RAM to respond. Zero wait state means the memory keeps up with the CPU, and a one wait state board is noticeably slower, maybe 15 to 20 percent.

q: What interleave should I use for a 386 hard disk?
a: Depends on the controller, but 3:1 is common for old MFM on an AT, while a good controller can manage 1:1 or 2:1. Run SpinRite or Calibrate to test each one and pick the fastest that works.

q: What is EISA and should I wait for it?
a: EISA is the 32-bit bus the Gang of Nine came up with as an answer to IBM's Micro Channel. It's compatible with ISA cards but expensive. For a single-user desktop ISA is fine, EISA matters for servers.

q: What is Unix like on a 286?
a: SCO Xenix 286 and a few others work, but the 286 has no paging hardware, so swapping whole processes is slow. Anything serious like SCO Unix, ISC, or Interactive 386/ix really wants a 386.

q: What is a 386 upgrade card for my 286?
a: Boards like the Intel Inboard 386/PC or the Kingston and Sota upgrades plug into a slot or replace the 286 chip, and give you a 386 running at 16 to 25MHz. Check that it fits your case and BIOS first.

q: What is a DOS extender?
a: It's a library that switches the CPU into protected mode so your program can use all your extended memory, then switches back to call DOS. Phar Lap 386 and Rational Systems are examples, and Lotus 1-2-3 3.0 uses one.

q: What is a cache controller on a 386 motherboard?
a: It's a chip set, like Intel's 82385, with fast SRAM, typically 32K or 64K, that holds recently used memory. It cuts the wait states from slow DRAM and gives a decent speedup on 25 and 33MHz boards.

q: What is protected mode?
a: It's a CPU mode on the 286 and up where programs get memory protection and can address more than 1MB, up to 16MB on a 286 and 4GB on a 386. DOS itself runs in real mode, so extenders like Phar Lap or DOS/4G bridge the gap.

q: What is the 286 limit on memory and why?
a: The 286 has 24 address lines, so it can address 16MB of RAM in protected mode. In real mode it is limited to 1MB like the 8086, and DOS stays in that mode, which is the real bottleneck.

q: What is the 386 stepping or B1 bug I keep hearing about?
a: The early 386 chips, marked with a double sigma, had a bug in 32-bit multiply and rare paging problems. Those chips are rated as 16-bit only, and Intel replaced them. Newer ones with the full 32-bit rating are fine.

q: What is the 486 and how much faster is it than a 386?
a: The 486 is Intel's new chip with built-in 8K cache and math coprocessor on the die. At 25MHz it runs about twice as fast as a 386 at 25MHz on most integer code, since many instructions take one clock instead of two or more.

q: What is the 80287XL and is it different from the plain 287?
a: The 287XL is Intel's newer CMOS part that runs cooler and uses less power. It's essentially an 80387SX core wired to work in a 286 socket, so it's a little faster than the older 287 at the same clock.

q: What is the 8K on-chip cache in the 486?
a: It's a small fast cache built into the chip that holds recently used code and data. It helps keep the CPU fed without waiting for main memory, and many boards add a second-level cache of 64K to 256K.

q: What is the HMA and why do people talk about it?
a: The High Memory Area is the first 64K less 16 bytes above 1MB, reachable in real mode on a 286 or better by switching the A20 line. DOS 5.0 can load itself there and free up conventional memory.

q: What is the Norton SI rating?
a: The System Information program in Norton Utilities compares your machine to the original IBM PC at 4.77MHz, rated as 1.0. A typical 16MHz 386 gives you somewhere around 12 to 15, a 25MHz 386 about 20 or more.

q: What is the difference between a 286 and a 386?
a: The 386 is a full 32-bit chip with 32-bit registers and a flat memory model, plus virtual 8086 mode for running several DOS sessions. The 286 is 16-bit and tops out at 16MB, and it can't switch back from protected mode without a reset trick.

q: What is the turbo button for?
a: It switches the CPU between full speed and a slowed down speed. Some older games and copy-protected software depend on the 4.77MHz timing of the original PC, so you drop out of turbo for those.

q: Which Unix can I run on a 386 PC?
a: SCO Unix System V/386, Interactive 386/ix, and Microport are the main ones, and SCO Xenix 386 is still around. You want at least 4MB of RAM and a decent ESDI or SCSI disk to make it pleasant.

q: Which compiler works best for 386 protected mode programs?
a: Watcom C 386 and MetaWare High C are the usual picks, using a DOS extender such as Phar Lap or Rational's DOS/16M. Microsoft C 6.0 only makes 16-bit code, so it won't give you 32-bit programs.

q: Which is better, a 16MHz 386SX or a 20MHz 286?
a: The SX at 16MHz is slightly faster on plain DOS code and far better if you want Windows 386 enhanced mode, DESQview, or OS/2 2.0 later. For pure DOS the two are close, so go with the SX for the upgrade path.

q: Why do some old games run way too fast on my 286?
a: Those games use CPU loops for timing instead of the system clock, so a faster chip speeds everything up. Try the turbo switch, or a slowdown utility, and newer games usually use the timer chip properly.

q: Why does my 286 run so slowly under Windows 3.0?
a: A 286 can only run Windows in standard mode, with no multitasking of DOS programs and no virtual memory. Add a couple megs of extended RAM and a SMARTDrive cache, and it gets better, but a 386 is the right chip for it.

q: Why does my 386 say Parity Error 1?
a: It means a memory chip on the motherboard failed or a SIMM isn't seated properly. Parity Error 2 refers to the expansion memory. Reseat the SIMMs and clean the contacts, and swap the modules if it comes back.

q: Why is my hard disk slow on my fast 386?
a: The disk is likely the bottleneck, especially an old MFM drive with a 1:1 interleave problem. Try a better interleave, a caching program like SMARTDRV, or move to an IDE, ESDI, or SCSI drive.

q: Will a 486 run my 386 software?
a: Yes, the 486 is fully compatible with the 386 instruction set and runs everything the same, only faster. It adds a few instructions, but programs written for the 386 don't need them.

q: Will my old 8-bit cards work in a 386?
a: Most do, since the ISA bus is the same one. Some old cards and clones are timing-sensitive on fast machines, so a few need the bus slowed down in the BIOS setup. Disk controllers are the usual troublemakers.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Can I mix 256K and 1 Mbit chips on my motherboard?
a: Usually not within one bank. Each bank must be filled with identical chips, and the board jumpers or switches must match the density. Check your manual, since many boards only support one chip type per bank.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Can I put more than 640K in my Commodore Amiga or Atari ST?
a: Yes, those use the 68000 and have no 640K limit. The Atari 520ST upgrades to 1 MB or 4 MB with a board, and the Amiga 500 takes a 512K expansion in the trapdoor. This is a PC problem.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Can I run DESQview with extra memory?
a: Yes, DESQview from Quarterdeck multitasks DOS programs and benefits a lot from extra RAM. On a 386 with QEMM it can give each program close to 640K. On a 286 or XT you are limited by EMS hardware.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Can I use extended memory on my 8088 XT clone?
a: No. The 8088 can only address 1 MB, so there's nothing above it to extend into. Your option is an EMS board such as an Intel Above Board or AST RAMpage, which bank-switches memory into a 64K page frame.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Do I need to add a math coprocessor to use more memory?
a: No, they're unrelated. A coprocessor like the 8087, 80287 or 80387 speeds up floating point math only. Extra RAM helps with larger programs and caches. Buy one if your software, like CAD or spreadsheets, uses it.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Does OS/2 1.x need a lot of memory?
a: Yes. OS/2 1.1 wants at least 2 MB on a 286 or 386, and more if you run several programs or Presentation Manager. It's real RAM hungry. Plan on 4 MB if you want to multitask comfortably.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Does Windows 3.0 need extended memory?
a: Yes, for 286 standard mode and 386 enhanced mode. It needs HIMEM.SYS loaded and recommends at least 2 MB. Real mode only uses conventional and EMS, and runs poorly compared to the others.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How do I find out how much conventional memory I have free?
a: Run CHKDSK and look at the last line, which shows bytes free in memory. Under DOS 4.0 or later you can use MEM as well. Third-party tools like Norton's SI or Quarterdeck Manifest give more detail.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How do I install memory chips without damaging them?
a: Power off and unplug the machine, and touch the metal chassis to discharge static. Match the notch on the chip with the socket, line up all the pins, and press down evenly. Bent pins are the usual problem.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How do I load DOS device drivers into upper memory?
a: With a 386 you can use QEMM's LOADHI or 386MAX's utilities to put drivers and TSRs in unused blocks between 640K and 1 MB. That frees conventional memory. It's tricky to get right, so exclude any areas your cards use.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How do I make a RAM disk in extended memory?
a: With DOS 3.3 add DEVICE=VDISK.SYS 360 /E to CONFIG.SYS, which makes a 360K disk in extended memory. Under MS-DOS use RAMDRIVE.SYS with the /E switch. Put your temp files or compiler on it for a big speedup.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How do I tell if my AT has 640K or 512K of base memory?
a: Look at your motherboard switches or run the SETUP disk. On an IBM AT the memory is configured in the setup program, and the base size must match the chips installed. CHKDSK will show the total.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How do I turn extended memory into expanded memory on a 386?
a: Use a memory manager like QEMM-386 from Quarterdeck or 386MAX from Qualitas. Add the device line to CONFIG.SYS and it builds EMS from your extended RAM. Compaq's CEMM does the same on Compaq DOS 3.31.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How do I upgrade my XT from 256K to 640K?
a: Fill the motherboard banks to the maximum your board supports, usually by swapping in 256K-bit DRAM chips, and set the DIP switches to match. If the board is limited to 256K, add a multifunction card with RAM and set it to start at that address.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How much RAM can a 286 address?
a: 16 MB, since it has 24 address lines. In practice most AT clones have a few megabytes at most. A 386DX can address 4 GB, though nobody is stuffing that into a desktop box.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: How much RAM should I get for Windows 3.0?
a: Get 2 MB to run at all in 386 enhanced mode, but 4 MB is more comfortable. With 1 MB, you're stuck in real or standard mode. Windows works best with a lot of extended memory and a disk cache like SMARTDrive.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Is a disk cache better than a RAM disk?
a: Usually yes. A cache adapts to what you actually use and writes changes back safely, while a RAM disk needs files copied in and is lost on power failure. Use a RAM disk only for fixed things like compiler temp files.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Is it worth buying an EMS board for my 286 or should I just use extended memory?
a: Depends on your software. Lotus 1-2-3 Release 2 wants EMS, while OS/2, Windows/286 and RAM disks like VDISK use extended. Many 286 boards, like the Above Board AT, can be jumpered to do either, so buy one of those.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Is it worth upgrading my 386 to 8 MB?
a: If you run Windows 3.0 in enhanced mode, OS/2, Unix or big spreadsheets, yes. For plain DOS programs, 2 to 4 MB is plenty. Prices on 1 Mbit chips are still high, so buy what you will use.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Should I buy SIMMs or SIPPs?
a: SIMMs. They're more widely used and easier to find than SIPPs. Both are small modules with several DRAM chips, but SIMMs use edge contacts into a socket, while SIPPs use fragile pins. Check what your motherboard takes.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What addresses do my video cards use that I must avoid?
a: Mono text uses B000-B7FF, CGA uses B800-BFFF, and EGA or VGA uses A000-BFFF. Plug-in BIOS ROMs for EGA/VGA sit at C000. Put your EMS page frame at D000 or E000 to avoid conflicts.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What does 'Parity Check 1' mean on boot?
a: It means the motherboard memory failed a parity test, so a chip is bad or loose. Reseat the RAM chips first. If it persists, find the failing bank with a diagnostic like Checkit or the POST error code.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What does 'zero wait state' mean in an ad?
a: It means the CPU never has to pause waiting on memory. Systems usually get this using page interleaving or a cache, with fast RAM. Check what the claim applies to, as some only mean certain memory accesses.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What does EMS 4.0 mean?
a: It's the Lotus/Intel/Microsoft Expanded Memory Specification version 4.0, released in 1987. It allows up to 32 MB of expanded memory and lets programs map more pages, so multitasking software can swap whole programs in and out.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What does LIM mean?
a: Lotus-Intel-Microsoft, the companies that wrote the expanded memory spec. You'll see LIM EMS 3.2 or 4.0 on boards and manuals. It means the board follows that standard, so programs like 1-2-3 and Symphony can use it.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What does XMS stand for?
a: Extended Memory Specification, written by Microsoft, Lotus, Intel and AST in 1988. It defines how programs get extended memory, the HMA, and upper memory blocks through a driver like HIMEM.SYS, so they don't fight over the same RAM.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What does the BIOS memory test do at startup?
a: The POST counts and checks your RAM, which is the number you see ticking up as the machine boots. If you have a lot of memory it can take a while. Some clone BIOSes let you skip it by pressing Esc.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is HIMEM.SYS?
a: It's Microsoft's extended memory manager, shipped with Windows/286 and Windows 2.1 and later. It follows the XMS spec so programs can allocate extended memory without stepping on each other. Put DEVICE=HIMEM.SYS in your CONFIG.SYS.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is QEMM?
a: Quarterdeck Expanded Memory Manager, a popular 386 memory manager that provides EMS, maps RAM into unused upper memory areas, and loads TSRs high. Its Optimize feature, in later versions, tunes your load order automatically.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is a TSR and why does it eat my memory?
a: A Terminate and Stay Resident program stays in conventional memory after it exits, to pop up on a hotkey. SideKick, print spoolers and mouse drivers are examples. Each one cuts into your 640K, so remove any you don't use.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is a wait state?
a: It's a clock cycle where the CPU idles because memory can't deliver data fast enough. Slow DRAM on a fast CPU forces wait states and drags performance. Zero wait state systems need fast RAM or cache.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is bank switching?
a: It's swapping different chunks of memory into the same address range, so a CPU with limited address space can use more RAM. EMS does this: a driver maps 16K pages of the card into the 64K page frame as needed.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is interleaved memory?
a: It splits RAM into two banks so that consecutive accesses alternate between them. While one bank is recovering, the other responds, which hides DRAM cycle time. It needs RAM in pairs of banks to work.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is shadow RAM?
a: It's a BIOS feature that copies the slow system and video ROM into faster RAM and runs it from there. It can speed up screen and BIOS calls. The RAM it uses is taken out of the 384K above 640K.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is the 640K barrier?
a: It's the limit of conventional memory under DOS on 8088 and 8086 machines. The CPU sees 1 MB, and IBM put video and ROM in the upper 384K, so programs get 640K. Anything beyond that takes tricks like EMS or extended memory.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is the A20 line?
a: It's the 21st address line on the 286 and up. IBM's AT keeps it gated off through the keyboard controller to mimic 8086 address wraparound. Memory managers switch it on to reach the memory just above 1 MB.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is the Intel Above Board?
a: It's Intel's popular memory expansion card for the PC, XT and AT, one of the first to follow the LIM EMS spec. The AT version can be set up as expanded, extended, or a mix, and holds up to several megabytes.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What is the page frame in EMS?
a: It's the 64K window, usually four 16K pages, in the upper memory area where the EMS driver maps expanded memory. Programs access EMS through that window. Typically it sits at segment D000 or E000.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What's SMARTDrive?
a: It's the disk caching driver that comes with Windows 3.0. It uses extended memory to hold recently read disk sectors so repeated reads are faster. Put DEVICE=SMARTDRV.SYS in CONFIG.SYS, and size it for your RAM.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: What's the difference between 80ns and 100ns RAM?
a: It's the access time. 80ns chips are faster than 100ns. You can generally use faster chips in a slower board, but not the reverse. Fast chips are needed for 12 MHz and higher AT machines or zero-wait-state operation.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Why does my 386 with 4 MB report only 3 MB extended?
a: Probably 640K of your 4 MB is used as base memory, and the rest is extended, which is about 3.3 MB. If you've got shadow RAM on, that copies ROMs into RAM and can eat some more. Check your BIOS setup.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Why does my PC with 1 meg of RAM only show 640K free in DOS?
a: Real-mode DOS can only address 1 MB total, and the top 384K is reserved for video, BIOS and adapter ROMs. That leaves 640K for programs. The rest of your RAM needs expanded or extended memory drivers to be useful.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Why does my RAM disk contents vanish after a reboot?
a: RAM loses its contents when power drops or the machine resets. Copy anything you want to keep back to the hard disk before shutting down. Put it in your batch file, or use a battery-backed RAM card.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Why does my program say 'Not enough memory' when I have 4 MB?
a: Most DOS programs only see conventional memory, which is limited to 640K minus DOS, drivers and TSRs. Your 4 MB must be set up as EMS or extended, and the program must support it. Check with CHKDSK or MEM.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Why is RAM so expensive right now?
a: DRAM prices rose sharply in 1988 and again in 1989 because of supply limits, the US-Japan chip trade agreement, and strong demand. Prices usually drop when new fabs come online. Shop mail order rather than local stores.

topic: memory: 640K, expanded and extended memory, RAM upgrades
q: Will my old EMS 3.2 board work with software that wants 4.0?
a: Usually the software runs, but only with the 3.2 feature set, meaning a 4 page 64K frame and 8 MB max. Programs that need 4.0 functions, like running multiple DOS programs in EMS, will not work properly.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Can I mix MFM and RLL drives on the same controller?
a: Not well. The controller writes in one encoding, so both drives get used with the same one. An MFM drive won't be reliable run as RLL unless it is certified for it. Use a controller for all of one type.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Can I put two hard drives in my PC?
a: Yes. Most AT controllers handle two ST-506 drives, which need different drive select jumpers and a twisted cable on the first. The second drive is D: in DOS. On SCSI you just set a separate ID.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Can I use a 3.5 inch drive in a full-size AT?
a: Yes. Buy mounting rails that adapt a 3.5 inch drive to a 5.25 inch bay. The Conner CP-3044 and CP-3104 are popular. They are lighter, use less power, and are quieter than full-height drives.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Can I use an RLL controller with my old MFM ST-225 to get more space?
a: Yes, people do it, turning a 20 meg ST-225 into about 30 meg. Low-level format it with the RLL controller and run a surface analysis. Many ST-225s throw bad sectors and some fail outright, so back up often.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Do I need a disk cache?
a: Yes, it makes a big difference. SMARTDRV.SYS from Windows 3.0 or PC-Kwik both work well. Even a 256K cache cuts the number of disk reads a lot. Use extended or expanded memory so it doesn't eat conventional RAM.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Do I need to park the heads before moving my computer?
a: On older drives like the ST-225, yes. Run a park program such as SHIPDISK or the one in Norton Utilities. Newer drives such as the ST-251 and most voice-coil drives auto-park when power is cut, so you needn't bother.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Do I need to worry about stray magnets near my hard disk?
a: Not much. The platters are sealed in a metal case, and the drive's own motor magnets are stronger than a typical speaker. Floppies are the ones to keep away from magnets, monitors, and telephones.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How do I find the best interleave for my drive?
a: Try a tool like SpinRite, Disk Technician, or the Norton Calibrate program. They test throughput at different interleaves and reformat to the best one. Calibrate does it without wiping your data, though back up first anyway.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How do I low-level format my hard disk on an XT?
a: Run DEBUG and type G=C800:5 at the dash prompt. That jumps into the controller's ROM format routine on most Western Digital XT controllers. The address varies by controller, so check your manual. Then run FDISK and FORMAT.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How do I partition a hard disk with FDISK?
a: Run FDISK, choose Create DOS Partition, and set it active so the machine boots from it. Reboot, then run FORMAT C: /S to put the system files on. DOS 3.3 lets you add an extended partition for the rest.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How do I recover a file I deleted by accident?
a: Stop writing to the disk right away. Use UNDELETE in DOS 5 or Norton Utilities' UnErase or PC Tools' Undelete. DOS only changes the first letter of the directory entry, so the data is often still there.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How do I tell if my drive is certified for RLL?
a: Look for RLL on the label or in the spec sheet. Seagate's ST-238 and ST-277R are examples. The drives have a better media and tighter tolerance. Regular MFM drives will often work, but at your own risk.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How fast is a typical hard disk of this era?
a: An old MFM drive like the ST-225 averages about 65 ms seek time. Better drives such as the Miniscribe 3425 do 85. Modern ones like the Quantum ProDrive 80S do about 19 ms. Under 28 ms is good for a 386.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How long do hard drives usually last?
a: Most vendors quote MTBF of 20,000 to 40,000 hours, but that's an average. A drive that survives the first few months usually runs for years. Heat, power surges, and shocks are what usually kill them.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How many devices can I put on a SCSI bus?
a: Eight IDs total, 0 through 7, and the host adapter takes one, usually 7. So you can chain seven devices. The bus needs terminators on both ends of the cable, and total cable length stays under 6 meters.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: How often should I back up?
a: Anything you cannot recreate should be backed up at least weekly, and daily if you work with it every day. Drives fail without warning. Keep a full backup plus incrementals of changed files.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Is it safe to leave my PC on all the time to avoid wearing out the drive?
a: Many people do, since start-up is when the heads and spindle are stressed. Heat is also a factor, so keep the case ventilated. A quality drive usually lasts either way. Just turn off the monitor.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Is it worth buying a SCSI drive for my 386 clone?
a: If you can afford it, yes. SCSI is faster, the drives are bigger, and you can add tapes or CD-ROMs later. But a good host adapter like an Adaptec 1540 costs a lot more than an ESDI or AT-bus setup.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: My AT BIOS doesn't have my drive type listed. What do I do?
a: Pick a type with fewer or equal cylinders and heads, or get a BIOS with user-definable type 47, like AMI or Phoenix. You can also use Disk Manager from Ontrack, which loads a driver and works around the table.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What SCSI host adapters work with Unix on a 386?
a: Adaptec 1542 and Western Digital WD7000 are well supported in SCO Unix and ISC 386/ix. Check the vendor's list before you buy because drivers are a bit scarce. Also Future Domain TMC-950 for the cheap end.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What are the common ST-506 drive types in the AT BIOS?
a: The AT BIOS has a fixed table of about 47 types, which is a problem. Type 2 is the 20 meg, 615 cylinders by 4 heads. Type 17 is the 30 meg ST-4038 at 733 by 5. Pick the closest match not exceeding your geometry.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What does MTBF mean on a drive spec sheet?
a: Mean Time Between Failures, in power-on hours. A rating of 30,000 hours does not mean a drive lasts 30,000 hours. It is a statistical figure over many drives, so take it with some salt.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What does SCSI stand for and how is it different from ST-506?
a: Small Computer System Interface, pronounced scuzzy. ST-506 is a dumb interface where the controller does the work. SCSI drives carry their own controller on the drive, and the bus can host up to seven devices.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What does ST-506 mean?
a: It's the Seagate interface from 1980 for their 5 meg 5.25 inch drive. Later MFM and RLL drives used the same signals. The controller handles all the data separation and encoding, and the drive just moves bits.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What does SpinRite do?
a: It's Steve Gibson's utility that does a non-destructive low-level reformat of each track, testing for marginal areas and moving data away from them. It also finds the best interleave. Many people run it every few months.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What does average access time mean?
a: It's the average time for the head to move to a random track, plus the wait for the right sector to come around. Manufacturers usually quote only seek time, so figure about 8 ms extra for rotation at 3600 rpm.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What does the DOS command CHKDSK /F do?
a: It looks for lost clusters and cross-linked files. With /F, it fixes the file allocation table and saves lost chains as FILE0000.CHK files. Do not run it from inside a DOS shell or Windows, or you may harm the disk.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What does the error 1701 at boot mean on my AT?
a: It means the BIOS cannot find or correctly talk to the hard disk. Check the cables, the drive type in SETUP, and whether the controller card is seated. Also check that the drive power connector is attached.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is SCSI termination?
a: It's a set of resistors on the ends of the cable that stop signals from reflecting back along the bus. Without them you get random errors and hangs. Normally the last device and the host adapter carry them.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is a RAM disk and should I use one?
a: It's a driver that sets aside RAM as a fast pretend drive, using VDISK.SYS or RAMDRIVE.SYS. Handy for compilers and temp files. But the contents are gone on power loss, so always copy results to the hard disk.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is a bad track table on the drive label?
a: It's a list of cylinder and head locations where the factory found flaws. You enter them in the low-level format program so those areas get marked bad. Keep the label; it's useful if you must reformat.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is a cluster and why does a tiny file take up so much space?
a: DOS allocates space in clusters, which are groups of sectors. On a 20 meg drive a cluster is 4K, so even a 100 byte file takes 4096 bytes. Bigger partitions have bigger clusters and more waste.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is a head crash?
a: It happens when a read/write head touches the platter surface and scrapes off magnetic coating. Usually a bump or shock while the drive is running does it. You lose data in that spot and sometimes the whole drive.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is a stepper motor drive versus a voice coil drive?
a: Stepper drives move the heads with a motor that clicks from track to track, which is slower and prone to drift with temperature. Voice coil drives use a servo and are faster, quieter, and more reliable. They auto-park too.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is an AT-bus or IDE drive?
a: It's a drive with the controller built in, plugged into a simple adapter on the AT bus using a 40-pin cable. Compaq and Conner began it. It's cheaper than SCSI, fast enough, and looks to the BIOS like an ST-506 drive.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is the Adaptec 1540?
a: It's a SCSI host adapter for ISA machines, with bus-mastering DMA and an onboard BIOS. It handles hard disks, tape, and CD-ROM. It's also popular in 386 PCs and works with Novell NetWare and UNIX.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is the Conner CP-3104?
a: It's a 3.5 inch 104 meg AT-bus drive with a voice coil actuator. It has about 29 ms average seek and costs a lot less than comparable full-size drives. They've proven popular and are quite reliable.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is the best way to back up a hard drive?
a: Floppies with BACKUP in DOS work but are slow. A tape drive like the Colorado or Archive QIC-40 or QIC-60 is much easier. Programs like Fastback Plus are quicker than DOS BACKUP and compress.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is the difference between ESDI and SCSI?
a: ESDI is a fast device-level interface based on ST-506 but with the data separator on the drive, giving 10 Mbit/s or more. SCSI is a system-level bus with intelligent commands. ESDI is for disks only, while SCSI handles other devices.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is the difference between MFM and RLL hard drives?
a: RLL packs data more tightly, using 26 sectors per track instead of 17 for MFM. That gives about 50 percent more capacity on the same platters. You need an RLL controller, and the drive has to be certified to handle it.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is the maximum hard disk size DOS 4.01 supports?
a: DOS 4.0 raised the partition limit beyond 32 meg, so a partition can be up to 512 meg with larger clusters. But 4.0 uses more memory and had bugs, which is why a lot of people stay on 3.3.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: What is the twist in the floppy and hard drive cable?
a: On ST-506 drives, the 34-pin control cable has a twist in lines 25 through 29. This sets the drive select, so the drive after the twist is drive 0 or 1. Without it both drives would answer at once.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Which is better for a 286: a 40 meg MFM or a 30 meg RLL?
a: Take the RLL setup if it costs the same, because the data rate is higher and the transfer is faster. A good certified 40 meg drive with an RLL controller would give you about 60 meg, but only if it's rated for it.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Why does my 40 meg drive show up as only 32 meg in DOS?
a: DOS 3.3 and earlier can't handle a partition larger than 32 meg. Make two partitions with FDISK, using an extended DOS partition for the second. Or get Compaq DOS 3.31 or a driver like Disk Manager, which gets around it.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Why does my SCSI chain not work when I add a second drive?
a: Check that each device has a different ID, and that only the two physical ends of the chain are terminated. Remove terminator packs from the middle drives. Bad termination is the cause of most SCSI headaches.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Why does my new SCSI drive not show up on my Mac?
a: Check the SCSI ID isn't 0 or 7, because the internal drive uses 0 and the Mac is 7. Make sure it is formatted with the Apple HD SC Setup or a program like Silverlining. Also check termination and cable.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Why is my hard drive getting slower over time?
a: Files become fragmented as you save and delete, so the heads jump around to read them. Run a defragmenter such as Norton Speed Disk, PC Tools Compress, or VOPT. Back up first and check the disk after.

topic: hard disks, SCSI, MFM and RLL
q: Why is my hard drive making a loud grinding noise?
a: Probably a failing bearing, or a head touching the platter. Back up everything now if it still reads. Stop using it if you hear scraping, because that can destroy the surface and your data.

q: Can I flip over a single sided disk and use the other side as a double sided disk?
a: People do it with a hole punch, but it's a gamble. Many single-sided disks are not certified on the back, so you risk lost data. Buying double-sided disks costs only a bit more and it's worth it.

q: Can I format a 360K 5.25 inch disk in my 1.2MB AT drive?
a: Yes, it'll read and write them, but a 1.2MB drive writes a narrower track than a 360K drive. Disks written in the AT drive may not read reliably in an old XT drive, so use them mainly on the same machine.

q: Can I read a Mac disk on a PC?
a: Not directly because the formats differ. You can use a utility like Apple File Exchange on a Mac with a SuperDrive to read and write PC disks. On a PC you need a product like Mac-in-DOS.

q: Can I use DOS 3.3 to format a 1.44MB disk?
a: No. DOS 3.3 doesn't support 1.44MB drives. You need DOS 3.3 plus a driver, or better, DOS 4.01 or MS-DOS 5.0 on machines where they are provided, or the one from the manufacturer.

q: Can a magnet really erase a floppy?
a: Yes, a strong enough magnet will damage the data. Speakers, motors, telephones with ringers, and TV sets all have magnets. Keep disks a foot or more away from them.

q: Can my Atari ST read MS-DOS disks?
a: Mostly yes. The ST uses a DOS-compatible format, so 720K disks formatted on a PC can be read, though some ST programs make disks with 9 or 10 sectors per track that a PC can't handle.

q: Do I need to clean my drives if I use them every day?
a: Cleaning every three months or so is plenty for most home use. If you start seeing read errors on disks that used to work fine, clean it and try again.

q: Do airport X-ray machines damage floppy disks?
a: Not in my experience. The X-ray itself doesn't harm disks. The conveyor belt motor and metal detector gates are more of a concern, so many people hand-carry disks around them just in case.

q: How can I use a floppy as a boot disk for a hard drive that will not start?
a: Make a boot floppy with FORMAT A: /S and copy over CONFIG.SYS, AUTOEXEC.BAT and tools like FDISK and CHKDSK. Boot from it, then you can reach the hard drive's C: files.

q: How do I copy a copy-protected game disk?
a: The protection often uses odd track formats that DISKCOPY can't copy. Programs like Copy II PC or Copywrite can sometimes do it. The legal position for backup copies is a gray area, so check the license.

q: How do I format a floppy in MS-DOS?
a: Type FORMAT A: at the prompt and follow the instructions. Add /S if you want it bootable with the system files. Under DOS 4.0 and later you'll also be asked for a volume label.

q: How do I get 1.44MB on a floppy when my drive only reads 720K?
a: You can't. A 720K drive lacks the head and electronics for 1.44MB. You need an HD drive, and your controller has to support the data rate, so check the controller card as well.

q: How do I know whether my AT drive is 1.2MB or 360K?
a: Run CHKDSK on a freshly formatted disk and look at the total bytes. You can also look at the drive in the CMOS setup, which lists drive A as 1.2MB or 360K. ATs use 1.2MB drives.

q: How do I make a backup of a disk on a one-drive PC?
a: Use DISKCOPY A: A: and swap the source and target disks when asked. It may take several swaps. The disks must be the same size and type, and it'll format the target as it goes.

q: How do I undelete a file I removed by accident from a floppy?
a: Stop writing to the disk right away. With DOS 5.0 unavailable, use Norton Utilities Unerase or PC Tools Undelete. They work as long as the space hasn't been reused.

q: How do I write-protect a 3.5 inch disk?
a: Slide the little tab in the corner so the square hole is open. With the hole open the disk is protected. With it closed you can write to it.

q: How do I write-protect a 5.25 inch floppy?
a: Cover the square notch on the side of the disk with a write-protect sticker. Those come in the box with new disks. A covered notch means the drive can only read the disk.

q: How long do floppy disks last?
a: Properly cared for, they can last for years, but I wouldn't count on more than five or so for important data. Make backups, and copy off old disks to fresh ones now and then.

q: How many files can I put in the root directory of a floppy?
a: On a 360K disk the limit is 112 entries, on 1.2MB it's 224, and on 720K it's 112. Subdirectories don't have that limit, so use them if you have many files.

q: How should I store floppy disks?
a: Keep them in their sleeves or a disk box, upright, away from heat, dust, and magnets. Don't put them on top of the monitor or near the telephone. Room temperature is best.

q: Is a 3.5 inch disk more reliable than a 5.25?
a: Generally, yes. The hard plastic shell, metal shutter and smaller size protect the disk surface from fingers and dust. It's much harder to damage one by accident.

q: Is it OK to leave a disk in the drive when I turn the computer off?
a: Better not to. A power surge as the machine switches on or off can scribble on the disk. Take the disk out first, and on 5.25 inch drives open the latch.

q: Is it safe to send floppy disks through the mail?
a: Generally yes. Put the disk in a stiff cardboard mailer, mark it Do Not Bend, and for 3.5 inch disks use a padded mailer. The X-ray machines at airports aren't a problem but magnets are.

q: Is it worth buying a 3.5 inch drive for my XT?
a: Yes if you swap files with newer machines, since the 3.5 inch disks are tougher and hold more. Get an external or a 5.25 inch bay adapter kit with a controller that supports it. Expect 720K on most XT setups.

q: What does 'General failure reading drive A' mean?
a: DOS can't make sense of the disk. Usually it's unformatted, formatted for another system, or has a bad boot sector. Try another disk first to rule out the drive, and if the disk is yours, try a utility like Norton's Disk Doctor.

q: What does 'Non-system disk or disk error' mean?
a: The disk in drive A isn't bootable. Take it out and press a key to boot from a disk that has the system files, or from the hard drive if you have one.

q: What does 'Sector not found reading drive A' mean?
a: DOS can't find the sector on the disk. The disk may be damaged, or the drive may be misaligned if it only happens with disks written elsewhere. Try the disk in another machine.

q: What does the 'DRIVER.SYS' line in CONFIG.SYS do?
a: It lets DOS set up an extra logical floppy drive, such as an external 3.5 inch drive on an older machine. You give the physical drive number and options like /F:2 for 720K.

q: What does the 'volume label' do on a floppy?
a: It's a name stored on the disk, up to 11 characters, set at format time with FORMAT /V or by the LABEL command. DIR and VOL show it, and it helps you tell your disks apart.

q: What does the DOS command DISKCOMP do?
a: It compares two floppies track by track and tells you if they are the same. It's handy after DISKCOPY to check the copy. Both disks must be the same format.

q: What does the Mac 800K disk use that a PC disk does not?
a: A Mac drive varies the spin speed depending on the track, so it can pack more sectors on the outer tracks. That's how it squeezes 800K onto a DD disk. PC drives spin at a constant speed.

q: What is ARC and why do people use it on floppies?
a: ARC is a file compression program by System Enhancement Associates that packs several files into one archive. It saves space on floppies and makes downloading from BBSs quicker. PKARC and PKXARC are faster versions of it.

q: What is a RAM disk, and is it faster than a floppy?
a: A RAM disk uses part of your memory as a pretend drive, via VDISK.SYS or RAMDRIVE.SYS. It's far faster than a floppy but the contents vanish when you turn off or reboot, so copy files back to disk.

q: What is a bad sector and what should I do about it?
a: It's a spot on the disk that can't hold data reliably. FORMAT marks them so DOS avoids them. If a once-good disk gains bad sectors, copy off your files and throw it away.

q: What is a disk label and where do I put it?
a: It's the paper sticker you write on to say what is on the disk. On 5.25 inch disks write on the label with a felt tip pen before you stick it on, never a ballpoint, since it can dent the disk.

q: What is a disk sector?
a: A sector is the smallest chunk the drive reads or writes, normally 512 bytes on PCs. Each track is divided into sectors, 9 per track on a 360K disk and 18 per track on a 1.44MB disk.

q: What is interleave and does it matter on floppies?
a: Interleave is the order that sectors are numbered on a track so the computer can keep up. Floppies on a PC are normally 1:1 and nothing to tune. It matters more with hard drives.

q: What is the best way to clean a floppy drive head?
a: Use a head cleaning disk with a few drops of cleaning fluid, run it for about 30 seconds. Don't do it too often since the cleaning disk is abrasive. Once every few months is plenty.

q: What is the capacity of an Amiga floppy?
a: A standard Amiga 3.5 inch disk holds 880K when formatted. It uses its own format with 11 sectors per track, so a PC drive can't read it without special software.

q: What is the difference between FORMAT and QuickFormat?
a: MS-DOS 5.0 isn't out, so there's no QuickFormat in DOS. Some Norton and PC Tools utilities have a quick format that only rewrites the directory and FAT, which is fast but doesn't check for bad sectors.

q: What is the difference between a double density and a high density 3.5 inch disk?
a: DD disks hold 720K on PC or 800K on a Mac, HD disks hold 1.44MB on PC. HD disks have a second hole in the corner and a different coating. You need an HD drive to format them as HD.

q: What is the difference between a hard sector and soft sector disk?
a: Hard sector disks have a row of punched holes marking sector starts, found on some older S-100 and Vector systems. Soft sector disks have just one index hole and the sectors are written when you format. PC and Mac disks are soft sector.

q: Which brand of floppy disks is best?
a: Maxell, Verbatim, 3M, and Sony have the best track record. Bargain no-name disks can be fine, but they have a higher failure rate. For important data I'd stay with a name brand.

q: Why can't I use a 1.2MB disk in a 360K drive after formatting it in an AT?
a: A disk formatted at 1.2MB uses 80 tracks, while a 360K drive only handles 40. The old drive can't line up with those narrower tracks. Use 360K disks for any disk going to older machines.

q: Why do I get 'Disk boot failure' when I turn on my PC?
a: The machine tried to boot from a disk without the system files. Either remove the data disk from drive A, or put in a bootable disk made with FORMAT /S or SYS A:.

q: Why does my 5.25 inch disk make a grinding noise?
a: It may be a bent or warped disk, a dirty head, or the disk not seated and latched in the drive. Take it out, and check the jacket for creases. If new disks do it too, the drive probably needs service.

q: Why does my Mac keep ejecting a disk and saying it is unreadable?
a: The disk is either bad or not initialized. The Mac offers to Initialize it, which erases it. If it has data you need, try another Mac or a recovery tool like Norton Utilities for Macintosh before initializing.

q: Why does my disk drive light stay on after I get a read error?
a: The drive is retrying the read, usually several times, before DOS gives up and shows Abort, Retry, Fail. Press R a few more times, and if it still fails, copy off what you can with a tool like Copy II PC or Norton Utilities.

q: Why is my floppy drive so slow compared to a hard disk?
a: A floppy spins at only 300 or 360 rpm, and the heads touch the disk. Transfer rates are around 250 to 500 kilobits per second. A hard disk spins about ten times faster.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Can I add memory to my EGA card?
a: Many EGA cards, including the IBM EGA, have a memory expansion daughterboard, which takes you from 64K to 128K and then 256K. The ATI and Paradise clones often have sockets for chips instead.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Can I plug my old CGA monitor into an EGA card?
a: Only if the card has a CGA mode and your monitor takes 15.7 kHz scan rates. Most EGA cards have DIP switches for this, but you will only get CGA resolution and colors, not EGA.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Can I use a Hercules card and a CGA card in the same PC?
a: Yes, since they use different addresses, you can run a Hercules mono and a CGA color board together with two monitors. Use the MODE command to switch, for example MODE MONO or MODE CO80.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Can I use a multisync monitor with all of these cards?
a: Yes, that is the point. NEC MultiSync and similar monitors handle 15 to 35 kHz or so, so they work with CGA, EGA, VGA and even some Super VGA modes. They cost more but save you from upgrading twice.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Can a VGA card display 16 colors in 640x480?
a: Yes, that is the standard VGA mode 12h. It is 4 bit planes at 640x480, and it needs 256K of video RAM. Windows 3.0 and many paint programs use this mode a lot.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Does VGA work with older software that supports EGA?
a: Mostly yes, since VGA is backward compatible with EGA and CGA modes. Some old programs poke the hardware directly and fail, but nearly all popular software like Flight Simulator and Lotus works fine.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Does a 386 need a faster video card?
a: Yes, video can become the bottleneck. A fast 16-bit VGA card with a good chipset, such as the Tseng ET4000 or Video Seven, can make Windows feel quite a lot snappier even on the same CPU.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How can I get 16 colors on a CGA card?
a: In text mode you get 16 colors at once, but in graphics mode just 4. Some games use tricks with the composite output to get 16 colors from a CGA card and a TV or composite monitor.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How do I run Lotus 1-2-3 graphics on a Hercules card?
a: Run the Lotus install program and pick the Hercules driver, or use the Graphics driver option to select it. Some programs need a Hercules emulator like SIMCGA to run CGA-only software.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How do I set the DIP switches on my EGA card?
a: The manual should show a table that matches your monitor type: CGA, EGA, or monochrome, and your primary display. If you do not have the manual, check the card's silk-screen or ask the maker.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How do I switch between color and mono on a dual-monitor PC?
a: Use the DOS MODE command, for example MODE MONO for the monochrome display or MODE CO80 for the color one. Some programs, like Turbo Debugger, let you use the second monitor directly.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How do I tell if my VGA card is 8-bit or 16-bit?
a: Look at the edge connector. An 8-bit card has just the one long slot connector, while a 16-bit card has a second shorter connector. The 16-bit ones are noticeably faster on a 286 or 386.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How many colors can EGA display at once?
a: Sixteen at a time, chosen from a palette of 64. That requires 128K of memory on the card, though. With only 64K you are limited to 4 colors in 640x350 mode.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How many pixels is 640x480 in total?
a: It's 307,200 pixels. At 16 colors that takes 4 bits per pixel, which is about 150K of memory, but VGA uses planes so it reserves 256K on the card.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: How much video memory do I need for 800x600 with 256 colors?
a: You need 512K minimum, since 800x600 at one byte per pixel is 480,000 bytes. For 1024x768 with 256 colors you need a full 1 MB on the card.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Is it OK to leave my monitor on all the time?
a: Not really. Phosphor burn-in is real, especially on monochrome with a static display, and the tube ages. Turn it off or use a screen blanker like Screen Saver in your AUTOEXEC.BAT if you are away often.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Is it safe to hot-swap the monitor cable on a running PC?
a: I wouldn't. It can damage the video card or monitor input. Power both off first, plug in the cable and tighten the screws, then power everything on. It takes about a minute.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Is it worth upgrading from EGA to VGA?
a: If you can afford it, yes. VGA cards are down to about $200 for decent ones, and 256 color games and 640x480 text look much better. You will need a new analog monitor, so budget for that too.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Is the color of a monochrome monitor important, green, amber or white?
a: It is mostly preference. Many people find amber easiest on the eyes for long sessions, green is common and cheap, and paper-white is best for desktop publishing. Try a few before buying.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: My monitor says 31.5 kHz. Is that VGA?
a: Yes. VGA 640x480 uses a 31.5 kHz horizontal scan rate at 60 Hz vertical, and the 720x400 text mode uses 31.5 kHz at 70 Hz. EGA monitors only do 21.8 kHz, so they cannot sync to that.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Should I buy a 14 inch or 12 inch monitor for my XT?
a: A 14-inch is easier to look at if you can afford it. For a Hercules or CGA setup, a 12-inch is fine. Bigger sizes only help if the resolution is high enough, otherwise the pixels just look chunky.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What does 'VGA' actually stand for and why is everyone excited about it?
a: Video Graphics Array, introduced by IBM with the PS/2 in 1987. It does 640x480 in 16 colors and 320x200 in 256 colors, with an analog output, so the picture is far smoother than EGA.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What does 'dot pitch' mean on a monitor?
a: It is the distance between phosphor dots of the same color on the screen. Smaller is sharper. 0.31 mm is typical for a decent color monitor, and 0.28 mm is considered very good.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What does 'non-glare' on a monitor do?
a: It reduces reflections from room lights, either by etching the glass or by coating it. Etched glass can make the image a bit softer, while a mesh screen filter you put on yourself cuts the glare but also dims the picture.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What does 256 colors in VGA mode 13h mean?
a: Mode 13h is 320x200 with one byte per pixel, so 256 colors from a palette of 262,144. That is what most VGA games use, such as the newer Sierra adventures, because programming it is easy.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What does interlaced mean for a monitor?
a: The screen draws odd lines first and even lines second, so it takes two passes per frame. It lets cheap cards reach high resolutions, but you will see flicker, especially at 640x480 or higher.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is Super VGA?
a: It is the name for cards that go beyond standard VGA, usually 800x600 in 16 colors, and sometimes 1024x768. Each maker does it differently, so you need a driver for your particular chipset.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is a Hercules card and why would I want one?
a: The Hercules Graphics Card gives you 720x348 monochrome graphics plus crisp MDA text on a TTL monochrome monitor. It's great for Lotus 1-2-3 and word processing, and a lot of software supports it.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is a composite monitor?
a: It takes one video signal combining color and sync, like a TV. You get the CGA composite output as a yellow RCA jack, but the picture is blurry compared to an RGB monitor, and fine text is hard to read.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is a good VGA card for under $200?
a: Look at the Paradise VGA Plus, the Video Seven VGA, or an ATI VGA Wonder. All have 256K and some have 512K, can do 800x600, and ship with drivers for Windows and Lotus.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is a video BIOS and can I upgrade it?
a: It is a ROM on the card that contains the firmware routines for text and graphics modes. On most cards it is soldered or socketed, and you can only replace it with a chip from the manufacturer, if they offer one.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the Plantronics ColorPlus card?
a: It is a CGA-compatible card with extra memory that gives 16 colors at 320x200 and 4 colors at 640x200. Only a limited number of programs support it, so check before you buy.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the best monitor for a Mac-like crisp display on a PC?
a: Look at a Hercules card with a good 12-inch or 14-inch TTL monochrome monitor, or an IBM-compatible with a VGA monochrome display. Paper-white monochrome VGA monitors are very sharp for desktop publishing.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the best way to clean the screen of my monitor?
a: Turn it off and unplug it, then wipe with a soft cloth lightly dampened with water or a glass cleaner. Spray the cloth, not the glass. Do not use harsh solvents on anti-glare coatings.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the difference between CGA and EGA?
a: CGA gives you 320x200 in 4 colors or 640x200 in 2 colors. EGA does 640x350 with 16 colors out of a 64 color palette, and the text is much sharper. EGA needs an EGA monitor, though.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the difference between a TTL and an analog monitor?
a: A TTL monitor takes digital on/off signals per color, so CGA and EGA are limited to a few levels. An analog one, like VGA, takes continuously varying voltages, so it can show 262,144 possible colors.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the difference between the IBM PS/2 Model 30 VGA and MCGA?
a: The MCGA in the Model 25 and 30 is a cut-down VGA built into the motherboard. It does 320x200 with 256 colors and 640x480 with 2 colors, but not the 16-color 640x480 mode or EGA modes.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the maximum resolution of EGA?
a: 640x350 with 16 colors, which needs 128K of video memory. On a monochrome EGA monitor you get the same resolution with different shades of intensity. The text mode is 80x25 with an 8x14 character cell.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the refresh rate of VGA?
a: The standard VGA 640x480 mode runs at 60 Hz non-interlaced, while the 720x400 text mode runs at 70 Hz. That is fine for most people, but a few are sensitive to flicker with a bright white background.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: What is the resolution of the original IBM monochrome display adapter?
a: The IBM MDA gives you 80x25 text with 9x14 character boxes, which looks very sharp, but no graphics at all. That is why Hercules created their card, which adds graphics to the same monitor.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Which is better, the Paradise or Tseng ET4000 VGA card?
a: The Tseng ET4000 is generally faster and has the best software support for 800x600 and 1024x768. Paradise cards are cheaper and fine for ordinary use. If you do Windows 3.0, I'd pick the Tseng.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Why can't I plug a VGA monitor into my EGA card?
a: The cables use different signals. VGA has a 15-pin connector with analog RGB, while EGA is a 9-pin digital connector. Even with an adapter, the scan rates do not match, so you would see nothing or risk the monitor.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Why do I get the wrong aspect ratio, like circles that look like ovals?
a: The program is assuming a different mode than what your monitor displays. Adjust the monitor's height and width controls, or choose a driver that matches your card and mode. Many CGA programs expect a 4:3 screen.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Why does my 8514/A flicker in 1024x768?
a: The IBM 8514/A runs 1024x768 interlaced at 44 Hz, which flickers on many monitors. A longer persistence phosphor helps, but a non-interlaced Super VGA card at 800x600 is often easier on the eyes.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Why does my CGA have snow on the screen?
a: The CPU and card contest for video memory, and if the program writes to it during the display refresh, you see sparkles. Good software waits for vertical retrace. Some clone cards do not have the snow problem.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Why does my screen shrink when I switch to a different video mode?
a: Different modes use different sync timings, and the monitor's picture size adjusts for each one. Most monitors have height and width knobs at the back, and you can adjust them per mode with a multisync.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Why does my text look fuzzy on my CGA monitor in 80 column mode?
a: CGA's 8x8 character cell is coarse, and composite monitors blur the colors together. Get a real RGB monitor, like the IBM 5153, and use a green or amber monochrome one if you mostly do text.

topic: monitors and graphics cards: CGA, EGA, VGA, Hercules
q: Why is my VGA monitor showing a black screen after I install Windows 3.0?
a: Probably the wrong driver or a Super VGA mode your monitor cannot sync. Boot with a standard VGA driver by running SETUP from DOS in the Windows directory, and choose VGA from the display list.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Can I plug a LaserWriter into my IBM PC?
a: Yes, through the serial port at 9600 baud, or with an AppleTalk card for the PC. You need software that outputs PostScript, such as Microsoft Word or Ventura Publisher with a PostScript driver. Set the serial port with the MODE command first.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Can I use Windows 2.0 with a PostScript printer?
a: Yes, there is a PostScript driver for Windows and it works with the LaserWriter Plus and other Adobe printers. Pick it in the Control Panel, and select the right port. Expect slow printing, since the PC has to send a lot of data.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Can I use an old Diablo daisy wheel printer with a modern PC?
a: If it has a serial port, yes. Set the baud rate and handshake to match, use a null modem cable if you must, and install the Diablo 630 driver in WordPerfect or Word. Some models need a Centronics converter box to work with the parallel port.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Can I use proportional spacing on a dot matrix printer?
a: Yes, if the printer supports it, usually through ESC p 1 on Epsons, or a control panel setting. Your word processor has to know about it, too, or margins and justification will be off. WordPerfect and Word both have drivers for it.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Can a dot matrix printer print graphics from a Macintosh?
a: Yes, the ImageWriter is made for that and prints bitmap graphics at 144 dpi in high quality mode. Third party printers like the Epson FX series work with a driver such as Orange Micro's Grappler. Output is rougher than a LaserWriter.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I clean my daisy wheel printer?
a: Remove the wheel and wipe the petals with a cotton swab dampened in alcohol. Also clean the platen and the carriage rail, with a light drop of oil on the rail if the manual says so. Keep the ribbon fresh, since a dirty one gives uneven print.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I fix jagged text from my ImageWriter?
a: Pick Best quality in the Print dialog, and use fonts sized at double the final size, like 24 point for 12 point text, which the ImageWriter prints at 144 dpi. Fonts such as New York and Geneva in 12 or 24 point look smoothest.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I get my Epson FX-80 to print in condensed mode from BASIC?
a: Send CHR$(15) with LPRINT before your text, like LPRINT CHR$(15);"hello". CHR$(18) turns condensed off again. You'll get about 17 characters per inch instead of 10.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I get my printer to print the full 80 columns on a Commodore 64?
a: Use a printer made for the Commodore serial bus like the MPS-801, or get an interface such as the Cardco G-Wiz to connect a normal Centronics printer. Then OPEN 4,4 and PRINT#4 as usual. A plain Epson won't work without the interface.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I make a PostScript file from my Mac application?
a: In System 6, hold Command-F while the Print dialog's OK button is clicked and the print starts, and a file called PostScript0 is created in the System Folder. Command-K gives you a file with the Mac's definitions. Use that to send to a service bureau.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I print a PostScript file to a printer from a Unix box?
a: Send it with lpr to a queue set up for the PostScript printer in /etc/printcap. The file has to begin with %! on the first line. If the printer is on a serial line, check the baud rate in the printcap entry matches the printer.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I print a screen dump on my IBM PC?
a: Press Shift-PrtSc and the PC sends the text screen to LPT1. For graphics screens on a CGA, run GRAPHICS.COM from DOS first, then use Shift-PrtSc. It works with IBM and Epson compatible printers.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I print in landscape on a LaserJet?
a: Send ESC & l 1 O to select landscape orientation, and use a landscape font from a cartridge or soft font set, since the fonts are bitmapped per orientation. Many programs like Lotus 1-2-3 have a setup string for that.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How do I set the top of form on my tractor feed printer?
a: Turn the printer off, line the perforation up with the tear bar, then power on. Most printers take the current paper position as top of form at that moment. Don't roll the platen knob while it's on or the registration will drift.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How fast is a typical laser printer compared to dot matrix?
a: An HP LaserJet II does 8 pages per minute at best, and a LaserWriter about the same. A 24-pin dot matrix in letter-quality mode might manage one page per two minutes. In draft mode the dot matrix can get 200 cps or so, about 2 or 3 ppm.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How long does a print head last on a dot matrix printer?
a: Typically around 100 to 200 million characters for good 9-pin heads, which is years for home use. Heads fail from overheating or broken pins, so avoid long solid black graphics. Replacement heads for an FX-80 cost around $50 to $80.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: How much memory does a laser printer need for a full page of graphics?
a: A full letter page at 300 dpi needs about one megabyte of printer RAM, since it's roughly 8.5 by 11 inches times 90000 dots per square inch. The original 512K LaserJet could only print a full-page graphic at 150 dpi. Add a memory board for 300.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Is a daisy wheel printer still worth buying over a 24-pin dot matrix?
a: If you only write letters and reports, a daisy wheel like the Diablo 630 or Juki 6100 still gives the sharpest text. But it's slow, noisy and can't do graphics or font changes without swapping wheels. For most people a 24-pin is the better buy.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Is it OK to refill laser toner cartridges?
a: Several shops will refill Canon SX cartridges for about half the price of a new one, and many people report good results. The risk is a leaky seal or worn drum, which can dirty the printer. HP doesn't recommend it, and it may affect your warranty.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Is the Apple LaserWriter IISC worth it over the IINT?
a: The IISC has a SCSI port and no PostScript or AppleTalk, so it works as a QuickDraw printer for one Mac at a time. It costs much less, around $2800. If you need PostScript or want to share it, get the IINT.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Is the HP DeskJet any good?
a: The DeskJet is a thermal inkjet that prints 300 dpi at about 2 pages per minute and costs a lot less than a laser at around $1000. The quality is close to laser on plain paper, but the ink can smear and run if it gets wet.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: My ImageWriter prints garbage when I connect it to a modem port, what's wrong?
a: Use the printer port, and make sure AppleTalk is turned off in the Chooser if you're printing straight to an ImageWriter. Check that the cable is a real ImageWriter cable with the right handshaking. Also make sure the printer is selected in the Chooser.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does 9-pin versus 24-pin mean on a dot matrix printer?
a: It's the number of wires in the print head. 9-pin machines like the Epson FX-80 look rough in text, while 24-pin ones like the LQ-500 or Panasonic KX-P1124 print denser dots and come close to letter quality. They cost more and run slower.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does LaserWriter mean for Mac users, and why is it so expensive?
a: The Apple LaserWriter is a 300 dpi laser printer based on the Canon engine, with a PostScript interpreter and its own 68000 CPU inside. That computer in the printer is a big part of the roughly $7000 price. You also get 35 built-in fonts.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does Linotronic mean and how does it relate to PostScript?
