a: The Linotronic 100 and 300 are typesetting machines from Linotype that use PostScript RIPs, with resolution up to 2540 dpi. You can send your PostScript file from your laser proof to a service bureau and get camera-ready film or paper.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does Postscript Level mean, and what is the difference with Type 1 and Type 3 fonts?
a: Type 1 fonts have hinting that keeps small text looking good at low resolution and are encrypted by Adobe, while Type 3 fonts have no hints, so they look worse at small sizes. Adobe has kept its Type 1 format private, but the Type 3 spec is open.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does cps mean in printer specs?
a: Characters per second. A Epson FX-85 is rated about 160 cps in draft mode, but that number is a best case at 10 cpi. Letter quality speed is far lower, typically 30 to 50 cps. A daisy wheel runs around 40 cps.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does dpi mean and does 300 dpi look good enough?
a: Dots per inch, the number of printed dots across one inch. 300 dpi is the standard for laser printers like the LaserJet and looks sharp for business documents. Typesetters run 1270 or 2540 dpi, which is noticeably crisper for fine print and photos.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does the DIP switch bank on the back of my printer do?
a: Those little switches set defaults like character set, form length, auto line feed, and slashed zero. Your manual has a table that lists each switch. Power the printer off when you change them, because many models only read them at power-up.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does the Fonts menu show for a LaserWriter, and what is Times, Helvetica, and Courier?
a: These are the built-in PostScript fonts. Times is a serif text face, Helvetica is a clean sans serif, and Courier is a typewriter look with each character the same width. The LaserWriter also has Symbol, Palatino, and a few others built in.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What does the SELECT button do versus ON LINE?
a: They're the same thing on different brands. It switches the printer between being ready for data from the computer and being offline, so you can use the form feed and line feed buttons. Press it again to go back online before printing.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is Adobe Type Manager?
a: It's a Macintosh utility for System 6 that draws smooth screen fonts and prints PostScript Type 1 fonts on non-PostScript printers like the ImageWriter. You install it in the System Folder, then add the outline fonts. Text looks much better at odd sizes.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is PCL?
a: Printer Command Language is HP's set of escape codes for the LaserJet and DeskJet. It handles fonts, margins and basic graphics, but it works with bitmapped or cartridge fonts rather than scalable outlines. Level 4 came with the LaserJet II.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is PostScript, in plain terms?
a: It's a programming language from Adobe that describes a page: text, lines, curves and images. The printer has an interpreter that turns that description into dots at whatever resolution it can manage. The same file looks good on a 300 dpi LaserWriter or a 2540 dpi Linotronic.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is a Centronics interface and why do I need a special cable?
a: It's the standard 36-pin parallel connector on most printers, with the PC end being a 25-pin D connector. You need a cable that matches, so buy a regular IBM printer cable. Keep it under about 10 feet or you may get garbage characters.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is a form feed and why does my printer eject a blank page?
a: A form feed is character 12 that tells the printer to advance to the top of the next page. Many programs send one at the end of a job. A blank sheet usually means your program sent an extra one or the page length setting is wrong.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is a print spooler and do I need one?
a: A spooler holds your print job in memory or on disk, then feeds it to the printer in the background so your computer is free to keep working. On a PC, the DOS PRINT command does this for text files. PrintMonitor does it on the Mac.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is a soft font?
a: It's a font file you download from disk to the printer's RAM before printing, which gives you more typefaces than the cartridges. Bitstream and Hewlett-Packard sell them for the LaserJet. Each size and orientation is a separate file, so they use a lot of disk space.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is an escape sequence and why do printers need them?
a: It's a string starting with the ESC character (decimal 27) followed by codes that tell the printer to change fonts, spacing, margins and so on. Epson's ESC/P set is the de facto standard for dot matrix. Your manual should list them in the back.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is the best way to print mailing labels with a dot matrix printer?
a: Buy continuous labels made for tractor feed and set the page length to match the label size, like 1 inch or 6 lines. Use a program such as PFS:File or a mail merge in WordStar. Tear them off carefully, and don't run them back through the machine.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is the difference between an HP LaserJet and a LaserWriter?
a: The LaserJet uses HP's PCL language and is mostly for PCs, with fonts in cartridges or downloaded. The LaserWriter uses PostScript and has scalable fonts. The LaserJet is cheaper and faster for plain text, but PostScript is better for graphics and layout.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What is the difference between draft and NLQ on my printer?
a: NLQ means near letter quality. The head makes two or more passes over each line and fills in the gaps between dots, so text looks cleaner but takes about a third as long. Use draft for proofs and NLQ for the final copy.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: What paper should I use in a laser printer?
a: Regular 20 lb copier paper works fine. Avoid cheap rough stock, glossy paper, and anything with a coating that melts in the fuser. Never run labels meant for dot matrix printers through it since the glue can melt and ruin the fuser.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Which is better for a printer connection, serial or parallel?
a: Parallel is easier and faster on a PC, and needs no setup. Serial lets you use longer cables, up to a few dozen feet at 9600 baud, but you have to match baud rate, parity and handshaking on both ends. Use parallel unless your printer is far from the computer.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Why does my laser printer leave a black streak down the page?
a: Most likely the toner cartridge is nearly empty or the drum is scratched. Take it out and shake it gently side to side to spread the toner. If the line stays, the cartridge is bad. Also check the corona wire for dirt.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Why does my printer print everything double spaced?
a: Your printer is adding a line feed after each carriage return and so is your software. Look for a DIP switch labeled auto line feed and turn it off. On an IBM PC you may also have a setting in the program itself.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Why does my ribbon wear out so fast and can I re-ink it?
a: Dot matrix ribbons are fabric loops that wear from the pins hammering them. You can re-ink them with a spray like Mac Inker or a ribbon re-inker kit, and it works fine a few times. Don't overdo it, since too much ink gums up the print head.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Why is my laser printer so much more than a dot matrix, if both just make dots?
a: A laser has a print engine with a drum, laser and fuser, a controller with memory and a CPU, and the toner. The result is crisp 300 dpi pages that dot matrix can't match. Prices have dropped, with the LaserJet IIP coming in around $1500.

topic: printers: dot matrix, daisy wheel, LaserWriter, PostScript
q: Why won't my printer work on the second parallel port, LPT2?
a: Check that your printer card or adapter is actually set as LPT2, since the port addresses 378h and 278h are set by jumpers. Then use the correct device name in DOS, like PRN or LPT2. Some programs only support LPT1.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Can I use a modem on a party line?
a: It can work, but if a neighbor picks up the phone during your call, you'll get dropped or see garbage. Noise on party lines also hurts at 2400. A private line is much better.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Can I use my 2400 baud modem at 9600 with software?
a: No, the speed is set by the modem hardware. No terminal program can make a 2400 bps modem go faster. Compression like MNP 5 can improve throughput on some files, but the line speed stays 2400.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Can I use my Macintosh with a Hayes compatible modem?
a: Yes, plug it into the modem port with a Mac modem cable, which is an 8 pin mini DIN to DB-25. Use a program like MicroPhone or Red Ryder. The AT commands are the same as on the PC.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Do I need a special phone line for a modem?
a: No, a regular voice line works fine. Just remember that someone picking up an extension will drop your call. Many people with a BBS or heavy usage get a second line installed so the family can still talk.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How do I connect my Commodore 64 to a modem?
a: The C64 needs a modem made for its user port, like the Commodore 1670 or 1660, or a RS-232 interface adapter for a standard modem. Most are 300 or 1200 baud. Use a terminal program like Novaterm.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How do I get my modem to redial a busy number?
a: Most terminal programs have a dialing directory with auto redial. You can also type ATDT then the number again, or use A/ to repeat the last command. Procomm and Telix can cycle through numbers until one answers.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How do I make my modem dial a number with the Hayes commands?
a: Type ATDT followed by the number for touch-tone, like ATDT5551212, then hit return. Use ATDP instead if you have a rotary line. You should get CONNECT when the other end answers.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How do I make the modem remember my settings?
a: Set what you want, then send AT&W to write it to non-volatile memory. On a Hayes 2400 or compatible, ATZ will restore them at power up. Older modems use DIP switches instead.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How do I run a BBS with my modem?
a: You need a modem set to auto-answer with ATS0=1, a dedicated phone line ideally, and BBS software like RBBS-PC, PCBoard or WWIV. Set the modem to reset itself when a caller hangs up so it's ready for the next call.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How do I set my modem to 8N1?
a: Set it in your terminal program, not the modem. 8N1 means 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, and it's what most BBSes and online services use. Some older systems want 7E1, so check what the other end uses.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How do I turn off call waiting when I'm using the modem?
a: In most areas you dial *70 before the number, like ATDT*70,5551212. The comma adds a pause. It only disables call waiting for that one call, and you should check with your phone company that your area supports it.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: How many bits per second can I really get from a 2400 baud modem?
a: About 240 characters per second at best, since each byte takes 10 bits on the line with start and stop bits. With protocol overhead you'll see roughly 200 to 230 cps on Zmodem.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Is Zmodem better than Xmodem?
a: Yes, by a good margin. Zmodem streams data without waiting for an acknowledgement on each block, uses a 32 bit CRC, and can resume after a dropped connection. Use it whenever the BBS offers it.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Is it worth upgrading from 1200 to 2400 baud?
a: Yes, if you spend much time online. 2400 modems are cheap now, often under $150, and halve your connect time and phone bill. Just make sure it's Hayes compatible and falls back to 1200 and 300.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What are the DIP switches on the back of my modem for?
a: They set things like DTR handling, result codes, echo, auto-answer and carrier detect. The manual has a table for them. On older Hayes style modems they define the power-up defaults.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What do the lights on my external modem mean?
a: On most Hayes style modems, CD is carrier detect, RD and SD show data received and sent, TR is terminal ready from your computer, and MR is modem ready. HS lights when you are at high speed, like 2400.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does ATH0 mean?
a: It tells the modem to hang up, going on-hook. If your software can't drop the line, you can type +++ first, wait a second for OK, then send ATH0.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does ATM0 do?
a: It turns the modem speaker off so you don't hear the dialing and handshake. ATM1 leaves it on until carrier is detected, and ATM2 keeps it on all the time. ATL sets the volume on many models.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does ATS0=1 do?
a: It sets register S0 to 1, which makes the modem auto-answer after one ring. That's what you want for running a BBS. ATS0=0 turns auto-answer off again.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does ATX4 mean?
a: It selects the extended result codes, including connect speed and busy and dial tone detection on Hayes 2400 compatibles. ATX0 gives only the basic codes. Many programs need X1 or higher to see CONNECT 2400.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does ATZ do?
a: It resets the modem to the settings stored in its memory, or the factory defaults on some models. Most terminal programs send it at startup so the modem is in a known state before dialing.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does CONNECT 1200/ARQ mean?
a: The modems connected at 1200 bps and are using an error correcting protocol, with ARQ meaning automatic repeat request. It means bad blocks get resent, so your file transfers will be cleaner.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does the S-register S7 do?
a: S7 is how many seconds the modem waits for carrier after dialing before giving up. The default is typically 30 seconds. On long distance calls with slow switching you may want to raise it to 45 or 60.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What does the comma do in a dial string?
a: A comma makes the modem pause, usually two seconds, set by register S8. It's handy for dialing 9 to get an outside line on an office phone system, like ATDT9,5551212.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is DTR and why does my modem hang up when I exit my program?
a: DTR is Data Terminal Ready, a line your computer raises to tell the modem it's in use. When the program quits, DTR drops and the modem hangs up if set to follow it with AT&D2. Use AT&D0 to ignore it.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is Kermit?
a: Kermit is a file transfer protocol and terminal program from Columbia University. It's slower than Zmodem but runs on almost anything, including mainframes and odd micros, and copes with 7 bit lines. It's free for universities.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is MNP and do I need it?
a: MNP is a set of error correction and compression protocols from Microcom. MNP 5 can roughly double throughput on text files. If you call other MNP modems, it saves you from line noise garbage, so it's nice to have.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is RTS/CTS flow control?
a: It's hardware handshaking using two wires on the serial cable. The modem drops CTS when its buffer is full so your computer stops sending. It's needed with error correcting modems at high speeds, where XON/XOFF can get lost.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is V.32?
a: It's the CCITT standard for 9600 bps full duplex over dial-up lines, using echo cancellation. Modems that support it are pricey, often over $1000, but they're getting cheaper. Only another V.32 modem will connect at that speed.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is Xmodem?
a: It's a file transfer protocol by Ward Christensen that sends 128 byte blocks with a checksum and resends bad ones. It's slow and chatty. Ymodem uses 1K blocks, and Zmodem is faster and can resume an interrupted transfer.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is a 16550 UART and do I need one?
a: The 16550 is a serial chip with a 16 byte buffer, replacing the 8250 and 16450. It helps if you run 9600 or higher, or multitask, since you won't drop characters. At 2400 under plain DOS you won't notice.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is a null modem cable?
a: It's a serial cable with the transmit and receive lines crossed so two computers can talk directly with no modems. You can buy one or wire a DB-25 cable with pins 2 and 3 swapped and pin 7 ground straight through.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the Hayes AT command set?
a: It's the command language Hayes introduced on the Smartmodem. Every command starts with AT for attention, like ATDT to dial or ATH to hang up. Nearly every modem maker copies it, which is why Hayes compatible is such a selling point.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the Hayes Smartmodem 1200?
a: It's the 1200 bps modem Hayes sold from 1982, with the AT command set built in. It set the standard that other makers copied. The Smartmodem 2400 followed later and works the same way.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the Telebit Trailblazer?
a: It's a high speed modem that uses PEP, a proprietary protocol with many carriers, to reach about 18,000 bps in one direction on good lines. It's popular on Usenet UUCP links. It only reaches that speed when talking to another Trailblazer.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the difference between Bell 212A and V.22bis?
a: Bell 212A is the American 1200 bps standard, while V.22bis is the CCITT standard for 2400 bps. Most 2400 modems in the US also talk 212A at 1200 and Bell 103 at 300 baud.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the difference between baud and bps?
a: Baud is signal changes per second, bps is bits per second. At 300 and 1200 baud-ish speeds they happen to be close, but a 2400 bps modem still runs at 600 baud, packing 4 bits into each signal change.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the difference between half duplex and full duplex?
a: In full duplex both sides can send at once, and echo comes back from the remote host. In half duplex you send or receive one at a time, and your own terminal echoes locally. If you see double characters, switch to full.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the difference between pulse and tone dialing in the modem?
a: Tone dialing uses the touch-tone frequencies and is faster, with ATDT. Pulse dialing, ATDP, clicks like a rotary phone and works on older exchanges. If tone doesn't work, your line may be pulse only.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What is the maximum cable length for an RS-232 serial cable?
a: The spec says about 50 feet at 19200 bps or less, though shorter cables are safer. Low speeds like 2400 often work fine at 100 feet or more with good shielded cable.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: What speed should I set my serial port to for a 2400 baud modem?
a: Set your computer to 2400 if the modem has no error correction or compression. With MNP 5 or V.42bis, lock the port at a higher rate such as 9600 or 19200 so the modem can use its compression without being throttled.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Which is better, an internal or external modem?
a: External is easier to move between machines and the blinking lights tell you what's going on, but it needs a serial port and a cable. Internal is cheaper and has its own UART, but you have to fiddle with IRQs and jumpers.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Which terminal program should I use on my IBM PC?
a: Procomm is popular and cheap as shareware, and Qmodem is also well liked. Telix is good too if you want scripts. All of them handle Xmodem, Ymodem and Zmodem transfers.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Why am I seeing each character I type twice?
a: Both your modem and the remote host are echoing. Turn off local echo in your terminal program or send ATE0 to the modem. If you see nothing at all, do the opposite and turn echo on.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Why can't my 2400 baud modem connect at 2400 on this line?
a: The line is probably too noisy or has poor quality, so the modems fall back to 1200. Try another call, make sure the phone cord is short and good, and move the modem away from monitors and power supplies.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Why do I have to wait before and after typing +++?
a: The Hayes escape sequence needs a pause of about one second on both sides of the three plus signs. That guard time keeps the modem from mistaking +++ in normal data for a command. Register S12 sets the delay.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Why do I see garbage characters when I connect?
a: Usually your terminal speed or parity doesn't match the remote system. Try 7E1 instead of 8N1, or change baud rate. Line noise can do it too, so hang up and redial to see if it clears.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Why does my modem dial but I don't hear anything?
a: Your speaker may be off, so try ATM1 first. If you still hear nothing, check the phone cord is plugged into the LINE jack and not PHONE. Also make sure your phone line works by plugging in a regular phone.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Why does my modem lock up my PC when I use COM3?
a: COM1 and COM3 usually share IRQ4, and COM2 and COM4 share IRQ3, so a mouse on COM1 can fight with a modem on COM3. Move the modem to COM2 or set the card to a free IRQ.

topic: modems, baud rates and Hayes AT commands
q: Why does my modem say NO CARRIER?
a: The modem lost or never found the other modem's carrier tone. Common causes are a wrong number, a noisy line, or the remote end hanging up. Try again, and check for call waiting clicking in on the line.

q: Can I call long distance BBSes without a huge phone bill?
a: Call in the evening or on weekends when rates drop, and use a compact service like PC Pursuit, which lets you call BBSes in many cities for about $30 a month, off-peak. A fast modem saves money too.

q: Can I run a BBS on a Mac?
a: Yes. Hypercard-based and dedicated programs such as Red Ryder Host, TeleFinder, and FirstClass are used. FirstClass has a nice graphical interface with a client program, and TeleFinder is easy to set up.

q: Can I use a BBS with a Commodore 64?
a: Yes. You need a modem like the Commodore 1670 or a Hayes-compatible with a user port adapter, plus a terminal program such as Novaterm. There are many C64 boards, most running at 300 or 1200 baud.

q: How can I tell whether a downloaded program has a virus?
a: Run a scanner such as McAfee's SCAN on it before running anything, and only trust files from boards that check uploads. Boot from a clean floppy and keep backups. Viruses like Stoned and Jerusalem are going around.

q: How do I find BBS phone numbers in my area?
a: Look for a local BBS list on the bigger boards, usually a file called something like BBSLIST.ZIP. User groups and computer stores often have printouts too. Computer Shopper and Boardwatch-type newsletters also list numbers.

q: How do I get started calling BBSes with my new modem?
a: You need a terminal program like Procomm, Telix, or Qmodem on a PC, or Red Ryder on a Mac. Set it to 8-N-1, dial a local board from a list, and register with your real name when asked. Start with local numbers to keep phone bills down.

q: How do I read my mail offline?
a: Use an offline reader. Download a QWK packet from a board running a QWK door, read and reply with a reader such as Qmail or SLMR, then upload your replies. It saves a lot of phone time.

q: How do I stop my phone line from clicking when I dial out?
a: Turn off the modem speaker with ATM0 or use ATL0 for lower volume. If it's call waiting, you need to add *70, on touch tone systems, in front of your dial string to disable it.

q: How much does it cost to run a BBS?
a: You need a dedicated phone line, about $15-30 a month, a modem, and a computer that stays on. A basic setup can be done with an old XT and a 2400 baud modem, and the software can be free or under $100.

q: Is Usenet the same as a BBS?
a: No. Usenet is a worldwide distributed set of newsgroups carried by Unix machines, mostly at universities and companies. Some BBSes have gateways that carry selected Usenet groups, but that is different from a stand-alone board.

q: Is a 2400 baud modem worth it over 1200?
a: Yes, if you do any downloading. A 2400 cuts file transfer times roughly in half, and prices have dropped to around $100-150 for Hayes-compatibles. Most boards now support 2400, though check that your local ones do.

q: Is it worth getting a second phone line for a BBS?
a: If you run a board, yes. Sharing a voice line means missed calls and angry family. A second residential line is cheap, and a dedicated line lets your board be up 24 hours.

q: Should I use ZIP or ARC for compressing files?
a: ZIP, from PKWARE, compresses better and is faster than ARC. Many boards now only take ZIP. Get PKZ110.EXE or the latest PKZIP from a good board and you can unpack both.

q: What BBS software should I run if I want to start my own board?
a: On a PC, look at PCBoard, Wildcat, RBBS-PC, or Opus for FidoNet. RBBS-PC is free, and PCBoard is commercial with lots of features. Try RBBS first if money is tight.

q: What are smileys like :-) for?
a: They show tone in text. Turn your head sideways and :-) is a smile. Use :-( for sad and ;-) for a wink. They help stop sarcasm from being read as an insult.

q: What are the best things to say in my first message on a board?
a: Say hello in the general area, mention what computer you have and what interests you. Keep it short, no ALL CAPS, and don't post the same message in many areas.

q: What does 'lurking' mean?
a: Reading messages without posting. It's a good idea when you join a new board or conference, so you learn the culture and avoid asking questions that were answered last week.

q: What does 8-N-1 mean?
a: It's 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. Nearly every BBS uses it these days. A few older or Unix-style systems want 7-E-1, so if you see garbage on connect, try switching.

q: What does 9600 baud cost now?
a: Prices have been dropping, but a 9600 bps modem, such as a US Robotics HST or a V.32 model, still often costs $500 to $1000. HST is common on boards, but it only talks to other HSTs at full speed.

q: What does ANSI mean on a BBS?
a: It means the board sends ANSI escape codes for color and cursor movement. Your terminal program has to emulate ANSI, and on a PC you may need ANSI.SYS loaded in CONFIG.SYS for it to work with some programs.

q: What does ARC mean on files I download?
a: ARC is an archive format from System Enhancement Associates that compresses one or more files into one. Use ARC or PKXARC to unpack them. PKZIP's .ZIP format is now replacing it on many boards.

q: What does the AT command set do?
a: It's the Hayes command set. You type AT followed by commands, such as ATDT5551212 to tone dial, ATH to hang up, or ATZ to reset. Most modems follow it and the manual has the S-registers.

q: What is FidoNet?
a: FidoNet is a network of BBSes running Fido software and compatibles that swap echomail and netmail overnight over phone lines. Messages hop between nodes, so you can talk to people across the world without a long distance call of your own.

q: What is MNP?
a: Microcom Networking Protocol is error correction built into some modems. Both ends must support it, and MNP 5 adds data compression. It makes transfers cleaner on noisy lines.

q: What is PC Pursuit?
a: A service from Telenet that gives you off-peak access to modems in dozens of cities for a flat monthly fee, around $25-30. You dial a local Telenet number, then connect through to the city you want.

q: What is a QWK packet?
a: A compressed bundle of new messages you download from a board in one go, designed by Mark Herring for the Searchlight-style readers. You read offline, write replies, and upload a REP packet on the next call.

q: What is a Telebit Trailblazer and why do sysops like it?
a: It's a high-speed modem using PEP, which gets up to about 18,000 bps on good lines when talking to another Trailblazer. Sysops of Usenet and FidoNet hubs like them for moving lots of mail fast.

q: What is a door on a BBS?
a: A door is an outside program the BBS runs for you, like a game, and then returns you to the board. Trade Wars and Legend of the Red Dragon style games are popular ones, though most are written in Turbo Pascal or C.

q: What is a flame war?
a: An argument that has dropped into personal insults, usually in public messages. The best response is to not reply, and sysops will often step in and lock the thread if it goes on.

q: What is a good init string for a 2400 baud modem?
a: Many Hayes-compatibles work fine with ATZ or AT&F, then ATM1 and ATS11=50 if needed. Check your manual, since commands differ between makers. Keep it simple and add things only if you have a problem.

q: What is a good terminal program for the Apple II?
a: ProTerm by Intrex is the popular one, with Z-Link and Applied Engineering's Data Link also in use. ProTerm handles Xmodem, Ymodem and Zmodem and works well with a Super Serial Card.

q: What is a node in a multi-line BBS?
a: Each phone line and modem on a multi-line board is a node. Systems like TBBS, Wildcat or Major BBS run several nodes at once so people can chat or play multiuser games online.

q: What is a pirate board?
a: A board that trades cracked commercial software, which is illegal copyright infringement. Sysops have been raided and equipment seized, so avoid them. Shareware and public domain files are the safe stuff.

q: What is a sysop?
a: The system operator, the person who owns and runs the board. They usually pay for the phone line and hardware out of pocket, so respect the rules and don't hog their line.

q: What is a trojan horse program?
a: It's a program that claims to do something useful but actually does damage, such as wiping your hard disk. Boards keep lists of known trojans, and the sysop will usually post warnings. Look for names flagged as bad before running anything new.

q: What is an upload/download ratio?
a: Many boards make you upload files in proportion to what you download, say 1 upload for every 10 downloads, to keep the file library growing. If you have nothing to upload, ask the sysop, as some will give credit for useful files.

q: What is shareware?
a: Software you can try free and copy to friends, but you are expected to pay the author if you keep using it. PC-Write, PC-File, and PKZIP are good examples, and registering often gets you a manual and updates.

q: What is the USR HST?
a: HST is U.S. Robotics' proprietary 9600 bps high speed technology, with a slow 300 or 450 bps back channel. Many sysops run HST because USR gave them a discount, so you will find many boards that support it.

q: What is the difference between a BBS and CompuServe?
a: CompuServe is a big commercial service charging hourly rates, often $6 to $12 an hour, with thousands of users. A BBS is usually a local hobbyist system that is free or cheap, but smaller and with fewer features.

q: What was the Great Renaming on Usenet?
a: In 1987 the Usenet groups were reorganized into the comp, sci, soc, rec, news, misc, and talk hierarchies from the old net.* names. Some boards that carry Usenet echoes still use odd names.

q: What's the difference between echomail and netmail?
a: Echomail is public conferences copied to every board that carries the area. Netmail is private, routed from one node to a specific person. Netmail can cost the sysop real long distance money, so be polite with it.

q: Where can I get a free ANSI terminal program?
a: Telix is shareware, and Qmodem has a shareware version too. For something free, grab the old public domain programs like Kermit or Pibterm from a local board's file area.

q: Which file transfer protocol is best, Xmodem, Ymodem or Zmodem?
a: Zmodem, if the board has it. It sends batches, resumes broken downloads, and is faster than Xmodem, which waits for an ack on every 128-byte block. Ymodem-G is quick too but needs an error-correcting modem since it can't retry.

q: Why do I get NO CARRIER right after connecting?
a: Usually a bad line or incompatible modem speeds or error control. Try a lower speed, disable MNP or V.42bis in your init string, and check for call waiting. A bad phone cord can also be the cause.

q: Why does my download keep failing with errors on Xmodem?
a: Probably line noise, which hits Xmodem's small blocks and checksum hard. Try Xmodem-CRC, or better Zmodem. Also turn off call waiting, which will wreck a transfer, by prefixing your dial string with *70 where available.

q: Why is ALL CAPS bad?
a: It reads as shouting and is hard to read. Use normal capitalization, and if you want to stress a word, put asterisks around it like *this*.

q: Why was I given only a little time on my first call?
a: Most boards limit new users to 30 or 60 minutes a day until the sysop validates you. Fill in your registration honestly and you will usually get upgraded access, with higher download limits, in a day or two.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Can I resume a broken Xmodem download?
a: Not with standard Xmodem. The only option is to start over. Zmodem is the one with real crash recovery, so ask your sysop to add it if the board doesn't have it.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Can I use Xmodem over a 9600 baud connection?
a: Sure, but it only gets a fraction of the speed because it waits for an ACK after every 128-byte block. On a long distance link the delay hurts even more. Zmodem or Ymodem-G would use that speed far better.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Can Kermit work over a 7-bit connection?
a: Yes, and that's one of its big strengths. It quotes the 8-bit characters with a prefix, so binary files survive a 7-bit link with parity. It's slower, but it works where Xmodem and Zmodem fail.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Does MacBinary matter for Xmodem transfers?
a: Yes. Mac files have a data fork and a resource fork, and MacBinary bundles them with the Finder info into one file. If you upload an application without it, the resource fork is lost and it won't run.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Does Xmodem work with 7-bit text files?
a: It works, but the padding in the last block is a Ctrl-Z, which most MS-DOS text tools treat as end of file anyway. On Unix you may need to strip the trailing junk. Binary files shouldn't care.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I download a file from a BBS with Xmodem?
a: Pick the file on the board and choose Xmodem when it asks. Then start the receive in your terminal program and give it a filename, since Xmodem doesn't send one. Most programs have a Receive File menu item.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I get back to my local Kermit from the remote one?
a: Type the escape character, usually Ctrl-] and then C. That returns you to the local Kermit prompt, where you give RECEIVE. After the transfer, type CONNECT to go back to the remote session.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I recover from a Zmodem transfer that hangs at the start?
a: Press Ctrl-X several times to cancel, then start again. Check that both sides use the same protocol and that flow control is set the same. Hardware flow control (RTS/CTS) is best if your modem and cable support it.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I send a file from my Unix box with Zmodem?
a: Get the rz/sz package, then type sz filename on the Unix side. Many terminal programs see the start sequence and begin receiving automatically. If yours doesn't, start a Zmodem receive by hand.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I send a whole bunch of files at once?
a: Use a batch protocol, either Ymodem or Zmodem. Mark the files on the BBS and they come down one after another with their names. With Xmodem you'd have to do every file by hand.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I speed up Kermit?
a: Try SET RECEIVE PACKET-LENGTH 1000 on both ends, and enable sliding windows if the versions support them. Also SET PREFIXING to cut escape overhead on a clean 8-bit line. MS-DOS Kermit 3.x handles this well.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I transfer a binary file with Kermit?
a: Type SET FILE TYPE BINARY on the sending and receiving side, or let newer versions detect it. Then SEND on one end and RECEIVE on the other. Without binary mode, text conversion can wreck the file.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How do I transfer files between a PC and a Unix machine with no modem?
a: Hook up a serial cable, run a terminal program on the PC, and use sz/rz or Kermit on the Unix side. Set the same baud rate and 8-N-1 on both. Kermit is a good choice if you lack rz and sz.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: How many retries does Xmodem do before giving up?
a: The usual limit is ten retries per block. After that the program cancels the transfer. Some programs let you change it. If you keep hitting the limit, the line is bad.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Is Kermit available for my Commodore 64 or Apple II?
a: Yes, Kermit has been ported to a huge list of machines, including the Apple II, Atari ST, Amiga and CP/M systems. Columbia's distribution has the sources, and many user groups carry disks.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Is Zmodem really better than Xmodem?
a: Yes, by a wide margin. Zmodem streams data with no per-block wait, uses a 32-bit CRC, sends filenames in batches, and can resume a broken transfer. On a noisy line it still beats Xmodem easily.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Is Zmodem safe over a packet network like Telenet or Tymnet?
a: Mostly yes, but the network may swallow some control characters like XON/XOFF. Zmodem can escape those with the -e option on sz. Otherwise you may hang on a PAD. Check what your PAD passes through.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Is it worth buying a terminal program just for Zmodem?
a: If you call BBSes much, yes. Procomm, Telix and Qmodem all do Zmodem, and some shareware options are cheap. The time you'll save on 1 MB downloads pays for it fast.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Should I turn off software compression when I use a compressing modem?
a: Don't send already compressed files like ZIP or ARC through modem compression, since it can't squeeze them and may even slow things down. Text compresses well, so let the modem do it there.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What are NAK and ACK in Xmodem?
a: ACK (ASCII 6) means the block was received correctly. NAK (ASCII 21) means it was bad and should be resent. The receiver starts the transfer by sending NAK, or the letter C in CRC mode.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What does Ctrl-X five times do during a transfer?
a: A string of Ctrl-X (CAN) characters aborts a Zmodem transfer. Eight in a row is the usual way to bail out. The receiving program watches for them, so you can kill a stuck session from the keyboard.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What does MNP have to do with file transfers?
a: MNP is error correction built into some modems, like those from Microcom. It makes the link look error-free, so streaming protocols like Ymodem-G work. It also can compress data, at levels 5 and up.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What does Ymodem mean, and how is it different from Xmodem?
a: Ymodem is Chuck Forsberg's extension of Xmodem using 1K blocks and CRC. The batch version sends a header block with the filename, size and date, so you can grab several files in one go without typing names.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What does ZRQINIT mean?
a: It's the Zmodem request-init frame the sender transmits to ask the receiver to start. If you see it, the receiver hasn't responded. Start your Zmodem receive, or check that the other end is really in Zmodem mode.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What does that string of **B00000000000000 mean on my screen?
a: That's a Zmodem header from the other end, asking to start a transfer. Your terminal program isn't set up to catch it automatically. Start a Zmodem receive from the menu, or use a program that auto-detects it.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What does the SET PARITY command do in Kermit?
a: It tells Kermit what parity the line uses so it can handle 8-bit data properly. With SET PARITY EVEN, for example, Kermit will use prefix quoting for the eighth bit. Use NONE when the line is clean 8-bit.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is DSZ?
a: DSZ is Chuck Forsberg's external protocol driver for MS-DOS, handling Xmodem, Ymodem and Zmodem. Many terminal programs and BBS packages call it, so you get the same dependable Zmodem everywhere. It's shareware.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is Xmodem and why does everybody use it?
a: Xmodem is Ward Christensen's 1977 protocol that sends data in 128-byte blocks, each with a block number and a checksum. The receiver ACKs good blocks and NAKs bad ones. It's simple, so nearly every terminal program supports it.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is Xmodem-1K?
a: It's Xmodem-CRC with 1024-byte blocks instead of 128. Fewer ACK waits means faster transfers on clean lines. Some people wrongly call it Ymodem, but real Ymodem adds batch support too.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is Ymodem-G?
a: Ymodem-G streams the blocks without waiting for an ACK on each one. It's very fast, but there's no retransmission, so one bad block aborts the transfer. Use it only over error-correcting modems like MNP or V.42.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is Zmodem crash recovery?
a: If a Zmodem download drops, you call back, start the same transfer, and it picks up where it stopped rather than from byte zero. The receiver needs to find the partial file. It saves hours on big files over 2400 baud.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is the best way to move files from a Mac to a PC over a null modem cable?
a: Run a terminal program on both, like Red Ryder on the Mac and Procomm on the PC. Connect with a null modem cable at 9600 or higher and use Zmodem or Xmodem. Mind the line endings on text files.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is the command to start receiving in C-Kermit?
a: At the C-Kermit prompt just type RECEIVE, and the file arrives under its original name. On the sending side you type SEND filename. If you're connected through a modem, you do the SEND from the remote Kermit and then escape back.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What is the difference between Xmodem and Xmodem-CRC?
a: Xmodem-CRC replaces the one-byte checksum with a 16-bit CRC, which catches many more errors. The receiver starts by sending 'C' instead of NAK. If the sender doesn't answer, good programs fall back to the checksum.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What settings do I need for binary file transfers?
a: Use 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. With 7 bits and parity, the high bit gets stripped and your binaries are ruined. Most protocols will fail outright if you're set to 7-E-1.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: What's the difference between Xmodem checksum and CRC in practice?
a: The checksum just adds up the bytes, so some errors cancel out and slip through. A 16-bit CRC catches nearly all burst errors. Use CRC whenever both ends support it, especially on noisy lines.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Where can I get C-Kermit or MS-DOS Kermit?
a: Anonymous ftp from cu20b.columbia.edu has the Kermit distribution, or you can order a tape or disks from Columbia University for a fee. Many BBSes and user groups also carry copies.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Which protocol should I use on a 2400 baud modem?
a: Zmodem if both sides have it. It's quick and recovers well. If not, Ymodem or Xmodem-1K on a good line, and Xmodem-CRC if the line is noisy. Kermit is the fallback for odd hosts.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Which terminal program for the PC supports the most protocols?
a: Telix and Procomm Plus both do Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem and Kermit, and Qmodem is similar. Most also take external protocol drivers like DSZ, which Forsberg's Omen Technology offers.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Who wrote Zmodem?
a: Chuck Forsberg of Omen Technology wrote it in 1986 under a Telenet contract. It's the same fellow who did Ymodem and the Professional-YAM terminal program. The rz and sz programs for Unix are his too.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why can't I get Zmodem to work through my Unix terminal server?
a: Terminal servers often eat control characters like Ctrl-S, Ctrl-Q, and sometimes strip the eighth bit. Try sz with -e to escape control characters, and check that the port is set to 8-bit transparent. If it still fails, use Kermit.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why do I see garbage on the screen while Zmodem is running?
a: That's just the data stream if your program isn't intercepting it, or a Zmodem sender that started while you weren't ready. If it keeps going, abort with Ctrl-X and start the receive in your terminal.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why does Xmodem make me type a filename when receiving?
a: Plain Xmodem sends only data blocks, with no header carrying the name or size. Your program has no idea what to call the file, so you have to supply one. Ymodem and Zmodem fix this by sending the name first.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why does my Xmodem transfer keep timing out?
a: Usually line noise, a mismatched protocol, or the sender not seeing your first NAK or C. Try Xmodem-CRC versus checksum, drop to a lower baud rate, and turn off call waiting. Also check that both ends use 8 bits, no parity.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why is Kermit so slow?
a: The default packet size is only 80 bytes and each packet waits for an ACK. It also quotes control characters, which adds overhead. Turning on long packets and sliding windows, if both ends support them, helps a lot.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why is Xmodem slower over Telenet than a direct call?
a: Every block waits for an ACK to cross the network and come back. Packet networks add delay, so you spend most of the time waiting. Zmodem doesn't wait, so it suffers much less.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why is my downloaded file a little bigger than the original?
a: Xmodem pads the last block to 128 bytes, usually with Ctrl-Z or nulls, since it doesn't send a length. Ymodem and Zmodem send the exact size, so no padding. It's usually harmless for archives like ARC or ZIP.

topic: file transfer: Xmodem, Ymodem, Zmodem, Kermit
q: Why is my file corrupted after a Kermit transfer?
a: Almost always text mode versus binary mode. In text mode Kermit converts line endings and can mangle executables or archives. Set FILE TYPE BINARY at both ends and send it again.

q: Can I get Usenet news over FidoNet?
a: Some gateways turn Usenet newsgroups into FidoNet echoes, and some also pass email between the two. Ask your net coordinator whether a gateway exists near you. The traffic is usually a trimmed set of groups.

q: Can I run FidoNet on an Amiga or Atari ST?
a: Yes. There's Fido-compatible software on both, such as Amiga ports of BinkleyTerm-style mailers and the Atari ST version of Fido. Selection is smaller than on the PC, but you can be a full node.

q: Can I run a FidoNet node on a Macintosh?
a: Yes, with Tabby, a Mac mailer, and a BBS such as Red Ryder Host or Hermes. They can send and receive FidoNet packets. Tabby is a popular choice for Mac nodes.

q: Can I send email from FidoNet to the Internet?
a: Only through a gateway node. Some, like 1:1/31 style gateways, route mail to Internet addresses, and often charge or require approval. Check the gateway list in your nodelist flags.

q: How do I become a point instead of a full node?
a: Ask a node that's willing to be your boss and they'll give you a point number such as 1:105/42.7. You run a mailer like Pointman or Binkley and call only that node. It's easier since you skip the nodelist and phone bills.

q: How do I get a FidoNet address for my BBS?
a: Find a local node or your net coordinator and ask for a node number. You'll need to run a compatible mailer, be reachable during national mail hour, and show up in the nodelist. Then you're a real node.

q: How do I request a file from another FidoNet system?
a: Send a file request, FREQ, from your mailer. You ask for a filename or a magic name like NODELIST, and the other system hands it over during the session. They have to have enabled requests.

q: How do I set up a FidoNet door game?
a: Doors run from your BBS using a drop file like DOOR.SYS or DORINFO1.DEF. Set the paths in the game's config, add a menu entry, and test locally first. Many games are shareware and ask for registration.

q: How do I start my own echo?
a: Talk to your net coordinator about a name and an area tag, then find a backbone or hub willing to carry it. Write a clear description and rules. It lives or dies by how many systems link up to it.

q: How does FidoNet routing work?
a: Mail goes from you to your hub, then to your net host, then to the region, and finally down to the destination net's host. Each level forwards it. You can also route direct if both agree.

q: How much will the phone bills cost me for a FidoNet node?
a: It depends on how far your hub is. A local hub costs nothing, but a long distance one at night rates may be a few dollars a month. Compressed packets and a fast modem help keep the bill small.

q: Is FidoNet better than a local BBS?
a: They aren't opposites. A local BBS gives you people nearby, while FidoNet connects your BBS to people everywhere and gives you far more conversations. Most sysops end up doing both.

q: Is FidoNet free to join?
a: There is no fee to join; the network is volunteer run. You pay for your phone calls and modem. Some nets ask for a small donation to cover long distance for the hub.

q: Is it worth running a FidoNet node on a 2400 baud modem?
a: Yes, for mail it's fine, since packets are compressed with ARC or ZIP and move fast. If you carry many echoes, 9600 helps a lot and cuts phone costs. A Hayes-compatible 2400 is what most nodes start with.

q: Should I use ZIP or ARC for my mail bundles?
a: ARC is the standard and everyone can unpack it. ZIP compresses a bit better and PKZIP is common now, so many nodes accept it. Check what your hub supports before you change anything.

q: What does 2:250/1 mean in a FidoNet address?
a: It's zone:net/node. Zone 2 is Europe, net 250 is a regional network, and node 1 is a system in it. Zones were added in 1988. North America is zone 1, and you may see a point number after a dot.

q: What does Crash mean on a netmail message?
a: Crash tells your mailer to call the destination directly instead of routing through your hub. It is faster but costs you a phone call, and the recipient has to accept crash mail. Don't abuse it, since some sysops get annoyed.

q: What does SEEN-BY mean on an echo message?
a: SEEN-BY lines are added to the bottom of echomail as it passes systems, listing which nodes already have it. Your tosser uses them so it won't send the message back. Don't edit them.

q: What does ZMH mean?
a: It means zone mail hour, the period each zone sets aside when nodes must accept FidoNet mail. Outside it, nodes can run normal BBS operations. In zone 1 it runs from 0900 to 1000 UTC.

q: What does the MO flag mean in the nodelist?
a: MO means mail only, so that system does not take BBS callers and is only there for mail. It is used for nodes that only exchange mail during the hours. Don't try to log in as a user.

q: What does the Pvt status mean in the nodelist?
a: Pvt means private. The phone number isn't published, and you have to get it from the sysop or your coordinator before you can call. Mail normally goes through the host instead.

q: What does the flag CM mean in the nodelist?
a: CM means continuous mail, so that node accepts mail 24 hours a day. Without it, a node only answers during mail hour. Check for CM before you try to crash a message at noon.

q: What is ARCmail?
a: It's FidoNet mail packets compressed with ARC, named by the day of the week extension, like .MO0 or .TU1. It cuts transfer time a lot. Your tosser unpacks them automatically if ARC is on your path.

q: What is EMSI?
a: EMSI is a handshake that lets two mailers swap information about themselves such as name, address, and supported protocols before transferring. It was proposed in 1990 to replace the older YooHoo handshake. Not every mailer has it yet.

q: What is FTS-0001?
a: It's the FidoNet technical standard describing the basic packet and message format, plus the mail transfer rules, all in one document. Systems that follow it can talk to each other. Other FTS documents cover nodelists and so on.

q: What is FidoNet Policy4?
a: It's the FidoNet policy document that came into use in 1989 and replaced older rules. It covers sysop conduct, echomail rules, and how disputes get handled. Every node is expected to read it.

q: What is Opus-CBCS?
a: Opus is a free-for-noncommercial-use BBS from Wynn Wagner that includes a mailer, so it was a favorite for FidoNet. It can handle echoes and netmail. Many nodes switched to Binkley plus a separate BBS for more flexibility.

q: What is YooHoo?
a: YooHoo is the handshake used in WaZOO sessions. The caller sends a YooHoo signal, the answerer replies with YooHoo info including its address and capabilities. After that both sides can move mail with the agreed protocol.

q: What is a Hold flag on a message?
a: Hold means the message waits at your system until the destination calls and picks it up. It's what you use for points, or when you can't afford the long distance call. Your mailer won't dial out for it.

q: What is a PATH line in echomail?
a: The PATH line records the nodes the message actually traveled through. Unlike SEEN-BY, it helps find out who is feeding loops or dupes. It starts to appear on newer software in 1988 or so.

q: What is a WaZOO session?
a: WaZOO is an FTS-0006 style mail session using Zmodem-like transfer to move mail packets and file requests in one go. It's faster than old XMODEM-based Bark. Binkley supports it, and so does FrontDoor.

q: What is a hub in a FidoNet net?
a: A hub collects mail from a group of nodes in a net and passes it to the host. It saves everyone phone calls by sitting at the middle. Hubs are chosen by the net coordinator.

q: What is a magic filename?
a: It's an alias a system sets up for a file request, such as NODELIST or FILES. The sysop maps the name to the real file. It saves the trouble of knowing the exact filename.

q: What is a network coordinator?
a: The NC is the person who keeps the nodelist segment for your net and is the mail hub for the net's nodes. They add and remove nodes, and route mail between your net and the region. It's a volunteer job.

q: What is a nodediff?
a: It's the weekly update file that lists just the changes since the last full nodelist. It's much smaller to download than the whole list. You apply it with a tool like the one that comes with most mailers.

q: What is a nodelist and where do I get it?
a: It's the weekly list of every FidoNet system with its number, name, phone number and flags. It goes out Fridays as NODELIST.nnn, where nnn is the day of the year. Grab it from your host or via file request, then compile it with your mailer's tool.

q: What is a scanner in FidoNet software?
a: A scanner looks through your message base for new echomail and netmail you wrote, then packs those messages for sending to your hub. It usually runs together with the tosser. Run it before each mail call or the outbound stuff just sits.

q: What is a sysop's responsibility on FidoNet?
a: A sysop must keep the system up for mail hour, pass on mail they route, and watch what goes through their system. They are also responsible for their users' posts. Read Policy and follow your coordinator.

q: What is a tosser?
a: It's a program that takes incoming mail packets and sorts the messages into your message base, and also bundles outgoing messages for your uplinks. Examples are Tick-style tools, Opus's Squish, and the old Fido's own. It's the middle piece between mailer and BBS.

q: What is an echo and how is it different from netmail?
a: Netmail is private mail from one node to another. An echo is a public conference, like a newsgroup, where messages get copied to every system carrying it. Echomail is moved around by a tosser like Opus or Squish-style tools.

q: What is an echomail moderator?
a: The moderator runs the conference, sets the topics and the rules, and can ask the hub to cut off someone who breaks them. In most echoes it is the one who started it. Read the rules file first.

q: What is national mail hour?
a: It's the time every FidoNet system in North America must be up for mail, 0900 to 1000 UTC, which is 4 to 5 AM Eastern. Zone mail hour differs in other zones. If you're a node, your BBS must take calls then and nothing else.

q: What is the best way to avoid dupes in echomail?
a: Run a dupe checker in your tosser, which keeps a list of message IDs it saw. Also get your feed set up properly so you don't get the same echo from two links. Loops are the usual cause.

q: What is the difference between XMODEM and YMODEM and Zmodem for mail transfers?
a: XMODEM sends 128 byte blocks and waits for each ACK, so it's slow. YMODEM sends 1K blocks, and Zmodem streams data and can resume after a break. For a FidoNet link, Zmodem or Bark and WaZoo-style handling is the best bet.

q: What is the difference between a region and a zone?
a: A zone is a big geographic area such as North America, and it contains several regions. A region is a group of nets, usually a state or part of one. Regions have a regional coordinator.

q: Which BBS software works with FidoNet?
a: Fido itself, Opus-CBCS, TBBS with a FidoNet door, PCBoard with add-ons, Wildcat, and RBBS-PC all work. Opus was designed with FidoNet in mind. Pick based on the features you want rather than only the network support.

q: Which mailer should I use, BinkleyTerm or FrontDoor?
a: BinkleyTerm is the most widely used and it's free in source form, so it's what most people run. FrontDoor is newer and more polished but costs shareware money. If you're just starting, go with Binkley and a good config file.

q: Why does my mailer keep getting BUSY from my hub?
a: Many nodes call the hub in the same minutes after mail hour starts. Set your mailer to retry a few times with random delays, and try an off-peak time that the hub allows. It's normal congestion.

q: Why does my netmail take a week to arrive?
a: Mail is stored and forwarded through hubs and hosts, and each hop waits for the nightly call. A message crossing several nets can take days. If anyone is down or short on cash, it stalls further.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Can I cancel an article I posted by mistake?
a: Yes, in rn press C at the article to issue a cancel control message. It only works for your own articles, and sites that already read it won't care. Do it quickly.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Can I get news on a 1200 baud modem?
a: You can, but reading interactively is painful, and a full feed won't fit. Use a few groups, and keep headers short with rn's options. A 2400 baud modem is a much better minimum.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Can I read Usenet on my PC at home?
a: Yes. Set up a UUCP package like UUPC or Waffle on MS-DOS, dial a nearby site, and get your news batched down by modem. It's slow at 2400 baud, so subscribe to only a few groups.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How do I find a particular post I read last week?
a: If it hasn't expired, use rn's ^Ng pattern search with a subject or the g command with a regular expression. Otherwise, ask the group or look for archives at a site such as uunet via FTP.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How do I get a copy of a program mentioned in a group?
a: Ask where it's archived. Many sites offer anonymous FTP, such as uunet.uu.net or wuarchive. Without FTP, ask the poster or use an archive server by mail and request it.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How do I mark everything in a group as read in rn?
a: Press c at the article prompt to catch up the group. rn asks you to confirm. At the newsgroup prompt you can type c too, which saves you from reading dull stuff you don't care about.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How do I post my first article to a newsgroup?
a: Read the group with rn, then press f to followup or run Pnews or inews-based posting from the shell to start a new thread. Fill in Newsgroups and Subject, write your text in the editor, save, and answer s to send. Try misc.test first.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How do I start a new newsgroup?
a: Follow the guidelines posted in news.announce.newgroups: propose it in news.groups, discuss for about a month, then call for votes. You need at least 100 more yes votes than no votes, and a two-thirds majority.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How do I unpack a shar file?
a: Save each part, strip the header lines before the #!/bin/sh line, and run sh on the file. For multipart archives, do them in order. Then read the README and run make.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How do I unsubscribe from a group in rn?
a: At the newsgroup prompt for that group press u. It changes the colon to an exclamation point in your .newsrc. To resubscribe, use a g followed by the group name.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How long does it take for a posting to reach everyone?
a: Depends on the feeds. Sites on the backbone using UUCP and dial-up may take a day or two. Sites on NNTP over Internet links can see it in minutes. Don't repost just because you can't see it yet.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: How much disk space does Usenet need?
a: A full feed in 1990 runs around 10 to 20 MB a day, so a two-week expire needs hundreds of megabytes. Small sites subscribe to a subset and expire quickly. Check your spool in /usr/spool/news.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Is it OK to post from my work account?
a: Check your employer's policy. Your posts carry your site name, and many people add a disclaimer saying opinions are their own. Remember that your boss can read what you say, and so can everyone else.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Is it OK to post my for-sale ad to all the groups?
a: No. Post once in misc.forsale or a local for-sale group. Posting everywhere wastes the network's bandwidth, which others pay for, and you will get angry mail.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Is it worth switching from rn to trn?
a: If you read busy groups, yes. trn, a threaded rn by Wayne Davison, shows the thread tree and lets you follow discussions. It's still rn at heart, so your commands and killfiles mostly carry over.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Is there a newsreader for the Mac?
a: Yes, with a UUCP or NNTP link you can use programs like Netnews on the Mac or ones in Unix-to-Mac setups. Most people on a Mac still telnet into a Unix host and run rn there.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Should I reply by mail or post a followup?
a: If your answer only helps the one person, mail it. If it's of general interest, or corrects something, post. Many people ask a question and get ten identical answers because everyone assumed nobody else would reply.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What are comp.sources groups?
a: They carry source code posted in parts called shars, for programs like games, utilities and libraries. comp.sources.unix, .misc, .games and .x are moderated. Save the parts and unpack with sh or unshar.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What are the big seven newsgroup hierarchies?
a: They are comp, misc, news, rec, sci, soc, and talk. Before the 1987 renaming, you had net.* groups like net.micro and net.games. The Great Renaming moved things into these categories.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does IMHO mean?
a: In My Humble Opinion. Others you'll see are BTW for by the way, FWIW for for what it's worth, and ROTFL for rolling on the floor laughing. Use them sparingly, and smileys such as :-) help show tone.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does RTFM mean?
a: Read The F-ing Manual. It's what you get told if you ask something clearly answered in the man page. Try man first, and if you still don't get it, say what you tried when you ask.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does expire do?
a: The expire program deletes old articles from the spool, usually run nightly from cron. Set the expire time in the history or explist file. Many sites keep articles for one to two weeks.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does the Followup-To header do?
a: It tells the posting software where replies should go, so a cross-posted thread can be steered to one group. Set it to poster if you want replies sent by mail only.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does the Path line in the header show?
a: It lists the machines that the article passed through, newest first, in bang-path form. Sites use it to avoid sending the article back to a machine that has already seen it.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does the alt hierarchy mean?
a: alt is the alternative hierarchy, started in 1987 or so by people who wanted groups without the backbone approval process. Anyone can create a group there, so you get everything from alt.sex to alt.fan.dave-barry. Not every site carries it.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does the line count in the header mean?
a: The Lines header shows how many lines are in the body of the article. It helps you judge whether it's worth the time on a slow terminal or modem. Very long postings are common in comp.sources.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What does the n do in rn?
a: At a group prompt, n skips to the next newsgroup with unread articles. Inside an article, n goes to the next unread article. Press q to quit the group, and the = key lists subjects.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is C News compared to B News?
a: B News was the older software, and it got slow with high volume. C News, written by Geoff Collyer and Henry Spencer at Toronto, is much faster at batching and expiring. Many sites switched around 1989.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is NNTP?
a: The Network News Transfer Protocol, defined in RFC 977 in 1986. It lets machines exchange articles over TCP/IP and lets a newsreader on one host fetch from a news server on another. It beats batching over UUCP.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is a FAQ and why do people keep telling me to read it?
a: FAQ means Frequently Asked Questions list. Regulars get tired of answering the same beginner question weekly, so someone compiles answers and posts them periodically. Check news.announce.newusers and the group itself before you ask.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is a bang path?
a: It's a UUCP address written as hosts separated by exclamation points, like uunet!decwrl!mysite!joe. Mail is forwarded host by host along the route. You need to know a path from your machine to theirs.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is a killfile and how do I use it?
a: A killfile is a per-group list of patterns rn uses to skip articles automatically. Press k in a thread to kill that subject, or use Ctrl-K to edit the file by hand. It saves lots of time in noisy groups.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is a moderated newsgroup?
a: It's a group where postings go to a moderator first, who approves or rejects them. Your article is mailed to the moderator automatically. comp.risks and comp.sources.unix are examples.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is a smiley and what does :-) mean?
a: Turn your head sideways: :-) is a smiling face, used to show that a remark is a joke. :-( is a frown and ;-) a wink. Sarcasm gets misread in plain text, so it helps.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is crossposting?
a: It's one article with several groups on the Newsgroups line, separated by commas. Readers see it once, in whichever group they read first. Keep it to a few related groups and set Followup-To.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is misc.test for?
a: It's the place to test your posting setup. Post a short message there and many sites will auto-reply, so you learn whether your article is propagating. Don't test in real discussion groups.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is rot13?
a: It's a simple letter-swap that shifts each letter 13 places. Posters use it to hide spoilers or offensive jokes, so only readers who choose to decode will see them. In rn, press Ctrl-X to decode the article.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is the .newsrc file?
a: It's in your home directory and lists each newsgroup with a colon if subscribed or an exclamation point if not, followed by ranges of read article numbers. rn updates it. Don't edit while rn runs.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is the Internet and how does Usenet relate to it?
a: The Internet is a network of networks running TCP/IP. Usenet is not a network but a set of machines exchanging news over UUCP, NNTP, and other links. Many Usenet sites aren't on the Internet at all.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is the Message-ID?
a: It's a unique identifier like <1234@host.edu>, generated when an article is posted. News software uses it to spot duplicates, and the References line uses it to link followups to originals.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is the difference between rn and readnews?
a: readnews is the older, simple reader that goes through articles one by one in order. rn, written by Larry Wall, is newsgroup-oriented with threading by subject, killfiles and pattern searches. Most people prefer rn.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: What is uuencode used for?
a: It turns a binary file into printable text so it can travel through news and mail. Use uuencode file file > file.uu to encode, and uudecode on the receiving side. Big files get split into several articles.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Where can I find the rules and guidelines for new users?
a: Look in news.announce.newusers. It carries regular postings like A Primer on How to Work with the Usenet Community and Rules for Posting to Usenet. Read them before your first post.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Why are there lines of garbage in a binary posting?
a: Those are uuencoded data. Save all the parts, concatenate them in order after removing the headers, and run uudecode. The first line says begin 644 filename.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Why do people put a signature in their posts?
a: The .signature file in your home directory is appended to posted articles with name, address and affiliation. Keep it to four lines at most. Long banners and drawings annoy people who pay for the transmission.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Why does my article show up twice on some systems?
a: Usually a message-ID problem or a loop between sites with a bad feed setup. Duplicates also appear if you post again because the first seemed not to appear. Articles can take hours or days to propagate, so be patient.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Why does rn say Unread news in a group but shows nothing?
a: Articles may have expired or been cancelled after the count was made. Your .newsrc just has a stale range. Press c to catch up and move on.

topic: Usenet itself: newsgroups, posting, newsreaders like rn
q: Why won't my reply by mail get to the poster?
a: The From or Reply-To address in the header may be a UUCP path that doesn't work from your site. Check the Path line and try a bang-path through a well-known site like uunet or decvax. Mapping data in comp.mail.maps helps.

q: Can I post a copy of a commercial program to the net?
a: No. Posting copyrighted software is piracy and you could get your site in trouble. Freeware and shareware are fine in the comp.sources groups or comp.binaries.ibm.pc, with the author's permission.

q: Can I post a message asking for money to make a get-rich-quick plan work?
a: Don't. Chain letters like the MAKE.MONEY.FAST ones are against the rules at nearly every site, and they get posters angry mail sent to their system administrators. People have lost their accounts over them.

q: Do I have to answer every flame aimed at me?
a: No. Not answering is often the strongest response. Readers can see who is being unreasonable, and most will think better of you for staying calm.

q: How do I cancel an article I posted by mistake?
a: On most systems, run the cancel command or use the cancel option in rn or readnews. It only works for your own articles, and it may not reach every site, so think before you post.

q: How do I create a new newsgroup?
a: Don't just make one. Post a proposal to news.announce.newgroups and news.groups, hold the discussion, then take a vote of about 21 days. You need at least 100 more yes votes than no votes, with two thirds yes.

q: How do I deal with someone who keeps sending me nasty mail?
a: Don't answer. If it goes on, send a short note to their system administrator at postmaster@their.site with copies of the messages. Most sites take harassment seriously.

q: How do I post my first article to a newsgroup without embarrassing myself?
a: Read the group for a couple of weeks first to see what's on topic. Pick a clear Subject line, keep your lines under 72 characters, and test in misc.test before posting for real.

q: How long should I wait before posting a follow-up to my own question?
a: Give it at least a few days, given how slowly news can spread. If you still have no answer, repost with more detail, and try a more specific group. Don't post a 'bump' the next morning.

q: How much of the original article should I quote when I reply?
a: Only enough to remind readers what you're answering, a few lines at most. Cut the signature and everything else. Quoting a whole 200-line article to add one line of reply wastes other people's phone bills.

q: How should I ask for help with a computer problem?
a: Tell people your machine, operating system version, the exact error message, and what you already tried. 'It doesn't work' gets no answers, but a short precise description often gets one in a day.

q: Is it okay to post a flame if someone really deserves it?
a: You may feel better, but you'll rarely change their mind, and the whole group has to read it. If you must write it, save it as a draft, sleep on it, and then probably delete it.

q: Is it okay to type in all capital letters?
a: No, it reads as shouting and people find it hard to read. Use normal upper and lower case. If you want to stress one word, put asterisks around it like *this*.

q: Is it rude to post a message asking people to e-mail me their answers?
a: It can be fine if you promise to post a summary later. That keeps the group from filling up with the same answers, and everyone gets the results. Do actually post the summary.

q: Is it rude to post a question that isn't about the group's topic?
a: Yes, it is. Check the group's name and charter first. If you aren't sure where to go, news.groups or a general group like misc.misc is better than guessing and annoying a technical group.

q: Is it worth reading news.groups and news.admin?
