a: If you plan to run a site or propose a group, yes. They cover how the net is run. Be warned they're also where some of the longest and most heated arguments on Usenet happen.

q: Is it worth replying to someone who flamed me in public?
a: Usually not. A calm one-line correction is fine if there's a real mistake. Otherwise wait a day before answering, because what you write angry always looks worse the next morning.

q: Should I correct someone's spelling in a public post?
a: Generally no. Spelling flames are a pet peeve of many readers and add nothing to the discussion. Many people are posting from slow terminals or in a second language.

q: Should I reply to the group or send mail to the person?
a: If your answer only helps the one person, send mail. If others would gain from it, post a followup. Plenty of people have posted the same answer an hour apart because nobody checked.

q: Should I use my real name when posting?
a: Most regulars do, and it makes people take you more seriously. Anonymous posting is possible through servers like anon.penet.fi, but it's frowned on in technical groups and fine in support groups where privacy matters.

q: What are the rules about advertising on the net?
a: Commercial ads in most groups are unwelcome, and on the Internet the NSFNET acceptable use policy forbids commercial traffic on its backbone. A brief note about a product, if it answers a question, is usually tolerated.

q: What does ':-)' mean at the end of a rude-sounding sentence?
a: It says the writer is joking. Without it, sarcasm is easy to miss and people take offense. It doesn't excuse a real insult, though.

q: What does 'BTW' mean?
a: By The Way. It marks a side comment that isn't the main point. Along with IMHO and FWIW, it's among the most common abbreviations in postings.

q: What does 'Followup-To' do in the header?
a: It tells the news software where replies should go. If a thread is drifting off topic you can set Followup-To: poster to push replies to mail, or name a better group to move the talk.

q: What does 'Spoiler' mean and do I need to warn people?
a: A spoiler gives away a plot twist in a movie, book or show. Put a warning in the Subject line and a few blank lines before the details, so people who haven't seen it can skip it.

q: What does 'Usenet is not the Internet' mean?
a: Usenet is a set of news groups carried over many networks, including UUCP dial-up links, BITNET gateways and the Internet. Many Usenet readers have no Internet access at all.

q: What does 'flame on' and 'flame off' mean?
a: Writers use <flame on> before a heated rant and <flame off> after, to show they know they're being intense. It warns the reader and lets you vent without people thinking you've gone off the deep end.

q: What does 'net.god' mean?
a: It's a half-joking name for a long-time user whose opinion carries weight, often someone who helped build the net. Respect them for their experience, but remember they can be wrong too.

q: What does 'on topic' mean?
a: It means what you post fits the subject of the group. A question about Amiga games doesn't belong in comp.sys.mac. Off-topic posts start arguments about where the discussion should go.

q: What does FAQ mean and why do people keep telling me to read it?
a: FAQ means Frequently Asked Questions. Most groups post a list of them every month or so, and reading it before you post saves everyone from answering the same question for the hundredth time. Check news.announce.newusers too.

q: What does IMHO stand for?
a: In My Humble Opinion. People put it in front of a statement to say it's their view and not a fact. It can soften a post a bit, which helps in a touchy argument.

q: What does ROTFL mean?
a: Rolling On The Floor Laughing. It's a reaction to something funny. Use it sparingly, since a post that is nothing but ROTFL adds nothing for the readers.

q: What does it mean when someone says 'Please take this to email'?
a: They think the argument is of no interest to the rest of the group. Move it to private mail and keep the newsgroup for the topic it's meant for.

q: What is 'Godwin's Law'?
a: Mike Godwin noted that as a Usenet thread grows longer, the chance of someone being compared to Hitler or the Nazis goes toward one. It usually means the discussion is over and the person who said it has lost the argument.

q: What is a .sig file?
a: It's a file called .signature in your home directory on Unix. The news software adds it to the end of each article you post. Keep it to your name, site and maybe a short quote.

q: What is a kill file and should I use one?
a: It's a file for rn that hides articles by a chosen author or subject. It's a good way to avoid someone who keeps starting fights. Use it instead of replying, and it saves your temper.

q: What is a smiley and how do I make one?
a: It's a sideways face made from punctuation. A colon, a dash and a close paren, :-), means you're joking, and :-( means unhappy. Use it when sarcasm could be taken the wrong way, since text has no tone of voice.

q: What is the 'Backbone Cabal' and does it control Usenet?
a: It was a loose group of administrators of the big backbone sites who handled group creation and news routing. Nobody owns Usenet, but those sites carried a lot of news, so their decisions had a lot of weight.

q: What is the Great Renaming?
a: In 1986 and 1987 the old net.* groups were reorganized into the comp, sci, rec, soc, talk, news and misc hierarchies. It made groups easier to find and gave the backbone sites a way to manage the load.

q: What is the difference between a flame and a criticism?
a: Criticism goes after the idea or the facts. A flame goes after the person. Saying your code has a bug is criticism, saying you're an idiot for writing it is a flame.

q: What is the single best piece of netiquette advice for a newcomer?
a: Lurk before you post. Spend a few weeks reading a group, learning its tone and its FAQ, and remember there's a real person reading each word you write. Treat them the way you'd like to be treated.

q: Why do people complain about long signatures?
a: Every line you add gets sent to thousands of machines, often over slow dial-up links that cost money per minute. The usual rule is four lines at most. Big ASCII art in a .sig will get you flamed.

q: Why do people use <grin> or <sigh> in text?
a: They stand in for facial expressions, which you can't see online. Putting <grin> after a barb shows you're not angry. They work like the smiley, so use whichever feels natural.

q: Why do some people put their replies below the quoted text and not above?
a: Because it reads like a conversation. Readers see the question first and your answer right after it. Trim the quote so each reply sits next to the part it answers.

q: Why does everyone hate it when I post test messages to a regular group?
a: A test post travels to thousands of sites and clutters the group. Use misc.test or a local test group such as ucb.test instead. Some sites in misc.test even send back an automatic reply.

q: Why does everyone say not to feed the trolls?
a: A troll posts bait on purpose to get a rise out of people. If you answer, you give them what they want and the thread grows. Ignore them and they usually move on.

q: Why does my posting take days to show up at other sites?
a: Many sites pass news along by UUCP over nightly phone calls, so each hop can add hours. Don't repost because you think it vanished, as you'll just make duplicates when the first one finally arrives.

q: Why was my article rejected as cross-posted too widely?
a: Posting one article to many groups at once annoys readers who see it in each. Pick the one or two groups that fit best. Use the Newsgroups line with commas and a Followup-To to keep replies in one place.

q: Can I run UUCP on an IBM PC?
a: Yes, there are ports such as Waffle, UUPC, and Xenix or Minix-based UUCP. UUPC is free and handles mail and news by dial-up. A 286 with a 2400 baud modem and a hard disk works fine.

q: Can I use a percent sign in an address?
a: Yes, the % hack is used for relaying, as in user%host2@host1. Host1 receives the mail, converts the % to @, and forwards to host2. Many gateways accept it, but some mailers refuse it.

q: How can I reach someone on the Internet from a UUCP-only site?
a: Route through a site with a gateway, like uunet!user@host.domain or ucbvax!host.domain!user. Many sites also run a smart mailer that accepts user@domain if they've set up a default route.

q: How can I tell how a message got to me?
a: Look at the Received: lines in the full headers, which show each machine and time stamp from the bottom up. On older UUCP mail, the From_ and >From lines show the path in reverse.

q: How do I check whether my UUCP jobs are stuck?
a: Run uustat -a to see queued jobs, and look in /usr/spool/uucp for C. and D. files that are piling up. Then check the LOGFILE and ERRLOG, and try a manual call with uucico -r1 -x9 -s sitename.

q: How do I compress news batches to save on phone time?
a: Use compress with 12 or 16 bit LZW, as in the compressed batch from csendbatch, which makes text about a third of its size. Both ends need the same version, and the receiving site runs cunbatch.

q: How do I find someone's email address?
a: There is no universal directory. Try the From line of their news postings, ask them by phone, or try the whois server at nic.ddn.mil for Internet folks. Usenet-addresses at mit-eddie also collects posters' addresses.

q: How do I get a copy of a file from a remote UUCP site?
a: Use uucp remotehost!/usr/spool/uucppublic/file /tmp. The remote side normally allows only the public directory, so ask the sysadmin to put the file there. Write ~ for uucppublic, as in remotehost!~/file.

q: How do I get a news feed?
a: Ask the admin of a site near you that carries news, ideally within your local calling area, and offer to pay for the phone costs. Posting a request to news.admin or a regional group can find you a feed.

q: How do I get my site on the UUCP map?
a: Write a map entry in the standard format with your site name, contact, phone, and links, then mail it to the regional map coordinator. The pathalias program will then include you in everyone's routing databases.

q: How do I send a binary file through mail?
a: Run it through uuencode first, which turns the binary into printable text, then mail that. The recipient saves the message and runs uudecode. Compress with compress first to save phone time.

q: How do I send mail to CompuServe from Usenet?
a: Use the user ID with a period instead of a comma, at compuserve.com, as in 71234.567@compuserve.com. The comma in the number confuses mailers, so the gateway wants the period. Check which gateway your site uses.

q: How do I send mail to someone on a UUCP site I've never heard of?
a: Find a well-known site you already talk to, then add the path from there, like ihnp4!bigsite!user. Check the UUCP maps posted in comp.mail.maps to find who connects to whom.

q: How do I set up an alias for a long bang path?
a: In Berkeley Mail, put a line in your .mailrc such as: alias joe decvax!harpo!bigsite!joe. Then just type mail joe. Sendmail users can also use the system aliases file, which needs newaliases afterward.

q: How much does a UUCP link cost?
a: The cost is mostly the phone bill: a 2400 baud call moves about 15 to 20K per minute, so a daily news feed of several megabytes adds up. A local number is best. UUNET also charges a modest fee.

q: Is Usenet the same thing as UUCP?
a: No. Usenet is the collection of newsgroups and the people who read them, while UUCP is one means of moving the articles around. News also travels by NNTP over the Internet and by other links.

q: Is it safe to leave uucp with no password?
a: No. Anyone who dials your modem can log in as uucp and read or send files. Always set a password, restrict commands in USERFILE and L.cmds, and keep uucp's shell set to uucico.

q: Is it worth getting a 2400 baud modem for UUCP?
a: Yes, if you move much news or mail. 2400 costs little more than 1200 and cuts phone time by half. If your neighbor site supports it, a Telebit Trailblazer with the g-spoof trick is faster still, but costly.

q: Should I use a domain name or a bang path in my signature?
a: Give both if you can. A domain address is more stable, but if your site only has UUCP, post a path starting from a well-known backbone site so people can reach you without guessing.

q: What does 'host unknown' mean?
a: Your mailer can't find the site name in its routing tables or in DNS. Check the spelling, try the full domain name, or route it through a gateway that knows it better, such as uunet.

q: What does MAILER-DAEMON mean in a bounce message?
a: It's your mail system reporting that it could not deliver your message. Read the body of the bounce, which usually says whether the host was unknown, the user was unknown, or the retries timed out.

q: What does Reply-To do?
a: It tells mail programs where replies should go, in place of the From address. It's useful when your From line is a poor route back, but it's easy to set wrong, so test it by mailing yourself.

q: What does rmail do?
a: rmail is the program that receives mail arriving by UUCP. It checks the From lines, adds the path information, and hands the message to the local mail delivery program for the recipient.

q: What does the ! in an address mean?
a: It separates hops in a UUCP route. Read left to right: the first machine is one you call directly, and each following machine is where that one forwards the message. The last name is the user.

q: What does the at sign mean in Internet addresses?
a: In user@host.domain, the part after @ names the machine or domain and the part before is the user. The domain goes from specific to general, such as host.cs.berkeley.edu, unlike bang paths, which read left to right.

q: What does the line in L.sys look like?
a: It reads like: bigsite Any ACU 2400 5551212 ogin: nuucp ssword: secret. That gives the site name, allowed times, device, speed, phone number, and then the expect and send chat script for logging in.

q: What does the tilde mean in uucp paths?
a: A leading ~ stands for the public directory, /usr/spool/uucppublic on most systems. So host!~/files/foo.tar.Z means that file in the public area. Quote or escape it if your shell expands the tilde itself.

q: What does uux do?
a: uux queues a command to run on a remote machine, and it's how mail gets delivered over UUCP. Mail typically runs something like uux - remotehost!rmail user, with the message text fed in as standard input.

q: What is BITNET and can I mail to it?
a: BITNET is a network of mostly IBM mainframes at universities, linked by leased lines. You can mail to it through gateways, using user%site.bitnet@gateway or a domain address like user@site.bitnet, depending on your mailer.

q: What is UUCP exactly?
a: It's Unix-to-Unix CP, a set of programs for copying files between Unix machines over phone lines or serial links. Mail and Usenet news both ride on top of it, using uucp and uux to queue and send jobs.

q: What is a .forward file?
a: A file in your home directory holding an address, and sendmail will send your mail there instead of to your mailbox. Put in something like bigsite!joe to forward to another system.

q: What is a backbone site?
a: A well-connected site that passes news to many others and keeps good uptime, like ihnp4, decvax, or seismo. Smaller sites get their feeds from a backbone or from another site nearby to save on long distance calls.

q: What is a domain name?
a: A name in the hierarchical system replacing the flat host table, with top-level parts such as .edu, .com, .gov, .mil, .org, .net and country codes like .uk. The DNS looks up the address of each name for you.

q: What is a mailing list and how do I join one?
a: It's an address that redistributes your message to subscribers. To join, mail a request to the list address with -request added, like info-unix-request@host, not to the list itself, which would annoy everybody.

q: What is pathalias?
a: Pathalias reads the map data and computes the cheapest route to each site, and it outputs a database of routes. Mailers like smail then use it so you can send to a name instead of typing the whole path.

q: What is the difference between From: and From_ lines?
a: The From_ line, with no colon, is the Unix mailbox separator added by the delivery program. The From: header is part of the message itself. Mail readers use From_ to split up the mailbox file.

q: What is the difference between UUCP and the Internet?
a: UUCP is dial-up batch transfer, so your mail hops machine to machine whenever the modems call, taking hours or days. The Internet uses permanent TCP/IP links and mail usually arrives in seconds.

q: What is the difference between mail and Mail?
a: Mail is the Berkeley mail program with folders, aliases, and better editing options, found on BSD systems. The older System V mail is plainer. Both use the same mailbox format, so you can switch freely.

q: What is the difference between uucp and cu?
a: uucp copies files in the background through a queue, while cu connects you interactively to a remote system through a modem or line. Use cu to test your modem and phone line before debugging uucico.

q: What is the etiquette for quoting in replies?
a: Quote only enough of the original to give context, with a > mark in front of each line, then add your reply. Posting the whole article back wastes bandwidth and phone bills for everyone down the line.

q: What is the limit on mail message size?
a: There's no universal limit, but many gateways bounce anything over about 50K and some over 64K. For large files, split them up or use uuencode and send in parts, and check with the sysadmin first.

q: What is uunet?
a: UUNET is a service run by Rick Adams that lets sites buy UUCP access, mail, and news feeds by dial-up for a fee. It also hosts a big archive of Usenet sources you can fetch by UUCP.

q: What's the difference between a Subject line and a Summary line in news and mail?
a: Subject is the topic and stays through the thread of replies. Summary is an optional line the poster uses to give a bit more detail about the article. Mail programs mostly show just the Subject.

q: Which is better, sendmail or smail?
a: For a small UUCP leaf site, smail is far simpler to configure and does the job. Sendmail is more powerful for networks with several kinds of transport, but its sendmail.cf file is famously hard to get right.

q: Why did my mail take four days to arrive?
a: Each UUCP hop may call only once or twice a day, often at night when rates are low. Four or five hops add up fast. A hung link or a down site along the path can add days more.

q: Why do some people have a path that begins with an exclamation point?
a: A leading bang tells the local mailer to use the path exactly as written, starting at the first named site, and not rewrite it. Some mailers add it to avoid wrong guessing about the first hop.

q: Why does my From line show a long ugly path?
a: The header shows the route the message took, with each machine adding itself. Replying with the raw path works only if all those links still exist. Look for a registered domain address in the signature instead.

q: Why does my mail to user@host.edu bounce from my UUCP machine?
a: Plain UUCP doesn't understand domain addresses. Either your site needs smail or sendmail with a smarthost configured, or you must route it by hand through a gateway such as uunet!host.edu!user.

q: Why does uucico say LOGIN FAILED?
a: The login or password sent doesn't match what the remote has. Check your Systems or L.sys line and the chat script, and confirm with the other admin that your uucp account and password are still valid.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Can I FTP from a machine that isn't on the Internet, like my home PC?
a: Not directly. You'd need a UUCP or BITNET link, or an FTP-by-mail server. Some sites offer ftpmail, where you email commands and they mail files back, usually uuencoded and split into pieces.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Can I telnet to a library catalog?
a: Yes, many universities have online catalogs open on the Internet. For example, try telnet to a university library host and log in as directed. Lists of them circulate on the net, and no account is usually needed.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Can I use FTP from a PC running DOS?
a: Yes. Packages like NCSA Telnet, FTP Software's PC/TCP, or the free KA9Q give you ftp and telnet on a PC with an Ethernet card. You'll need an IP address from your network administrator.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Do I need to be at a university to get on the Internet?
a: Not strictly, but most access comes through universities, research labs, or companies with a connection. Some regional networks like NEARnet or BARRNet sell links to businesses. Otherwise, UUCP and Usenet access is easier to get.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How can I tell if a remote host is up?
a: Use ping hostname. If it replies, the host is reachable on the net. No reply doesn't always mean it's down, since a gateway in between may be unavailable.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I escape out of a stuck telnet session?
a: Press Ctrl-] to get the telnet> prompt, then type quit or close. If the session is totally dead, the escape character still works because it is handled by your local client.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I find out the IP address for a host name?
a: Try nslookup hostname on a Unix box with the domain name system. Older sites use the HOSTS.TXT file from the NIC. Numbers look like 128.32.1.1, four numbers separated by dots.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I get RFC 959?
a: FTP to nic.ddn.mil, log in as anonymous, cd to rfc, and get rfc959.txt. Some mirrors like ftp.uu.net also keep copies. It describes the FTP protocol in detail.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I get a list of files on an FTP server?
a: Type dir for a long listing with sizes and dates, or ls for just names. Look for files named README, ls-lR, or INDEX, which many archive sites keep to describe what they have.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I log in to a remote machine over the Internet?
a: Use telnet. Type telnet hostname, for example telnet nic.ddn.mil, and you get that machine's login prompt. You need an account there unless the site offers a public login. Escape back to the telnet prompt with Ctrl-] if things hang.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I resume an interrupted FTP download?
a: Most FTP clients of this era can't. You usually have to restart from the beginning. Some newer ones support the restart command, but the server has to as well. For big files, try a less busy time of day.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I see who is logged on to a remote host?
a: Try finger @hostname, which many hosts answer with a list of current users. finger user@host gives details on one person. Some sites turn fingering off for privacy or security reasons.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I telnet to a port other than the default?
a: Put the port number after the host name, like telnet host 25. That is handy for testing a mail server by hand. The default port for login is 23.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: How do I upload a file with FTP?
a: Use put localfile at the ftp prompt, after you cd to the right remote directory. Anonymous users can usually only write to a directory like incoming, if the site has one. Most just allow reading.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Is FTP password sent securely?
a: No. Both FTP and telnet send your username and password in plain text across the net, so anyone on the wire can read them. Don't use a sensitive password on a remote account over a shared network if you can avoid it.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Is it OK to FTP large files in the middle of the day?
a: Better not. Many sites ask you to fetch large files outside local business hours, since links are slow and shared. Check the welcome banner or README for the site's rules.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Is it worth getting a 9600 baud modem to use the net?
a: If you dial a Unix host, yes. 2400 baud is okay for mail but painful for file transfers and news. A 9600 modem like the Telebit Trailblazer or a V.32 model costs a lot, but saves time if you use it daily.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Is the NSFNET the same as the Internet?
a: Not quite. NSFNET is a high-speed backbone funded by the National Science Foundation that links regional networks, running T1 lines since 1988. It is one major part of the Internet, which is the collection of all the TCP/IP networks.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What does 'binary' versus 'ascii' mean in ftp?
a: Ascii converts line endings between the two machines' text conventions, which is good for text files between Unix and a VMS or DOS box. Binary sends bytes unchanged and is required for anything that isn't plain text.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What does 'ftp: connect: Connection timed out' mean?
a: Your packets aren't getting an answer. The host may be down, or a gateway or link along the way is broken. Try ping to see if it is reachable, and try again later.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What does 'telnet: Unknown host' mean?
a: Your machine's resolver could not find that name. Check the spelling, or try the numeric IP address instead. If that works, your name server or hosts table is the problem.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What does TCP/IP mean?
a: It is the protocol suite the Internet runs on. IP moves packets from host to host, and TCP sits on top to give reliable, ordered connections. Telnet, FTP, and SMTP all run over TCP.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What does a .Z file mean and how do I open it?
a: It's compressed with the Unix compress program. Run uncompress file.Z, or zcat file.Z to pipe it out. If it's file.tar.Z, uncompress it first and then run tar xvf on the result.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What does the ftp command 'hash' do?
a: It prints a # mark for each block transferred, so you can see the transfer is actually moving. Handy on slow links when you can't tell a stall from a long file. Just type hash before your get.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What does the ftp command 'passive' mean?
a: I'd not count on it. Standard FTP of this era has the server open the data connection back to your machine, and that is all. Just stay with the usual get and put, and ask your administrator if firewalls cause problems.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is Archie?
a: It's a service from McGill University that gathers file listings from anonymous FTP sites and lets you search by file name. You telnet to an Archie host and log in as archie, then use the prog command to search.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is Kermit and how does it differ from FTP?
a: Kermit is a file transfer protocol for serial lines and modems, free from Columbia University. FTP needs a TCP/IP network connection. If you dial in to a host, use Kermit or Zmodem to move files to your PC.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is NCSA Telnet?
a: It's free TCP/IP software from the National Center for Supercomputing Applications for PCs and Macs. It gives you telnet, an FTP server, and terminal emulation including Tektronix graphics, over Ethernet or serial lines.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is RFC and where do I find them?
a: RFC means Request for Comments, the numbered documents that define Internet protocols. FTP is RFC 959 and telnet is RFC 854. You can get them by anonymous FTP from nic.ddn.mil in the rfc directory.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is a domain name like .edu or .com?
a: The last part is the top-level domain. edu is for educational schools, com for commercial, gov for government, mil for military, org and net for others, and two-letter codes such as uk or de for countries.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is a gateway in Internet terms?
a: It's a machine, nowadays often called a router, that connects two networks and forwards IP packets between them. Your host sends off-network traffic to its default gateway.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is a good terminal program for dialing in to a Unix host?
a: On a PC, Procomm or Kermit work well, and on a Mac, Red Ryder or MacTerminal. Kermit is free and also does file transfer, which is useful when you have no TCP/IP, just a serial line.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is anonymous FTP?
a: It's a way to grab public files from a server without an account. You ftp to the host, log in as anonymous, and give your email address as the password. Then cd to a directory like pub and get what you want.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the 'incoming' directory on some FTP servers?
a: It's a place where anonymous users are allowed to upload. Usually you can write there but not list or read the files. Put the file there and send mail to the admin to tell them about it.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the .cshrc trick to see ftp banner text?
a: There isn't one. The banner is sent by the server when you connect and displays automatically. If you want less clutter, some clients have a verbose toggle; type verbose to turn that output off.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the .tar extension?
a: Tar means tape archive. It bundles many files and directories into one file. Extract with tar xvf file.tar and list with tar tvf file.tar. Often it's then compressed to .tar.Z.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the ARPANET?
a: It's the packet-switched network started by DARPA in 1969 that connected research sites and universities. It now sits alongside NSFNET and regional networks as part of the larger Internet, all using TCP/IP.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the Internet Worm everyone is talking about?
a: In November 1988 a program written by Robert Morris Jr. spread through Sun and VAX Unix machines, using bugs in sendmail and fingerd and guessing passwords. It slowed thousands of hosts and led to CERT forming at Carnegie Mellon.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the difference between BITNET and the Internet?
a: BITNET links mostly IBM mainframes using store-and-forward file transfer, not TCP/IP. You can't telnet or ftp across it directly, but mail gateways between the two work well.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the difference between ftp and telnet?
a: Telnet gives you an interactive terminal session on a remote machine. FTP is for moving files between machines. You can't browse files with telnet in a way that saves them locally, and FTP won't let you run programs remotely.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is the mget command for?
a: It fetches multiple files by wildcard, like mget *.c. By default ftp asks yes or no for each file, so type prompt first to toggle that off if you want them all without questions.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What is uuencode and why do I need it?
a: It turns binary data into printable ASCII so it survives mail and Usenet. You run uuencode file file > file.uu, and the recipient runs uudecode. The result is about 35 percent bigger than the original.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: What should I use as the password for anonymous FTP?
a: By custom, your email address, like jsmith@cs.wisc.edu. Some servers log it, and a few reject logins that don't look like an address. Plain guest also works at some sites, but your address is the polite choice.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Where can I find a list of anonymous FTP sites?
a: Check the periodic posting in comp.sources.wanted or news.answers style lists of anonymous FTP sites. Archie is a newer experiment from McGill that indexes them, if your site has access to it. Otherwise ask in comp.misc.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Which is better for sending files, FTP or email?
a: FTP for anything big or binary. Email is okay for small text, but gateways often limit message size and mangle binaries, so you'd have to uuencode, which makes the file about a third larger.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Why do my downloaded programs come out corrupted after FTP?
a: You probably transferred a binary file in ascii mode. Type binary (or type image) at the ftp prompt before you get anything that is a tar, compressed, or executable file. Ascii mode mangles line endings and trashes binaries.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Why does ftp say 'Login incorrect' for anonymous?
a: Many sites are configured for either ftp or anonymous. Try both. Some also limit the number of anonymous users, or restrict by the domain you come from, so a reverse lookup of your address may matter.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Why does my FTP connection say 'Connection refused'?
a: The remote host isn't running an FTP server, or it's down, or it blocks you. Try again later and check the host name. If telnet to port 21 also refuses, the daemon is not listening.

topic: the ARPANET and the early Internet: FTP, telnet, anonymous FTP
q: Why is my FTP transfer so slow?
a: Check the load on both ends and the path between. Long hops across 56k lines or a congested gateway cut throughput a lot. Try early morning or late night in the remote time zone and use a closer mirror if there is one.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Can I rename a file in Unix? I can't find a rename command.
a: Use mv oldname newname. Moving and renaming are the same operation. If newname already exists it gets overwritten without asking unless you use mv -i on a BSD system.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Can I use wildcards in Unix like I did with *.* in MS-DOS?
a: Yes, but the shell expands them. Use * for any string and ? for one character. Note that * alone matches everything not starting with a dot, and *.* only matches names containing a dot.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Can a Unix filename have spaces in it?
a: Technically yes, anything except a slash and a null is legal. In practice it's a pain because the shell splits on spaces, so you must quote the name. Stick to letters, digits, dots and underscores.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How can I compare two files to see what changed?
a: Use diff file1 file2. It lists lines to add, delete or change. For a quick yes or no, cmp tells you whether they differ, and where the first difference is.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I append to a file instead of overwriting it?
a: Use >> instead of >. So echo hello >> notes adds a line to the end of notes, creating it if it doesn't exist yet.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I change the owner of a file?
a: Use chown newowner file. On BSD only root can do it, and on System V you can give files away if you own them. Use chgrp to change the group.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I copy a whole directory with all its subdirectories?
a: Use cp -r olddir newdir on BSD and most modern systems. On older System V machines without -r, tar is safer: cd to the source and run tar cf - . | (cd /dest; tar xf -).

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I delete a directory that has files in it?
a: Use rm -r dirname, which removes everything below it. Be careful, there is no undelete on Unix. Plain rmdir only works on empty directories.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I find a file when I forgot which directory I put it in?
a: Use find, for example find / -name memo.txt -print. It can be slow on a big disk, so start from your home directory first. Remember the -print, since older versions print nothing without it.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I find out how much disk space I am using?
a: Try du -s on your home directory, which totals the blocks used. To see how full the whole filesystem is, use df. Block sizes differ between BSD and System V, so check your man page.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I get a file's date changed to now without editing it?
a: Use touch filename. It updates the modification time, and creates an empty file if it doesn't exist. Make uses these times to decide what to rebuild.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I get back to my home directory after wandering around?
a: Just type cd with no arguments and you land in $HOME. In csh you can also use cd ~. Either one works from anywhere, so you never need to type the full path.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I list files sorted by date, newest first?
a: Use ls -t. Add -l to see the dates, and -r to reverse the order so the newest comes last, which is handy when the list scrolls off the screen.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I look at a long file one screen at a time?
a: Use more filename, and press space for the next page. On System V you might have pg instead. Plain cat will just scroll past faster than you can read.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I make a compressed archive of a directory to send to someone?
a: Run tar cf - dirname | compress > dirname.tar.Z. The other side can do zcat file.tar.Z | tar xf -. Then uuencode it if you need to mail it, since mail doesn't carry binary.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I make a file that only I can read?
a: Run chmod 600 filename. That gives you read and write and takes everything away from group and others. For a directory use chmod 700 so nobody else can even list it.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I make a new directory?
a: Use mkdir dirname. If you want to create several levels at once, older mkdir won't do it, so make each level in turn. Newer ones support -p for that.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I print the directory I am currently in?
a: Type pwd. It prints the full absolute path of your current working directory. It's handy after a few cds when you've lost track of where you are.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I see all my files, including the ones that start with a dot?
a: Use ls -a. Files starting with a dot, like .profile and .login, are hidden from plain ls. If you want to skip . and .. as well, System V and BSD ls on newer systems take -A.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How do I see who else can read my files?
a: Run ls -l and look at the last three permission characters, which are the others, and the middle three for your group. Also check the directory permissions, since a readable file in an open directory is exposed.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: How long can a filename be on Unix?
a: On BSD 4.2 and later filesystems, and System V Release 3 with the right filesystem, 255 characters. Older System V filesystems only allow 14, so keep names short if you share files across machines.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Is it safe to put . in my PATH?
a: It's risky. Someone could leave a program named ls in a directory you visit and you'd run it. If you must, put it last in your PATH, and never for root.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Is it worth learning vi, or should I stick with ed?
a: Learn vi. It's on practically every Unix system, and being a full-screen editor it's far easier than ed for real work. Emacs is nicer but not always installed, so vi is the safe bet.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does cat file1 file2 > file3 do?
a: It joins file1 and file2 end to end and writes the result into file3. The > is output redirection. Be careful, if file3 already exists it gets overwritten.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does chmod 755 do?
a: It sets rwxr-xr-x. The 7 gives the owner read, write and execute (4+2+1), and each 5 gives group and others read and execute (4+1). It's the usual setting for scripts and programs.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does drwxr-xr-x mean?
a: It's a directory (d). The owner can read, write and search it (rwx), while group and others can read and search but not change it (r-x). In octal that's 755.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does ls -F do?
a: It adds a mark after each name: a slash for directories, an asterisk for executables, and an @ for symbolic links. It's a quick way to tell what is what without ls -l. It's on BSD and most newer System V.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does ls -l show me?
a: The long listing: permissions, link count, owner, group, size in bytes, modification date, and name. The first character of the permissions tells you the type, a dash for a plain file, d for a directory, l for a symbolic link.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does the man command do and how do I search for a command by topic?
a: Man displays the manual page for a command, like man ls. To search by keyword use man -k topic, or apropos on BSD, if your admin has built the whatis database.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does the number after the permissions in ls -l mean?
a: It's the link count. For a plain file it's usually 1, more if there are hard links. For a directory it's at least 2, counting its own entry and the dot entry inside it.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does the s in -rwsr-xr-x mean?
a: It's the setuid bit. When someone runs the program, it runs with the file owner's privileges instead of their own. That's how passwd can update /etc/passwd. Be very careful with setuid root programs.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does the sticky bit on /tmp do?
a: With the t bit set on a directory, users can only remove or rename files they own, even though everyone can write there. That's why /tmp shows drwxrwxrwt on BSD-derived systems.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does the tilde mean in a path like ~bob/src?
a: In csh and ksh, ~bob expands to bob's home directory, and a lone ~ means your own. The shell does the expansion, so older Bourne shells don't understand it.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What does the x in the Makefile name or a file ending .c or .o mean?
a: Nothing special to Unix itself, it's just convention. A .c is C source, .o is a compiled object file, .h a header, and .a an archive library. The compiler and make go by those suffixes.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What happens to the files if I rm a directory by accident?
a: They're gone. Unix has no trash can, and the blocks go back to the free list. Your only hope is last night's backup, so ask your administrator, and consider using rm -i.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is an inode?
a: It's the on-disk structure holding a file's owner, permissions, size, timestamps and pointers to its data blocks. The directory entry just maps a name to an inode number. Use ls -i to see the numbers.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is in /etc and should I be poking around in there?
a: It holds system configuration files like passwd, group, fstab and rc. Looking is fine and a good way to learn, but only root can change most of it, and a typo there can keep the machine from booting.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is the difference between /bin and /usr/bin?
a: Originally /bin held the essential programs needed to boot and /usr/bin held the rest because /usr was on a separate disk. Nowadays the split varies by vendor, and Sun puts many in /usr/bin.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?
a: A hard link is another directory entry pointing at the same inode, so it must be on the same filesystem. A symbolic link, made with ln -s, is a small file holding a pathname and can cross filesystems and point to directories.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is the difference between a relative and an absolute path?
a: An absolute path starts with a slash and begins at the root, like /usr/spool/mail. A relative path starts from wherever you are now, so docs/memo means the docs directory under your current one.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is the dot-dot in cd .. ?
a: The two dots mean the parent directory, and a single dot means the current directory. So cd .. moves you up one level, and ../.. goes up two.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is the group in file permissions for?
a: It lets a set of users share files without opening them to everyone. Each file has one owner and one group. On BSD you can belong to several groups, on older System V only one at a time, with newgrp to switch.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is the root directory?
a: It's the top of the filesystem tree, written as a single slash. Everything else, /bin, /usr, /etc, /tmp and your home directory, hangs below it. Not to be confused with the root user's home directory.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: What is umask and why do my new files come out as 644?
a: The umask is a mask of permission bits removed from newly created files. A umask of 022 strips write for group and others, giving 644 for files and 755 for directories. Set it in your .profile or .login.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Which is better for a beginner, csh or sh?
a: Csh is nicer to use interactively, with history and job control, but sh is better for writing scripts. Many people use csh at the prompt and sh for scripts. Ksh does both well if your system has it.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Why can't I make a hard link to a directory?
a: Only root can on most systems, because links to directories can create loops that break fsck and find. Use a symbolic link with ln -s if you have BSD or SVR4, which handles directories fine.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Why does it say Permission denied when I try to cd into a directory?
a: The directory lacks execute (search) permission for you. On a directory, x means you can pass through it. Ask the owner to chmod it, or if it's yours, try chmod +x on it.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Why does ls show my files in a weird order, with capital letters first?
a: Ls sorts by ASCII value, and all uppercase letters come before lowercase. So Makefile lists ahead of apple. It is not alphabetical in the dictionary sense.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Why does my directory show a size of 512 or 1024 bytes when it's empty?
a: A directory is itself a file containing name and inode entries, and it takes at least one block. The size shown is that block allocation, not the size of the files inside.

topic: Unix basics: files, directories, ls, cd, permissions
q: Why won't my shell script run when I type its name?
a: Probably it isn't executable, so chmod +x it. It may also be that the current directory isn't in your PATH, in which case type ./script instead.

q: Can I run a shell command from inside vi?
a: Yes, type :!command, for example :!ls, and vi runs it and then waits for return. If you want a whole shell, use :sh and press control-D to come back.

q: Can I use regular expressions in vi searches?
a: Yes. You get . for any character, * for repeats, [abc] for sets, ^ and $ for line ends. Use \< and \> for word boundaries. It's basic regular expressions like grep, not the extended kind.

q: How can I make vi wrap long lines as I type?
a: Set :set wrapmargin=8, which breaks lines automatically 8 columns from the right edge. It only breaks at spaces, and it won't reformat existing text.

q: How can I undo a mistake in vi?
a: Press u in command mode to undo the last change. Original vi only has one level, so pressing u again redoes it. Capital U restores the whole current line if you haven't left it.

q: How do I append to the end of a file I'm editing from a different file?
a: Use :r otherfile after going to the last line with G. Or to write part of your buffer out, :10,20w newfile saves lines 10 to 20, and :10,20w >> newfile appends them.

q: How do I change a word?
a: Put the cursor at the start of the word and type cw, then the new text, then ESC. A dollar sign marks the end of the part being replaced while you type.

q: How do I copy and paste lines in vi?
a: Yank with yy for one line, or 3yy for three, move the cursor, and press p to put them below the current line. P puts them above. dd followed by p moves lines around.

q: How do I define a shortcut key in vi?
a: Use :map. For example :map g Gdd would run those keys when you press g. In insert mode use :map! instead. Avoid keys you already use, and control characters need a control-V in front to be entered.

q: How do I delete a whole line?
a: Type dd in command mode. Put a count in front to delete several lines, so 5dd kills five lines. The deleted lines go in a buffer and you can bring them back with p.

q: How do I delete all blank lines in a file?
a: Use :g/^$/d. The g command runs d on every line matching the pattern, and ^$ matches an empty line. Lines with just spaces won't match.

q: How do I delete from the cursor to the end of the line?
a: Press D, or d$ which does the same thing. Capital C does the same but also puts you in insert mode so you can type the replacement.

q: How do I edit more than one file at a time?
a: Start with vi file1 file2 and use :n to go to the next file after saving. For switching back and forth, :e file works and :e# returns to the previous one. Yank into a named buffer like "a to carry text between files.

q: How do I filter text through a Unix command like sort from inside vi?
a: Use !} sort or, for a range of lines, something like :1,10!sort. Text goes through the command and gets replaced by the output. Use u if you don't like what came out.

q: How do I get to the beginning and end of a line?
a: 0 (zero) goes to the first column and $ goes to the end of the line. The caret ^ goes to the first non-blank character.

q: How do I get vi to show whether I'm in insert mode?
a: Type :set showmode. It prints INSERT at the bottom of the screen. Older versions of vi don't have the option, but the 4.3BSD and System V Release 3 ones do.

q: How do I go to a particular line number in vi?
a: Type the number followed by G, like 120G, or use :120 and return. Control-G shows the current line number and file name at the bottom.

q: How do I go to the end of the file?
a: Press capital G. With a number first, like 25G, you jump to that line. 1G or gg is not needed, just 1G takes you to the top.

q: How do I join two lines together?
a: Put the cursor on the first line and press capital J. It pulls the next line up and puts a space between them.

q: How do I mark a spot in the file and come back to it?
a: Press m followed by a letter, like ma, to set a mark. Later type 'a to jump to the line of that mark or `a for the exact position. d'a deletes from here to the mark.

q: How do I move forward one word at a time?
a: Press w to go to the start of the next word and b to go back one word. e goes to the end of the word. Capital W, B and E treat punctuation as part of the word.

q: How do I quit vi without saving my changes?
a: Hit ESC, then type :q! and press return. The bang tells vi to throw away your edits. Plain :q will refuse if the buffer has been modified.

q: How do I read another file into the one I'm editing?
a: Use :r filename to insert that file below the cursor line. You can also do :r !command to read in the output of a shell command, like :r !date.

q: How do I replace every occurrence of foo with bar in the file?
a: Use :%s/foo/bar/g from command mode. Without the g only the first match on each line changes. Add a c at the end if you want vi to ask before each change.

q: How do I save and exit at the same time?
a: Type :wq from command mode, or ZZ (two capital Z's) which does the same thing but only writes if the file changed. Either one works fine.

q: How do I scroll the screen a page at a time?
a: Control-F moves forward a page and control-B goes back. Control-D and control-U scroll half a screen down and up.

q: How do I search for a word in a file?
a: Type /word and return to search forward, or ?word to search backward. Press n for the next match and N to go the opposite direction.

q: How do I set the tab width in vi?
a: Use :set tabstop=4 or :set ts=4. That changes how tabs are displayed, not what's in the file. Other programs and printers will still treat a tab as 8 columns.

q: How do I swap two characters I typed in the wrong order?
a: Put the cursor on the first one and type xp. The x deletes it and p puts it back after the next character, so the pair is swapped.

q: I got a message saying 'file is locked' or 'recovery' after my terminal hung up. Did I lose my work?
a: Probably not. vi saves the buffer when the line drops. Run vi -r filename, or just vi -r to list recoverable files, and you'll likely get most of your changes back. You may also get mail from vi about it.

q: I started vi and everything I type does weird things. What's going on?
a: vi starts in command mode, where keys are commands, not text. Press i to enter insert mode and then type your text. Hit ESC when you're done to get back to command mode.

q: Is it worth learning vi if I just want to edit a few config files?
a: Yes. Every Unix system has it, and when you're in single-user mode or on someone else's machine it may be the only editor you get. A dozen commands will carry you a long way.

q: Is there a vi for my IBM PC?
a: Yes, there are a few. Mortice Kern Systems sells MKS vi, and there are shareware clones like Stevie that run on the PC and Atari ST. They're close enough to the real thing for basic use.

q: Is there a way to see invisible characters like tabs and end-of-line?
a: Try :set list. Tabs show as ^I and each line ends with a $. It's good for finding stray trailing spaces or tabs where you wanted spaces.

q: Is vi or emacs better?
a: Depends who you ask. vi is on every Unix box and starts fast, so it's what you can count on. Emacs is more powerful but big and slow on a loaded machine, and you may not have it installed.

q: What are the named buffers in vi?
a: You can yank or delete into buffers a through z by typing "a before the command, as in "ayy. Paste with "ap. Unlike the default buffer they survive other deletes, so you can move text between files.

q: What do h j k l do?
a: They move the cursor left, down, up and right. They were picked because they sit on the home row of the ADM-3A terminal Bill Joy used. Once you get used to them you won't want arrow keys.

q: What does 'No write since last change' mean?
a: You tried to quit with :q after modifying the file. Either save with :w first or use :q! to leave and discard the changes.

q: What does 'Not an editor command' mean?
a: You typed a colon command that ex doesn't recognize, usually a typo or a command from a different vi. Check your spelling and that you were in command mode.

q: What does :set nu do?
a: It turns on line numbers along the left of the screen. The numbers aren't part of the file. Turn them off with :set nonu.

q: What does the % key do?
a: It jumps to the matching parenthesis, bracket or brace. Handy for C programmers who lose track of nesting. Put the cursor on one and press %.

q: What does the R command do?
a: Capital R puts you in replace mode, where what you type overwrites the existing text until you press ESC. Lowercase r replaces just a single character and returns right away.

q: What does the dot command do?
a: The period repeats your last change. If you did dw to delete a word, pressing . deletes the next word too. It saves a lot of typing.

q: What does the tilde (~) at the left of the screen mean?
a: Those are lines past the end of your file. They aren't part of the text, vi just shows ~ for empty screen lines. Nothing to worry about.

q: What is autoindent and should I use it?
a: :set ai makes a new line start with the same indentation as the one above. It's very handy for C code. Use control-D at the start of a line to back up one shiftwidth.

q: What is the difference between i and a in vi?
a: i inserts text before the cursor and a appends after it. Capital I inserts at the start of the line and capital A appends at the end of the line.

q: What is the difference between vi and ex?
a: They're the same program. ex is the line editor and vi is its visual mode. Type Q in vi to drop into ex, and type vi at the ex prompt to return.

q: Where do I put my vi settings so I don't have to type them every time?
a: Put them in a file called .exrc in your home directory, one ex command per line without the colon. You can also set the EXINIT environment variable. vi reads these when it starts up.

q: Why does my screen get garbled in vi, and how do I fix it?
a: Line noise or a message from write or mail can scribble on the screen. Press control-L to redraw it. If it still looks wrong, check that your TERM variable matches your terminal.

q: Why does vi beep at me when I press the arrow keys in insert mode?
a: Many terminals send escape sequences for arrows, and vi sees the ESC as the end of insert mode. Use h, j, k, l for movement instead. They work on any terminal.

q: Why does vi say 'Out of memory' or 'Temporary file too large' when I open a big file?
a: vi keeps a temp file in /tmp or /usr/tmp, and the file system there is probably full. Clean out old files, or set the directory option to some other place with more room. Splitting the file with split also helps.

q: Can Emacs show me the line number?
a: M-x line-number-mode puts the line number in the mode line, though in older versions you may only have what-line (M-x what-line). M-x goto-line jumps to a given line.

q: Can I run Emacs under X11?
a: Yes, version 18.5x has X support if you build it with the X11 option in config.h. You get its own window with mouse use. Otherwise just run it in an xterm like any terminal program.

q: How can I run a shell command from Emacs?
a: M-! runs a single command and shows the output. M-x shell starts a shell in a buffer, where you can edit and scroll through the output like any text.

q: How can I undo a mistake in Emacs?
a: Type C-x u or C-_ to undo. Repeat it to go back further. If you undo too far, make any other command in between and then undo again, which redoes the changes.

q: How can I use Emacs with TeX?
a: Use tex-mode or latex-mode, which come with 18.5x. C-c C-b runs TeX on the buffer, and C-c C-l shows the log. There's also the AUC TeX package on ftp for more features.

q: How do I bind a key to a command in my .emacs?
a: Use (global-set-key "\C-cg" 'goto-line). Stick to C-c followed by a letter, since those are reserved for users. Don't rebind keys like C-x ones that the standard setup uses.

q: How do I change the case of a word?
a: M-u makes the word after the cursor uppercase, M-l lowercase, and M-c capitalizes it. For a region, use C-x C-u and C-x C-l.

q: How do I compile my program without leaving Emacs?
a: Type M-x compile and give it your make command. Output goes to a *compilation* buffer, and C-x ` jumps to the source line of each error in turn.

q: How do I cut and paste a region?
a: Set the mark with C-SPC (or C-@), move to the other end, then C-w kills the region. Move somewhere else and C-y pastes it. M-w copies without deleting.

q: How do I do search and replace?
a: M-x replace-string replaces everywhere after the cursor without asking. M-% (query-replace) asks at each match: y to replace, n to skip, ! to do all the rest, q to quit.

q: How do I edit two files at once and copy between them?
a: Visit both with C-x C-f, then switch between buffers with C-x b. Or split with C-x 2 and use C-x o to jump between windows. Kill in one and yank in the other.

q: How do I get Emacs to indent my C code properly?
a: Use c-mode, which comes on automatically for .c files. TAB re-indents the current line, and M-C-\ indents the region. You can adjust c-indent-level and the brace settings in your .emacs.

q: How do I get a list of all the commands with a certain word in them?
a: Use C-h a (command-apropos) and give it a word like "buffer" or "mail". It lists matching commands and what keys they're on. Handy when you know what you want but not the name.

q: How do I get auto-fill so lines wrap automatically?
a: M-x auto-fill-mode turns it on for the buffer. Text modes can have it by default if you add (setq text-mode-hook 'turn-on-auto-fill) to your .emacs. Set the column with C-x f.

q: How do I get to the start or end of a file?
a: M-< goes to the beginning of the buffer and M-> goes to the end. C-a and C-e go to the line ends, and C-v and M-v page down and up.

q: How do I make Emacs open a file the right mode for my extension?
a: Add to auto-mode-alist in your .emacs, like (setq auto-mode-alist (cons '("\\.pl$" . perl-mode) auto-mode-alist)). Or put -*- mode: foo -*- on the first line of the file.

q: How do I quit Emacs?
a: Type C-x C-c. If you have unsaved buffers it will ask whether to save each one. If you're stuck in a prompt, hit C-g first to get out of it.

q: How do I read my mail in Emacs?
a: Use M-x rmail. It reads your inbox file, and you move messages with n and p, delete with d, reply with r, and send new mail with C-x m. Quit with q.

q: How do I record a macro?
a: Press C-x ( to start, type your keystrokes, then C-x ) to stop. C-x e replays it. A numeric argument like C-u 100 C-x e repeats it a hundred times.

q: How do I save a file in Emacs?
a: C-x C-s saves the current buffer to its file. C-x C-w asks for a new name and writes it there, like Save As.

q: How do I search for text in Emacs?
a: C-s starts an incremental search forward and C-r goes backward. Type the string and it jumps as you type. Hit C-s again for the next match and RET to stop.

q: How do I transpose two letters I typed backwards?
a: Put the cursor between them and press C-t. M-t swaps two words, and C-x C-t swaps two lines. They are quick to use once you remember them.

q: I hit some keys and now my screen is split in two. How do I get back to one window?
a: Type C-x 1 to keep only the window you're in. C-x 0 isn't there in the older versions, so use C-x 1. C-x 2 splits again if you want it back.

q: Is Emacs better than vi?
a: Depends who you ask, and that argument has run on Usenet for years. Emacs is bigger and slower to start, but you can extend it and run mail and shells inside it. vi is small and on every Unix box.

q: Is GNU Emacs really free?
a: Yes, under the GNU General Public License you can copy it and give it away, and you get the source. You can sell copies too, but you must pass on the same freedoms and the source.

q: Is it worth learning Emacs if I only edit small files?
a: Probably, if you'll be at a Unix machine a lot. The basic keys take a day to learn, and they work in many other programs too. If you only do quick edits, a simpler editor is fine.

q: Is there a way to use Emacs over a slow modem link?
a: Yes, but it's painful at 1200 baud. Turn off fancy things, use C-s sparingly, and try setting baud-rate. Emacs adapts its redisplay to the speed, and M-x edit-options can help. Many people use ed or MicroEmacs there.

q: My Backspace key brings up help instead of deleting. How do I fix that?
a: Your terminal sends C-h for backspace. Easiest fix is to swap the keys with keyboard-translate-table in your .emacs, or use C-x DEL. Many people just bind help to F1 or M-x help-for-help.

q: What are the files with # around the name?
a: Those are auto-save files, like #foo.c#. Emacs writes them every 300 keystrokes or so. If the system crashes, use M-x recover-file to get your work back. They're deleted when you save normally.

q: What are the main differences between Emacs 18 and the older Emacs 17?
a: Version 18 was released in 1986. It was faster, had many bug fixes, and added things like better Lisp support and more modes. Anything older than 18.5x should be upgraded if you can.

q: What are those files with a tilde at the end of the name?
a: Emacs makes a backup of the old version the first time you save, with ~ added to the name. You can delete them. To stop it set make-backup-files to nil in your .emacs.

q: What does "Mark set" mean?
a: You pressed C-SPC or C-@, which put an invisible marker at the cursor. The text between mark and cursor is the region. C-x C-x swaps the cursor and the mark so you can see where it is.

q: What does "Symbol's value as variable is void" mean?
a: You referenced a variable that hasn't been set. Usually it's a typo in your .emacs or a package you use before loading it. Use setq to define it first, or check the spelling.

q: What does C-h do in Emacs?
a: It's the help prefix. C-h c tells you what a key does, C-h f describes a function, C-h a searches commands by keyword, and C-h ? lists the options. Some terminals send backspace as C-h, which is annoying.

q: What does C-x mean in the Emacs docs?
a: C-x means hold down Control and press x. M-x means Meta, which is the ESC key if your keyboard has no Meta key. Press ESC, let go, then press x.

q: What does the .emacs file do?
a: It's your startup file in your home directory, written in Emacs Lisp. Emacs loads it every time you start. Put your key bindings, variable settings and hooks there.

q: What is Elisp?
a: Emacs Lisp is the dialect of Lisp that Emacs is extended with. Most of the editor's commands are written in it. You can try expressions by typing them in *scratch* and hitting C-j, or use M-x eval-expression.

q: What is GNUS?
a: It's a newsreader that runs inside GNU Emacs, written by Masanobu Umeda. It reads news over NNTP or from a local spool. You get groups, subjects, and replies using Emacs keystrokes.

q: What is Gosling Emacs?
a: It's James Gosling's Emacs for Unix, written in C with an embedded language called Mocklisp. It was sold commercially by UniPress. GNU Emacs grew out of the same ideas, but is a separate program.

q: What is MicroEmacs?
a: It's a small Emacs-style editor by Dave Conroy, later extended by Daniel Lawrence. It's in C, portable to MS-DOS, Atari ST, Amiga and Unix, and uses the usual Emacs keys. It has its own macro language, not Lisp.

q: What is a major mode?
a: A major mode sets up Emacs for the kind of text you're editing, such as text-mode, c-mode, or lisp-mode. It changes things like indentation and syntax. Only one is active in a buffer at a time.

q: What is a minor mode?
a: It's an extra feature you can switch on along with a major mode, like auto-fill or overwrite mode. You can have several on at once. They show in the mode line in parentheses.

q: What is dired?
a: It's the directory editor, started with C-x d. You get an ls -l listing you can move around in. Press d to flag files for deletion, x to do it, and f to visit a file.

q: What is the best way to learn Emacs?
a: Start the built-in tutorial with C-h t. It takes about half an hour and teaches the basic cursor and editing commands. After that, use C-h k and C-h f to look things up.

q: What is the difference between a buffer and a file in Emacs?
a: A buffer is the copy of the text you're editing in memory. The file on disk doesn't change until you save with C-x C-s. That's also why a crash can lose your edits.

q: What is the kill ring?
a: It's where text goes when you kill it with C-k or C-w. C-y yanks back the latest one, and M-y right after replaces it with the previous kill. So you can move several chunks around.

q: What's the difference between M-x and ESC x?
a: Nothing really. If your keyboard has no Meta key, ESC acts as a prefix, so ESC then x is the same as M-x. Type them one after the other, don't hold ESC.

q: Where do I get GNU Emacs?
a: You can get it by anonymous ftp from prep.ai.mit.edu in pub/gnu. Version 18.57 or so is current. Or send $150 to the Free Software Foundation in Cambridge for a tape.

q: Why does Emacs say "Buffer has been modified; kill anyway?"
a: You tried to kill a buffer with changes you didn't save. Say no and save with C-x C-s first. If you really want to throw away the changes, answer yes.

q: Why is Emacs so big?
a: It carries a Lisp interpreter and a lot of Lisp code for modes, mail, and so on. On a Sun-3 the running process is a megabyte or more. It runs fine with 4 MB, but on a small machine with 2 MB it will swap.

q: Will Emacs run on my PC under MS-DOS?
a: Not GNU Emacs, as far as I know, since it needs a big address space. There are small clones like MicroEmacs, Freemacs and Mince that run fine on a PC XT or AT.

q: Does the Bourne shell have aliases or command history?
a: No, neither. That's one reason people use csh interactively. If you want that in an sh-style shell, look for ksh from AT&T, which has both and vi or emacs line editing, if your site has it licensed.

q: Does the Bourne shell have functions?
a: Yes, in System V Release 2 and later you can define name() { commands; } and call it with arguments as $1, $2. Older V7 style sh doesn't have them, and csh has no functions at all.

q: How can I do arithmetic in sh?
a: Use expr, as in i=`expr $i + 1`. Remember to put spaces around the operator, and escape * as \*. It is slow since it starts a new process every time. ksh has built-in let for this.

q: How can I see what a shell script is doing when it fails?
a: Run it with sh -x script, which prints each command after expansion as it runs. sh -v prints the lines as they are read. In csh the same options exist as csh -x and csh -v.

q: How do I change the prompt in sh?
a: Set the PS1 variable, like PS1='$ ' or PS1="`uname -n`\$ " in .profile. PS2 is the continuation prompt, usually >. The Bourne shell can't show the current directory by itself.

q: How do I do arithmetic in csh?
a: csh has @ built in. Try @ i = $i + 1, with spaces around everything. It handles integers only, but it's much faster than calling expr.

q: How do I find out what happened to my PATH in csh when I change it?
a: csh keeps a hash table of commands, so after changing path run rehash. Without it, new programs in a new directory won't be found. Typing set path=($path /usr/local/bin) also works, followed by rehash.

q: How do I get the number of arguments in a csh script?
a: Use $#argv, and the arguments themselves are $argv[1], $argv[2] and so on. In sh the count is $# and the arguments are $1, $2, up to $9, then use shift for more.

q: How do I keep csh from logging me out when I press Control-D?
a: Do set ignoreeof in your .cshrc. Then you must type logout to leave. Setting it can also stop you from accidentally leaving from a shell when your terminal sends a stray end-of-file.

q: How do I loop over files in sh?
a: Write for f in *.c; do echo $f; done. You can use any word list after in. If you leave out the in part, it loops over the script arguments.

q: How do I make an alias in csh?
a: Type alias ll 'ls -l' and put it in your .cshrc to keep it. You can use !* in the alias to get at the arguments, like alias h 'history \!*'. The Bourne shell has no aliases at all.

q: How do I pipe the output of one command into another?
a: Put a | between them, like ls -l | more. The first command's stdout becomes the second one's stdin. In csh, use |& if you also want stderr in the pipe.

q: How do I read a line of input in a sh script?
a: Use read var. It takes one line from stdin and puts it in var, and with several names it splits into words. In csh the equivalent is set var = $< .

q: How do I redirect both stdout and stderr to a file in csh?
a: Use command >& file. That sends both to the file. If you want them split, csh can't do it directly; run it in sh with a subshell, like (command > out) >& err.

q: How do I redirect stderr to a file in sh?
a: Use command 2> errfile. To send stderr to the same place as stdout, use command > file 2>&1. Order matters, the 2>&1 must come after the > file.

q: How do I run a command in the background?
a: Put an & at the end of the line, like make > log 2>&1 &. The shell prints a job number or PID. Use nohup in front if you want it to survive logging out.

q: How do I set an environment variable in csh?
a: Use setenv NAME value, with no equals sign. For example setenv EDITOR vi. A plain set NAME=value only makes a shell variable that child programs won't see.

q: How do I set an environment variable in sh?
a: Assign it and then export it: TERM=vt100; export TERM. Without the export, programs you start won't see it. On the newer System V sh you can do it in one line, but the two-step way works everywhere.

q: How do I set the prompt in csh?
a: Use set prompt = "`hostname`% " in your .cshrc. In a prompt you can put !, which stands for the history number. Check that it's only for interactive shells with if ($?prompt).

q: How do I stop csh from overwriting files with > by accident?
a: Do set noclobber. Then > won't overwrite an existing file and complains instead. If you really want to, use >! file to override it.

q: How do I suspend a running job and put it in the background in csh?
a: Hit Control-Z to stop it, then type bg to continue it in the background. Use fg to bring it back, and jobs to list what you have. This needs job control in your kernel, which BSD has.

q: How do I test if a file exists in sh?
a: Use if test -f file; then ...; fi, or the bracket form [ -f file ]. -d checks for a directory and -r, -w, -x check permissions. Leave spaces around the brackets, since [ is really a command.

q: How do I use a variable that's not set in csh without an error?
a: Test it first with $?name, which is 1 if set and 0 if not. Using an unset variable gives "Undefined variable". In sh an unset variable is just empty, and ${name-default} gives a default.

q: How do I use more than nine arguments in a sh script?
a: Only $1 through $9 are available directly. Use shift to throw away $1 and slide the rest down, then $9 is the tenth argument. Loop with while test $# -gt 0; do ...; shift; done.

q: How do I write a loop in csh over a list of files?
a: Use foreach f (*.c) then your commands, such as cc -c $f, and finish with end. Each pass puts a file name in $f. The sh equivalent is for f in *.c; do ...; done.

q: Is it a good idea to write scripts in csh?
a: Not really. csh has quirks, like no way to redirect stderr alone, trouble with functions and weird quoting and parsing of if/while on one line. Most folks write scripts in sh and keep csh for typing at the terminal.

q: Should I switch from csh to ksh?
a: If you can get it, yes for most people. ksh gives you csh's history and job control plus the sh syntax you need for scripts, so you only learn one language. Just remember it's an AT&T licensed product, not free on every machine.

q: What are the backquotes for?
a: Command substitution. Text between backquotes is run, and its output replaces it on the line, so d=`date` stores the date in d. They're hard to nest in sh; you have to escape the inner ones with backslashes.

q: What does !! mean in csh?
a: It repeats the previous command line. !$ is the last word of the previous line, and !abc runs the most recent command starting with abc. Handy, but be careful with !* and rm.

q: What does #!/bin/sh at the top of a script mean?
a: On BSD and System V Release 3 kernels, the first line tells exec which interpreter to run for the file. Without it, a csh user's script may get run by csh instead of sh. Older systems may ignore it, so a lone # on line one is the fallback.

q: What does $$ mean in a shell script?
a: It is the process ID of the shell running the script. People use it to make unique temp file names, like /tmp/foo.$$, so two copies of the script don't clobber each other.

q: What does $* and $@ mean in sh?
a: Both expand to all the command line arguments. Inside double quotes, "$*" becomes one single word, while "$@" keeps each argument separate. You almost always want "$@" if arguments may contain spaces.

q: What does nohup do?
a: It runs a command immune to hangups, so it keeps going after you log out. Output goes to nohup.out if you don't redirect it. Use it like nohup make all &.

q: What does rehash do?
a: It rebuilds csh's internal table of where commands live in your path. Run it after you install a new program, or csh will say Command not found. hashstat shows how well the hash is doing.

q: What does the .cshrc file do and how is it different from .login?
a: .cshrc is read by every csh you start, including shell escapes and scripts. .login is read only once at login, after .cshrc. Put aliases and set variables in .cshrc, and terminal setup and setenv PATH in .login.

q: What does the dot command do in sh?
a: A line like . file reads and runs the commands in the current shell instead of a new one. That's how you reload .profile after editing it. In csh the equivalent is source file.

q: What does the set command do in sh?
a: With options it turns on shell flags, like set -x for tracing. With words it sets the positional parameters, so set `date` puts the day in $1 and the month in $2. Alone, it lists all your variables.

q: What does the trap command do?
