a: It catches signals in sh scripts. For example trap 'rm -f /tmp/x.$$; exit' 1 2 15 cleans up if you hang up, hit interrupt, or get killed. Signal 0 runs it at exit.

q: What is $? in sh?
a: It is the exit status of the last command. Zero means success and anything else is a failure. In csh the same thing is $status.

q: What is a here document?
a: It's the << syntax that feeds lines in your script to a command's stdin, up to a terminator word. For example cat << EOF, text, then EOF on a line alone. Variables get expanded unless you quote the terminator.

q: What is ksh and is it worth getting?
a: ksh is David Korn's shell from AT&T Bell Labs, mostly compatible with sh but with history, aliases, job control and command line editing. If your system ships it with SVR4 or you can afford the license, it's well worth it.

q: What is the difference between sh and csh?
a: sh is the Bourne shell, the original and best for scripts. csh is the Berkeley C shell, with history, aliases and job control that make it nicer to type at, but its syntax is odd. Most people script in sh and log in with csh.

q: What is the difference between single and double quotes in the shell?
a: Single quotes pass everything literally. Double quotes still let $variables, backquotes and backslashes work. So echo '$HOME' prints $HOME, while echo "$HOME" prints your directory.

q: What is the meaning of the tilde in csh, like ~bob?
a: ~ is your home directory, and ~bob is the home directory of user bob. That's a csh feature that sh does not have. Some newer shells like ksh also understand it.

q: Which file does sh read when I log in?
a: Just .profile in your home directory, after /etc/profile on System V. Plain sh has no startup file for subshells, so anything you want there needs to be exported from .profile.

q: Why do I get "test: argument expected" in my script?
a: A variable in your test was empty, so test saw fewer arguments than expected. Quote it like [ "$x" = yes ]. Some old versions of test also choke if the variable starts with a dash.

q: Why does csh say "Too many arguments" when I use *?
a: The wildcard expanded to more names than the shell or kernel allows, usually about 10240 bytes on a lot of systems. Use find with xargs, or loop through smaller patterns, instead of one huge glob.

q: Why does my cd in a script not change my directory?
a: A script runs in a child shell, and a directory change there dies with it. Run it with . script in sh or source script in csh, so it runs in your shell. Or make it an alias in csh.

q: Why does my script print "if: Expression Syntax" in csh?
a: csh expressions are picky about spaces and parentheses, and a variable that is empty or unset breaks them. Write if ($x == foo) then with spaces around the operator. Check that $x is set with $?x first.

q: Why does my shell script work from sh but fail when I run it from csh?
a: Probably csh is running it itself, since it has no #! line. csh will hand scripts starting with # to csh, otherwise to sh. Put #!/bin/sh on the first line, or run it explicitly as sh script.

q: Why doesn't Control-Z work on my System V machine?
a: Older System V kernels, up through SVR3, have no job control, so the tty driver doesn't support stopping jobs. Some vendors add it, and SVR4 will have it with the new sh and ksh. Otherwise use layers on a 5620 terminal if you have one.

q: Can grep search for two words at once?
a: With egrep, yes: egrep 'foo|bar' file. Plain grep has no alternation, but fgrep accepts several strings if you put them on separate lines inside one quoted argument.

q: Can sed do more than one edit in one pass?
a: Yes, give it several -e options or put the commands on separate lines in a script file and use -f. Each line of input goes through all the commands in order.

q: Can sed edit a file in place?
a: Not in any sed I know of. It writes to stdout, so send it to a temp file and then mv that over the original. Some people use ed or ex scripts when they really want in-place edits.

q: How can I get a list of all usernames from /etc/passwd?
a: Try awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd. The -F: sets the field separator to a colon, and the login name is the first field. cut -d: -f1 also works on System V.

q: How can I pass a shell variable into an awk program?
a: Put the program in double quotes carefully, or better, end the command with var=value before the file name, like awk '{print x}' x=$HOME file. That assignment happens after BEGIN though. nawk has -v for it.

q: How can I pipe stderr in csh?
a: Use cmd |& other in csh, which sends both stdout and stderr down the pipe. You can't separate them in csh easily. If you need to, run the pipeline under sh -c instead.

q: How can I see which processes of mine are running without grep showing up in the list?
a: Use ps -ef | grep '[s]hell' style patterns. The bracket trick makes the grep command line not match its own pattern. Otherwise add a second grep -v grep to the pipeline.

q: How do I add up a column of numbers with awk?
a: awk '{s += $1} END {print s}' file sums the first column. The END block runs once after the last line is read. Uninitialized variables start at zero, so no setup is needed.

q: How do I change the field separator in awk?
a: Use -F on the command line, like awk -F: '...', or set FS in a BEGIN block. A tab is awk -F' '. Some old awks only take a single character for FS, so check yours.

q: How do I convert upper case to lower case in a pipe?
a: tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' does it on BSD, and tr '[A-Z]' '[a-z]' on older System V. Use it as cmd | tr A-Z a-z. Note that tr only reads stdin and cannot take a file name.

q: How do I count the lines that match a pattern?
a: Use grep -c pattern file. It prints just the number of matching lines, not the number of matches, so two hits on one line count once.

q: How do I delete blank lines from a file?
a: sed '/^$/d' file removes empty lines. If lines might hold only spaces or tabs, use sed '/^[ ]*$/d' instead, though some seds want a literal tab typed in.

q: How do I find the ten most common words in a text file?
a: tr -cs 'A-Za-z' '\012' < file | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10. That is the classic one from Bentley's Programming Pearls column. Old System V tr wants bracket syntax, like '[A-Za-z]'.

q: How do I get grep to show lines around the match?
a: Standard grep can't. Some versions of grep have no context option at all. You can do it with awk or sed, or get one of the free greps from comp.sources.unix that supports context.

q: How do I grep for a line containing a literal dot or star?
a: Put a backslash in front, like grep 'version 1\.2' file. Inside brackets they are already literal, so [.] works too. Use single quotes so the shell does not eat the backslash.

q: How do I make grep ignore upper and lower case?
a: Use grep -i pattern file. That works on BSD and System V grep both. Very old V7 greps don't have it, so on those you have to write a [Ss][Ee] bracket pattern by hand.

q: How do I print just the third column of a file with awk?
a: awk '{print $3}' file will do it. Fields are split on whitespace by default. If your file uses colons or something else, add -F: before the program.

q: How do I print only lines 10 through 20 of a file?
a: sed -n '10,20p' file does it. The -n turns off automatic printing, so only the lines you ask for with p appear. Add 20q to stop reading early on a big file.

q: How do I print only lines longer than 80 characters with awk?
a: awk 'length > 80' file works. With no action given, awk prints each line for which the pattern is true. On old awk you may need length($0) > 80 instead.

q: How do I put a newline in the replacement text with sed?
a: Put a backslash followed by an actual newline in the script, like s/,/\<newline>/g typed over two lines. Sed can't take \n in the replacement on most systems, only in the pattern on a few.

q: How do I replace every occurrence of foo with bar in a file using sed?
a: sed 's/foo/bar/g' file > newfile. Without the g only the first match on each line changes. Don't redirect back to the same file or you will empty it; use a temp file and mv.

q: How do I search for a string in all files under a directory tree?
a: find . -type f -print | xargs grep string. On systems without xargs use find . -type f -exec grep string {} /dev/null \;. The /dev/null makes grep print file names.

q: How do I search for a word in all the files in a directory?
a: Use grep word *. If you want to know which files match without seeing the lines, add -l. Note that it won't descend into subdirectories, so use find with xargs grep for that.

q: How do I see the first few lines of command output?
a: Pipe it to head, like ps -ef | head. On older systems without head, sed 10q does the same thing. The command may get a broken pipe signal when head quits, which is normal.

q: How do I sort a file and remove duplicate lines?
a: sort file | uniq will do it, or sort -u file on System V and newer BSD. Remember uniq only collapses adjacent identical lines, so the sort comes first.

q: How do I tell sed to only change lines that match some pattern?
a: Put an address in front, like sed '/^Subject:/s/Re: //' file. The substitute runs only on lines matching that address. You can also use line numbers or ranges like 1,10s/a/b/.

q: How do I use part of the match again in sed?
a: Mark the part with \( and \) in the pattern, then refer to it as \1 through \9 in the replacement. For example s/\(.*\) \(.*\)/\2 \1/ swaps two words.

q: Is it worth learning awk if I already know Perl?
a: Perl is a superset in practice and faster on big jobs, but awk is on every Unix box and Perl often isn't. For quick one-liners awk is fine and you can count on it being there.

q: Is there a limit to how many commands I can chain with pipes?
a: No fixed small limit in the shell, but each stage is a process, so you are bound by your process table. Chains of five or six are common. Pipe buffers are about 4K to 10K on most systems.

q: Is there a way to use awk to print the last field on each line?
a: Yes, awk '{print $NF}' file. NF is the number of fields on the current line, so $NF is the last one. It works even when the lines have different numbers of fields.

q: Is there a way to watch data going through a pipe?
a: Put tee in the middle, like cmd1 | tee /tmp/look | cmd2. It copies its input to the file and also passes it on. That is the best way to debug a long pipeline stage by stage.

q: What do BEGIN and END mean in an awk program?
a: BEGIN actions run once before any input is read, good for setting FS or printing headers. END actions run after the last line, good for totals. Neither is tied to any line of input.

q: What does $0 mean in awk?
a: It is the whole current input line. $1 is the first field, $2 the second, and so on. If you assign to $0 awk resplits the fields, and if you assign to a field it rebuilds $0.

q: What does 2>&1 mean?
a: In the Bourne shell it sends file descriptor 2, standard error, to wherever descriptor 1 is going. So cmd > out 2>&1 puts both in out, and cmd 2>&1 | more pages both. csh doesn't have it; use >& there.

q: What does ^ and $ mean in a grep pattern?
a: The ^ matches the start of a line and $ matches the end. So grep '^From ' finds mail message headers in a mailbox, and grep 'x$' finds lines ending in x.

q: What does awk stand for?
a: It's the initials of the authors, Aho, Weinberger and Kernighan, from Bell Labs. The book The AWK Programming Language by those same people came out in 1988 and is well worth owning.

q: What does sed stand for?
a: Stream editor. It reads input a line at a time, applies your editing commands, and writes the result to standard output. It was written by Lee McMahon at Bell Labs, based on ed.

q: What does the -v option to grep do?
a: It inverts the match, so grep prints only the lines that do NOT contain the pattern. Handy for stripping comments out of a file, like grep -v '^#' file.

q: What does the pipe symbol do in the shell?
a: It connects the standard output of the command on the left to the standard input of the command on the right. So ls | wc -l counts your files without making a temp file.

q: What is a named pipe, and how is it different from a regular pipe?
a: A named pipe, or FIFO, is a pipe with a name in the filesystem, made with mknod name p. Unrelated processes can open it. System V has them, and BSD only got them recently, so check your system.

q: What is nawk and why is it different from awk?
a: nawk is the new awk that came with the 1988 book and System V Release 3.1 and 4. It adds functions, getline, multiple -f files and more string functions. Old awk lacks those, so check which one you have.

q: What is the & in a sed substitute command?
a: In the replacement part, & stands for whatever text the pattern matched. So s/[0-9]*/(&)/ wraps the number in parentheses. Write \& if you want a real ampersand.

q: What is the difference between > and | ?
a: The > sends output to a file, while | sends it to another program. If you write ls > wc you create a file named wc and run nothing. You want ls | wc.

q: What is the difference between grep, egrep and fgrep?
a: grep uses basic regular expressions, egrep adds extended ones like + ? | and parentheses, and fgrep only searches fixed strings but can take many at once with -f. fgrep is usually fastest for plain words.

q: Which is faster, grep or awk for simple matching?
a: grep, by a good margin. It is a tight little program built for one job, while awk has to parse a program and split fields. Use awk when you need columns or arithmetic, not for plain matching.

q: Why do I get 'Broken pipe' when I run a command into head?
a: Head exits after it has printed what you asked for, and the writing program gets a SIGPIPE when it next writes to a closed pipe. It is harmless. The writer was just told nobody is listening.

q: Why do people put /dev/null on a grep command line?
a: With only one file grep doesn't print the file name. Adding /dev/null as a second file makes it show the name for each match, and it never matches anything itself. It's an old trick with find -exec.

q: Why does grep '*.c' not list my C files?
a: Because grep takes a regular expression, not a shell wildcard. The * means zero or more of the previous character. You want ls | grep '\.c$', or just ls *.c.

q: Why does my sed command say 'command garbled'?
a: Usually a typo in the script, like a missing slash or an unescaped slash inside the pattern. Pick another delimiter if your text has slashes, for example s,/usr/bin,/bin,. Also quote the script so the shell leaves it alone.

q: Why does my shell script with a pipe lose a variable I set inside the loop?
a: In the Bourne shell a while loop at the end of a pipe runs in a subshell, so changes to variables vanish when it ends. Redirect the file into the loop with < file instead of using cat file |.

q: Why does ps -ef | grep foo always show the grep itself?
a: Because the grep process is running with foo on its command line while ps looks. Use ps -ef | grep foo | grep -v grep, or write the pattern as [f]oo so it doesn't match itself.

q: Can I run Unix programs on a VAX running VMS?
a: Not directly. You can port them using VAX C, but expect trouble with Unix-specific calls and file names. Some sites run Eunice or buy the VMS-based Unix-like tools, but if you need real Unix, run Ultrix on that machine instead.

q: Can I run VMS on a non-DEC computer?
a: No, not legitimately. VMS only runs on VAX hardware, and a few approved clones. Some folks run a PDP-11 with RSX or RSTS, which are different. If you want VMS-like tools elsewhere, look at the DCL lookalikes that exist for Unix.

q: Can I use a PC as a terminal for my VAX?
a: Yes. Run a terminal emulator such as Kermit or Procomm in VT100 mode over a serial line. Set 9600 baud, 8 bits, no parity, and set the VMS side to match with SET TERMINAL. DEC also sells DECnet-DOS for PCs on Ethernet.

q: How can I get the Usenet news on a VAX running VMS?
a: You need a news package such as the VMS port of C News or the NNTP-based VMS news software, plus a UUCP or Internet link. Many sites run Bnews ported by folks at various universities. Expect to spend a weekend on setup.

q: How can I tell which VMS version I am running?
a: Type SHOW SYSTEM at the prompt, which shows the version in the header line, or use WRITE SYS$OUTPUT F$GETSYI("VERSION"). The first line after login often shows it too, such as VAX/VMS V5.1.

q: How do I back up a disk on VMS?
a: Use the BACKUP utility. For a full image backup, mount a tape and type BACKUP/IMAGE DUA0: MUA0:SAVE.BCK/SAVE_SET. Image backups need a standalone system for the system disk. For files, BACKUP/RECORD with /SINCE does incrementals.

q: How do I copy a file to another VAX over DECnet?
a: Use COPY with the node name in the spec, like COPY FILE.TXT NODEB::DISK$USER:[SMITH]FILE.TXT. You may need to put username and password in quotes after the node name unless a proxy account is set up.

q: How do I delete all old versions of a file in VMS?
a: Use PURGE. PURGE file.ext keeps only the highest version. Add /KEEP=3 if you want the latest three. Without a filespec it purges everything in your current directory, so be sure where you are.

q: How do I find a file anywhere on a VMS disk?
a: Use DIRECTORY with the ellipsis wildcard, like DIRECTORY DUA1:[000000...]FILENAME.EXT. It walks every subdirectory from the top. It can be slow on a big disk but works on all versions.

q: How do I get a directory listing sorted by date on VMS?
a: Use DIRECTORY/DATE with the /SINCE or /BEFORE qualifiers to filter by date. VMS DIRECTORY has no real sort option, so people pipe through SORT after sending output to a file, or just live with the alphabetical order.

q: How do I give another user access to my files?
a: Use SET PROTECTION, like SET PROTECTION=(G:R,W:R) FILE.TXT, for group and world read. For finer control, VMS 4.x and up have ACLs, set with SET ACL or EDIT/ACL, where you can name specific users with identifiers.

q: How do I print a file on a VMS system?
a: Use PRINT filename. Add /QUEUE=name for a specific printer, /COPIES=n for multiples, and /FORM if you need special paper. SHOW QUEUE shows what's waiting, and DELETE/ENTRY=n removes your job from the queue.

q: How do I read a Unix tar tape on a VAX?
a: VMS cannot read tar natively. Either get a public domain VMS tar program from the net, or move the data over Ethernet or serial with kermit. Check the tape blocksize too, because the VMS tape driver is picky about it.

q: How do I recover a forgotten SYSTEM password?
a: Do a conditional boot with SYSBOOT, set UAFALTERNATE to 1, and let it use a minimal alternate UAF, or boot with the startup set to minimal and fix the record. Only do this on a machine you manage, and follow the manual's steps carefully.

q: How do I see who else is logged on to my VAX?
a: Type SHOW USERS at the DCL prompt. It lists each process with its username, terminal, and PID. SHOW USERS/FULL gives more detail if you have the privileges. For a quick check of one person, try FINGER if your site has it installed.

q: How do I set my terminal to 132 columns?
a: Type SET TERMINAL/WIDTH=132 on a VT100 or VT220. The terminal itself must also switch modes, which you can do from its setup screen or by sending the escape sequence ESC [ ? 3 h. Without both, lines wrap oddly.

q: How do I stop a runaway process of mine?
a: Type SHOW SYSTEM or SHOW USERS to get the PID, then STOP/ID=pid. If it's on your terminal, Ctrl-Y gets you to the DCL prompt and then you can type STOP. Ctrl-C only interrupts, it may not kill it.

q: How do I submit a batch job on VMS?
a: Put your DCL commands in a .COM file and type SUBMIT JOB.COM. Add /QUEUE=name to pick a queue, /AFTER=time to delay it, and /NOTIFY to get a message when it finishes. Output goes to JOB.LOG in your directory.

q: How do I write a simple DCL command procedure?
a: Put DCL commands in a file ending in .COM and run it with @FILENAME. You can use symbols, IF-THEN-ENDIF, GOTO labels, and parameters named P1 to P8. Use $ at the start of every command line.

q: How much memory can a MicroVAX II hold?
a: The MicroVAX II maxes out at 16 megabytes on its memory boards. Most people run with 5 to 9 MB. VMS likes memory, so if it's paging a lot, more RAM is the cheapest upgrade you can buy.

q: Is VMS better than Unix for a small department?
a: Depends on what you run. VMS has better clustering, batch queues, security, and support from DEC, and it's solid for commercial and lab work. Unix is cheaper, more portable, and has better tools for programmers. Ultrix gives you BSD on a VAX if you want that.

q: Is it worth upgrading from VMS 4.7 to 5.0?
a: Version 5 adds the new TPU editor, better clustering, and many bug fixes, but also changes a lot of things. Wait for 5.1 or a later patch release if you can, read the release notes thoroughly, and back up everything before you try it.

q: Is the VAX 8800 worth it for a university computing center?
a: If you have a few hundred users and heavy number crunching, yes. It's a dual-processor machine at about 12 VUPs, and runs in a VAXcluster. The price runs well into seven figures, so compare against a few VAX 6000s in a cluster.

q: Should I buy a VAXstation or a MicroVAX for a lab?
a: If you need graphics, get a VAXstation like the 2000 or 3100, which runs DECwindows on VMS. If it's just a multiuser box for terminals, the MicroVAX is cheaper and has the same CPU. VAXstations also work well as cluster workstations.

q: What are VUPs?
a: VAX Unit of Performance. One VUP equals the speed of a VAX-11/780. A VAX 8650 is about 6 VUPs and the 8800 is around 12. DEC uses it to compare their machines, though real speed depends heavily on your workload.

q: What does %SYSTEM-F-EXQUOTA mean?
a: You exceeded one of your account quotas, such as disk quota, open file limit, or buffered I/O limit. For disk, try PURGE and delete junk. For other quotas, the system manager must raise them in the authorization file with AUTHORIZE.

q: What does Ctrl-T do on VMS?
a: It prints a one-line status of your current process: the time, node, username, current image, CPU time, page faults, and I/O count. It's useful for checking whether a long job is still doing anything or is hung.

q: What does PID mean in SHOW SYSTEM output?
a: It's the process identification number, an 8-digit hex value that uniquely names each process. You use it with STOP/ID=pid or SET PROCESS/ID=pid to control a process other than your own.

q: What does SYS$SYSDEVICE refer to?
a: It's a logical name pointing to the disk you booted VMS from, where the system directories like SYS$SYSTEM and SYS$LIBRARY live. Using logicals like that instead of real device names keeps your command files working when disks get moved.

q: What does a MicroVAX 3600 offer over a MicroVAX II?
a: The 3600 uses the CVAX chip and is about 3 VUPs, roughly three times faster than a MicroVAX II. It runs on the Q-bus too, takes up to 64 MB of memory, and is a popular choice for departmental servers.

q: What does the %SYSTEM-F-NOPRIV error mean?
a: It means you tried something your account lacks the privilege for. Check SHOW PROCESS/PRIVILEGES to see what you have. Ask your system manager for the needed one, like OPER or SYSPRV, rather than hoping it goes away.

q: What does the BACKUP error ACCONFLICT mean?
a: An access conflict. Another process has the file open for writing, so BACKUP cannot read a consistent copy. Use /IGNORE=INTERLOCK to copy it anyway, understanding the saved file might be inconsistent, or wait until the file is closed.

q: What does the DCL command SET DEFAULT do?
a: It changes your default device and directory, like cd on Unix. For example SET DEFAULT DUA1:[SMITH.WORK] moves you there. SET DEFAULT [-] goes up one directory level, and SHOW DEFAULT tells you where you are.

q: What does the SET TERMINAL/INQUIRE command do?
a: It asks the terminal for its identity and sets VMS to treat it as that type. It works for DEC terminals like the VT100 and VT220 that answer the request. For other terminals, use SET TERMINAL/DEVICE_TYPE=VT100 or similar by hand.

q: What is AUTOGEN?
a: It's the VMS procedure, SYS$UPDATE:AUTOGEN.COM, that recalculates SYSGEN parameters based on your hardware and observed usage from the last run. Run it after adding memory or disks, then reboot so the new values take effect.

q: What is DECnet and do I need it?
a: DECnet is Digital's networking protocol suite, letting VAXes share files, run remote tasks, and send mail. If you have more than one DEC machine on Ethernet or serial links, it's well worth setting up. Phase IV is the current version.

q: What is DECwindows?
a: It's DEC's graphical user interface for VMS, built on the X Window System from MIT, with the Motif toolkit. It first shipped with VMS 4.7 and needs a VAXstation or an X terminal. It uses lots of memory, so plan on at least 8 MB.

q: What is RMS?
a: Record Management Services is the part of VMS that handles files and records. It provides sequential, relative, and indexed organizations. Most languages on VMS go through RMS, which is why ISAM files are so easy to use on VAX.

q: What is VMS Mail and how do I send to someone on another node?
a: Type MAIL, then SEND, and answer the To: prompt. For another DECnet node, use NODE::USER. For Internet or Usenet addresses you need a gateway, often written as IN%"user@host.domain" if the site has MX or PMDF installed.

q: What is a VAXcluster?
a: It's a group of VAX systems and disk controllers like the HSC50 joined by the CI bus or Ethernet, sharing disks, queues, and a common user authorization file. To users it looks like one big system, and if one node dies the others carry on.

q: What is a logical name in VMS?
a: It's an alias for a device, directory, or any string, set with DEFINE or ASSIGN. For example DEFINE WORK DUA1:[SMITH.WORK] lets you type WORK:FILE.TXT. They live in process, group, or system tables depending on your qualifiers.

q: What is the VMS SYSGEN utility used for?
a: SYSGEN lets you view and change system parameters and load device drivers. SHOW/ALL lists parameters, and the CONNECT command sets up new devices like a terminal line or printer. Be careful with WRITE ACTIVE and WRITE CURRENT.

q: What is the best editor on VMS, EDT or TPU?
a: EDT is the old standby and works on any terminal, with a line mode and a keypad mode. EVE, the TPU-based editor from VMS 5.x, is more flexible and programmable. Many people use EDT out of habit, but EVE is where DEC is heading.

q: What is the difference between SPAWN and ATTACH?
a: SPAWN creates a subprocess so you can run DCL commands without leaving your current program. ATTACH switches your terminal back to another process, like the parent. Use LOGOUT to end the subprocess and return to the parent.

q: What is the difference between VAX C and VAX FORTRAN for scientific work?
a: FORTRAN is the usual choice for number crunching on VAX. DEC's compiler is very good, has vectorizing support on the 9000 series later, and works well with the VMS runtime library. VAX C is fine but mostly used for systems or ported code.

q: What is the difference between a VAX 11/780 and a MicroVAX II?
a: Both are about 1 MIPS, which is why the 780 is the VUP baseline. The 780 is a big multi-cabinet machine on the SBI bus, while the MicroVAX II is a small box on a Q-bus with far lower cost, power, and cooling needs.

q: Why do I get a file locked error when two people open the same file?
a: RMS controls sharing through file access options. If the first program opened it without allowing shared access, others get a locked or privilege violation error. Programs must open with the right share flags for concurrent readers or writers.

q: Why does VMS keep making file.txt;1 and file.txt;2?
a: VMS never overwrites a file when you edit it. It creates a new version with the next number and leaves the old one. That's handy for undoing mistakes, but you have to PURGE now and then or your quota fills up.

q: Why does my VT220 show garbage characters on VMS?
a: Likely a mismatch of baud rate, parity, or character set. Check the terminal setup matches the host port, usually 8 bits and no parity. If you see odd accents, the terminal is in 7-bit mode while VMS sends 8-bit, so set SET TERMINAL/EIGHT_BIT.

q: Why is my VAX so slow when everyone logs in?
a: Probably memory or disk I/O rather than CPU. Run MONITOR SYSTEM and MONITOR PAGE to check page faults and look at disk queue lengths. If you're paging heavily, add memory or tune your working set parameters with AUTOGEN.

q: Can I put a Sun-3 tape drive on a SPARCstation?
a: If it is a SCSI drive, probably yes. Sun's tape devices use the st driver, and a 1/4 inch QIC cartridge drive is /dev/rst0. Make sure the target number does not clash with your disk.

q: Can I run SunView and X11 on the same Sun?
a: Yes, they can coexist. You start X from a shell inside SunView or, better, from the console with xinit. X11R4 builds fine on SunOS 4.0 or 4.1, and many people are moving to it from SunView.

q: Can I use a PC monitor or a regular terminal as a Sun console?
a: Yes, if you set the keyboard-less machine to use ttya as console. Unplug the keyboard and connect a terminal at 9600 baud to serial port A. The monitor will then talk through the serial line.

q: Can a Sun-3/50 run SunOS 4.1?
a: Yes, SunOS 4.1 supports Sun-3 machines, including the 3/50, but it will be slow with only 4 MB. I would recommend at least 8 MB, and do not expect X11 to run well on that machine.

q: Does Sun's cc support ANSI C prototypes?
a: Not the stock one in SunOS 4.1. You need to buy the ANSI C compiler as a separate unbundled product, or use GNU gcc, which is free and works well on both Sun-3 and Sun-4.

q: How big should my swap space be on a Sun?
a: A common rule is two to three times the physical memory, though you can get by with less. For a 16 MB machine, 32 to 48 MB of swap is reasonable, and you can add more with swapon.

q: How do I add more swap on SunOS?
a: Make a file with mkfile 20m /export/swap2 and then run swapon /export/swap2. Put it in /etc/fstab to keep it after reboot. This feature came with SunOS 4.0, so older versions need a partition.

q: How do I back up my Sun to tape?
a: Use dump, for example dump 0usf 54000 /dev/rst0 /usr, for a full level 0 backup. Restore with restore or restore -i. For smaller jobs tar cvf /dev/rst0 directory works fine.

q: How do I boot my Sun from a different disk?
a: At the monitor prompt, type b sd(0,1,0) to boot from SCSI target 1 on Sun-3. On Sun-4 it works the same way, and the arguments are controller, unit, and partition. Check your target numbers first.

q: How do I check a filesystem after a crash?
a: Boot single user and run fsck on each filesystem, for example fsck /dev/rsd0a. Answer yes to its fixes, and then reboot. Always use the raw device, which has the r in front.

q: How do I compile a program with the Sun C compiler?
a: Use cc -o prog prog.c, with -O for optimization. SunOS ships the BSD-flavoured cc, and on Sun-4 it generates SPARC code. If you want ANSI C, get gcc from the GNU distribution instead.

q: How do I find out what version of SunOS I am running?
a: Type uname -a or cat /etc/motd. On older 3.x systems, uname may not exist, so try /usr/bin/what on /vmunix. SunOS 4.0 and 4.1 will show up in the uname -r output.

q: How do I find the Ethernet address of my Sun?
a: Look at the banner on power-up, which prints Ethernet address 8:0:20:xx:xx:xx. Once running, ifconfig le0 shows it too on some versions, and Sun addresses always begin with 8:0:20.

q: How do I get gcc running on my Sun?
a: Get the gcc source from prep.ai.mit.edu by FTP and build it with the stock cc. Configure it for sun3 or sun4 and then rebuild it with itself. You need about 20 MB of free disk space.

q: How do I get on Usenet or the Internet from a Sun?
a: Get a feed from a nearby site, often by UUCP over a modem, and install C News or B News. For Internet access you need a TCP/IP connection, and SunOS already includes the stack and sendmail.

q: How do I make a Sun boot into single user mode?
a: At the monitor prompt, type b -s. You get a root shell with only the root filesystem mounted, so run fsck and mount -a if you want to do real work.

q: How do I mount a remote disk using NFS?
a: Make sure the server lists the directory in /etc/exports and runs exportfs, then on your machine do mount server:/usr/local /usr/local as root. Add it to /etc/fstab to have it mounted at boot.

q: How do I print to a PostScript laser printer from my Sun?
a: Set up an entry in /etc/printcap with the printer's serial or network address and use lpr -Pname file. For plain text, run it through enscript first so the printer gets PostScript.

q: How do I see my YP password entry?
a: Run ypcat passwd or ypmatch yourname passwd. If you want to change your password in the YP map, use yppasswd instead of passwd, since plain passwd only changes the local file.

q: How do I set the date and time on a Sun?
a: As root, run date yymmddhhmm, for example date 8912311530. For a network, run timed or ntp so that machines stay in sync. The battery-backed clock keeps time while the power is off.

q: How do I set up a diskless Sun client?
a: On the server, add the client to /etc/hosts, /etc/ethers, and /etc/bootparams, then create root and swap directories under /export and run the add_client script. Start rarpd and tftpd as well.

q: How do I set up a modem on a Sun serial port for dial-out?
a: Use /dev/ttya or ttyb with tip and put a line in /etc/remote for your modem's speed. Make sure no getty is running on that port in /etc/ttytab, then run tip modemname.

q: How do I use rlogin and rsh to get to other Suns?
a: Add the remote hostname to the ~/.rhosts file on the target, or to /etc/hosts.equiv. Then rlogin host gives you a session without a password, and rsh host command runs a single command.

q: How much memory do I need to run SunOS 4.1 comfortably?
a: 8 MB will run it, but 16 MB is far nicer, especially with X and a compiler going. Diskless clients swap over the network, so memory matters even more there.

q: I forgot the root password on my Sun, what can I do?
a: Boot single user with b -s from the monitor, which on older SunOS gives you a root shell without a password. Then edit /etc/passwd to blank the root entry. Newer versions may ask for it, so boot from tape.

q: Is SunOS 4.1 a Berkeley or System V Unix?
a: Mostly BSD at its core, with a lot of System V compatibility added. You get /usr/5bin for the SysV versions of commands and the SysV-style libraries if you need to compile AT&T code.

q: Is a SPARCstation 1 worth it over a Sun 3/60?
a: Yes if you can afford it. The SPARCstation 1 runs at about 12 MIPS against roughly 3 for the 3/60, and costs only a bit more. Just remember you will have to recompile any Sun-3 software you have.

q: What are Sun's rev levels of the 3/50, 3/60, and 3/160?
a: The 3/50 and 3/60 are 68020 desktop models at 15 MHz and 20 MHz, and the 3/160 is a deskside VME machine at 16.7 MHz. The 3/60 has a better graphics option and can take up to 24 MB of RAM.

q: What do the sd0a and sd0b names mean?
a: sd is the SCSI disk driver, 0 is the unit, and the letter is the partition. By convention a is root, b is swap, g is usually /usr, and c covers the whole disk.

q: What does NFS stand for and what does it do?
a: Network File System. It lets one Sun mount directories from another over Ethernet so they look like local disks. You export on the server in /etc/exports and mount on the client with the mount command.

q: What does NIS or Yellow Pages do?
a: It shares files like /etc/passwd, /etc/hosts, and /etc/group across all machines in a domain from one master server. Sun renamed it NIS but most people still say YP, and commands like ypcat and ypmatch still use that name.

q: What does bad trap or panic mean on my Sun?
a: The kernel hit a fatal fault and halted. Write down the message, and after the reboot run fsck. Frequent panics usually point to bad memory, a failing disk, or a kernel driver bug.

q: What does sendmail.cf do and why is it so awful to edit?
a: It is the config file telling sendmail how to rewrite addresses and route mail. Its syntax is cryptic, so start from Sun's main.mc or a sample from the net and change only the few things you need.

q: What does the color frame buffer cg2 versus cg4 mean?
a: cg2 is an older 8-bit color board for Sun-3 and Sun-4 VME machines, while cg4 is a cheaper 8-bit card with a monochrome plane on top, used in the 3/60 and 4/110. Both give 256 colors.

q: What does the ok prompt or the > prompt mean when my Sun stops booting?
a: That is the PROM monitor. A > prompt means the old monitor, so type b to boot or c to continue after a break. Newer machines show an ok prompt from the Forth monitor, where you type boot.

q: What is NeWS and should I bother with it?
a: NeWS is Sun's PostScript-based window system, using a PostScript interpreter in the server. It is nice technically, but most third-party software is written for X11, so I would learn X first.

q: What is a QIC-24 tape versus QIC-150?
a: QIC-24 holds 60 MB and QIC-150 holds 150 MB or more. Sun SCSI drives usually read the older formats, but a QIC-24 drive cannot read a QIC-150 tape. Check the density option when you write.

q: What is a Sun 386i and does it run Sun software?
a: It is an Intel 80386 machine running SunOS 4.0, with some PC compatibility. It does not run SPARC or 68k binaries, so software support is thinner. I would pick a SPARC or Sun-3 instead.

q: What is the Sun Workstation's biggest weakness compared to an HP or DEC?
a: Mostly price for the larger configurations, and early SunOS releases were buggy. On the other hand, the Sun has a huge software base, NFS everywhere, and a good deal on price per MIPS against the VAXstation.

q: What is the Sun type 4 keyboard Stop-A for?
a: Stop-A, or L1-A, drops the machine into the PROM monitor, halting the OS. Type c to continue if you hit it by accident, though sometimes the filesystems will be messy and you may need fsck.

q: What is the Sun386i or Sun-3 hostid?
a: It is a unique machine ID stored in the PROM, and many licensed packages use it for node-locked license keys. Run hostid to see it. The first byte tells you the architecture, for example 17 for Sun-3.

q: What is the best way to add a second disk to a Sun?
a: Get a SCSI disk, set its target to something unused like 1, cable it, and format it using the format program on SunOS 4. Then use newfs, make a mount point, and add a line to /etc/fstab.

q: What is the difference between SunOS 3.5 and 4.0?
a: 4.0 brought a new virtual memory system, shared libraries, dynamic linking, and a lot of kernel changes based on System V ideas. It was buggy early on, and 4.0.3 is the one to run before 4.1.

q: What is the difference between a Sun-3 and a Sun-4?
a: Sun-3 uses the Motorola 68020 and Sun-4 uses Sun's own SPARC RISC chip, first shipped in the 4/260 in 1987. Sun-4 is several times faster, but binaries are not compatible between the two, so you need to recompile.

q: What is the file /etc/ethers for?
a: It maps Ethernet addresses to hostnames so rarpd can answer a diskless machine asking who it is at boot. Each line is the 48-bit address like 8:0:20:1:2:3 followed by the hostname.

q: Why does ifconfig show le0 on my machine but ie0 on another?
a: le is the Lance Ethernet chip used on newer machines like the SPARCstation and 3/80. ie is the older Intel 82586 interface used on Sun-3 and early Sun-4 models. Both are the same to the user.

q: Why does my NFS server say stale file handle?
a: The file or directory was deleted or the filesystem was recreated on the server while you had it mounted. Unmount and remount on the client, and kill any process still sitting in the old directory.

q: Why is my Sun screen slow when I use the 1152x900 display?
a: A monochrome bwtwo is fast because it moves one bit per pixel. Color boards move eight bits per pixel, so scrolling and window moves take longer. Make sure you are not using a software frame buffer.

q: Can I get a hard disk for my NeXT instead of the optical drive?
a: Yes, later cubes and the NeXTstation ship with SCSI hard disks, like 330MB and up. The original machine can use external SCSI drives too, and you can boot from them if you load the system on them.

q: Can I read Mac or DOS floppies on the NeXT?
a: The cube has a 2.88MB floppy drive, which also handles 1.44MB DOS disks with the right software. Mac disks are harder, and many people just move files over Ethernet with ftp instead.

q: Can I run my Unix software on the NeXT?
a: Mostly yes. Plenty of BSD source compiles with minor changes, and you get sockets, NFS and the usual tools. Some System V code needs porting work, and X11 programs need an X server, which you have to add.

q: Can I send voice messages in NeXT Mail?
a: Yes, you record from the microphone and attach the sound to a message. The other person needs a NeXT or other software that reads NeXT mail to hear it, though.

q: Can I use a regular PostScript printer with my NeXT?
a: Yes, an Apple LaserWriter or any PostScript printer on the network works. Add it with the Printer setup in the system software and print from any app.

q: Can I use a regular keyboard and mouse with the NeXT?
a: The NeXT keyboard and mouse connect through the monitor and use a custom connector. Third-party PC or Mac parts will not plug in, so you use the NeXT ones.

q: Can the NeXT talk to Sun workstations on a network?
a: Yes. It has built-in Ethernet, runs TCP/IP, and supports NFS, so you can mount Sun filesystems and use rlogin, telnet and ftp. It fits fine into a mixed Unix shop.

q: Does the NeXT run Mac or MS-DOS programs?
a: Not natively. There is no official emulator for either, so you need software written or ported for NeXTstep, or a Unix program you compile yourself.

q: Does the NeXT run X Windows?
a: Not natively, since the window system is Display PostScript. Third-party X servers exist and let you run X clients, but NeXTstep itself is a different environment.

q: How big is the NeXT monitor?
a: It's a 17 inch monochrome display at 1120 by 832 pixels, about 92 dpi. It plugs into the cube through the same cable that carries power to the display.

q: How do I add a new user on a NeXT?
a: Use the UserManager application, which edits the NetInfo database for you. On the command line you can also use niutil, but UserManager is far less error-prone.

q: How do I get a command line on the NeXT?
a: Open the Terminal application, or type >console as a user name in the login window to drop to a text console. From there you have the usual Unix shell.

q: How do I log in as root on a NeXT?
a: Type root as the user name in the login window. By default the root account has no password, so set one with passwd right away, especially if the machine is on a network.

q: How do I reboot a hung NeXT?
a: Often you can log in over the network and kill the stuck process. If not, the power key on the keyboard or the switch on the back will restart it, but you risk a filesystem check on the next boot.

q: How much RAM does a NeXT need?
a: The cube comes with 8MB and takes up to 16MB on the original board using 1MB SIMMs. NeXTstep is happier with more, and 8MB feels cramped once you run Mail, Edit and a couple of other apps.

q: How much does a NeXT cost?
a: The original 1988 announcement said $6,500 for the cube with monitor, optical drive and keyboard, though that was for universities. Add the laser printer at around $2,650. Real-world setups with extra RAM and a hard disk run well above that.

q: Is a NeXT better than a Mac II?
a: For programming, networking and multitasking, yes, the NeXT is much stronger. For software choice, color and price, the Mac II wins, so it depends what you plan to do.

q: Is the NeXT a good machine for a college student?
a: If your school has the education discount of around $5,000, it's a strong machine for programming and writing papers, with the printer and dictionary built in. But check software for your major first, because the library is small.

q: Is the NeXT really running Unix?
a: Yes. The OS is NeXTstep, built on the Mach kernel from Carnegie Mellon with 4.3BSD compatibility. You get csh, vi, cc, TCP/IP and NFS, with a graphical shell on top.

q: Is the NeXT worth it for a hobbyist?
a: Only if you like programming and want a fun Unix machine. The cost is high, and a PC clone or Mac has far more off-the-shelf software. NeXT makes sense if the Application Kit appeals to you.

q: Is the optical disk any good as the main drive?
a: It holds 256MB and is removable, which is nice for backups and moving data around. But it is slow, with seek times around 90 ms or worse, so most people want a hard disk for swap and everyday work.

q: Is there a spreadsheet for the NeXT?
a: Lotus announced Improv for the NeXT, a new kind of spreadsheet which lets you rearrange tables by dragging headings. Wingz from Informix is also talked about for the machine.

q: NeXT or a Sun SPARCstation, which should I buy?
a: The SPARCstation is faster, runs more commercial Unix software and has color options. The NeXT is nicer to use, has better development tools and costs less in the education market.

q: What CPU does the NeXT use?
a: The original NeXT Computer has a Motorola 68030 at 25 MHz with a 68882 floating point chip. The newer NeXTcube and NeXTstation announced in 1990 move to the 68040.

q: What comes bundled with the NeXT?
a: You get NeXTstep, Mail, Edit, Preview, the Digital Librarian with Webster's and the Oxford Quotations, Shakespeare, plus the developer tools and Interface Builder. Mathematica is bundled on some configurations too.

q: What does the DSP chip in the NeXT do?
a: It's a Motorola 56001 digital signal processor. It handles sound, modem-style work and number crunching, and the Sound Kit uses it for CD-quality 16-bit stereo output and for recording from the microphone.

q: What does the Dock do on NeXTstep?
a: It's the column of icons at the upper right of the screen where you keep your favorite applications and the Workspace Manager. You launch programs by double-clicking an icon, and running ones get a dot beside them.

q: What does the NeXT boot monitor do?
a: It's a small ROM monitor you get at a > prompt, for starting up or diagnosing the machine. You can boot from different devices, run tests and set parameters before NeXTstep loads.

q: What does the column browser view mean?
a: Each directory opens as a column to the right of its parent, so you can see the whole path at once. Click a folder and its contents appear in the next column, and files show in the last one.

q: What exactly is the NeXT computer?
a: It's a workstation from Steve Jobs's company NeXT, Inc. Black magnesium cube, 68030 CPU, Mach-based Unix, Display PostScript screen, and a 256MB optical disk. Aimed at universities and researchers at first.

q: What is Display PostScript?
a: It's Adobe's PostScript imaging model used to draw the screen as well as the printer. What you see in a window uses the same fonts and graphics model as the page you print, so WYSIWYG is pretty exact.

q: What is Interface Builder?
a: It's the tool for laying out windows, buttons and menus by drawing them, then wiring them to your Objective-C objects by dragging connections. You can make a working app with surprisingly little code.

q: What is NetInfo?
a: NetInfo is the NeXT database for system administration data like users, groups, hosts and printers. It replaces flat files such as /etc/passwd for many purposes and can be shared across machines on a network.

q: What is Objective-C and do I need to learn it for the NeXT?
a: It's C with Smalltalk-style objects added, using bracket message syntax like [obj doThing]. NeXTstep's Application Kit is written in it, so yes, you will want it for native apps. Plain C and C++ via the GNU compiler also work.

q: What is a NeXTstation?
a: It's the smaller, cheaper pizza-box style machine announced in 1990 with a 68040 CPU. The grayscale version lists at $4,995, and there's a color model with a color monitor available.

q: What is the Digital Librarian?
a: It's a full text search program that comes with the NeXT. It indexes books like the Oxford Quotations, Webster's dictionary and the works of Shakespeare, and you can search them in seconds.

q: What is the NeXT Mail application like?
a: It's a normal Unix mail system with a graphical front end. The notable part is that messages can contain voice, images and formatted text, which other NeXT users can see and hear directly.

q: What is the NeXT laser printer?
a: It's the NeXT Laser Printer, a 400 dpi engine from Canon with a PostScript-compatible interpreter driven by the cube itself. It connects through a dedicated port, not Ethernet, and costs around $2,650.

q: What is the NeXTdimension?
a: It's a board for the NeXTcube with its own Intel i860 processor, driving 32-bit color video at 1120 by 832. It also adds video capture, so it appeals to people doing graphics.

q: What is the Workspace Manager?
a: It's the NeXT equivalent of the Mac Finder, showing files in a column browser. You can open, copy and delete files, launch apps and eject the optical disk from it.

q: What is the difference between NeXTcube and the original NeXT Computer?
a: The NeXTcube uses a 68040 at 25 MHz, roughly three times quicker than the 68030, and has NeXTbus expansion slots. The original has a 68030 and no real expansion slots.

q: What kind of Ethernet connection does the NeXT have?
a: The first cubes have a thin Ethernet BNC connector built in. Later models also offer a twisted-pair 10BaseT port, so check which one you need before buying cable.

q: What word processors are available for the NeXT?
a: WriteNow was ported to it, and Edit handles rich text. Serious publishing people look at FrameMaker, which has been announced for NeXT. The software list is still short compared with the Mac.

q: Where can I buy a NeXT?
a: Direct from NeXT, through university sales, or from Businessland, which started selling them in 1989. NeXT also has authorized dealers in several cities. Call the 800 number to find the nearest one.

q: Which compiler does the NeXT use?
a: It ships with the GNU C compiler, modified to support Objective-C, plus gdb as the debugger. So existing C programs generally compile with little trouble.

q: Which version of NeXTstep should I be running?
a: If you still have 1.0, move to 2.0 which came out in 1990. It speeds up the system, adds a better file viewer and improves networking. Get it from your NeXT dealer or university rep.

q: Why does everyone say the NeXT is so hard to find software for?
a: Because it is a new platform with a small installed base, so developers have little reason to port. The ones who do like Objective-C and Interface Builder, but you won't see shelves of boxed software yet.

q: Why does the NeXT only have a grayscale display?
a: The MegaPixel display is 1120 by 832 with four shades of gray, which kept cost and memory down. Color arrives with the NeXTstation Color and the NeXTdimension board announced in 1990.

q: Why is my NeXT so slow when I open several programs?
a: Probably it's swapping. Mach uses virtual memory, and with 8MB and an optical drive the paging is painful. Adding RAM or a hard disk helps more than anything else.

q: Can I get C for my Amiga or Atari ST?
a: Yes. On the Amiga there's Lattice C and Manx Aztec C, and on the Atari ST there's Mark Williams C and Alcyon C, which ships with the developer kit. Gcc has also been ported to both.

q: Can I pass an array to a function by value?
a: No, C passes only a pointer to the first element, so the function works on the original array. If you want a copy, you have to make one yourself, or wrap the array in a struct, which ANSI compilers can pass by value.

q: Can I use // for comments in C?
a: No, only /* */ is standard C. Some compilers may take // as an extension, but you can't count on it, and comments of the /* */ kind don't nest, so watch out when commenting out code.

q: How can I find out where my program is crashing without a debugger?
a: Put fprintf(stderr, ...) calls at key places and watch where the output stops. Use stderr because it's unbuffered, so you won't lose the last messages when the program dies.

q: How can I tell how big an int is on my machine?
a: Use sizeof(int), or look at limits.h for INT_MAX if you have an ANSI compiler. It's 16 bits on most PCs and 32 bits on VAXes and Sun workstations, so don't assume.

q: How do I convert a string to an integer?
a: Call atoi(s) for the quick way, or strtol(s, &end, 10) if you want error checking, since atoi can't tell you whether the string was really a number. Both are declared in stdlib.h on ANSI systems.

q: How do I declare a function that takes a variable number of arguments?
a: With an ANSI compiler, include stdarg.h, declare the function with an ellipsis after at least one named argument, and use va_start, va_arg and va_end. Older compilers use varargs.h, which works a bit differently.

q: How do I do bit manipulation in C?
a: Use & to mask, | to set, ^ to toggle, ~ to invert, and << and >> to shift. For example flags |= 0x04 sets a bit and flags &= ~0x04 clears it. Use unsigned types for shifts so the sign bit doesn't surprise you.

q: How do I generate random numbers in C?
a: Call srand(seed) once, then rand() each time you want one. rand returns 0 to RAND_MAX, which is only 32767 on many PCs. Seed with time(NULL) for different sequences, and be aware the low bits of rand are often not very random.

q: How do I get command line arguments in C?
a: Declare main(int argc, char *argv[]). argc is the count including the program name, and argv[0] is the program name itself. argv[argc] is a NULL pointer, so you can also walk the list until you hit it.

q: How do I link a C program with assembly routines on a PC?
a: Assemble with MASM or TASM using the same memory model, and have the routine save BP, SI and DI. C passes arguments right to left on the stack and the caller cleans up, with the name prefixed by an underscore.

q: How do I open a file in binary mode on MS-DOS?
a: Add a b to the mode string, as in fopen("data.bin", "rb"). Without it, DOS compilers translate CR-LF to newline and treat Control-Z as end of file, which will wreck binary data.

q: How do I pass a pointer to a function so it can change my variable?
a: Pass the address with &x and declare the parameter as a pointer, then assign through it with *p = value. That's how scanf works, and why you need the & in front of your variables.

q: How do I read a whole line from the keyboard without overflowing my buffer?
a: Use fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin) if your library has it. Avoid gets(), since it has no way to know how big your buffer is and a long line will trash whatever is next to it in memory.

q: How do I use make with a C program?
a: Write a Makefile with a target, its dependencies, and a tab-indented command line, for example prog: main.o util.o followed by cc -o prog main.o util.o. Then just type make and it recompiles only what changed.

q: How do I write a function that returns a pointer to a string?
a: Return a pointer to static storage, a string literal, or memory from malloc. Never return the address of a local array, because it's gone when the function returns and you'll get garbage.

q: How do I write a macro that takes arguments?
a: Use #define SQUARE(x) ((x)*(x)) and put parentheses around every argument and the whole body. Beware that SQUARE(i++) evaluates i++ twice, because macros are just text substitution.

q: Is C case sensitive?
a: Yes, count and Count are different names. Keywords are all lowercase. Be careful because some older linkers only look at the first six characters of external names, and may ignore case entirely.

q: Is it a good idea to use goto in C?
a: Rarely. Most of the time a loop, break or continue is clearer. One accepted use is jumping out of several nested loops or to a common cleanup section at the end of a function.

q: Is it safe to call free on a NULL pointer?
a: In ANSI C, yes, free(NULL) does nothing. Some older Unix libraries may crash on it, so if you're porting to old systems it's safer to test for NULL first.

q: Is it worth learning C if I already know Pascal?
a: Yes, you'll pick it up quickly. Most of the Unix world and a lot of PC software is written in C, so it's very useful. Just be ready for less hand-holding, because C won't catch array bounds errors for you.

q: What does 'near' and 'far' pointer mean on a PC compiler?
a: On the 8086 a near pointer is a 16-bit offset within one 64K segment, while a far pointer carries segment and offset in 32 bits. Far pointers reach the whole megabyte but are slower and have odd comparison rules.

q: What does 'segmentation violation' mean on my Unix box?
a: Your program touched memory it doesn't own. Usually it's a bad or NULL pointer, running off the end of an array, or a string that lost its terminating zero. Compile with -g and look at the core file with dbx or adb.

q: What does the error 'lvalue required' mean?
a: You're trying to assign to something that isn't a variable or memory location, like a function result or an expression. A common cause is writing something like a + 1 = b, or incrementing an array name.

q: What does the register keyword do?
a: It hints to the compiler that a variable is heavily used and should be kept in a CPU register. Modern optimizing compilers often ignore it, and you can't take the address of a register variable.

q: What does the static keyword do?
a: Inside a function it makes a variable keep its value between calls. On a global variable or function it hides the name from other source files, so it can't collide with names elsewhere in the program.

q: What does the volatile keyword mean?
a: It's new in ANSI C. It tells the compiler that a variable may change behind its back, like a hardware register or something altered by a signal handler, so it must reread it each time rather than caching it in a register.

q: What is ANSI C and should I care?
a: It's the standard X3.J11 finished in 1989 and adopted by ISO in 1990. The big changes are function prototypes, void pointers, const and volatile. If you're buying a new compiler, make sure it claims ANSI support.

q: What is a core dump?
a: When a Unix program crashes, the system writes an image of its memory to a file named core. You can load it into a debugger like dbx or adb along with the executable to see where the program died.

q: What is a typedef and why would I use one?
a: typedef gives a new name to an existing type, like typedef struct node NODE. It makes declarations shorter and lets you change a type in one place, which helps a lot when porting between machines.

q: What is a union used for?
a: A union lets several members share the same storage, so it holds one of them at a time. It's handy for saving space or for variant records, but you must remember yourself which member you last stored.

q: What is gcc and where do I get it?
a: It's the GNU C compiler from the Free Software Foundation, which is ANSI-ish, optimizes well, and is free. You can fetch the source by anonymous FTP from prep.ai.mit.edu, or order a tape from the FSF.

q: What is lint and should I run it?
a: lint is a Unix tool that checks your C for suspicious things like mismatched argument types, unused variables and missing returns. Yes, run it regularly, since it finds bugs the compiler lets through.

q: What is the best book to learn C?
a: Kernighan and Ritchie, The C Programming Language, is the standard. The second edition from 1988 covers ANSI C. If you want something gentler, Kelley and Pohl's A Book on C is a good tutorial.

q: What is the difference between #include <file.h> and #include "file.h"?
a: Angle brackets search the system include directories only. Quotes look in the current directory, or the directory of the source file, first and then fall back to the system directories. Use quotes for your own headers.

q: What is the difference between ++i and i++?
a: ++i increments first and yields the new value, while i++ yields the old value and then increments. On their own as statements they do the same thing, though on some older compilers ++i generates slightly better code.

q: What is the difference between a pointer and an array in C?
a: An array is a block of storage; a pointer is a variable holding an address. They look alike because an array name turns into a pointer to its first element in most expressions, but sizeof and assignment treat them differently.

q: What is the difference between a string literal and a char array?
a: A literal like "hello" is a constant array that you shouldn't modify, and some compilers put it in read-only memory. char s[] = "hello" makes your own writable copy that you can change.

q: What is the difference between getc and fgetc?
a: getc may be implemented as a macro, so it can evaluate its stream argument more than once and is faster. fgetc is always a real function. Don't pass getc an argument with side effects like fp++.

q: What is the difference between malloc and calloc?
a: malloc(n) gives you n bytes of uninitialized memory. calloc(n, size) allocates room for n items and zeroes it all. Both return NULL when they fail, so check the result every time.

q: Which is better for a beginner, Turbo C or Microsoft C 5.1?
a: Turbo C 2.0 is cheaper, compiles much faster, and its integrated editor is great for learning. Microsoft C 5.1 generates somewhat tighter code and comes with CodeView, which is a nice debugger, but it's slower and clunkier.

q: Which memory model should I use in Turbo C for a big program?
a: Large or huge if you need lots of code and data, but they are slower. Medium is a good compromise when your code is big but your data fits in 64K. Small is the fastest if everything fits in 64K each.

q: Why can't I compare two strings with == in C?
a: Because == on char pointers compares addresses, not contents. Use strcmp(a, b), which returns zero when the strings are equal. Remember it returns nonzero for different strings, so if (strcmp(a,b)) means not equal.

q: Why do I get a 'null pointer assignment' message when my Borland program exits?
a: Somewhere your program wrote through an uninitialized or NULL pointer, which clobbered the bytes at the bottom of the data segment. Borland checks them at exit. Look for pointers you never set before storing through them.

q: Why does 'char c = getchar()' fail to detect EOF?
a: getchar returns an int so EOF, which is -1, can be told apart from a real character. If you store it in a char, it may get truncated, or on machines with unsigned chars it never equals EOF. Use an int.

q: Why does my compiler say 'undefined symbol _main' at link time?
a: The linker found no main() in your object files. Either you left it out, misspelled it, or forgot to list the file containing it on the link line. Check for a stray semicolon or brace ahead of it, too.

q: Why does my int main() code fail on some systems when I don't return anything?
a: The exit status that gets passed to the shell or to make comes from what main returns. If you fall off the end without a return, the status is undefined on some systems, so end with return 0 or call exit(0).

q: Why does my program print garbage when I use printf with a long int?
a: You need %ld, not %d. On a PC int is 16 bits and long is 32, so printf with %d only picks up half the value. Arguments to printf aren't type checked, so the compiler won't warn you.

q: Why does my while(!feof(fp)) loop process the last line twice?
a: feof only becomes true after a read has already hit end of file. Test the return value of your read instead, like while (fgets(buf, sizeof buf, fp) != NULL), and you won't get the extra pass.

q: Why does scanf leave a newline behind that messes up my next getchar?
a: scanf with %d or %s stops before the newline and leaves it in the input buffer, so the next getchar reads it. Read whole lines with fgets and then use sscanf on the line to avoid this.

q: Why is my C program so much slower than the assembler version?
a: A good compiler is usually within a factor of two, but small PC compilers can be worse. Try the optimizer switches, use register variables in the inner loop, and profile with prof on Unix to find the hot spot first.

q: Can I use inline assembly in Turbo Pascal?
a: Turbo Pascal 6.0 has a built-in assembler with asm...end blocks. In earlier versions you can use the inline statement with hex bytes, or link a .OBJ made with MASM or TASM.

q: Can I use overlays in Turbo Pascal to fit a large program?
a: Yes, in 5.0 and later, with the Overlay unit. Mark the units with {$O+}, call OvrInit with the .OVR file name, and the system loads units in as needed.

q: Can I write TSR programs in Turbo Pascal?
a: Yes, but it's tricky. You use Keep from the Dos unit and hook interrupts with SetIntVec. Set the heap and stack sizes small with {$M}, and be careful with DOS calls inside interrupt handlers.

q: Can Turbo Pascal 3.0 programs be compiled in 4.0 without changes?
a: Not quite. 4.0 dropped chain and execute, changed graphics into units, and dropped the old overlay system, so expect to rewrite parts. The Turbo 4.0 package includes a conversion utility called UPGRADE.

q: Does Turbo Pascal support real numbers with more precision?
a: The Real type is 6 bytes with about 11 digits. With a coprocessor or in 5.0 emulation mode, you can use Single, Double, Extended and Comp by turning on {$N+}.

q: How can I make my Turbo Pascal executable smaller?
a: 4.0 and later use smart linking, so unused procedures are dropped. You can also avoid pulling in big units like Graph, and use short strings rather than large arrays. Packing the .EXE with a tool like LZEXE helps too.

q: How can I sort an array fast in Pascal?
a: Use Quicksort instead of bubble sort. It averages about n log n comparisons, so for thousands of items it is far faster. Write it recursively with a partition procedure.

q: How do I call a DOS command from within my Pascal program?
a: In 4.0 and up, use Exec from the Dos unit, for example Exec('C:\COMMAND.COM', '/C DIR'). You must shrink the heap with {$M} so DOS has memory to run the command.

q: How do I change the text color in Turbo Pascal?
a: With the CRT unit, call TextColor(n) and TextBackground(n). Colors are 0 to 15, so TextColor(14) gives yellow. Add 128 to the foreground color for blinking text.

q: How do I check if a file exists in Pascal?
a: Assign the file, turn off I/O checking with {$I-}, try Reset, then turn it back on with {$I+} and test IOResult. If IOResult is 0 the file exists.

q: How do I compile a Turbo Pascal program to an .EXE file instead of running it in memory?
a: In Turbo Pascal 4.0 and up, open the Compile menu and change Destination from Memory to Disk, then hit F9 to make. You'll get a stand-alone .EXE in the current directory.

q: How do I do graphics in Turbo Pascal?
a: In 4.0 and later, use the Graph unit and call InitGraph with a driver such as CGA, EGA or VGA. The .BGI driver files must be where InitGraph can find them, or give it the path.

q: How do I get more than 64K of data in Turbo Pascal?
a: Global data and the stack are each limited to 64K, but you can use the heap with New and GetMem for dynamic data. Arrays still can't exceed 64K each, so use pointers to chunks.

q: How do I get the current date and time from DOS in Pascal?
a: Use GetDate and GetTime from the Dos unit in 4.0 and later. GetDate gives year, month, day and day of week, and GetTime gives hour, minute, second and hundredths.

q: How do I pass command line parameters to my Pascal program?
a: Use ParamCount to get the number of arguments and ParamStr(n) to get each one as a string. ParamStr(0) in 3.0 and up gives the program name in later versions.

q: How do I read a single keypress without waiting for Enter?
a: Use the CRT unit and call ReadKey, which returns a char. If you want to just test whether a key is waiting, use KeyPressed first.

q: How do I read a text file line by line?
a: Assign the file to a name, Reset it, and loop while not Eof(f) doing ReadLn(f, s). Close it when finished. A string variable holds one line up to 255 characters.

q: How do I set the unit directory in Turbo Pascal 5.0?
a: Go to Options, then Directories, and set the Unit Directories field to the path holding your .TPU files. Separate several directories with semicolons.

q: How do I turn off Ctrl-Break in my program?
a: Set CheckBreak := False in the CRT unit. That stops Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Break from killing the program in the middle of your code.

q: How do I use the integrated debugger in Turbo Pascal 5.0?
a: Press F8 to step through the lines, F4 to run to the cursor, and Ctrl-F7 to add a watch expression. Make sure Debug Information is turned on under Compiler options.

q: How do I write directly to screen memory in Turbo Pascal?
a: Color text memory starts at segment $B800 and mono at $B000. Use Mem[$B800:offset] or declare an array at absolute $B800:0. Each character takes two bytes: character and attribute.

q: How do I write to the printer in Pascal?
a: With the Printer unit, add uses Printer; then writeln(Lst, 'text'). Without it, you can assign a text file to 'PRN' and write to that.

q: How much does Turbo Pascal cost?
a: Turbo Pascal 5.0 lists at $149.95 from Borland, and the earlier 3.0 was $69.95 in the 1980s. Mail order houses often sell it for less than list.

q: Is Turbo Pascal 5.0 worth upgrading to from 4.0?
a: Yes, if you debug much. 5.0 adds an integrated debugger with breakpoints and watches, overlays, and a faster compiler. It's a solid upgrade for the price.

q: Is Turbo Pascal as fast as C?
a: For most work, close. The compiler generates decent 8086 code and compiles very quickly. Optimizing C compilers from Microsoft often produce somewhat faster code on tight loops, but the difference rarely matters.

q: Is there a way to do object-oriented programming in Turbo Pascal?
a: Yes, version 5.5 added objects with inheritance, virtual methods and constructors. Declare them with the object keyword and use the manual's examples as a guide.

q: Should I use goto in Pascal?
a: Almost never. Pascal has while, repeat and for loops that cover most cases. The one common use is jumping out of nested loops to an error exit, and you must declare the label.

q: What are sets in Pascal and how do I use them?
a: A set is a collection of values from an ordinal type, such as set of char. Use in to test membership, like if ch in ['A'..'Z'] then. Turbo Pascal limits sets to 256 elements.

q: What does Error 112: Case constant out of range mean?
a: Turbo Pascal case labels must fit in the range 0 to 255 or -32768 to 32767 for the selector type. Your constant is outside what the selector can hold, such as using a byte selector with a label of 300.

q: What does Error 2: Identifier expected usually mean?
a: The compiler found something that isn't a name where it wanted one. Look at the line above the pointer too, since a missing semicolon or a stray reserved word is often the real culprit.

q: What does Runtime error 200 mean in Turbo Pascal?
a: That's a divide by zero. It usually shows up on fast Pentium-class... no, on fast 286 and 386 machines when a CRT unit delay loop calibrates badly; otherwise check your code for a division where the divisor can be 0.

q: What does forward mean in Pascal?
a: It lets you declare a procedure's header before its body so two routines can call each other. Write the header with forward; and later give the body without repeating the parameters.

q: What does the {$I filename} directive do?
a: It includes another source file at that point during compile, as if you had typed it in. It is useful for splitting a big program or sharing common declarations, because Turbo Pascal 3.0 had no units.

q: What does the {$R+} directive do?
a: It turns on range checking, so array index and subrange errors give a runtime error 201 instead of silently trashing memory. Use it while debugging and turn it off with {$R-} for speed.

q: What does var mean in a parameter list?
a: It passes the parameter by reference, so changes inside the procedure affect the caller's variable. Without var, you get a copy and the original stays untouched.

q: What is a pointer and why would I need one?
a: A pointer holds the address of a variable you allocate at run time with New. You need them for linked lists, trees, and anything whose size isn't known when you write the program.

q: What is a record and how is it different from an array?
a: An array holds items of the same type indexed by number. A record groups named fields of different types, such as a name string, an age integer and a salary real.

q: What is a unit in Turbo Pascal?
a: A unit is a separately compiled module with an interface section for what it exports and an implementation section for the code. Turbo Pascal 4.0 introduced them, and they are saved as .TPU files.

q: What is the .TPU file for?
a: It is the compiled form of a unit. Turbo Pascal links it into your program, so you don't recompile the source each time. You need the .TPU in the unit directory when you compile.

q: What is the best book to learn Pascal?
a: Kathleen Jensen and Niklaus Wirth's Pascal User Manual and Report is the standard reference. For learning, Borland's own Turbo Pascal manuals are good, and Ellis Horowitz and others have decent textbooks.

q: What is the difference between Pascal and Turbo Pascal?
a: Standard Pascal is the Wirth language as defined by ISO and ANSI. Turbo Pascal is Borland's dialect with extras: strings, units, direct screen and DOS access, and a very fast integrated compiler.

q: What is the difference between Read and ReadLn?
a: Read takes the values you ask for and leaves the rest of the line in the buffer. ReadLn also discards the rest of the line, so it moves to the next input line.

q: What is the difference between a function and a procedure?
a: A function returns a value and can be used in an expression, while a procedure just does something. Both can take var parameters if you need to hand back several results.

q: What is the heap and what is the stack?
a: The stack holds local variables and return addresses for procedures. The heap is the free memory you get from New and GetMem. In Turbo Pascal they grow toward each other in your 640K.

q: Which is better for a beginner, Turbo Pascal or Turbo C?
a: Pascal is easier to learn. Its strict typing catches mistakes early and the syntax reads clearly. Turbo C is faster to get into trouble with, but C is more useful if you plan to work on Unix.

q: Why does Write of a real show something like 1.2345678901E+02?
a: That's the default floating format. Give field widths, like Write(x:8:2), to print 8 characters wide with 2 decimal places and get plain fixed-point output.

q: Why does my program crash when I use too much recursion?
a: Each call eats stack, and the default Turbo Pascal stack is 16K. Raise it with the {$M} directive, for example {$M 65520,0,655360}, or rewrite the routine to use a loop.

q: Why does my program run slowly when I use Writeln to the screen?
a: Standard Writeln goes through DOS and handles Ctrl-C checks. Using the CRT unit makes output direct to the BIOS or video memory and is much faster, especially with DirectVideo true.

q: Why does my program say Error 3: Unknown identifier when I use ClrScr?
a: ClrScr lives in the CRT unit. Put a uses Crt; line right after the program line and it will compile fine.

q: Why is my string only 255 characters long?
a: Turbo Pascal strings are length-byte strings, with the length in byte 0, so 255 is the max. For longer text, use an array of char or a linked list of string chunks.

q: Can BASIC programs call machine language routines?
a: Yes. On the PC use DEF SEG and CALL with an address, and on a C64 use SYS or USR. Put the routine in memory with POKEs from DATA statements or BLOAD it from a file.

q: Can I have more than one statement on a line?
a: Yes, separate them with a colon, like A=1:B=2:PRINT A+B. It saves memory on small machines, but very long lines get hard to read and edit.

q: Can I run BASIC programs from my Apple II on an IBM PC?
a: Not directly. Applesoft and GW-BASIC are different dialects, and things like PEEK, POKE, HPLOT and HGR have no PC equivalent. Simple text programs usually port with some editing, but graphics and sound must be rewritten.

q: Can I run BASIC under DOS 4.0 without GW-BASIC installed?
a: Not directly. MS-DOS ships with GW-BASIC or BASICA, depending on the OEM, but some vendors leave it out. You can buy QuickBASIC, or the QBASIC-less DOS disk may still include the interpreter on the supplemental disk.

q: Can I use BASIC to write to the serial port?
a: Yes. OPEN "COM1:1200,N,8,1" AS #1, then PRINT #1 to send and INPUT$(1,#1) or LOC(1) to check for received characters. It works fine for a simple terminal program at 1200 or 2400 baud.

q: How can I make a BASIC program wait for a keypress?
a: Loop on INKEY$ until it returns something, like A$=INKEY$: IF A$="" THEN GOTO the same line. On older machines, use GET A$ on Commodore or Apple, or INPUT if you can accept pressing Return.

q: How can I save my BASIC program so I can read it in a text editor?
a: Use SAVE "FILE.BAS",A to write it as plain ASCII. Without the A option GW-BASIC stores it in a tokenized binary format that editors will show as garbage.

q: How do I PEEK and POKE the screen on a C64?
a: Screen memory starts at 1024 and color memory at 55296. POKE 1024,1 puts an A in the top left corner, and POKE 55296,2 makes it red. Screen codes differ from ASCII, so check the chart in the manual.

q: How do I clear the screen in GW-BASIC?
a: Use the CLS statement. Just put CLS on a line by itself at the start of your program, or type it at the Ok prompt. It clears the text screen and homes the cursor.

q: How do I draw a circle on a CGA screen in BASIC?
a: Use SCREEN 1 or 2, then CIRCLE (160,100),50 for a circle centered at that point with a radius of 50. Add a color number after the radius if you want a color. SCREEN 1 gives 320x200 in four colors.

q: How do I draw a line or box in BASIC?
a: LINE (10,10)-(100,50) draws a line on the graphics screen. Add ,,B for a box outline or ,,BF for a filled box. Add a color number before the B to change the color.

q: How do I get graphics on an EGA card with BASIC?
a: Use SCREEN 7, 8, 9 in QuickBASIC 4.0 or later, which give 16 colors in resolutions up to 640x350. GW-BASIC 3.2 and later also support these modes, but older versions only know CGA.

q: How do I get random numbers in BASIC?
a: Use RND. On the IBM PC, RND returns a number between 0 and 1, so INT(RND*6)+1 gives a die roll. Put RANDOMIZE TIMER at the top, or the same sequence comes up every run.

q: How do I get sound out of the PC speaker with BASIC?
a: SOUND takes a frequency in Hz and a duration in clock ticks, for example SOUND 440,18 gives about a second of A. BEEP just makes the standard beep. PLAY lets you write music with strings like "CDEFG".

q: How do I get the current date and time in BASIC?
a: DATE$ and TIME$ return the system date and time as strings on the PC. TIMER gives seconds since midnight, which is handy for timing code or seeding RANDOMIZE.

q: How do I make a menu in BASIC?
a: PRINT the choices, take a key with INKEY$ or INPUT, and use ON X GOSUB or ON X GOTO to jump to the right routine. In QuickBASIC, SELECT CASE is cleaner.

q: How do I make a random-access file in BASIC?
a: OPEN "DATA.DAT" FOR RANDOM AS #1 LEN=50, define the record with FIELD or a TYPE in QuickBASIC, then GET #1,n to read record n and PUT #1,n to write it.

q: How do I print a number with two decimal places?
