a: Use PRINT USING "####.##";X on most PC BASICs. It rounds and lines up the decimal point, so it's good for money columns. Plain PRINT will give you however many digits it likes.

q: How do I read a file one line at a time in BASIC?
a: OPEN the file FOR INPUT AS #1, then loop with LINE INPUT #1, A$ until EOF(1) is true. Then CLOSE #1. LINE INPUT keeps commas in the line, which plain INPUT would split.

q: How do I sort an array in BASIC?
a: A bubble sort is simplest: nested loops that swap neighbors when out of order. It's slow past a few hundred items, so use a Shell sort or quicksort for bigger lists. SWAP A(I),A(J) saves a temp variable.

q: Is BASIC on the Amiga any good?
a: AmigaBASIC from Microsoft ships with early versions of the Workbench and handles windows, menus, and sound fairly easily. It's slow, though, so serious people look at AC/BASIC or Lattice C.

q: Is QuickBASIC worth buying if I already have GW-BASIC?
a: Yes, if you write programs bigger than a few pages. QuickBASIC 4.5 compiles to real EXEs, has no line numbers, supports SUB and FUNCTION procedures, and has a decent editor. It runs several times faster than the interpreter.

q: Is it possible to compile GW-BASIC programs?
a: Yes, with the Microsoft BASIC Compiler (BASCOM) or QuickBASIC, which handles most GW-BASIC code. Save the program in ASCII with SAVE "NAME",A first if the compiler complains about format.

q: Is there a way to use more than 64K in GW-BASIC?
a: Not for program and variables, which are stuck in one 64K segment. You can reach other memory with DEF SEG, PEEK and POKE, and QuickBASIC 4.5 lets you use far strings and arrays up to 64K each.

q: What does ?OUT OF MEMORY mean on my Commodore 64?
a: You have used up the roughly 38K of free BASIC RAM. Large arrays and long strings are the usual cause. Try shrinking your DIMs, using integer arrays with the % sign, or splitting the program into chunks that CHAIN with LOAD.

q: What does BASIC stand for, and who made it?
a: Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code. John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz wrote it at Dartmouth in 1964. Microsoft's versions on micros started with Altair BASIC in 1975.

q: What does DEFINT A-Z do?
a: It makes every variable starting with letters A through Z an integer unless you say otherwise. Integer math is faster and uses less memory, but you can't store decimals or values past 32767 in them.

q: What does RUN do compared to CONT?
a: RUN clears all variables and starts from the first line. CONT continues after you hit Ctrl-Break or a STOP, keeping the variables, but you can't continue if you edited the program in between.

q: What does Type mismatch mean?
a: You are mixing a string and a number, like assigning A$=5 or adding a string to a number. Use STR$ to turn a number into text and VAL to go the other direction.

q: What does the ON ERROR GOTO statement do?
a: It sends the program to an error-handling routine instead of stopping when a runtime error occurs. In the routine, ERR gives the error number and ERL the line. End with RESUME or RESUME NEXT.

q: What does the REM statement do?
a: REM marks a comment that BASIC ignores. You can also use a single quote in most PC versions. On small machines, comments eat memory, but they are worth it when you come back later.

q: What does the dollar sign mean at the end of a variable name?
a: It marks a string variable, so A$ holds text and A holds a number. A percent sign makes it an integer, and an exclamation mark or pound sign marks single or double precision on most PC BASICs.

q: What is a good book for learning QuickBASIC?
a: Microsoft's own Learn BASIC Now is easy for beginners, and the manuals that come with 4.5 are decent. For deeper stuff, Peter Norton's and Waite Group books on BASIC are well liked.

q: What is a good way to speed up a slow BASIC program?
a: Use integer variables, move constants out of loops, avoid repeated string concatenation, and put frequently called subroutines early in the program on interpreters. Failing that, compile it.

q: What is the best BASIC for the Atari ST?
a: The ST ships with ST BASIC from Atari, which is slow and buggy. Most people buy GFA BASIC, which is fast, structured, and has good access to GEM graphics.

q: What is the best way to learn programming, BASIC or Pascal?
a: BASIC gets you running programs in an afternoon, so it's fine for starting. Pascal teaches better habits with structure and types. If you pick QuickBASIC, you get a bit of both.

q: What is the difference between GOSUB and GOTO?
a: GOTO just jumps and never comes back. GOSUB jumps to a subroutine and returns to the next statement when it hits RETURN. Using GOSUB keeps your program much easier to follow.

q: What is the difference between INPUT and LINE INPUT?
a: INPUT stops at commas and may print a question mark, so a comma in the answer splits it into fields. LINE INPUT takes the whole line, spaces and commas included, into one string.

q: What is the difference between PRINT and LPRINT?
a: PRINT sends output to the screen, LPRINT sends it to the printer, normally the one on LPT1. Everything else works the same, including semicolons and commas for spacing. Make sure the printer is online first or the program will hang.

q: What is the difference between SCREEN 1 and SCREEN 2 on a CGA?
a: SCREEN 1 is 320x200 with four colors from a palette. SCREEN 2 is 640x200 in just black and white. Choose by whether you need color or finer horizontal detail.

q: What is the difference between Turbo BASIC and QuickBASIC?
a: Borland's Turbo BASIC is cheap, compiles very fast, and has a good integrated editor. QuickBASIC has wider support, a better debugger, and more third-party libraries. Both are mostly compatible with GW-BASIC code.

q: What is the maximum size of a string in BASIC?
a: On GW-BASIC and most PC versions it is 255 characters. QuickBASIC allows up to 32767 characters in a variable-length string. On a C64 it is also 255.

q: Which is faster, GW-BASIC or compiled QuickBASIC?
a: QuickBASIC compiled to an EXE is much faster, often five to ten times for number crunching. GW-BASIC interprets every line each time it runs. Using integer variables helps in both.

q: Why does LOAD"*",8,1 work but plain LOAD"*",8 not do what I want on my C64?
a: Without the ,1 the program loads where BASIC starts. With ,1 it loads to the address saved in the file, which is what machine language programs need. For BASIC programs use the plain version.

q: Why does my FOR loop with STEP 0.1 not end where I expect?
a: 0.1 can't be stored exactly in binary, so the counter drifts a little and may miss the final value. Loop with integers and divide, like FOR I=1 TO 10 and use I/10 inside.

q: Why does my INKEY$ loop miss arrow keys?
a: Arrow keys return a two-character string, CHR$(0) followed by a scan code, such as CHR$(72) for up. Check LEN(A$)=2 and look at the second character with ASC(RIGHT$(A$,1)).

q: Why does my program say Syntax error in a line that looks fine to me?
a: Often the error is in a DATA line or a typo somewhere else, since BASIC reports the line it was reading. Check for a misspelled keyword, a missing quote, or a reserved word used as a variable name like NAME or LEN.

q: Why does my program stop with Subscript out of range?
a: You used an array index higher than you DIMmed, or lower than zero. Without a DIM the limit is 10, meaning elements 0 to 10. Check your loop bounds and remember arrays start at 0 unless you use OPTION BASE 1.

q: Why is my string array so slow when I add lots of items?
a: String handling triggers garbage collection, which can pause the interpreter for seconds when memory fills up. On a C64 or Apple, calling FRE(0) occasionally forces it at a time you choose rather than at random.

q: Can I run assembly programs on an Atari ST?
a: Yes, the ST uses a 68000. Devpac from HiSoft is the popular assembler, and you call TOS through TRAP #1 for GEMDOS, TRAP #2 for GEM, and TRAP #14 for XBIOS.

q: Can I use inline assembly in Turbo C?
a: Yes, Turbo C 2.0 supports asm statements, but you need TCC with the -B option or a #pragma inline so it can call TASM. Borland's Turbo C++ also handles it that way.

q: Can the Apple IIgs be programmed in 65816 assembly?
a: Yes. The 65816 runs 6502 code and adds 16-bit registers and 24-bit addressing. APW, the Apple Programmer's Workbench, includes an assembler and linker, and Merlin 16 is a popular alternative.

q: Does a disassembler exist that I can use to learn from other people's code?
a: Try Sourcer or the disassembler in Periscope, or just use DEBUG's U command for small stuff. Reading what compilers produce with Microsoft's /Fa option or Turbo C's -S is also a great way to learn.

q: How can I make my inner loop faster on an 8088?
a: Keep data in registers, not memory. Unroll the loop, use LOOP or string instructions where possible, and avoid MUL and DIV. Remember the 8088's 8-bit bus makes each memory word access cost extra cycles.

q: How can I read a key without waiting on the 8086?
a: Call INT 16h with AH=1 to check if a key is waiting. The zero flag tells you. If one is there, call INT 16h with AH=0 to fetch it. AL has the ASCII, AH the scan code.

q: How do I call an assembly routine from Microsoft C?
a: Write it as a PROC with the C calling convention, push BP, and read arguments from the stack at BP+4 onward. Return values in AX, or DX:AX for longs. Preserve SI, DI, BP, and segment registers.

q: How do I clear a register fast on the 6502?
a: There's no clear instruction for A, so use LDA #0. For X and Y use LDX #0 or LDY #0. To clear memory use STA after loading a zero.

q: How do I find out which CPU my program is running on?
a: Push the flags with bits 12-15 set, pop them back, and see what stuck. On an 8086 those top bits always read as ones. On a 286 they clear in real mode, and a 386 has extra tests.

q: How do I get command line arguments in a .COM program?
a: DOS puts the command tail in the PSP at offset 80h. The first byte is the length and the text follows from 81h, ending with a carriage return, usually with a leading space.

q: How do I get started with assembly language on my IBM PC?
a: Get MASM or Borland's Turbo Assembler, plus a copy of Peter Norton's Programmer's Guide to the IBM PC. Start with small .COM programs and use DEBUG to step through them. Learn the 8086 registers first.

q: How do I hook an interrupt in DOS?
a: Use INT 21h function 35h to get the old vector, save it, then function 25h to install yours. Chain to the old handler when you're done, and don't poke the interrupt table directly unless you must.

q: How do I multiply quickly on a 6502 without a MUL instruction?
a: Use shift and add. ASL doubles the value, so multiplying by 10 is shift left once, shift left twice and add the original, then add the doubled value. For general cases use a shift-and-add loop.

q: How do I print a character to the screen using DOS?
a: Put the character in DL, set AH to 2, and execute INT 21h. For a whole string, put its address in DX, end it with a dollar sign, set AH to 9, and call INT 21h.

q: How do I read a sector from a floppy in assembly?
a: Use INT 13h with AH=2. Put the sector count in AL, cylinder in CH, sector in CL, head in DH, drive in DL, and the buffer in ES:BX. Carry set means an error, with the code in AH.

q: How do I switch to 320x200 256 color mode on a VGA card?
a: Set AX to 0013h and call INT 10h. Video memory then sits at segment A000h, one byte per pixel, with offset equal to y times 320 plus x.

q: How do I test if a number is zero in 8086 code?
a: Use OR AX,AX or TEST AX,AX, then JZ. CMP AX,0 works but is a byte longer. All of these set the zero flag without changing AX in the TEST case.

q: How do I write a delay loop that works on any speed PC?
a: Don't count instructions. Watch the BIOS timer tick at 0040:006C, which updates about 18.2 times a second, and wait for it to change. Loops run differently on a 4.77 MHz XT than on an AT.

q: How does the Z80 differ from the 8080?
a: The Z80 runs all 8080 opcodes and adds index registers IX and IY, block moves like LDIR, bit test instructions, and a shadow register set. Mnemonics differ too, so Zilog code reads differently.

q: Is it worth learning assembly now that we have Turbo Pascal and Microsoft C?
a: Yes, for speed-critical routines and for understanding what your machine does. Most people write in C or Pascal and drop to assembly for inner loops, graphics, and interrupt handlers.

q: Is self-modifying code a good idea?
a: Generally not. It breaks in ROM, confuses debuggers, and can misbehave on chips with a prefetch queue like the 286 and 386. It may save a few bytes on a 6502, but think twice.

q: Is the 80286 worth coding specially for?
a: Mostly no. A few instructions like PUSHA and shifts by immediate counts help, but then your code won't run on 8088 machines. Unless you're protected-mode bound, stay with 8086 code.

q: What are segments and why does the 8086 have them?
a: Segments let a 16-bit processor address one megabyte. The physical address is the segment times 16 plus the offset. It's awkward, but that's how you reach beyond 64K.

q: What does JNZ check?
a: It jumps if the zero flag is clear, meaning the last result wasn't zero. After CMP it means the operands were not equal. JNE is just another name for the same opcode.

q: What does LEA do and how is it different from MOV?
a: LEA loads the effective address of an operand, not the contents. LEA BX,table puts the offset in BX. MOV BX,table with MASM may fetch the word at that address instead, depending on syntax.

q: What does REP MOVSW do?
a: It copies CX words from DS:SI to ES:DI, adjusting SI and DI by the direction flag. It's the quickest way to move a block of memory on the 8086, much faster than a hand-coded loop.

q: What does XOR AX,AX do?
a: It sets AX to zero. It's shorter than MOV AX,0 and a little faster on the 8086 and 286, so everyone uses it. It also clears the carry flag, which is worth remembering.

q: What does the AX register do on an 8088?
a: AX is the main 16-bit accumulator. It splits into AH and AL, the high and low bytes. Many instructions like MUL, DIV and IN/OUT work fastest or only with AX or AL.

q: What does the Amiga's copper do and can I program it in assembly?
a: The copper is a coprocessor that changes custom chip registers in sync with the video beam. You write a copper list in memory, point COP1LC at it, and it runs each frame.

q: What does the CLD instruction do?
a: It clears the direction flag so string instructions like MOVSB, LODSB and STOSB move forward, with SI and DI incrementing. Use STD if you want them to count down instead.

q: What does the carry flag mean?
a: It's set when an unsigned add overflows past the register size or a subtract needs a borrow. Shifts and rotates also move bits through it. Use ADC and SBB for multi-byte math.

q: What does the instruction NOP actually do?
a: Nothing, it just takes a cycle or so. People use it for tiny delays, to pad code for alignment, or as a placeholder to patch over later in DEBUG. On the 8086 it's really XCHG AX,AX.

q: What happens when an interrupt occurs on an 8086?
a: The CPU pushes the flags, CS and IP, clears the interrupt and trap flags, and jumps through the vector table at address 0 using the interrupt number times four. IRET restores everything.

q: What is a BIOS call and why would I use it instead of hitting hardware?
a: A BIOS call is a software interrupt like INT 10h for video or INT 13h for disk. It works across different clone hardware, though slower than direct access. Use it where portability matters.

q: What is a TSR and how do I write one?
a: A TSR is a Terminate and Stay Resident program like SideKick. Hook an interrupt, then exit with INT 27h or INT 21h function 31h, giving the number of paragraphs to keep in memory.

q: What is the 8087 and can I use it from assembly?
a: The 8087 is the math coprocessor for the 8088 and 8086. You use ESC-prefixed instructions like FLD, FADD and FSTP, and MASM assembles them with the 8087 mnemonics. Add a FWAIT before reading results.

q: What is the best book for learning 6502 assembly?
a: Lance Leventhal's 6502 Assembly Language Programming is the standard. For Apple II, Randall Hyde's Using 6502 Assembly Language is good, and for the C64 the Programmer's Reference Guide covers the hardware.

q: What is the difference between SHR and SAR?
a: SHR shifts right and fills the top bit with zero, for unsigned numbers. SAR keeps the sign bit, so it divides signed numbers by two properly. Both put the shifted-out bit in carry.

q: What is the difference between a macro and a subroutine?
a: A macro is pasted in by the assembler every time you use it, so it's fast but bigger. A subroutine exists once and is called, which saves space but costs the CALL and RET.

q: What is the fastest way to write to the CGA screen?
a: Write straight into video memory at segment B800h. Don't go through the BIOS or DOS. For graphics modes, remember CGA interleaves even and odd scan lines at offsets 0000h and 2000h.

q: Which assembler is better, MASM or TASM?
a: TASM assembles a lot faster and has an Ideal mode with cleaner syntax, but also runs MASM mode fine. MASM 5.1 is the standard though, so if you share source use MASM syntax.

q: Which is better for the Commodore 64, a cartridge assembler or a disk-based one?
a: Cartridge assemblers like the Final Cartridge or Action Replay tools load instantly and survive crashes better. Disk-based ones like Merlin-style packages usually offer more features and bigger source files.

q: Why do some people say the 68000 is easier than the 8086?
a: It has a flat 32-bit address space, sixteen general-purpose registers, and regular instructions. No segment juggling, and most operations work on any register, so code is cleaner to write.

q: Why does my 68000 program get an address error?
a: The 68000 faults on word or long accesses at odd addresses. Make sure your data is aligned with an EVEN directive and that you're not using a byte pointer for word-sized moves.

q: Why does my MASM program say phase error between passes?
a: MASM guessed a forward reference size on pass one and found it wrong on pass two. Add explicit SHORT, PTR or segment overrides on the forward jump or reference, or try the /D option to see the listings.

q: Why does my program crash when I RET from a subroutine?
a: Most likely your stack is unbalanced, so RET pops the wrong address. Check that every PUSH has a matching POP and that you didn't CALL into something that leaves extra bytes on the stack.

q: Why does my program hang when I use STI and CLI around a long routine?
a: With interrupts off the timer tick and keyboard stop being serviced. Keep CLI sections to a few instructions. Disabling them for long periods can lose keystrokes and break the system clock.

q: Why is my DEBUG session showing weird numbers for my program?
a: DEBUG uses hexadecimal for everything. Add an h suffix in your own source only when assembling with MASM. In DEBUG's A command, numbers are always hex, so 100 means 256 decimal.

q: Can I run Lisp on an IBM PC?
a: Yes, but you want a 386 and several megabytes. Golden Common Lisp and Allegro for the PC exist, and XLISP by David Betz is free and runs on small machines. PC Scheme from TI is another good option.

q: Can I write a program that modifies itself in Lisp?
a: Yes, since code is just lists you can build one and hand it to EVAL. It works, but it's usually better to use macros, which do the same thing at compile time and are far easier to debug.

q: Can Lisp programs be turned into standalone executables?
a: Most implementations let you save the running image, such as with save-lisp in Lucid or dumplisp in Franz, but the file is big, often several megabytes. Newer compilers are working on tree shakers to trim it, but don't expect tiny files.

q: Can a computer ever beat a chess master?
a: They're getting close. Deep Thought from Carnegie Mellon has beaten grandmasters in some games, and Hitech has played at master level. Brute-force search is winning over clever knowledge, but a world champion is still a few years away.

q: How do I debug a Lisp program?
a: Use TRACE on the function to see calls and return values, and STEP to walk through forms. When an error drops you into the break loop, look at the backtrace, usually :b or :bt depending on your Lisp. Sprinkling PRINT works too.

q: How do I get Lisp running on my Mac?
a: Try Allegro Common Lisp from Franz or Coral Common Lisp, which is now Macintosh Allegro Common Lisp. Coral's is cheap and runs on a Mac Plus with 2 MB, though 4 MB is far more comfortable. Also look at ExperLisp.

q: How do I read a file one line at a time in Common Lisp?
a: Open it with WITH-OPEN-FILE and call READ-LINE in a loop, e.g. (with-open-file (s "data.txt") (loop for line = (read-line s nil) while line do (print line))). The nil makes it return nil at end of file instead of an error.

q: How do I set up Emacs for Lisp programming?
a: Use M-x lisp-mode or lisp-interaction-mode, and with GNU Emacs 18 you can run an inferior Lisp with M-x run-lisp. Tab indents the current line properly and C-M-f and C-M-b move over whole expressions.

q: How do I write a factorial function in Lisp?
a: Try (defun fact (n) (if (<= n 1) 1 (* n (fact (- n 1))))). Common Lisp has bignums so (fact 100) just works and gives you all 158 digits.

q: How much memory do I need to run Common Lisp?
a: On a Unix workstation, 8 MB is the practical minimum and 16 MB is nicer for Lucid or Allegro. On a Mac, 2 MB barely works with Coral and 4 MB is better. Swapping makes the garbage collector painfully slow.

q: Is Common Lisp or Scheme better for a beginner?
a: Scheme is much smaller and cleaner, and Abelson and Sussman's Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs uses it. Common Lisp is bigger but is what most commercial AI shops use. For learning, start with Scheme.

q: Is Common Lisp too slow for real programs?
a: Not with a good compiler. Declare your types with DECLARE and use fixnum arithmetic and you can get within a factor of two or so of C on many things. Interpreted code is a lot slower, so always compile with COMPILE-FILE.

q: Is it worth learning Lisp if I mostly program in C?
a: I think so. Even if you never use it professionally, it changes how you think about recursion, data structures and abstraction. And if you want to work in AI, you'll almost certainly run into it.

q: Is there a free Lisp for Unix?
a: Yes, try Kyoto Common Lisp, which compiles via C and is available cheaply, or GNU Emacs Lisp, which is not Common Lisp but is handy. Franz Lisp from Berkeley is also around. Also check Scheme implementations like MIT Scheme.

q: What book should I read to learn Lisp?
a: Winston and Horn's LISP is a good beginner text, and Touretzky's Common Lisp: A Gentle Introduction to Symbolic Computation is gentle indeed. Once you know the basics, Steele's Common Lisp: The Language is the reference you want.

q: What does 'dynamic scoping' mean and why did Common Lisp go lexical?
a: With dynamic scoping a free variable gets its value from whoever called you, not where you were written. Lexical scoping looks at where the code sits, which makes closures work properly. Common Lisp adopted it from Scheme, though special variables stay dynamic.

q: What does 'frame' mean in AI?
a: A frame is a data structure from Marvin Minsky's 1975 paper that holds slots describing a stereotyped situation, with default values and inheritance. Object systems and tools like KEE are built on the same idea.

q: What does CAR and CDR actually stand for in Lisp?
a: They're leftovers from the IBM 704 where Lisp was first done: Contents of Address part of Register and Contents of Decrement part of Register. Nobody cares about the hardware now, just think first and rest. Common Lisp also gives you FIRST and REST.

q: What does MAPCAR do?
a: It applies a function to each element of a list and returns a list of the results. For example (mapcar #'1+ '(1 2 3)) gives (2 3 4). MAPC does the same but throws the results away, and MAPCAN splices them together.

q: What does the quote mark do in Lisp?
a: The quote stops evaluation, so 'foo gives you the symbol FOO instead of its value, and '(1 2 3) gives the list without trying to call 1 as a function. It's short for (quote foo).

q: What is CLOS?
a: The Common Lisp Object System, an object-oriented layer with classes, multiple inheritance and generic functions that dispatch on all arguments. It grew out of Flavors and LOOPS and is being standardized by the ANSI X3J13 committee. PCL is a portable version you can run now.

q: What is Cyc?
a: Doug Lenat's project at MCC in Austin, started in 1984, to hand-enter a huge base of common sense knowledge, around a million assertions, so programs stop being brittle. It runs on Lisp and is a ten-year effort.

q: What is ELIZA and can I get the source?
a: ELIZA is Joseph Weizenbaum's 1966 program that imitates a Rogerian psychotherapist by pattern matching on your sentences. Versions in Lisp are in Norvig's and Winston's books, and Emacs has one called doctor, try M-x doctor.

q: What is OPS5?
a: It's a forward-chaining production system language from Carnegie Mellon, and the Lisp version is widely available. XCON at DEC was written in it. It uses the Rete algorithm to match rules efficiently.

q: What is Scheme and who made it?
a: A small Lisp dialect created by Gerald Sussman and Guy Steele at MIT in 1975. It has lexical scope, first-class continuations and a tiny core. The IEEE standard for it was approved in 1990.

q: What is a Lisp 'property list'?
a: Each symbol has a list of alternating names and values you read with GET and set with (setf (get 'sym 'prop) value). It was an early way to attach data to symbols. Hash tables are often better for large sets.

q: What is a Lisp machine and is it worth buying one?
a: It's a workstation with hardware built to run Lisp fast, like the Symbolics 3600 or TI Explorer. They're great environments but cost $50,000 or more. Sun-4 and similar workstations running Lucid or Franz Lisp are catching up for much less.

q: What is a Lisp macro and how is it different from a function?
a: A macro gets its arguments unevaluated and returns a new piece of code, which is then evaluated in its place. Functions get evaluated arguments. You use DEFMACRO with backquote to build things like new control structures such as WHILE.

q: What is a closure?
a: A function bundled with the variable bindings that were visible where it was created. You can make a counter with (let ((n 0)) #'(lambda () (incf n))), and each call remembers its own n. Scheme and Common Lisp both support them.

q: What is a neural network and is it the same as AI?
a: It's a program made of many simple connected units that learn by adjusting weights, usually by backpropagation. It's part of AI but very different from symbolic Lisp-style work. The PDP books by Rumelhart and McClelland are the standard intro.

q: What is backward chaining versus forward chaining?
a: Forward chaining starts from known facts and fires rules to derive new ones. Backward chaining starts from a goal and works back to see what facts would prove it. MYCIN and Prolog work backward, while OPS5 works forward.

q: What is garbage collection and why does my Lisp pause?
a: Lisp allocates memory for you and periodically finds and reclaims what's no longer used. On small machines a full GC can freeze you for many seconds. Ephemeral or generational collectors on Symbolics machines make it much less noticeable.

q: What is machine learning, really?
a: It's programs that improve with experience. Examples are Samuel's checkers player, decision tree induction like Quinlan's ID3, and neural nets trained with backpropagation. The Machine Learning journal started in 1986 if you want to read more.

q: What is natural language processing and how far along is it?
a: It's getting computers to parse and understand human language. Parsing with ATNs and unification grammars works for limited domains, and database front ends like Intellect sell commercially. Open-ended understanding is still far off.

q: What is tail recursion and does my Lisp optimize it?
a: A tail call is the last thing a function does, so it can reuse the stack frame and run in constant space. Scheme requires this. Common Lisp doesn't, though many compilers do it, so use DO or LOOP if you need to be safe.

q: What is the AI winter people keep talking about?
a: Lisp machine makers like Symbolics and LMI are struggling as cheap Sun workstations take their market, and expert system hype is cooling off as companies find the systems hard to maintain. Funding is getting harder to find.

q: What is the Common Lisp standard?
a: Guy Steele's Common Lisp: The Language, published in 1984 and revised in a second edition in 1990, defines it. ANSI committee X3J13 is working on the official standard. Most vendors follow Steele pretty closely.

q: What is the Lisp function APPLY for?
a: It calls a function on a list of arguments, so (apply #'+ '(1 2 3)) gives 6. Handy when you have the arguments in a list at run time. FUNCALL is the same except you list the arguments separately.

q: What is the Symbolics 3600 and who uses it?
a: It's a Lisp machine from Symbolics in Cambridge, running Genera, with a great window system and debugger. Universities, the DARPA labs and some companies like Boeing and Lockheed use them. Prices run from about $50,000 up to well over $100,000.

q: What is the Turing test?
a: Alan Turing proposed in 1950 that if a person talking by teletype can't tell a machine from a human, the machine should be called intelligent. Nothing has come close to passing it, though ELIZA fooled a few people briefly.

q: What is the difference between AI and expert systems?
a: AI is the whole field of making machines do things that take intelligence. Expert systems are one practical branch that encodes a specialist's knowledge as rules, like MYCIN for blood infections or XCON at DEC configuring VAX orders.

q: What is the difference between EQ, EQL, EQUAL and EQUALP?
a: EQ tests for the identical object, so it's unreliable for numbers. EQL also works on same-type numbers and characters. EQUAL compares lists and strings structurally, and EQUALP is looser still, ignoring case in strings and comparing numbers by value.

q: What is the difference between Lucid and Franz Common Lisp?
a: Both are commercial Common Lisps for Unix workstations. Lucid has a strong compiler and is popular on Sun and HP machines, while Franz Allegro grew out of Franz Lisp and has good Unix integration. Try both, as they offer evaluation periods.

q: What is the difference between SETQ, SETF and LET?
a: SETQ assigns to a variable and SETF is the general version that also assigns to places like (car x) or (aref a 3). LET creates new local variables and doesn't change existing ones. Use SETF in new code.

q: What is the difference between a list and an array in Common Lisp?
a: A list is a chain of cons cells, so reaching the nth item takes n steps. An array gives constant time access with AREF but can't grow cheaply. Use lists for small or changing data and arrays or hash tables for big lookups.

q: Where can I get XLISP?
a: It's by David Betz and has been posted on comp.sources and is on many BBSs. It's a small Lisp with object extensions that runs on the PC, Amiga, Atari ST and Unix. Source is included so it's easy to build.

q: Which is better for expert systems, Prolog or Lisp?
a: In the US most people use Lisp, and tools like KEE, ART and Knowledge Craft are built on it. Prolog is popular in Europe and Japan and is nice for rule matching and search. Either works fine, so pick what you can get support for.

q: Why does everyone say Lisp has too many parentheses?
a: Because every expression is written as a list in prefix form, so they pile up at the end. A decent editor like Emacs with lisp-mode matches them and indents for you, and after a while you read the indentation instead.

q: Why does my Lisp function return NIL when I expected a list?
a: Most likely your last form is something like a SETQ inside a loop or a PRINT that returns something else, or your COND has no clause matching. Lisp returns the value of the last form evaluated. Check for a missing default T clause.

q: Why is Lisp used so much for AI?
a: Symbols and lists are built in, code is data so programs can reason about programs, and you can try things interactively without a compile cycle. That makes it good for exploratory work where you don't know the design yet.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Are backups really the best protection against viruses?
a: Yes, nothing beats them. Keep several generations, don't overwrite your only good copy, and scan before you back up. If a virus gets through, a clean backup beats any cleanup program.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Are there viruses for the Amiga?
a: Yes. The SCA virus is the best known, and it's a boot block virus that spreads from floppy to floppy and shows a message after a number of copies. VirusX and Xcopy-type tools can check and repair your boot blocks.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Can I get a virus from a data disk with no system files on it?
a: Yes. If you leave an infected floppy in drive A: and reboot, the PC tries to boot from it, and a boot sector virus gets loaded. You'll get a Non-system disk message, but the virus is already in memory.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Can I get a virus from just reading my mail or Usenet news?
a: Not from plain text. A virus has to be run, and mail and news are only text. The risk is in programs you pull off a BBS or from uuencoded files and then run, so scan before you run.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Can Macs get viruses, or is that only a PC problem?
a: Macs get them too. nVIR and the Scores virus are fairly common, and in 1988 the MacMag peace virus spread through commercial software. Run Disinfectant or Virex and be careful with shared disks.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Can a virus infect my hard disk through a modem download?
a: Yes, if the program you download is infected and you run it. Scan new downloads before you run them, and try not to run programs from unknown uploaders. Plain text files and ZIP archives won't infect you until you run what's inside.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Did the Internet worm erase files?
a: No, it didn't delete anything. The damage was that it kept infecting machines that were already running it, so the load climbed until they were unusable. Admins lost days cleaning up, and mail was down at many sites.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Does Stoned destroy my data?
a: Usually not on purpose, but it can bite. It hides the original boot record in a spot on the disk that on some disks, especially old 360K floppies, holds directory entries, so files can get trashed. Clean it off and back up first.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Does a low-level format get rid of a boot sector virus?
a: It will, but it also wipes all your data, so it's a last resort. Usually it's enough to boot from a clean floppy and clean the boot sector with a scanner, or to rewrite it with SYS on a floppy.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: How can I check a downloaded .EXE file is safe?
a: Scan it with an up-to-date scanner, and compare the size and checksum with what the author posted, if they posted any. Run it first on a floppy-only system, or on a machine without anything important.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: How can I keep floppies from being infected?
a: On a 5.25 inch disk, put a write-protect tab over the notch. On a 3.5 inch disk, slide the tab open. A write-protected disk can't be infected. Also, don't boot with a stray floppy in drive A:.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: How can I tell if my floppy has the Brain virus?
a: Run DIR or VOL on the disk and see if the volume label has changed to (c)Brain. Floppy access will also feel slower, and CHKDSK may report less free memory than normal. A scanner like McAfee's SCAN will confirm it.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: How did the Internet worm get into machines?
a: It used three ways in. One was the DEBUG command in sendmail, another was a buffer overflow in fingerd, and the third was guessing passwords and trusting rsh and .rhosts relationships. Any one of them was enough to get a copy running.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: How do I boot from a clean floppy?
a: Make a bootable DOS disk from a known-good copy with FORMAT A: /S, copy your scanner onto it, and write-protect it. Put it in drive A: and reboot. That way no virus is loaded in memory while you scan.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: How do I find nVIR on my Macintosh?
a: Open the System file with ResEdit and look for resources of type nVIR. If you see them, you're infected. It's easier to run John Norstad's Disinfectant, which is free and checks every file for you.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: How many machines did the Internet worm hit?
a: The usual estimate is about 6,000 machines, roughly a tenth of the Internet back then. Nobody knows the exact number, because many sites cut their network links to get away from it.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Is Disinfectant really free?
a: Yes, John Norstad at Northwestern gives it away as freeware. You can grab it from sumex-aim.stanford.edu by anonymous FTP or off most Mac BBSes. He updates it whenever a new Mac virus turns up, so get the newest version.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Is Virex worth buying for the Mac?
a: If you don't mind paying, Virex from HJC Software is solid and gets updates. But Disinfectant is free and does an excellent job on known Mac viruses, so try it first. Plenty of people use both.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Is a boot sector virus different from a file virus?
a: Yes. A boot sector virus lives in the first sector of a floppy or hard disk and loads before DOS does. A file virus attaches to .COM or .EXE programs and runs only when you start them. Brain and Stoned are boot sector viruses.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Is it illegal to write a virus?
a: It depends where you are. In the U.S. the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986 covers unauthorized access and damage to computers, and the Morris case showed it will be used. Several states also have computer crime laws.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Is it worth paying for a commercial antivirus like Norton or Central Point?
a: If you run a business or have many machines, yes. Symantec's Norton Antivirus and Central Point Anti-Virus come with manuals, support and updates. At home, SCAN and F-Prot are fine for much less.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Is shareware antivirus software worth using?
a: Yes. SCAN from McAfee, F-Prot from Fridrik Skulason and Flu_Shot+ from Ross Greenberg are well respected and cheap or free to try. Update them every few months, because they only catch the viruses they already know about.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Is the Internet worm a virus or a worm?
a: Strictly it's a worm. A virus attaches itself to other programs, but a worm is a stand-alone program that copies itself from machine to machine over the network. People still say virus when they mean either, though.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Should I be worried about pirated games?
a: A bit. Cracked games get passed around on floppies, and that's how Stoned, Brain and Ping-Pong spread. Scan every disk, even from friends, and keep write protect on whenever you only need to read it.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Should I use FORMAT to clean up my floppies?
a: A real FORMAT of a floppy clears the boot sector and removes the virus along with the files. Quick or unconditional options can leave things behind, so use a regular FORMAT on suspicious floppies, after copying the files you need.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What are checksum programs and do they work against viruses?
a: They record a checksum for each program, and if the file is changed later, the number won't match. That finds viruses the scanner doesn't know yet. It can't tell you what the virus is, though, and you need a clean baseline first.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What does "resident" mean for a virus?
a: A resident virus stays in memory after it's loaded and hooks into DOS or BIOS calls, so it can infect each disk or file you touch. Stoned and Brain both stay resident, and your free memory will drop slightly.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What does Friday the 13th have to do with viruses?
a: Some viruses, Jerusalem the best known, have a trigger date. On Friday the 13th they delete programs you run. If you haven't scanned yet, back up your files and don't use the machine that day.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What does nVIR do to a Mac?
a: nVIR infects the System file and any application you run, adding nVIR resources to them. After a while infected Macs may beep when you start programs, and some variants make MacinTalk say Don't panic. Disinfectant will remove it.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What does the Cascade virus do?
a: Cascade infects .COM files, and on certain dates the characters on your screen start to fall to the bottom in a heap. It looks strange, but it's just a display effect. Remove it with SCAN and CLEAN-UP.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is CERT, and why was it set up?
a: CERT is the Computer Emergency Response Team at Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute. DARPA set it up in November 1988 after the Internet worm, so sites would have one place to report and get help with security problems.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is a computer virus, exactly?
a: It's a program that copies itself into other programs or disks without you knowing. Every time you run an infected program or boot from an infected floppy, it gets a chance to spread. Some do damage, some just sit there and annoy you.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is a logic bomb?
a: A logic bomb is code that sits quietly until a condition is met, like a date or a particular user being removed from a payroll file, and then does damage. It doesn't copy itself, so it isn't a virus.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is comp.virus?
a: It's the Usenet side of the VIRUS-L digest, a moderated list started in 1988 at Lehigh by Ken van Wyk. People post virus reports, scanner news and questions. Read the FAQ before you post, and don't send viruses around.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is the Brain virus?
a: Brain is a boot sector virus for IBM PCs, written by two brothers in Lahore, Pakistan, and found in 1986. It spreads on 360K floppies and slows down disk access. Look at the volume label of an infected disk and you'll see (c)Brain.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is the Christmas tree worm?
a: It was a program that spread on IBM mainframe networks in December 1987. It showed a Christmas tree on your screen and, without being asked, mailed itself to everyone in your NAMES file, which clogged BITNET and IBM's internal network.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is the Dark Avenger virus?
a: Dark Avenger is the name taken by a virus writer in Bulgaria, and also the name of his virus from 1989. It infects files fast and corrupts data slowly, so you may have backups full of bad files before you notice.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is the Jerusalem virus?
a: It's a file virus found in Israel in 1987 that infects .COM and .EXE files. On Friday the 13th it deletes any program you run. It also makes infected programs grow, which is how you can spot it.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is the Peace virus on the Mac?
a: The Peace virus, also called MacMag, was written to show a message of universal peace on March 2, 1988 and then delete itself. It got into the commercial Aldus FreeHand disks. Disinfectant and other tools detect it.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is the Ping-Pong virus?
a: Ping-Pong, also called Bouncing Ball, is a boot sector virus that appeared in Italy in 1988. After a while a little ball bounces around your screen. It's harmless apart from that, but it will take up memory and floppy space.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What is the Scores virus on the Mac?
a: Scores is a Mac virus that shows up in 1988 and attacks the System file, and it seems aimed at some particular applications. Look for odd Scrapbook and Note Pad icons, then run Disinfectant, which removes it.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What was the Internet worm?
a: On November 2, 1988, a program spread across the Internet and loaded down thousands of Sun 3 and VAX machines running BSD Unix. It copied itself from host to host through holes in sendmail and fingerd, and kept starting new copies until the machines crawled.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: What was the Lehigh virus?
a: Lehigh turned up at Lehigh University in late 1987. It infected COMMAND.COM and after four infections it trashed the disk. It was discovered fast because the damage was so quick, which kept it from spreading far.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Where can I get a virus scanner?
a: Check your local BBS file areas or anonymous FTP sites such as simtel20.army.mil. McAfee's SCAN and CLEAN-UP, F-Prot and Disinfectant for the Mac are all there. Download from a trusted site and check that the scanner is a current version.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Where did the Stoned virus come from?
a: As far as anyone can tell it came from New Zealand, around 1987 or 1988. It's become one of the most common viruses on PC floppies. Some versions say Legalise Marijuana, but that's all the message does.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Which is better, McAfee SCAN or Flu_Shot+?
a: They do different jobs. SCAN checks your disks for known viruses on demand, and Flu_Shot+ sits in memory and warns you when a program tries something suspicious. I run both, and I run SCAN on any new disk.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Who wrote the Internet worm?
a: Robert T. Morris, a Cornell grad student. He was convicted in January 1990 under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. In May he got three years' probation, 400 hours of community service and a fine of about $10,000.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Why can't a scanner catch every virus?
a: A scanner looks for strings and patterns of viruses that are already known. A new virus, or a modified one, won't be on its list. That's why you keep updating the scanner and also use a checksum or memory-resident guard.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Why does CHKDSK show less memory than it should?
a: Possibly just drivers and TSRs, but a memory-resident virus can also take a few KB. Brain takes about 7K. Compare with a clean boot from a write-protected floppy, and if the numbers differ, scan the machine.

topic: computer viruses: Brain, Stoned, nVIR, the Internet worm
q: Why does my PC say "Your PC is now Stoned!" when I boot?
a: You've got the Stoned virus. It's a boot sector virus that shows that message on roughly one boot in eight. Boot from a clean, write-protected floppy and use a scanner such as SCAN or F-Prot to remove it from your hard disk.

q: Can I append another dump to the same tape?
a: Yes, with the no-rewind device such as /dev/nrst0 on a Sun. Each dump becomes a separate file on the tape, and you can skip forward with mt fsf. Make sure the tape has room.

q: Can I back up my Macintosh to a tape drive?
a: Yes, there are SCSI tape drives for the Mac from companies like Tecmar and Mountain, with backup software such as Retrospect from Dantz. Retrospect is also good for backing up over AppleTalk.

q: Can I back up while users are logged in on a Unix machine?
a: You can, but files being written may come out inconsistent. For dump the safest way is single-user mode, or at least unmounting the filesystem. Otherwise expect an occasional bad file on restore.

q: Can I copy a whole disk with dd?
a: Yes, dd if=/dev/rsd0c of=/dev/rst0 bs=64k copies a raw disk to tape. It copies every block, even unused ones, so it takes longer than dump. Restoring needs a disk of the same size or larger.

q: Can I use a VCR to back up my Amiga?
a: Yes. Products like Backer from Ecosoft plug into the video port and record data on ordinary VHS tape, about 200MB on a two-hour tape. It's cheap but you should verify your tapes regularly.

q: Do I need to degauss tapes before reusing them?
a: No. Writing over a tape erases the old data, and the drive's erase head does the job. Bulk erasing is only needed if you want to destroy data without rewriting.

q: Do floppy disks wear out sitting in a drawer?
a: They last for years if kept cool and dry, but I wouldn't count on one beyond five or so. Copy important archives to fresh media periodically, and keep two copies.

q: Does the Amiga have a built-in backup program?
a: Not really. The Workbench disk gives you Copy and DiskCopy, but for a hard drive you want something like Quarterback, which backs up a partition to floppies and can restore single files.

q: How can I store an 800K disk image with the Mac?
a: Use DiskCopy from Apple to make an image file of the floppy, which you can keep on your hard disk or send out by modem. Copying files in the Finder works too, but an image preserves the boot blocks.

q: How can I tell if my backup is any good?
a: Verify it. Most programs have a compare option, like tar's d option or the verify setting in Fastback. The real test is restoring a few files to another directory and checking them.

q: How do I back up an Atari ST hard disk?
a: Programs like Fast Copy or the backup utility that came with your hard disk software write the partition to floppies. Back up the partition to files first if your software supports it, and keep the disk count manageable with compression.

q: How do I back up my files on a VAX/VMS system?
a: Use the BACKUP command, such as BACKUP/IMAGE DUA0: MUA0:SAVE.BCK/SAVE_SET for a full disk. Use /SINCE=BACKUP for an incremental. Add /VERIFY if you want it to compare the files afterwards.

q: How do I back up my hard disk to floppies under MS-DOS?
a: Use BACKUP from DOS, like BACKUP C:\*.* A: /S to include subdirectories. Have plenty of formatted disks ready and label them in order. Restore with RESTORE A: C:\*.* /S. Test a restore before you trust it.

q: How do I back up over the network from one Unix machine to another?
a: Pipe through rsh to the machine with the tape drive, such as tar cf - /home | rsh tapehost dd of=/dev/rmt0 bs=20b. BSD dump can also use the remote tape host with the host:device form.

q: How do I make a tar backup to tape on a Sun?
a: Try tar cvf /dev/rst0 /home to write to the first SCSI tape drive. Use the rewinding device, and tar tvf /dev/rst0 afterward to check the table of contents. For whole filesystems use dump instead.

q: How do I restore a single file with dump?
a: Run restore -i from a directory you can write to, with -f giving the tape device. Use ls and cd to browse, add the filename, then type extract. Only the files you've marked get restored.

q: How long does a DC600A tape last?
a: With care, a few years or a few hundred passes. Heat, dust and stray magnetic fields shorten that. Retension it now and then and replace tapes used heavily for daily backups.

q: How many generations of backups should I keep?
a: Keep at least three sets and rotate them, the old grandfather-father-son scheme. That way, if the latest tape is bad or you discover a problem a week later, you still have an older copy.

q: How much data fits on a DC300XL cartridge?
a: A DC300XL holds about 40MB in the QIC-40 style formats. Older QIC-11 drives wrote around 20MB on the same tape type, so check your drive's format before buying media.

q: How often should I back up my system?
a: Depends how much work you can afford to redo. Most people do a full backup weekly and an incremental daily. If losing a day of work would hurt, back up daily.

q: Is a removable Bernoulli drive good for backups?
a: Iomega's Bernoulli Box is quite good. A 20MB cartridge is fast to write and quite durable, but the cost per megabyte is higher than tape, so it suits people who also want quick access to the data.

q: Is a tape drive worth it for a 40MB hard disk?
a: Yes, if you value your data. Floppies for 40MB means about 30 disks and a lot of babysitting. A QIC-40 drive runs a few hundred dollars and lets you back up unattended overnight.

q: Is it OK to compress files before writing them to tape?
a: You can, using compress on Unix, but one bad spot can ruin everything after it in the compressed stream. Many people prefer drives or software that compress in small blocks, or leave files uncompressed.

q: Is it safe to use PKZIP to back up files?
a: It's fine for archiving selected files, and compression saves floppies. But it's not a complete system backup, since it won't track changes well. Use it for data directories, and test archives with PKUNZIP -t.

q: Should I keep my backups in the same room as the computer?
a: Better not. A fire or theft takes both. Keep at least one recent set somewhere else, such as at home or in a fireproof safe in another building.

q: What can I do about a tape that stretched or broke?
a: If it snapped, you can splice it with a splicing kit for reels, but cartridges are best sent to a data recovery firm. Copy off whatever you can read and replace the tape.

q: What does 6250 bpi mean?
a: It means bits per inch, the recording density on 9-track tape. 6250 bpi uses GCR encoding and holds about 140MB on a 2400-foot reel. Older tapes are 1600 or 800 bpi and hold much less.

q: What does QIC stand for?
a: Quarter-Inch Cartridge, the industry committee and the standard for tapes of that size. You'll see QIC-24, QIC-120, QIC-150 and so on, each number naming a format and roughly how it's written.

q: What does Retrospect do?
a: It's Dantz's Macintosh backup program. It does full and incremental backups to tape, floppies, or removable disks, and can back up other Macs over a network. It keeps a catalog, so restoring a file is easy.

q: What does it mean to retension a tape?
a: You wind the cartridge fully to the end and back to even out the tension in the tape. It helps prevent read errors and is worth doing on new tapes and ones that sat unused for months.

q: What does mt do on Unix?
a: mt controls the tape drive. For example, mt -f /dev/nrst0 rewind rewinds it, fsf 2 skips forward two files, and status shows the drive's state. It's what you use to position a tape before a restore.

q: What is Fastback?
a: It's a popular PC backup program from Fifth Generation Systems that writes to floppies quickly by formatting and writing in one pass. It can also back up to tape on later versions, and it compresses a bit.

q: What is a DAT drive?
a: Digital Audio Tape adapted for data. It uses a 4mm cartridge and helical scan like a VCR, and holds around 1.3GB on a 60-meter tape. Drives are expensive, around $1500 or more, but it's very compact.

q: What is a QIC-40 tape drive?
a: It's a quarter-inch cartridge drive that hooks to your floppy controller and stores about 40MB on a DC2000 cartridge. Cheap, but slow, and you must format the tape first, which can take an hour or more.

q: What is a streaming tape drive?
a: It's a drive that writes continuously at full tape speed rather than stopping and starting for each block. It needs a steady data feed, but gives the best capacity and speed in return.

q: What is an image backup?
a: It copies the whole disk, structure and all, rather than file by file. You restore it to get an identical disk, which is quick for a total recovery. Picking out single files can be harder, though.

q: What is an incremental backup?
a: It saves only files changed since the last backup. With dump you use levels: level 0 is a full dump, and a higher level saves everything changed since the last lower level. It's much faster than a full dump.

q: What is the best way to store floppy backups?
a: Keep them in a box away from heat, dust and magnets, such as monitors and speakers. Write-protect them, label them with date and contents, and stand them upright in a sleeve.

q: What is the blocking factor in tar?
a: It's the number of 512-byte blocks written per tape record. The default is 20 on many systems, so 10K records. Larger records are better for streaming drives, but the reader must use a matching value.

q: What is the difference between a backup and an archive?
a: A backup is a copy for recovering from loss, normally rotated and overwritten. An archive is a long-term record of data you want to keep, such as a finished project, and it shouldn't be reused.

q: What should I label on a backup tape?
a: Write the date, the machine name, the filesystem or directories, the dump level, and the tape number in the set. Also note the software and block size used. Six months later you won't remember.

q: What's the capacity of an Exabyte drive?
a: The EXB-8200 uses 8mm video cassettes and holds about 2.3GB per tape. It connects by SCSI. Many sites use it for backing up networks of Suns because of its capacity and low media cost.

q: What's the difference between a floppy tape drive and a SCSI tape drive?
a: Floppy-interface drives like QIC-40 are cheap and slow, around 5MB a minute. SCSI drives are faster, hold more, and use a host adapter, but cost more. SCSI is the better choice on Unix systems.

q: What's the difference between tar and cpio?
a: Both pack files into one archive. tar is simpler and found everywhere, while cpio takes its file list from stdin, like find . -print | cpio -o, and handles special files better. System V folks lean on cpio, BSD folks on tar.

q: Which is better, 9-track or cartridge tape?
a: 9-track reel tape is faster and universal for exchanging data between mainframes and minis, but the drives are huge and costly. Cartridge drives are smaller and cheaper, so for a workstation or PC they make more sense.

q: Why does DOS BACKUP say Insert backup diskette 02 in drive A?
a: It's asking you to swap disks because the first one filled up. Number your disks carefully, since RESTORE needs them in sequence. Also have the disks formatted ahead of time or BACKUP will lose time formatting.

q: Why does my tape drive keep shuttling back and forth?
a: Streaming drives need data fed fast enough. If your disk or computer can't keep up, the drive stops, rewinds a bit, and restarts, which is called shoe-shining. Try a faster disk, bigger buffer, or less multitasking during the backup.

q: Why does tar say Directory checksum error?
a: Tar found a block that isn't a valid header. Often it's a blocking factor mismatch, so try the b option with the same value used when writing, or the tape is damaged or not a tar archive.

q: Why is my tape backup so slow?
a: Common reasons are a slow controller, a fragmented disk, small block sizes, or software compression. On Unix, use a larger blocking factor, like tar with b 20. On a PC, avoid running other programs.

q: Will DOS 3.3 RESTORE read disks made by DOS 2.0 BACKUP?
a: Mostly not reliably. The backup file format changed between DOS versions, and later versions of RESTORE may complain. Keep the DOS version you used to make the backup around.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Can I put a picture into a WordPerfect document?
a: With 5.0 and 5.1 you can. Press Alt-F9 for Graphics, choose Figure, and Create, then enter the file name of a .WPG or other supported graphic. You will see it only in View Document, not in normal edit mode.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Can I run WordPerfect on my Atari ST or Amiga?
a: Yes, WordPerfect has versions for the Atari ST and the Amiga, and also for the Macintosh and the Apple IIGS. They are not file-for-file identical to the PC version, but WordPerfect can convert between them.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Can I use proportional fonts in WordStar?
a: WordStar 5.0 and 5.5 support proportional spacing on printers that can do it, such as laser printers and many 24-pin dot matrix models. Older versions stick mostly to fixed pitch unless you use special patches.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Can WordPerfect read Microsoft Word files?
a: Not directly in 5.0, but WP 5.1 can convert some formats with the Convert program that ships with it. The safest route is to save as plain ASCII or RTF from Word and import that, though formatting will suffer.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Does WordStar have a spell checker?
a: WordStar Professional Release 4 and later include SpellStar, and earlier versions need a separate add-on like MailMerge's companions or a third-party tool. In WordStar 4 and later you press Ctrl-O L, or use the menu, to check the document.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How can I move a paragraph in WordPerfect?
a: Put the cursor on the paragraph and press Ctrl-F4, then choose 2 for Paragraph and 1 for Move. Pick Retrieve, move the cursor to the new place, and press Enter. Block and Ctrl-F4 works for any selection.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I center a line of text in WordPerfect?
a: Put the cursor at the start of the line and press Shift-F6, then type the text and press Enter. You will see a [Cntr] code in Reveal Codes. You can also center a whole page top to bottom from the Shift-F8 menu.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I change the font in MacWrite?
a: Select the text, then pick a typeface from the Font menu and a size from the Size menu. Fonts are installed with the Font/DA Mover on System 4 and earlier, so check that the font is in your System file.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I change the line spacing to double in Word 5.0 for DOS?
a: Select the paragraphs, press Alt-F, then choose Format Paragraph and set Line spacing to 2. Or press Alt-2, the shortcut for double spacing. Alt-1 goes back to single spacing.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I count the words in a WordPerfect document?
a: WP 5.0 has no word count in the main menu, but the spell checker, Ctrl-F2, gives the word count when it finishes checking. Pick the Word Count option at the end of the check.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I do a footnote in WordPerfect 5.0?
a: Press Ctrl-F7 for Footnote, choose 1 for Footnote and then 1 for Create. Type your note on the edit screen and press F7 to return to the document. Numbering and placement at the page bottom are automatic.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I do a mail merge in WordPerfect 5.0?
a: You need a primary file with the letter and a secondary file with the data. In the primary, press Shift-F9 for Merge Codes and enter fields like ^F1^ for the first field. Then Ctrl-F9 and choose Merge to combine the two.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I get a block of text to be bold in WordStar?
a: Type Ctrl-P then B at the start of the text and again at the end. The ^B marks show on screen, and the text prints bold. Ctrl-P S does underline the same way.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I get an Epson FX-80 to print in WordPerfect 5.0?
a: Use Shift-F7, choose Select Printer, add the Epson FX-80 from the list of .PRS driver files that came on the Printer disks, and set the port to LPT1. Then pick it and press Select.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I get the Mac to hold a long document in Word without slowing down?
a: Use the Save As command with a new name once in a while to cut the fast save clutter, and keep the file under around 30 pages. Word 4.0 also lets you split chapters into files and use Include to link them.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I make WordPerfect start with my own margins and tab settings?
a: Put the settings at the top of a document and save it as a template, or change the Initial Codes in Shift-F1 Setup, under Initial Settings. That makes every new document start with the codes you want.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I make WordPerfect stop making .BK! backup files?
a: Those are from the timed or original backup options. Press Shift-F1 for Setup, choose Backup, and turn off the original backup option. Timed backup makes the temporary files, which are erased when you exit normally.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I make a header on every page in WordPerfect 5.0?
a: Press Shift-F8, pick 2 for Page, then 3 for Headers. Choose Header A, say Every Page, and type your text. Use ^B in the text for the automatic page number.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I print two copies of a document in MacWrite?
a: Choose Print from the File menu and type 2 in the Copies box of the dialog, then click OK. On an ImageWriter you can also pick Best, Faster or Draft quality at that same dialog.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I save a WordPerfect file as plain ASCII text?
a: Press Ctrl-F5 for Text In/Out, choose 1 for Save, and then 3 for Generic Word Processor, or use DOS Text. Give the file a new name. Formatting codes are stripped, so keep the original WP file as well.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I search and replace in WordPerfect?
a: Press Alt-F2 for Replace, answer Y or N for confirm, type the search text, press F2, type the replacement and press F2 again. Searches go forward from the cursor, so go to the top of the document first.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I see the hidden codes in WordPerfect 5.0?
a: Press Alt-F3, which is Reveal Codes. The screen splits and shows your text with codes like [HRt] and [Bold] in the bottom half. Press Alt-F3 or F1 again to go back to normal editing.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I set tabs in WordPerfect 5.1?
a: Press Shift-F8 for Line format, choose 8 for Tab Set, then move the cursor and type L, C, R or D for left, center, right or decimal tabs. Ctrl-End clears tabs to the right of the cursor.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How do I undelete text in WordPerfect?
a: Press F1 for Cancel and choose 1 to restore the last deletion. It remembers the last three deletions, and you can step through them with option 2 for Previous Deletion.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: How much hard disk space does WordPerfect 5.1 need?
a: A full install takes around 4 to 5 megabytes with the speller, thesaurus and printer files. You can run it from floppies, but a hard disk is much nicer. You'll want at least 512K of RAM, preferably 640K.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Is MacWrite still any good now that Word 4.0 is out?
a: For short letters it's fine and quick. Word 4.0 does far more, like outlines, styles, glossaries and long documents, but it's bigger and slower. Pick based on what you write most.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Is Word for DOS hard to learn compared to WordPerfect?
a: Word uses menus with the Esc key and a command line at the bottom, so it's easy to explore without memorizing keys. WordPerfect needs the function key template at first but is quick once learned. Both do the job.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Is WordPerfect better than Microsoft Word for DOS?
a: WordPerfect has the bigger user base, better printer drivers and a cleaner screen, so it's the safe choice in most offices. Word 5.0 has styles and a nicer menu system, but many folks find WP faster once the function keys are learned.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Is it OK to use a mouse with WordPerfect?
a: WordPerfect 5.1 supports a mouse and pull-down menus, which you get with Alt-equals or a right click. Earlier versions have no mouse support at all. Word 5.0 for DOS also supports a mouse.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Is it worth upgrading from WordPerfect 4.2 to 5.0?
a: Yes if you do anything beyond plain letters. 5.0 adds a real graphics mode, better columns, tables of contents, and a much bigger set of printers. It does need more disk space and memory, so make sure you have 384K or more.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What are function key templates for and do I need one for WordPerfect?
a: It's a plastic strip that sits over the function keys, listing the commands for Shift, Ctrl, Alt and plain keys in colors. It's very handy at first, and most people stop looking at it after a few weeks.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What does Ctrl-F10 do in WordPerfect?
a: It starts defining a macro in WordPerfect 5.0. Give it a name or an Alt-letter key, type a description, then do the keystrokes and press Ctrl-F10 again to stop. Alt plus that letter plays it back.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What does Ctrl-K S do in WordStar?
a: It saves your file and keeps you in the document so you can continue editing. Ctrl-K D saves and returns you to the opening menu, and Ctrl-K X saves and exits to DOS.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What does the Ctrl-Q Ctrl-S command do in WordStar?
a: It moves the cursor to the start of the line. Ctrl-Q D goes to the end of the line, and Ctrl-Q R and Ctrl-Q C jump to the top or bottom of the file. Those are the quick-movement commands.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What does the Print Preview or View Document do in WordPerfect?
a: Press Shift-F7 then 6 for View Document in WP 5.0. It shows the page as it will print, including margins, headers and graphics, so you can check layout without wasting paper. Press F7 to return.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What does the dot command .PA do in WordStar?
a: It forces a page break at that point when the file prints. Dot commands start in column one of a line, and they don't print; they just control things like margins, headers and page length.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What does the number after WordStar like 3.3 or 4.0 mean for my disk files?
a: It's the version, and the files are mostly compatible since WordStar uses high-bit-set characters for soft hyphens and word wrap. Opening in non-document mode, with N, gives a plain text file that anything can read.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What does the ruler in Word for the Mac do?
a: It sets the tabs, indents and line spacing for the selected paragraphs. Drag the markers to change margins and indents, and click the tab icons to set left, center, right or decimal tabs. Use Show Ruler in the Format menu.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What is WYSIWYG and which of these word processors have it?
a: It stands for What You See Is What You Get, meaning the screen looks like the printed page. MacWrite and Word for the Mac have it. DOS versions of WordPerfect and WordStar show codes on screen, though WP's View Document is close.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What is a style in Word 4.0 for the Mac?
a: A style is a saved set of character and paragraph formatting that you name, like Heading or Body Text. Change the style definition and every paragraph using it updates, which beats reformatting by hand.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What is a thesaurus function in word processors like WordPerfect?
a: It lets you put the cursor on a word and press Alt-F1 to see synonyms and antonyms. Pick one by its letter and it replaces your word. It needs the WP{WP}US.THS file in your WP directory.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What is the best word processor for a Macintosh Plus?
a: Microsoft Word 4.0 is the heavy hitter for long documents and has styles, while MacWrite is simpler and lighter on memory. WriteNow is quick and small if you have only 1 meg. Try demos before you buy.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: What is the difference between a soft return and a hard return in WordPerfect?
a: A soft return [SRt] is the automatic wrap at the right margin, and WordPerfect moves it if you edit. A hard return [HRt] is what you insert with the Enter key, and it stays put until you delete it.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Which word processor handles tables and columns best, WordPerfect or Word?
a: WordPerfect 5.1 has a real Tables feature, while Word 5.0 uses tabs and side-by-side paragraphs. For newspaper style columns, both do the job well. Word on the Mac is nice for page layout types of work.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Why does MacWrite say there's not enough memory on my 512K Mac?
a: MacWrite is a memory hog, especially with pictures in the file. Close desk accessories, use the Finder rather than MultiFinder, and split long documents into smaller files. A Mac Plus with 1 meg helps a lot.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Why does my WordPerfect document print with the wrong margins on a laser printer?
a: Laser printers can't print to the paper's edge, usually about a quarter inch is unprintable. Set your margins to at least 0.25 inch, and make sure you picked the right printer driver and paper size definition in Shift-F7.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Why does my dot matrix printer print garbage from WordStar?
a: Usually the printer is set to the wrong mode, or WordStar was installed for a different printer with WINSTALL. Check the DIP switches and the cable, and then run the install program to choose your model.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Why does my text jump to the next line when I type in WordStar?
a: That's word wrap at the right margin. If you want to see the true line breaks, turn on the ruler and check the margin settings with Ctrl-O R. Soft wraps appear without the dot or the less-than sign in the margin.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Why is my WordPerfect so slow to scroll on my XT?
a: An 8088 at 4.77 MHz is slow, and 5.0 does a lot of work on screen. Try turning off timed backup, using a disk cache, and avoid the graphics mode screens. A faster AT or 286 helps the most.

topic: word processors: WordPerfect, WordStar, MacWrite, Word
q: Why won't my WordPerfect file open on another PC?
a: Most likely the other machine has an older version, since WP 5.0 files can't be read by 4.2. Save it in the older format from the other machine's Text In/Out, or save as DOS text with Ctrl-F5 to make an ASCII file.

q: Can Excel on a Mac and Excel on a PC share files?
a: Mostly yes. Excel 2.2 on the Mac and Excel 2.1 for Windows use the same file format, so you can move files by network or by DOS-formatted floppy using Apple File Exchange. Fonts and column widths might shift slightly.

q: Can Excel read Lotus 1-2-3 files?
a: Yes. Excel opens .WKS and .WK1 files directly with File Open, and it can save back in Lotus format too. Some 1-2-3 macros won't translate, and a few formatting details may be lost, so check your totals.

q: Can I make graphs in 1-2-3?
a: Yes, use /Graph. Pick a type like Line, Bar or Pie, set X for labels and A through F for data ranges, then View to see it. You need a graphics card such as CGA or Hercules. To print, save with Save and use PrintGraph.

q: Can I run 1-2-3 from a floppy-only system?
a: Yes, but it's awkward. Release 2.01 wants the system disk in A and a data disk in B, and it prompts you to swap disks for the help file and drivers. A hard drive makes life much easier.

q: Can I use 1-2-3 as a database?
a: For small stuff, yes. Put field names in a row, records below, and use /Data Query to find or extract records based on a criterion range. It is limited to what fits in memory, so for serious work get dBase.

q: Does 1-2-3 have an undo?
a: Release 2.2 and later have Alt-F4 for Undo, but only if you turn it on, and it takes memory. Earlier versions have none, so save before you do anything drastic like /Range Erase or a big /Copy.

q: Does Excel for Windows need a mouse?
a: It's much nicer with one, but you can use the keyboard. Alt opens the menus and the arrow keys move around. Excel 2.1 runs under Windows 2.x or the Windows runtime that ships with it.

q: How can I make a cell display a dollar sign and two decimals in 1-2-3?
a: Use /Range Format Currency, enter 2 for decimal places, and select the cells. Use /Worksheet Global Format Currency if you want it for the whole sheet. Note the format only changes display, not the stored value.

q: How can I tell which version of 1-2-3 I have?
a: The opening screen shows the release number with the copyright notice. Inside the program, the /Worksheet Status screen shows memory use and settings. Files saved as .WKS came from release 1A, and .WK1 from release 2 and later.

q: How do I calculate a loan payment in a spreadsheet?
a: Use @PMT(principal,interest,term) where interest is per period. For a $10,000 loan at 12 percent annual over 36 months, use @PMT(10000,.12/12,36), which comes to about $332.14 per month.

q: How do I change the default directory in 1-2-3?
a: Use /Worksheet Global Default Directory and type the path, like C:\DATA. Then choose Update to save it so it's there next time you start. Otherwise 1-2-3 uses whatever directory you launched it from.

q: How do I combine data from two worksheets in 1-2-3?
