a: Use /File Combine. You can copy an entire file or a named range into the current sheet, and choose Add or Subtract to do arithmetic on cells. Put the pointer where the incoming upper left corner should go first.

q: How do I copy a formula down a column without changing the column letter?
a: Use /Copy, then pick the source cell and the destination range. References are relative by default, so row numbers adjust. If a column must stay put, use $ before the letter, like $B2.

q: How do I enter a date in 1-2-3?
a: Use @DATE(year,month,day), for example @DATE(88,3,15), which gives a serial number. Then apply /Range Format Date to display it as 15-Mar-88. Serial 1 is January 1, 1900, so you can subtract dates to get days.

q: How do I find the average of a range ignoring blanks?
a: @AVG(A1..A20) skips empty cells and labels, so it only averages cells containing numbers. But a zero you typed in does count, so leave truly unknown values blank rather than entering 0.

q: How do I freeze titles so headings stay on screen when I scroll in 1-2-3?
a: Put the cell pointer just below and to the right of the rows and columns you want to keep, then use /Worksheet Titles and choose Both, Horizontal or Vertical. To undo it, use /Worksheet Titles Clear.

q: How do I get rid of a range I named by mistake?
a: Use /Range Name Delete and pick the name from the list, or /Range Name Reset to wipe all of them. Deleting a name doesn't change the cells, but formulas using the name will turn into plain addresses.

q: How do I lock cells so nobody overwrites my formulas in 1-2-3?
a: Use /Range Unprotect on the cells that may be edited, then turn on /Worksheet Global Protection Enable. All the other cells become locked. Remember it's only protection against accidents, not real security.

q: How do I make 1-2-3 print my spreadsheet on one page?
a: Use /Print Printer Range to set the area, then Options Margins and Setup. For wide sheets send the compressed string \015 as Setup for most Epson-compatible printers, which gives about 132 columns. Then Align and Go.

q: How do I make a number show as a percent?
a: Use /Range Format Percent and give the number of decimals. Enter .15 and you'll see 15%. In Excel you can also type 15% directly into the cell and it will understand.

q: How do I print a 1-2-3 graph?
a: Save it first with /Graph Save, which makes a .PIC file. Quit to the access menu and start PrintGraph, choose Image-Select, pick the file, then Align and Go. It's a separate program, which is a pain, but it works.

q: How do I round a number to two decimals in a formula?
a: Use @ROUND(number,2) around the formula, like @ROUND(A1*B1,2). Formatting only changes how the number looks, so if you want the stored value rounded for later sums, you need @ROUND.

q: How do I sort a list in 1-2-3?
a: Use /Data Sort. Set the Data-Range to your records (not including the headers), then set Primary-Key to a cell in the column you want to sort on, choose A or D for ascending or descending, and Go.

q: How do I total a column of numbers in Lotus 1-2-3?
a: Put the cell pointer under the column and type @SUM( then point to the first cell, type a period, move to the last cell, close the paren and hit Enter. Something like @SUM(B2..B20). Beats typing +B2+B3+B4 any day.

q: How much memory do I need to run 1-2-3 release 2?
a: Release 2.x needs 256K minimum, but you'll want 512K or 640K for decent size models. Everything lives in conventional RAM, so big sheets hit the 640K wall. Lotus/Intel/Microsoft expanded memory (EMS) helps with release 3.

q: Is Excel on the Mac any good compared to Multiplan?
a: Much better. Excel gives you real fonts, charts, and menus you can use with the mouse, plus it handles bigger sheets. Multiplan is fine but looks dated and uses the R1C1 style references that many people dislike.

q: Is Lotus Symphony worth looking at?
a: Symphony puts spreadsheet, word processing, database and communications in one program, and it's fine if you like integrated software. Its spreadsheet is mostly 1-2-3 compatible but it eats memory and is slower. Most people just run 1-2-3 plus a word processor.

q: Is it worth buying a math coprocessor just for spreadsheets?
a: If you do heavy recalculation on large models, yes. An 8087 or 80287 can cut recalc times by half or more and 1-2-3 uses it automatically. For small budget sheets you won't notice, so save your money.

q: Is it worth upgrading from Lotus 1-2-3 release 2.01 to 2.2?
a: If you run big models, yes. 2.2 adds file linking improvements, SmartIcons are not there but the better printing and the ability to undo-ish cleanup help. Cost is modest for registered users, and your .WK1 files carry over untouched.

q: What are the limits on worksheet size in 1-2-3 release 2?
a: The sheet is 256 columns (A to IV) by 8192 rows. In practice RAM runs out long before that. Release 3 adds multiple sheets stacked in a third dimension, if you can afford a 286 and extended memory.

q: What does @VLOOKUP do?
a: It looks up a value in the first column of a table and returns something from another column in the same row. @VLOOKUP(key,range,offset) with offset 0 being the first column. Table must be sorted ascending for it to find things properly.

q: What does CALC at the bottom of the screen mean?
a: It means you're in manual recalc mode and the sheet has changes that haven't been calculated yet, so displayed values may be stale. Press F9 to recalculate. It goes away once the sheet is up to date.

q: What does ERR mean in a 1-2-3 cell?
a: ERR means the formula cannot be calculated, usually division by zero, a bad range name, or a reference to a cell that holds an error. Check each cell the formula points to. Wrap divisions in @IF(B1=0,0,A1/B1) to avoid it.

q: What does NA mean in a cell?
a: NA stands for not available. It comes from the @NA function, which you can put in a cell as a placeholder for missing data. Any formula depending on that cell will also show NA, so you can easily spot gaps.

q: What does the /Data Fill command do?
a: It fills a range with a series of numbers. Give it the range, a start value, a step and a stop value. Handy for making row numbers or year headings like 1985, 1986 without typing each one.

q: What does the /Worksheet Global Zero command do?
a: It lets you hide zero values or show them as a label of your choice in release 3 or later releases of 2.x. Hiding zeros makes a sheet look much cleaner, but remember they're still there when you add things up.

q: What does the tilde mean in a macro?
a: The ~ stands for the Enter key. So {?} aside, a macro like /RE~ would press slash, R, E and Enter, erasing the current cell. Other special keys use braces, like {DOWN} or {EDIT}.

q: What is Quattro and how does it compare to 1-2-3?
a: Quattro is Borland's spreadsheet, out in 1987. It reads 1-2-3 files, offers a 1-2-3 compatible menu, has better graphics and costs far less. Quattro Pro in 1990 adds more. Compatibility with complicated macros isn't perfect.

q: What is a circular reference?
a: It's a formula that depends on its own result, like putting +A1+B1 into A1. 1-2-3 shows CIRC in the status line. Find the cell that points back to itself and fix the formula.

q: What is a data table in 1-2-3?
a: It's a what-if tool under /Data Table. You set up a formula, list different input values, and 1-2-3 fills in the results for each one. Table 1 varies one input and Table 2 varies two, good for loan payment charts.

q: What is a macro in 1-2-3 and how do I write one?
a: A macro is a label that holds keystrokes, which 1-2-3 replays for you. Type the keys as text, like '/FS~, name the cell with /Range Name Create using a backslash and a letter such as \A, then run it with Alt-A.

q: What is the best way to back up my spreadsheets?
a: Copy your data files to a floppy at the end of each session, and keep two sets of disks rotated. Also save to a new filename now and then, like BUDGET1, BUDGET2, so you can go back if you wreck the current one.

q: What is the difference between a label and a value?
a: A value is a number or a formula, a label is text. 1-2-3 decides by your first keystroke. Labels get a prefix character: ' for left aligned, " for right, ^ for centered. Labels count as zero in sums.

q: What is the difference between relative and absolute cell references?
a: A relative reference like A1 changes when you copy the formula to another cell. An absolute one like $A$1 stays fixed. In 1-2-3 press F4 while editing a formula to cycle through the $ combinations.

q: What was VisiCalc and does anyone still use it?
a: VisiCalc was the first spreadsheet, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston for the Apple II in 1979. Lotus 1-2-3 pretty much replaced it on the IBM PC. Some people still run it on old Apple IIs, but it's a museum piece now.

q: Which is better for a small business, Lotus 1-2-3 or Excel?
a: 1-2-3 is the standard on PCs and runs fine on a plain XT or AT. Excel is nicer looking and has real graphics, but it needs Windows and a 286 with a couple megs of RAM to be pleasant. On a Mac, Excel is the obvious pick.

q: Why do I get a row of asterisks in a cell?
a: The number is too wide for the column. Widen it with /Worksheet Column Set-Width, or use a format with fewer decimals. The value is still stored correctly in the cell.

q: Why does my 1-2-3 formula show the formula text instead of the answer?
a: You probably started the entry with a letter, so 1-2-3 took it as a label. Begin formulas with +, a digit, or a paren, like +A1*B1. Also check /Range Format Text isn't set on that cell.

q: Why does my sum come out one cent off?
a: Your cells display two decimals but hold more digits, so the sum of the displayed values differs from the true total. Wrap the individual formulas in @ROUND(...,2) so the stored values match what you see.

q: Why is my spreadsheet recalculating so slowly?
a: Big sheets with lots of formulas take time, especially without a math coprocessor. Switch to manual recalculation with /Worksheet Global Recalculation Manual, then press F9 when you want an update. An 8087 chip speeds things up noticeably.

q: Can FileMaker handle pictures?
a: Yes, there is a Picture field type for pasting or importing graphics from the Clipboard. They make the file grow fast. A Sound type is there too for HyperCard-style recordings. Keep pictures small, or put the data on a hard disk.

q: Can I run dBase programs without buying dBase for each machine?
a: Not with dBase itself, the license is per copy. Compilers like Clipper from Nantucket or Quicksilver let you compile your .PRG files into a standalone .EXE. You can give that to users with no royalty.

q: Can I use dBase on a Novell network?
a: Yes, dBase III Plus is multi-user. You open files with USE ... EXCLUSIVE or SHARED, and lock with FLOCK() or RLOCK() before editing. Run SHARE on DOS 3.x as well. A dBase III Plus network pack is needed, so check your license.

q: How can I change the structure of a database that already has data?
a: Use MODIFY STRUCTURE. You can add, delete, or resize fields, but don't rename a field and change something else in the same pass, or you'll lose that field's data. Back up the file first, and rebuild the indexes after.

q: How can I move my FileMaker data into Excel?
a: Use Export from the File menu and pick Tab-Separated Text, then choose the fields in order. Open the text file in Excel. Sort first, since the export comes out in the current sort order of the found records.

q: How can I print mailing labels in dBase III?
a: Type CREATE LABEL to design the label, then LABEL FORM yourlabel TO PRINT. It takes the size and number across from the form, so set that to match your stock. Add a FOR clause if you only want certain zip codes.

q: How can Lotus 1-2-3 read my dBase files?
a: Release 2 has the Translate utility, which converts between .WKS and .DBF. You can also export a database with COPY TO file TYPE WKS or APPEND FROM with TYPE WKS. Fields come across as columns and field names as headings.

q: How do I copy just a few fields to a new dBase file?
a: Use COPY TO newfile FIELDS name, city, phone. You can add FOR to select records too. This writes a new .DBF with only those fields in the order you list, and doesn't touch the original.

q: How do I delete records in dBase III for good? I did DELETE but they still show up.
a: DELETE only marks records. They stay in the file until you type PACK, which rewrites the .DBF without them. Be sure you have a backup first, because PACK can't be undone. Until then RECALL brings them back.

q: How do I find all records where the name starts with SMITH?
a: Use LOCATE FOR LASTNAME = "SMITH" and then CONTINUE for each next one. dBase's single equals does a partial match from the left unless SET EXACT is ON. With an index on the name, SEEK "SMITH" is far quicker.

q: How do I find records between two dates in FileMaker?
a: Switch to Find mode and type the first date, two periods, and the second date in the date field, like 1/1/90...12/31/90. Or use the greater-than and less-than symbols. Click Find, or press Enter.

q: How do I get rid of the "Too many files are open" error in dBase?
a: Edit CONFIG.SYS and set FILES=20 and BUFFERS=15 as the manual says, then reboot. Every open .DBF, .NDX and .DBT counts against that limit. dBase III Plus won't run with the DOS default of 8.

q: How do I link two dBase files together, like customers and orders?
a: Open the customer file in work area 1 and the order file in area 2, indexed on customer number. Then in area 1 type SET RELATION TO CUSTNO INTO ORDERS. When you move in the first file the second follows.

q: How do I make a calculation field in FileMaker?
a: In Define Fields type a name, pick Calculation as the type, and click Create. Then build the formula in the dialog, such as Price * Quantity. Pick the result type, number or text, to match what you need.

q: How do I make a date field in dBase print as month/day/year?
a: SET DATE AMERICAN is the default, which gives MM/DD/YY. To get a four-digit year you can't use the century switch in dBase III, so build the string with STR(YEAR(date),4) and the rest, or use DTOC. SET DATE BRITISH or ITALIAN give other orders.

q: How do I make dBase III sort my customer file by last name?
a: For a quick report use INDEX ON UPPER(LASTNAME) TO CUSTNAME. That makes an .NDX file and the records read in order. SORT TO makes a whole new database file, which is slower and uses more disk, so I'd go with INDEX.

q: How do I print a report from dBase without writing a program?
a: Use CREATE REPORT to lay out columns, totals and headings, then run REPORT FORM name TO PRINT. Add FOR to filter and SUMMARY to print totals only. Index or sort the file first so groups come out in order.

q: How do I print labels in FileMaker?
a: Use the New Layout command and choose Labels. Pick a standard Avery size or type in your own, place the fields, and print from that layout. Run a Find first if you only want a subset of records.

q: How do I sort a dBase file by date? Indexing on the date field comes out wrong when I mix fields.
a: Dates won't join cleanly with character fields in an index expression. Use DTOS(DATE) to turn the date into a YYYYMMDD string, so the sort order holds. For example INDEX ON LASTNAME+DTOS(ORDERDATE) TO NAMEDATE.

q: How do I use macros in dBase III, the ampersand?
a: The & substitutes the contents of a character variable as program text. If X="LASTNAME" then LIST &X works as LIST LASTNAME. It's handy for field names chosen by users, but it's slower than ordinary expressions.

q: How many records can FileMaker handle?
a: It's limited more by disk and memory than by a fixed count. Files with tens of thousands of records work fine on a Mac with a hard disk, though finds and sorts get slow on a Plus or SE. Give it 1 meg or more.

q: How much memory do I need to run dBase III Plus?
a: The manual calls for 256K, but you want 384K or more for any real work, especially with programs. Free memory goes quickly when you have TSRs loaded. 640K is the comfortable choice, and dBase IV needs more.

q: I have a CP/M machine and dBase II. How do I get my data into dBase III on a PC?
a: Get the files over by serial or a disk-conversion program, then COPY TO ... DELIMITED or SDF from dBase II. In III, use APPEND FROM with the same DELIMITED or SDF option into a file with a matching structure. Rebuild the indexes after.

q: Is FileMaker any good for a small business on a Mac?
a: Yes, for a mailing list, inventory or invoice jobs it's about the easiest Mac database around. You design layouts by dragging fields. For big relational needs look at 4th Dimension or Helix, because FileMaker can only do lookups between files.

q: Is dBase IV worth upgrading to from dBase III Plus?
a: Not for 1.0. It has the Control Center, SQL and multiple-index .MDX files, but it's slow, hungry for memory and has plenty of bugs. If III Plus works for you, wait for the 1.1 maintenance release.

q: Is it OK to put dBase files on a RAM disk to go faster?
a: It works great for read-only lookups and indexing jobs. Any changes are lost if power drops, so copy the files back to the hard disk when you finish. Don't use it for your only copy of live data.

q: What can I do about the dBase IV bugs? Mine locks up on indexing.
a: Check that you have the latest release. Ashton-Tate has been shipping fixes, and 1.1 corrects a lot. Make sure your system has enough free memory, since dBase IV wants a lot, and keep backups of every file.

q: What does "Record is not in index" mean?
a: Your index doesn't point to the record you tried to use, usually because the file was changed when the index wasn't open. REINDEX will fix it. Always open the indexes with the file, using USE name INDEX name1.

q: What does "Syntax error" mean when the command looks right to me?
a: It means dBase didn't understand something on that line. Check for a missing closing quote or parenthesis, a field name over 10 characters, or a reserved word used as a variable. Type the command at the dot prompt by itself to see what part fails.

q: What does SET TALK OFF do?
a: It stops dBase echoing the results of commands, such as record numbers after a REPLACE or the values from STORE. You put it at the top of every program so the screen stays clean. SET TALK ON turns it back on for debugging.

q: What does ZAP do in dBase?
a: ZAP removes every record in the open database at once and leaves the structure alone. It's PACK on a file where everything is marked deleted. It asks "Zap C:CUSTOMER.DBF? (Y/N)" unless SET SAFETY is OFF, so read the prompt.

q: What does the .DBF extension mean?
a: It's the file for a dBase database holding records. The .NDX is an index, .DBT is memo text, .PRG is a program, .FRM is a report form and .LBL is a label. Many other programs read .DBF too, such as Lotus 1-2-3 Release 2.

q: What is Clipper and why do people use it?
a: Clipper is a dBase compiler from Nantucket. You compile .PRG files to .OBJ, link them with RTLINK or Plink86, and get an .EXE that runs much faster than interpreted dBase. It reads .DBF and .NDX files, and Summer '87 added more compatibility.

q: What is FoxPro and is it compatible with dBase?
a: FoxPro is Fox Software's follow-up to FoxBase+, out in 1989. It reads .DBF files and runs most dBase III code. It has windows and mouse support and a built-in Rushmore speedup, and it uses compact .CDX indexes.

q: What is a layout in FileMaker?
a: A layout is how the data shows on screen or on paper. One file can have many layouts, such as a data entry form, a list, and a label or envelope layout. Switch between them with the pop-up in the corner.

q: What is a lookup in FileMaker?
a: A lookup copies a value from a second file into a field in the current file, based on a matching field. You set it in the field's Entry Options. It lets you put a price list in one file and use it in an invoice file.

q: What is a memo field and how big can it be in dBase III?
a: It's a field for free text. The text goes in a separate .DBT file and the .DBF holds a 10-byte pointer. In III Plus a memo can reach about 4000 characters when editing, with a bit more in some programs. Don't forget to copy the .DBT too.

q: What is a summary field in FileMaker?
a: It's a field that adds up or averages a field across a set of records, like total sales for a found set. You put it in a subsummary part of a layout, sorted by the break field, to see totals per group.

q: What is the Ashton-Tate Developer's Kit or runtime?
a: It's a license that lets you distribute dBase applications to people who don't own dBase. dBase III has a runtime option and dBase IV added its own. Check the licence terms and the price, which many find high next to Clipper.

q: What is the difference between dBase II and dBase III?
a: dBase III is the 16-bit MS-DOS rewrite. It allows 128 fields and 4000 bytes per record, against 32 fields and 1000 bytes in dBase II, and the file format changed. It also gets 10 work areas and a bigger memo field.

q: What is the dot prompt?
a: It's the single period dBase shows when it waits for a command, the interactive mode. You can type USE, LIST, and BROWSE straight at it. III Plus starts in the Assistant menu instead, so press Escape to get to the dot.

q: What is the maximum number of records dBase III can handle?
a: The manual says a billion records or about 2 billion bytes per file. You'll run out of disk long before that. Remember that one record can't exceed 4000 bytes and a file can have only 128 fields.

q: What's the best way to back up a dBase database?
a: Close everything and copy the .DBF, .DBT memo files and your .PRG files to floppy with DOS COPY or BACKUP. Index files can be rebuilt, so you can skip them. Do it daily, and keep more than one set of disks.

q: What's the difference between FIND and SEEK in dBase III?
a: FIND takes a literal with no quotes and only works with character keys. SEEK takes an expression, so you can search for a variable or a number or date key. I'd use SEEK all the time, because FIND can't use memory variables without a macro.

q: What's the difference between FileMaker II and FileMaker Pro?
a: Pro is Claris's 1990 revision. It has the same file format and an interface of more power: scripts, multiple windows, and better layout tools. If you run System 6 or 7 with a couple of megs, it's a worthwhile upgrade.

q: Which is faster, dBase III Plus or FoxBase+?
a: FoxBase+ from Fox Software, by most accounts, usually a few times faster on indexing and queries. It reads the same .DBF and .NDX files and runs the same programs. It's still cheaper than buying a Clipper license for every user.

q: Which should I learn first, dBase or FileMaker?
a: It depends on your machine. On a Mac, FileMaker is quicker to learn and you'll make a working database in an afternoon. On a PC, dBase is the standard, and its programming language is worth the time if you want custom systems.

q: Why does dBase say "Index file does not match database"?
a: The .DBF changed since the index was built. Usually someone edited it without the index open, or you used a different version of the file. Open the database and run REINDEX, or rebuild with INDEX ON.

q: Why does my dBase program run so slow?
a: Common causes are too few BUFFERS in CONFIG.SYS, no index on the field you search with LOCATE, and a lot of file opening inside loops. Use SEEK, SET TALK OFF, and keep your files open to speed it up.

q: Why is my FileMaker file so big after I deleted records?
a: FileMaker doesn't always shrink the file when records go. Use Save a Copy As to write a compressed copy of the file, which squeezes out the empty space. It's also a good way to repair a damaged file.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Can I print PageMaker documents to a file for the typesetter?
a: Yes. In PageMaker 3 you can hold down Command-F while clicking OK in the Print dialog to save a PostScript file to disk. Download the fonts you need to include. The service bureau then sends that file to the imagesetter.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Can I run PageMaker on an Atari or Amiga?
a: No, PageMaker is only on the Mac and on the PC with Windows. On the Atari ST you have Calamus and Timeworks Publisher, and on the Amiga there is PageSetter and Professional Page. They are cheaper but the file compatibility is limited.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Can I use PostScript fonts on a non-PostScript printer?
a: Yes, with Adobe Type Manager on the Mac, which rasterizes Type 1 fonts for the ImageWriter or a QuickDraw laser. You still need the printer fonts installed beside the screen fonts. Without ATM the screen shows only the installed bitmap sizes.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Can I use Word documents in PageMaker?
a: Yes. Use Place to bring in the Word file and PageMaker keeps most of the character and paragraph formatting, including styles with the same names. Do your editing in Word and the layout in PageMaker, because round-tripping isn't reliable.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Does a bigger point size always mean readable body text?
a: No. Body text in books and newsletters is generally 9 to 11 points, and the typeface changes how big it looks, since x-height varies. Check proofs on paper, because the screen at 72 dpi is not a good guide.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How can I refill or save money on toner cartridges?
a: Local refill shops will recharge Canon engine cartridges for around half the price of a new one. Quality varies, so try one before buying several. Shaking the cartridge gently can get a few more pages when the print gets faint.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How can I scan a photo for PageMaker without it printing muddy?
a: Scan at no more than twice your halftone screen frequency, so about 150 dpi for a 75 lpi screen. Save as TIFF and adjust contrast in the scanning software or Digital Darkroom first. Higher resolution just makes huge files without better output.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How do I get PageMaker to print crop marks on my LaserWriter?
a: In the Print dialog check Crop marks, and make sure your paper size is bigger than your page. Letter-size paper won't leave room for marks on a full page, so use Tabloid on an imagesetter or shrink the page setup.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How do I get a PC to talk to a LaserWriter?
a: The easiest way is the serial port at 9600 baud with a PostScript driver, or LocalTalk with a card such as the TOPS or Apple's LaserWriter-compatible card. The printer's serial port needs a switch setting to be used.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How do I install fonts on a Mac with System 6?
a: Use the Font/DA Mover. Open the Fonts suitcase, copy the font into your System file, and restart any programs. Or use Suitcase or Font Juggler if you have a lot of fonts and don't want to bloat the System.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How do I make a drop cap in PageMaker?
a: PageMaker 3 has no automatic drop cap. Type the letter in its own text block at a large size, then place it next to the paragraph and set the text to wrap around it with Text wrap. You can also indent the first lines with a text block placed above.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How do I make a layout fit on a LaserWriter if my page is tabloid?
a: In the Print dialog use the Reduce to fit option, or print Tiling to get the page in letter-size pieces and tape them together. Tabloid proofs are best sent to a service bureau with a Linotronic or a large format printer.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How do I put page numbers on every page in PageMaker?
a: Go to the master page, make a text block where you want the number, and type Command-Option-P. It shows as LM or RM on the master and turns into the right number on each page. Do it on both left and right masters if you use facing pages.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How do I rotate text in PageMaker?
a: PageMaker 3 cannot rotate text in the layout. You can rotate whole pages with the Tall or Wide setting in Page Setup. For angled headlines make them in Illustrator or Freehand, save as EPS, then place that.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How much RAM do I need to run PageMaker 3.0 on a Mac?
a: Officially 1MB will start it, but 2MB is more realistic and 4MB is comfortable with MultiFinder. Pages with scanned graphics eat memory fast. A hard disk is a must too.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: How much memory does the LaserWriter Plus have and does it matter?
a: It has 1.5MB, and about 400K of that is available for fonts and pages. Full-page graphics at 300 dpi need about a megabyte just for the bitmap. If you download lots of fonts you may hit a limit VM error.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Is Times the same as Times Roman?
a: Mostly. Adobe's Times Roman is the PostScript font in the LaserWriter, and Apple's Times is the bitmap font that matches it. Linotype also sells Times Roman, and the metrics are very close but not always identical, so line breaks can shift on a different printer.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Is Ventura Publisher OK on a 286?
a: It works, but slowly. With 640K of RAM and EMS memory you can do a 20 page chapter, but redraws drag. A 386 with a disk cache makes a big difference, and a graphics card with a full page display helps.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Is a 20 MB hard disk enough for PageMaker work?
a: It will be tight. PageMaker takes about 1MB, but fonts, the System and some scanned images will fill it quickly. A 40 or 80MB drive is a more comfortable buy, and you should budget for a backup system.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Is it worth getting a scanner like the HP ScanJet?
a: If you work with photos regularly, yes. The ScanJet does 300 dpi with 256 grays and costs about $1,500 to $2,000. For a few images a month it's cheaper to have a service bureau scan them.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Is the LaserWriter IINT really worth the extra money over the SC?
a: If you do real layout, yes. The IINT has a true PostScript interpreter in the box, with 35 resident fonts and 2MB RAM. The SC uses QuickDraw and no PostScript, so you can't print EPS files or use PostScript fonts at full quality.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Should I buy a Mac or a PC for desktop publishing?
a: For now the Mac is the better bet. WYSIWYG display is built in, fonts are simpler, and almost all service bureaus and designers use it. A 386 PC with Windows 3.0 and PageMaker 3.0 is catching up, but it costs more setup time.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What are the best fonts for a newsletter?
a: A readable serif such as Palatino, Times or New Century Schoolbook for body, and Helvetica or Avant Garde for headings. Stick with two families at most, and be consistent with sizes. Fancy fonts make it look cluttered.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What does 300 dpi mean for a laser printer?
a: It means 300 dots per inch, both across and down. That's fine for drafts and body text but visibly rough next to a typesetter, which runs 1270 or 2540 dpi. Many people print a laser original and have a service bureau output the final.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What does PostScript error limitcheck mean?
a: Your page is too complex for the printer, usually a path with too many points, like a huge autotraced or curved shape. Simplify the drawing, split it into pieces, or lower the flatness setting. More printer RAM does not always fix it.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What does WYSIWYG actually mean?
a: It means what you see is what you get, so the screen layout matches the printed page. On a Mac that's mostly true for layout, but at 72 dpi it's not exact, especially for fine type spacing. Real proofing still needs a printout.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What does leading mean?
a: Leading, pronounced ledding, is the space from one baseline to the next, measured in points. 10 point type on 12 point leading is written 10/12. It comes from the strips of lead typesetters used to put between lines.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What does lpi mean on a halftone?
a: It's lines per inch, the screen frequency of the halftone dots. Newspapers use around 85, magazines 133 to 150. A 300 dpi laser printer can only manage about 53 to 60 lpi before you lose gray levels.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is Adobe Illustrator good for compared to MacDraw?
a: Illustrator makes PostScript outlines with Bezier curves, so the output is smooth at any size and prints at the full printer resolution. MacDraw is object-based but uses QuickDraw and is limited to 300 dpi. For logos and type effects, Illustrator wins.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is Encapsulated PostScript?
a: EPS is a PostScript file with a header describing its bounding box, plus an optional low-res PICT preview. Programs like Illustrator and Freehand save it, and PageMaker can place it. It prints sharp on a PostScript printer, but you only see the preview on screen.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is a bleed and how do I do it?
a: A bleed is when ink runs off the edge of the paper. You extend the artwork about an eighth of an inch beyond the trim line, then the printer trims it. Laser printers can't print to the edge, so you need an imagesetter or a bigger sheet.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is a gutter?
a: It's the blank space between two columns of text. Typical gutters are a pica or so, around 12 points. In the inside margin of a facing-page spread the term can mean the area where the pages bind.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is a point and how many are in a pica?
a: A point is 1/72 of an inch, near enough. There are 12 points to a pica and 6 picas to an inch. Type size and leading are both measured in points.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is a service bureau?
a: It's a shop that outputs your PostScript files on a Linotronic imagesetter at 1270 or 2540 dpi onto paper or film. You bring a disk, they print it, and you pay by the page. Ask what format they want before you start.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is a style sheet in PageMaker?
a: It's a named set of formatting, such as font, size, leading and indents, that you apply to paragraphs in one click. Change the style and every paragraph using it updates. PageMaker 3.0 has them, and they are the key to consistent long documents.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is a widow and an orphan?
a: A widow is a short last line of a paragraph stranded at the top of a column or page. An orphan is the first line of a paragraph left alone at the bottom. Both look bad, and Ventura and Quark can control them while PageMaker 3 makes you fix them by hand.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is kerning?
a: Kerning is adjusting the space between two particular letters, such as AV or To, so they don't look too far apart. PageMaker has automatic pair kerning for fonts with kern tables, and you can nudge pairs by hand with Command-Delete or the arrow keys on a Mac.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is the Adobe Type Library?
a: It's Adobe's collection of licensed PostScript typefaces, including Palatino, Garamond, Futura and Bodoni. You can buy them as packages for the Mac or PC. They're Type 1 fonts, and are hinted for good looks at small sizes.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is the difference between TIFF and PICT?
a: TIFF is a bitmap format made for scanned images and supports gray scales, and it's the best choice for halftones. PICT is the Mac's native format that holds bitmaps and QuickDraw objects, and it prints at 72 dpi unless it's drawn with objects.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is the difference between a Linotronic 100 and 300?
a: Both are PostScript imagesetters from Linotype. The L100 prints at 1270 dpi and the L300 at 2540 dpi, and the 300 is faster and sharper. For halftones at fine screens the 2540 is worth the extra per-page cost.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is the difference between a screen font and a printer font?
a: The screen font is a bitmap that draws type on your monitor at certain sizes. The printer font holds the outline the PostScript printer uses at any size. You need both installed for good results, and if the printer font is missing you get Courier or jaggies.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: What is the difference between serif and sans serif?
a: Serifs are the little strokes at the ends of letters, as in Times or Palatino. Sans serif faces such as Helvetica have none. Serif is usually easier to read in long body text, and sans is common in headlines and captions.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Which is better for desktop publishing, PageMaker or Ventura Publisher?
a: Ventura is stronger on long documents, with tagged styles and automatic tables of contents and indexes. PageMaker is easier for newsletters and ads where you want to place things freely. Ventura runs under GEM on the PC, and PageMaker has Windows and Mac versions.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Why do my fonts look different on screen than printed?
a: The screen shows a 72 dpi bitmap and the printer uses the outline at 300 dpi or more, so spacing differs a bit. If you see a font printing in Courier, the printer font isn't loaded. Turn on Precision Bitmap Alignment to improve the match.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Why do my line breaks change when I send the file to the service bureau?
a: They probably have different fonts or different versions of them. Even small metric differences move words to another line. Send them the exact fonts you used or ask them to confirm they have the same ones.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Why does PageMaker say it can't find the linked graphic?
a: Links point to the original file by name and folder, and PageMaker can't find it if you moved or renamed it. Keep the graphics in the same folder as the publication. When you open it, PageMaker will ask you to locate the missing files.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Why does my PageMaker file take forever to save?
a: PageMaker writes the whole publication out on a Save, and big bitmap graphics make that slow. Use Save as periodically, because it compacts the file and often shrinks it a lot. Keep your graphics reasonable in size too.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Why does my text print with jagged edges on the ImageWriter?
a: The ImageWriter is only 144 dpi and uses bitmap screen fonts. Install the font in sizes that match what you print, or use Best quality mode, which prints at twice the size and reduces it. For smooth type you need a LaserWriter.

topic: desktop publishing: PageMaker, fonts, laser printing
q: Why is my laser printer printing so slowly with graphics?
a: The printer has to process the page and then rasterize it, and a Mac sending a large bitmap over LocalTalk is slow at about 230 kilobits. A 300 dpi TIFF can take several minutes. Lowering the scan resolution makes it faster.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Are the Amiga arcade ports as good as the real arcade machines?
a: The best ones come close, like R-Type and Xenon 2. Most lose some detail or speed. The Amiga's sound is great, so music often sounds better than the coin-op.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Are the Nintendo games better than computer games?
a: They are different. A Nintendo is cheap and plugs into the TV, with good arcade-style games like Super Mario Bros. A computer gives you adventures, simulators, and strategy games that the console can't match.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Can I fly in Flight Simulator over places besides Chicago and Seattle?
a: Yes, Microsoft sells Scenery Disks for different areas of the US, and Japan. There are also third party disks from Mallard and others. You load them through the scenery menu and set your location by coordinates.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Can I make backup copies of my game disks?
a: Many games use copy protection that stops DISKCOPY, so you'd need a copier utility like Copy II PC. Check whether the publisher offers a backup disk for a few dollars, as some do.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Can I play Infocom games on my Commodore 64?
a: Yes, most of them came out for the 64 on 5.25 inch disks, but loading from a 1541 drive is slow. The bigger games like Trinity were not released for it, so check the box before you buy.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Can I use an Atari joystick on my IBM clone?
a: Not directly. The Atari stick is digital and the PC port reads analog resistance. There are adapters, but they're hit or miss, so buy a proper PC joystick.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Do I need a math coprocessor for Falcon AT?
a: No, but a faster CPU helps a lot. Falcon on a 4.77 MHz XT crawls. A 286 at 12 MHz is okay and a 386 is much better. Turn off some detail options if the frame rate is bad.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Does Out Run on the Atari ST run smoothly?
a: It is playable but not as fast as the arcade. Frame rate drops when the road gets busy. The music is good, and you can pick the soundtrack like in the original.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Does Sound Blaster work with most games?
a: Many newer games support AdLib, and the Sound Blaster is AdLib compatible and adds digitized sound. Check the box to see if the game lists it. Older games just use the PC speaker.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How come the PC version of Pac-Man looks worse than the arcade game?
a: PCs had limited graphics and sound, with just the speaker and four colors on CGA. Ports were often rushed. Anything on an Amiga, ST or even a Nintendo looks closer to the arcade.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I get Gunship to start the engine on a Commodore 64?
a: Follow the checklist in the manual: battery, fuel, rotor brake off, then start the engines. Pay attention to the torque gauge so you don't overstress the rotor. Take off slowly rather than yanking the collective.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I get Sierra's King's Quest to take typed commands properly?
a: Use simple verb-noun commands like OPEN DOOR or GET KEY. The parser only understands a limited vocabulary. If it says it doesn't know a word, try a synonym.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I get around copy protection that asks for a word from the manual?
a: You can't legally skip it, so keep the manual handy. Some games use a code wheel, like Monkey Island will. Just keep the original disks and manual close and make backups for yourself.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I get out of the maze in Zork I?
a: Drop an item in each room to tell them apart, since the maze rooms look the same. Find the skeleton with the key and coins, and then the way to the Cyclops Room. Mapping carefully is the real answer.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I get past the babel fish dispenser in Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy?
a: You need to put the towel over the drain, put the satchel in front of the panel, then the robot cleans up and the fish comes out. Catch it in your hand with the cleaning device blocked. Be patient, it takes several steps and the order matters.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I get the maximum score in Zork I?
a: The max is 350 points. Collect all the treasures and put them in the trophy case in the living room. You also get points for entering places, so explore everything, and then finish the game by going to the Stone Barrow.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I land a plane in Microsoft Flight Simulator without crashing?
a: Line up with the runway, slow to about 70 knots in a Cessna, flaps down, and keep the nose slightly up. Reduce throttle to idle just over the runway and let it settle. Watch your sink rate on the vertical speed indicator.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I make a boot disk to play games with enough memory?
a: Format a floppy with FORMAT A: /S, then add a short CONFIG.SYS with FILES=20 and BUFFERS=10, and a plain AUTOEXEC.BAT. Boot from it to free up the most conventional memory.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I run an old game that's too fast on my new 386?
a: Turn off the turbo button if your machine has one, or use a slowdown program like MOSLO. Some games tie timing to CPU speed, so a 4.77 MHz mode may help.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How do I save my game in Zork on an IBM PC?
a: Type SAVE at the prompt, and it asks for a file name. You need a formatted disk with free space, so format a spare one before you start. RESTORE loads it back later.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: How much memory do I need for Ultima V?
a: It needs 256K on a PC, though 512K is safer. You'll want a hard disk or at least two floppy drives, because there are a lot of swapped disks. An EGA card helps with the graphics.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Is Leather Goddesses of Phobos worth buying?
a: If you like funny, slightly naughty text adventures, yes. It has Tame, Suggestive and Lewd modes, and the scratch-and-sniff card is a gimmick that's fun once. The puzzles are on the easy side compared to Infocom's harder games.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Is SimCity worth buying?
a: Yes, it's a different kind of game where you build and run a city. There's no winning, which some people find odd, but it's very addictive. It runs fine on most PCs, Macs and Amigas.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Is Test Drive worth buying for a PC?
a: If you want to drive a Ferrari or Porsche on mountain roads, it's good fun. The graphics on EGA are decent. It is a bit short on variety, though, and the cops get annoying.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Is Wing Commander good on a 286?
a: Not really. It's built for a 386 with VGA and plenty of memory, and it's slow and jerky on a 286. You'll also want a sound card to hear the music.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Is a hard drive worth getting just for games?
a: If you play big games like Ultima or Sierra adventures, yes. It saves a lot of disk swapping and loads faster. A 20 MB drive is enough for several games at current prices.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Is a joystick better than a keyboard for flight sims?
a: Yes, a joystick is much better for smooth control. On a PC get an analog stick and calibrate it with the game's menu. Cheap ones drift, so a CH Products stick is worth the extra money.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What does "TSR" mean and why do games complain about it?
a: It means Terminate and Stay Resident, a program that stays in memory, like a mouse driver or SideKick. It uses up your 640K, and games sometimes need every byte. Boot from a clean floppy with a minimal CONFIG.SYS.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What does "XYZZY" do?
a: It's a magic word from Colossal Cave Adventure, the original text adventure. It moves you between the building and a spot in the cave. Some later games like Zork have it as an in-joke too.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What does "You are likely to be eaten by a grue" mean in Zork?
a: A grue is a monster that lives in dark places. If you walk around without a light source, it will get you. Keep your lamp lit and don't wander in the dark, and you'll be fine.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What does "joystick port" mean on my PC?
a: It's the 15-pin game port on a game card or multi-I/O card. You plug an analog PC joystick into it. A Commodore or Atari joystick won't work without a special adapter.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What does ILS mean in Flight Simulator?
a: It stands for Instrument Landing System. Tune NAV 1 to the ILS frequency for your runway, then follow the localizer and glideslope needles to line up for landing. It helps a lot at night or in cloud.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What does the INVISICLUES booklet do?
a: Infocom sold hint booklets with the answers printed in invisible ink. You rub a special marker over a question and the hint appears, one level at a time. That way you only see as much help as you want.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What does the Infocom "Z-machine" do?
a: It's a virtual machine that Infocom wrote so the same game file runs on many computers. Each computer only needs a Z-machine interpreter, which is why one story file can run on an Apple II, IBM PC and Amiga.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What is a good arcade port for the IBM PC?
a: Not many are great, but Arkanoid, Out Run and Prince of Persia are decent on EGA or VGA. Make sure you have a fast enough machine, or the gameplay is choppy.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What is the best chess program for a home computer?
a: Chessmaster 2000 is a popular choice with good play and a nice interface. Sargon III is also strong. Both run well on a 286, and the higher levels take a long time to think.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What is the best way to learn to dogfight in F-15 Strike Eagle?
a: Fire your Sidewinders when the target is locked and in front of you. Use chaff and flares when a missile is chasing you. Fly low to avoid radar and don't waste missiles at long range.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What is the best way to map a text adventure?
a: Use graph paper and draw each room as a box with exits as lines. Note objects and any odd exits, like up, down and diagonal ones. Mapping saves hours in Zork's maze.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What is the difference between CGA, EGA and VGA for games?
a: CGA shows 4 colors at 320x200, EGA gives 16 colors from a palette of 64, and VGA gives 256 colors in mode 13h. VGA cards and monitors cost more, but games look much better.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: What is the difference between Zork I, II and III?
a: They are three separate games in one story. Zork I is the Great Underground Empire and treasure hunting, II has the Wizard and the Carousel Room, and III is shorter and more puzzly with the Dungeon Master. Play I first.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Which Infocom game should a beginner start with?
a: Try Seastalker, Wishbringer or The Hitchhiker's Guide. Infocom marks them Introductory or Standard level on the box. Zork I is also a good start. Save the Expert titles like Spellbreaker and A Mind Forever Voyaging for later.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Which Macintosh has the best games, the Plus or the SE?
a: The games run on both, but the SE is faster and has an expansion slot. Color needs a Mac II. Most good titles like Shufflepuck and Dark Castle are black and white and work on any of them.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Which flight simulator is best on the IBM PC, Flight Simulator or something else?
a: Microsoft Flight Simulator 3.0 is the standard for civilian flying and it runs on nearly everything. If you want combat, Falcon from Spectrum HoloByte or F-19 Stealth Fighter from MicroProse are better. It depends what you want to do.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Which has the better version of Gauntlet, the Atari ST or the C64?
a: The ST version is closer to the arcade, with better graphics and four-player play with an adapter. The C64 is playable but the screen is small and the sound is weaker. Go with the ST if you have one.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Which is better for a first PC game, King's Quest III or Space Quest II?
a: Space Quest II is a bit friendlier since it's funny and less fiddly. King's Quest III has time pressure with the wizard that annoys beginners. Save often in either one.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Why do I keep dying in Space Quest?
a: Sierra games kill you for lots of small mistakes, so save before every new room. Press F5 to save and F7 to restore. You'll die less if you look at everything first.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Why does Infocom's Planetfall keep killing me with Floyd around?
a: Floyd himself is harmless. You probably ran out of food or sleep, which the game tracks. Eat the ration, sleep when it tells you you're tired, and don't ignore the hunger warnings.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Why does Tetris keep slowing down on my Tandy 1000?
a: Tetris is fine on a Tandy at normal speed, but if you have a turbo switch make sure it's on. Also check that no TSR programs are loaded, since they can take up CPU time.

topic: computer games: Infocom, flight simulators, arcade ports
q: Why does my flight sim run so slowly on my 8088?
a: The 8088 is just too slow for the 3D graphics. Try turning off scenery detail, using CGA instead of EGA, or dropping the display options. An accelerator board or a faster 286 machine is the real fix.

q: Can I get a Moog cheaply?
a: Used Minimoogs run around $800 to $1,500, since Moog stopped making them in 1981. A Korg Mono/Poly or Roland SH-101 gives similar sounds for less, and also costs less to fix.

q: Can I record audio on my PC?
a: Not much in real time yet, at least not well. A Sound Blaster or Covox Speech Thing can sample at about 8 bits and 12 kHz, but long recordings fill a hard disk quickly. A Mac with Sound Designer is better.

q: Can I use my Commodore 64 for MIDI?
a: Yes, but you need an add-on interface cartridge, such as those from Passport, Sequential or Datel. Then software like Steinberg Pro-16 or Passport's sequencer will work. The SID chip itself doesn't speak MIDI.

q: How can I record my MIDI songs onto cassette?
a: Run the synth outputs into a mixer, then send the mix to your cassette deck's line inputs. Use Dolby noise reduction and keep levels below distortion. A four-track cassette recorder like the Tascam Portastudio lets you layer more.

q: How do I get a good sound out of a Sound Blaster?
a: The Sound Blaster has a Yamaha YM3812 FM chip with 9 voices, so tweak your patches in the software and use good speakers. Also keep the card's volume mid-level, since cranking the mixer adds hiss.

q: How do I hook my Atari ST up to my synth?
a: The ST has MIDI IN and OUT ports built in, so you just need standard MIDI cables. Connect ST OUT to the synth's IN, and synth OUT to ST IN if you want to record. Then run a sequencer like Cubase or Notator.

q: How do I sync my drum machine to my sequencer?
a: Use MIDI clock. Set the sequencer to send clock and start/stop, and set the drum machine to external or MIDI sync. Both then follow the same tempo at 24 pulses per quarter note.

q: How do I tune two synths together?
a: Play the same note on each and adjust the tuning knob or parameter until the beating stops. Digital synths usually have a master tune setting, with A=440 Hz as standard. Analog ones drift, so let them warm up first.

q: How does the NES make its sound?
a: The NES has a 2A03 CPU with a built-in sound unit, offering two pulse waves, a triangle, a noise channel and a rough 1-bit DPCM channel. That's five channels, so composers get clever with arpeggios.

q: How many MIDI channels are there?
a: There are 16 channels per MIDI cable. Each message is tagged with a channel number, and each instrument can be set to listen to one or more channels. For more than 16 you need multiple ports.

q: How much disk space does a minute of CD quality audio take?
a: About 10 megabytes for a stereo minute at 44.1 kHz, 16 bit. That's 176,400 bytes per second. A standard 20 MB hard drive would hold only a couple of minutes.

q: Is it worth buying a reverb unit?
a: Yes if you record anything. Even a cheap Alesis MIDIverb at about $250 makes dry synths sound much bigger. Many keyboards have onboard effects, but a separate unit gives you more control.

q: Is the Korg M1 any good?
a: It sold very well since 1988. It has 16-bit PCM samples, a built-in sequencer, effects, and 8-part multitimbral playing. It gives you a lot for around $2,000, and the piano and organ sounds are common on records.

q: Is the Roland MT-32 worth buying for PC games?
a: If your games support it, yes, Sierra and LucasArts titles sound great on it. It's an LA synth module with 32 partials and needs a MPU-401 compatible interface like the Roland MPU-401 or LAPC-I. It costs about $500.

q: Is the Yamaha DX7 hard to program?
a: Yes, quite. It has six operators, 32 algorithms and only a tiny LCD with membrane buttons. Most people use ROM cartridges or an editor program on a computer, such as a DX7 patch editor on the Atari ST.

q: What does 'DAT' mean for recording?
a: DAT is Digital Audio Tape, a small cassette format from Sony that records 16-bit at 44.1 or 48 kHz. It's the best way to mix down your songs, but decks cost about $1,000 and up.

q: What does 8-bit versus 16-bit sampling mean?
a: It's how many bits describe each sample's amplitude. 8-bit gives 256 levels and is noticeably hissy, about 48 dB of range. 16-bit gives 65536 levels and roughly 96 dB, which is CD quality.

q: What does ADSR stand for?
a: Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release. It's an envelope that shapes how a note's volume or filter changes over time. Attack, decay and release are times, while sustain is a level.

q: What does MIDI THRU do?
a: THRU passes along an exact copy of whatever arrives at the MIDI IN. It lets you daisy-chain several instruments from one controller. Don't chain too many, since timing gets sloppy after three or four devices.

q: What does MPU-401 mean?
a: It's Roland's MIDI interface for PCs, with a UART mode and an intelligent mode. Most PC music software supports it, and other makers clone it. It's basically the standard way to attach MIDI gear to a PC.

q: What does a low pass filter do?
a: It lets frequencies below a cutoff pass and cuts those above it. Sweeping the cutoff makes the classic synth wah sound. Resonance boosts the area around the cutoff and can give a squelchy tone.

q: What does polyphonic mean on a synth?
a: It means the synth can play several notes at once. A monophonic synth like a Minimoog plays one at a time. A Juno-106 has 6 voices, so you can play six-note chords.

q: What does quantize do?
a: It snaps your recorded notes to the nearest beat division, such as 16th notes, so sloppy timing gets tightened up. Use it carefully because too much can make it sound robotic. Many sequencers allow partial quantize.

q: What is FM synthesis?
a: It's frequency modulation, where one oscillator, called a modulator, changes the pitch of another, the carrier, at audio rate. This makes rich, bell-like tones. Yamaha's DX7 made it famous in 1983.

q: What is General MIDI?
a: Nothing official yet for the general market, but Roland's new Sound Canvas and its GS format, introduced in 1991, define a standard patch map so a sequence plays with the same instrument sounds on different modules.

q: What is MIDI and why does every keyboard seem to have it now?
a: MIDI is Musical Instrument Digital Interface, a serial standard from 1983 that lets synths, drum machines and computers send note and control data to each other. It runs at 31.25 kbaud over 5-pin DIN cables. It carries notes, not audio.

q: What is SysEx?
a: System Exclusive messages are MIDI data specific to one manufacturer's device. They are used to dump patches and settings to a computer or another synth, so you can back up and edit them.

q: What is a MIDI file?
a: A Standard MIDI File is a format that stores sequence data so different programs can read the same song. There are type 0, one track, and type 1, multi-track. Most sequencers can save and load them.

q: What is a Roland TB-303?
a: It's a small bass synth and pattern sequencer from 1982 that Roland sold as a guitarist's bass accompaniment. It flopped, so used ones are cheap. Chicago house producers now use its squelchy sound.

q: What is a patch?
a: A patch is a stored sound setting in a synth, with all its oscillator, filter, envelope and effects parameters. Different makers also call it a program or a voice. You can save them on cartridges or by MIDI SysEx dump.

q: What is a sequencer?
a: A sequencer records and plays back note events, either as hardware like the Roland MC-500 or as software on a computer. Then it sends them out by MIDI to your synths, so you can edit, quantize and layer parts.

q: What is a tracker or Soundtracker?
a: It's an Amiga program from 1987 that plays four-channel sample-based modules written as columns of notes in a pattern grid. You can share the .MOD files, which contain the samples with the song.

q: What is a vocoder?
a: It analyzes the spectrum of your voice with filter bands and applies it to a synth sound, so the synth appears to talk. Korg, Roland and Sennheiser make them. It's the robot voice effect on many records.

q: What is aftertouch?
a: It's pressure applied after a key is down, which sends extra MIDI data for vibrato or filter changes. Channel aftertouch applies to all notes, but polyphonic aftertouch is rarer and tracks each key.

q: What is multitimbral?
a: A multitimbral synth can play different sounds on different MIDI channels at the same time, such as bass, piano and strings. The Roland D-110 and Korg M1 are examples, each with 8 parts.

q: What is the AdLib card?
a: It's a PC sound card from 1987 with a Yamaha YM3812 (OPL2) FM chip, giving nine voices or six plus five percussion. Lots of games support it, and it's the most common PC music standard.

q: What is the Roland D-50 known for?
a: It uses Linear Arithmetic synthesis, combining short PCM attack samples with synthesized sustain parts. It came out in 1987 and has a signature sound with its built-in chorus and reverb. Programming it can be fiddly.

q: What is the Roland TR-808?
a: It's a classic analog drum machine from 1980 with 16 steps, handclaps, a deep kick and cowbell. It is discontinued but common secondhand, and is used all over hip hop and dance records.

q: What is the SID chip in the C64?
a: The SID is the MOS 6581, a three-voice synth chip with four waveforms per voice, ADSR envelopes, ring mod, sync and a programmable analog filter. It's why the C64 sounds better than most home computers.

q: What is the Yamaha YM2612?
a: It's the six-channel FM chip in the Sega Genesis (Mega Drive), a close relative of the OPN family. It works alongside a Z80 and a TI sound chip that handles PSG sounds.

q: What is the difference between MIDI and a .MOD file?
a: MIDI files hold only note instructions, so they sound different on every synth. MOD files contain the actual samples plus the note patterns, so they sound the same wherever they're played.

q: What is velocity sensitivity?
a: It means the keyboard measures how hard you hit each key and sends a velocity value from 1 to 127 in the MIDI note-on message. Synths use it to control volume or brightness. Cheap ones lack it.

q: What software should I use for MIDI on the Mac?
a: Performer from Mark of the Unicorn and Vision from Opcode are common choices. You need a MIDI interface for the serial port, such as the MIDI Time Piece. Studio Vision lets you mix audio too.

q: What's a good sampler for a beginner?
a: The Akai S900 is popular in studios, and the Ensoniq Mirage is the cheaper choice at about $1,700 new. Used Mirages go for less. For a computer there's the Amiga with Soundtracker, which is very cheap.

q: What's the difference between analog and digital synths?
a: Analog synths make sound with voltage-controlled oscillators and filters, which drift and sound warm. Digital synths compute waveforms with chips and stay stable in tune. Many modern ones, like the D-50, mix sampled attacks with digital synthesis.

q: Which MIDI sequencer is best on the Atari ST?
a: Cubase from Steinberg and C-Lab Notator are the top two, and both use tight timing. Cubase has a more flexible arrange page, while Notator offers good score printing. Pick one and learn it well.

q: Which is better for music, Amiga or Atari ST?
a: For MIDI sequencing the ST wins, since it has built-in MIDI ports and a very tight timing reputation. The Amiga has four-channel 8-bit sampled sound, so it is better for tracker modules and sample-based stuff.

q: Why does my MIDI keyboard play a note then hang forever?
a: You probably got a stuck note because a note-off message was lost, perhaps from a bad cable or from stopping the sequencer mid-note. Send an all-notes-off or panic command, or just turn the synth off and on.

q: Why is there MIDI delay when I chain a lot of devices?
a: MIDI is serial at 31.25 kbaud, so each three-byte note takes about 1 ms. Big chords or dense controller data can queue up and be audibly late. Use multiple MIDI outs to split the load.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Can I do animation in Deluxe Paint?
a: Yes. Version II lets you draw frames on separate pages and play them back, and you can use color cycling for effects. For real animation Aegis Animator or Videoscape 3D give you more control, saving to Amiga ANIM files.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Can I print a Deluxe Paint picture on my dot matrix printer?
a: Yes, use the Print command with the Amiga Preferences set to your printer. It supports Epson-compatible and ImageWriter printers, and color ones like the Okimate or Epson JX-80. Use Preferences to choose dithering for grays.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Can MacPaint do color?
a: No, MacPaint is strictly black and white, with 38 patterns for shading. For color on a Mac II you want something like SuperPaint 2 or Studio/8, or PixelPaint, which handle 256 colors.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I display a ray traced image on my VGA card?
a: Most tracers write a TGA or GIF file, and you view it with a program like CSHOW or VPIC. With a standard VGA you get 256 colors out of 262,144, so the picture is dithered or color-quantized.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I draw a perfect circle in MacPaint?
a: Pick the oval tool and hold down Shift while you drag. That constrains it to a circle. Same trick with the rectangle tool gives you a square. Double-click the tool to toggle fill if you want a solid shape.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I get a screen shot on a Mac?
a: Press Command-Shift-3 and the whole screen is saved as a MacPaint file named Screen 0 on your startup disk. It works on a Mac Plus or later with System 3.0 or newer. You can then open it in MacPaint.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I make a custom brush in Deluxe Paint?
a: Use the Brush selection tool, the dotted rectangle or lasso, and drag around the part of the picture you want. When you let go, that area becomes your brush and follows the pointer. Press b to pick it up quickly.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I make a drop shadow in MacPaint?
a: Select your object, copy it, then fill the copy with a gray pattern using the paint bucket. Paste it behind, offset a few pixels down and right, and the original goes on top. Use Edit, Backward to arrange layers if needed.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I post a picture to Usenet?
a: Convert it to GIF, run it through uuencode to make plain text, split it into pieces under about 50K, and post to comp.graphics or alt.binaries.pictures. Readers then uudecode the pieces back into the file.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I rotate a point in 2D?
a: For an angle a, the new x is x cos a minus y sin a, and the new y is x sin a plus y cos a. That rotates around the origin. For another center, subtract the center first, rotate, then add it back.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How do I zoom in to edit pixels in MacPaint?
a: Choose Fatbits from the Goodies menu, or double-click the grabber hand. You get a magnified view where each click toggles a single pixel. Handy for cleaning up icons and fixing jaggies.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How many colors can the Amiga show at once?
a: In normal modes you get up to 32 colors from a palette of 4096. Hold-And-Modify mode lets you show all 4096 at once, though with some color fringing limits. Interlace doubles vertical resolution to 400 lines on NTSC.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: How much memory do I need for a 640 by 480 picture with 256 colors?
a: One byte per pixel, so 640 times 480 is 307,200 bytes, about 300K. For 24-bit true color, multiply by three to get roughly 900K. That's why 24-bit boards cost so much.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Is Deluxe Paint II worth upgrading from the first version?
a: Yes, I'd say so. II adds perspective rotation, better stencils, more screen modes including overscan, and proper brush handling. It's also a good deal at about 100 dollars from EA.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Is Super VGA worth buying?
a: If you want 800 by 600 in 16 colors or 256 colors at 640 by 480, yes. Check for software support though, since there's no standard yet. Each chipset has its own mode numbers, so you need drivers for each program.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Is there a version of Deluxe Paint for the IBM PC?
a: Yes, Deluxe Paint II came out for MS-DOS and works with EGA and the new 256-color VGA cards. It will run best with a mouse. You get the same tools as on the Amiga, but no color cycling on plain EGA.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What book should I read to learn computer graphics programming?
a: Foley and van Dam, Fundamentals of Interactive Computer Graphics, is the standard text, though the newer 1990 edition adds more. For something cheaper, Hearn and Baker or Rogers' Procedural Elements are good.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What do I need to run a ray tracer on a PC?
a: A math coprocessor, like an 8087 or 80287 or 80387, helps hugely, since ray tracing is all floating point. Without one, a simple scene can take several times longer. A 386 with a 387 is about the best you can get.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What does 'frame buffer' mean?
a: It's the memory that holds the image being displayed, one value per pixel. The video hardware reads it constantly and sends it to the monitor. Bigger buffers hold more colors, so a 24-bit board needs three bytes per pixel.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What does Deluxe Paint do that other Amiga paint programs don't?
a: Deluxe Paint from Electronic Arts has color cycling, brushes you can grab and rotate, stencils, gradient fills and animation by palette and page flipping. Most Amiga artists use it, and it's the one that pushes the 32-color modes best.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What does Mode X mean on a VGA card?
a: It's an unofficial 320 by 240 mode with 256 colors and square pixels, made by tweaking the VGA registers. It lets you use multiple video pages and gives faster drawing. Games programmers are starting to use it.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What does a genlock do?
a: It syncs your computer's video output to an outside video signal and lets you overlay computer graphics on top of live video or tape. Amiga owners use them to add titles and graphics for video production.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What does color cycling mean in Deluxe Paint?
a: It rotates a range of palette entries so colors appear to move, without redrawing anything. Draw a waterfall in a ramp of blues, set a cycle range, and the water flows. It costs almost no CPU time.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What does dithering mean?
a: It's a way to fake more shades or colors using patterns of the ones you have. For example, a mix of black and white dots looks gray from a distance. It's how MacPaint patterns look like gray and how photos get printed on laser printers.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What does the lasso tool do in MacPaint?
a: It lets you draw a loose outline around an object, and when you let go it shrinks to fit the black pixels inside. Then you can drag, copy or cut just that shape without grabbing the white around it.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is 'overscan' in Amiga paint programs?
a: It lets the picture extend into the border area around the normal screen, up to about 704 by 480 interlaced on NTSC. It's used for video titling so no border shows. Deluxe Paint II supports it.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is Fractint?
a: A free fractal program for the PC by the Stone Soup Group. It draws Mandelbrot and Julia sets and many others, uses integer math so it's fast without a coprocessor, and supports EGA, VGA and many SuperVGA cards.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is GIF and should I use it?
a: GIF is CompuServe's Graphics Interchange Format, with up to 256 colors and LZW compression. It's become the standard for posting pictures on BBS systems and Usenet because every platform has a viewer.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is Gouraud shading?
a: You calculate the lighting at each vertex of a polygon and then interpolate the colors across the surface. It makes curved objects look smooth, much better than flat shading, though it misses sharp highlights that Phong shading gets.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is HAM mode on the Amiga?
a: Hold-And-Modify. Each pixel either takes a color from a 16-color palette or holds the previous pixel's color and changes just one of red, green or blue. Great for photos and ray traced images, awkward for painting.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is Sculpt 3D?
a: Sculpt 3D, from Byte by Byte, is an Amiga ray tracing program. You build objects from polygons in a modeler and then render with shadows and reflections. Sculpt-Animate 4D adds animation. Renders can take hours, even with accelerators.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is a PostScript printer, and do I need one for graphics?
a: PostScript is Adobe's page description language, which draws shapes and text as math, at the printer's full resolution. An Apple LaserWriter prints 300 dpi, and Illustrator output looks much crisper than a bitmap sent to an ImageWriter.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is a Targa file?
a: TGA is the format from Truevision for their Targa and Vista boards. It stores 8, 16, 24 or 32-bit images, optionally run-length compressed. Many renderers and paint programs can write it because it's simple and handles true color.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is a Z-buffer?
a: It's an extra array holding the depth of each pixel. When you draw a polygon you only update a pixel if it is nearer than what's stored. It solves hidden surface removal simply, but costs a lot of memory.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is a fractal and how do I draw one?
a: A fractal is a shape with detail at every scale. The Mandelbrot set is the famous one: for each point c, iterate z becomes z squared plus c and color by how fast it escapes past 2. Fractint for the PC does this quickly.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is a good program for drawing on the Mac with Bezier curves?
a: Adobe Illustrator 88 does Bezier curves well and prints to PostScript printers. Aldus FreeHand is a competitor and is also good. Both want a Mac Plus or better with at least 1 megabyte, preferably 2.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is a polygon fill algorithm?
a: The usual way is the scan line fill. For each horizontal line you find where it crosses the polygon edges, sort the crossings, and fill between pairs. It handles concave shapes fine. Foley and van Dam covers it well.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is anti-aliasing?
a: It smooths the stair-step edges on diagonal lines by blending edge pixels with the background. In a ray tracer you do it by shooting several rays per pixel and averaging the colors. It costs render time but looks much better.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is ray tracing in plain English?
a: You fire a ray from the eye through each pixel on the screen and see what object it hits. Then you trace more rays toward lights, and into mirrors or glass, to figure out shadows, reflections and refraction. It gives very realistic pictures but takes forever.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is the Amiga blitter?
