a: It's a custom chip that moves blocks of memory and draws lines and fills very quickly without bothering the 68000. Paint programs and games use it to move bobs and brushes around the screen smoothly.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is the difference between EGA and VGA?
a: EGA is 640 by 350 with 16 colors from a palette of 64. VGA gives 640 by 480 with 16 colors, or 320 by 200 with 256 colors from a palette of 262,144. VGA also uses analog output instead of digital.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is the difference between Gouraud and Phong shading?
a: Gouraud interpolates colors between vertices. Phong interpolates the surface normals and calculates lighting per pixel, so you get proper specular highlights. It looks better but is much slower, so ray tracers and high-end workstations use it.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is the difference between MacPaint and SuperPaint?
a: MacPaint is bitmap only. SuperPaint from Silicon Beach has both a paint layer and a draw layer with object-oriented shapes you can resize and edit later. It also reads and writes MacPaint files.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What is the difference between bitmap and vector graphics?
a: A bitmap is a grid of pixels, like MacPaint, and gets blocky when enlarged. Vector graphics store lines and curves as math, like in MacDraw or Illustrator, so they scale and print cleanly at whatever resolution the printer has.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: What ray tracers are available for free?
a: DKBTrace by David Buck is popular and runs on the Amiga, PCs and Unix. Also look for the Vivid and QRT programs, and the MTV raytracer from Mark VandeWettering. All are available on comp.sources and various bulletin boards.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Which is better for graphics, an Amiga or an Atari ST?
a: The Amiga has more colors, 4096 against 512, plus the blitter and good sound. The ST is cheaper and has a sharp monochrome mode at 640 by 400 that is great for DTP. For paint and animation, I'd take the Amiga.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Why do my scanned photos look so bad on my Mac?
a: A one-bit screen can only show black or white, so halftoning or dithering has to fake grays. Scan at 150 to 300 dpi, use the scanner's halftone setting, and try cleaning up with Fatbits. A gray-scale scanner with Digital Darkroom gives better results.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Why does ray tracing take so long?
a: Every pixel needs at least one ray tested against every object in the scene, and reflections and shadows add more rays. A 640 by 480 image has over 300,000 pixels, so complex scenes can run for hours or days on a PC or Amiga.

topic: computer graphics: MacPaint, Deluxe Paint, ray tracing
q: Why is my MacPaint picture only 576 by 720 pixels?
a: That's the MacPaint document size, fixed at 576 wide by 720 high, which fits an 8 by 10 inch area at 72 dpi on the ImageWriter. The screen only shows part of it, so scroll with the grabber hand.

q: Can I add a hard disk to a Toshiba T1100 Plus?
a: No, the T1100 Plus came with only floppy drives, and there's no internal slot for a hard disk. You can add memory and an external expansion box, but if you need a hard drive, buy a model such as the T1200.

q: Can I connect a laptop to a desktop to transfer files?
a: Yes, use a null modem cable on the serial ports and a program like Laplink or the DOS MODE command with a terminal program such as Procomm. Laplink is simplest, and 115200 baud is quick enough for most files.

q: Can I leave my laptop plugged in all the time?
a: Generally yes, since the charger tops off the battery. But NiCads like to be used, so run it down once in a while. Leaving it hot and plugged in for months can shorten the life of the cells.

q: Can I run CP/M on a laptop?
a: Only on machines with a Z80 CPU, like the Kaypro 2000 or the Osborne. On an IBM compatible you would need a CP/M-86 version or an emulator, but nearly all new software is for DOS now.

q: Can I run Windows on a laptop with an 8088 CPU?
a: Windows 2.x will run in real mode but slowly, and Windows 3.0 needs at least a 286 for real mode and a 386 for 386 enhanced mode. On an 8088 stick with DOS programs, they'll be far happier.

q: Can I use a regular modem with my laptop?
a: Yes, plug any serial modem into the RS-232 port using a standard cable. Some laptops like the Toshiba T1000 or T1200 have an internal 1200 baud modem option, which saves you carrying an extra box.

q: Can a laptop be used with an external monitor?
a: Most can. Look for a CGA or RGB connector on the back, and plug in a monitor of the matching type. Some models like the Toshiba T3100e have VGA out as well, but check the manual first.

q: Do laptop floppy drives work with regular PC disks?
a: Yes, a 720K or 1.44M 3.5 inch drive reads disks formatted on any PC with the same drive type. A 1.44M drive reads 720K disks, but be careful when formatting a 720K disk in a 1.44M drive.

q: How can I tell how much battery I have left?
a: Some models show a gauge on screen or an LED on the keyboard that blinks when the battery is low. Otherwise you have to go by time used. Don't wait for the low warning to save your work.

q: How do I add memory to my laptop?
a: Most laptops use a proprietary memory card or module from the maker, so you have to buy the right one. Third parties like Kingston sell cheaper compatibles. Check the manual, since some models need DIP switch changes after adding RAM.

q: How do I back up my laptop's hard disk when it has no tape drive?
a: Use the DOS BACKUP command to floppies, like BACKUP C:\*.* A: /S. Better yet, copy your data directories with a utility such as Fastback, which is quicker and can span disks more neatly.

q: How do I park the heads on my laptop hard drive?
a: Run the park utility that came with the machine, or use SHIP on Compaq systems. Many newer drives auto-park when power drops, but it's still a good idea to park before you move it around.

q: How do I print from my laptop to a desktop printer?
a: Use the parallel port with a standard Centronics cable and print from your application as you would on a desktop. Make sure to choose the printer driver for your model in the program's setup menu.

q: How do I set the time and date on my laptop when the battery dies?
a: Type DATE and TIME at the DOS prompt and enter the right values. If the machine keeps losing them, the backup battery for the clock is probably dead and needs replacing.

q: How fast is a 2400 baud modem compared to 1200?
a: It's twice as fast, so a file that takes 10 minutes at 1200 will take about 5 at 2400. If your laptop will be used on long distance calls, the saved time pays for the extra cost quickly.

q: How long should a NiCad battery last in a laptop?
a: Expect around two to four hours on most machines, less if you use the hard disk or backlight a lot. Fully discharge it now and then, since NiCads get a memory effect if you keep topping them off half full.

q: How much RAM do I need in a laptop for Lotus 1-2-3?
a: 640K is plenty for Lotus 1-2-3 version 2.01 and for most spreadsheets. If you want to run version 3.0 you'll need a 286 or better with extended memory, at least 1M of it.

q: How much does a decent laptop cost right now?
a: Prices run from about $1,000 for a basic 8088 machine like the Toshiba T1000 to $5,000 or more for a 386 with a hard disk. Around $2,500 to $3,500 buys a good 286 with 20 or 40 megabytes.

q: Is a trackball available for a laptop?
a: Yes, several, such as Microsoft's mouse on the serial port and small clip-on trackballs. A few laptops have a built-in port for them. Most older programs can use a serial mouse with a driver loaded in CONFIG.SYS or AUTOEXEC.BAT.

q: Is it safe to carry a laptop through airport X-ray machines?
a: The X-ray itself won't hurt your disks. The magnetic fields of the conveyor motor and metal detector can in rare cases, so keep floppies away from the detector and walk your disks around instead of sending them through if you're worried.

q: Is the Atari Portfolio a real computer?
a: Yes, it's a palmtop with an 80C88 CPU, a 40 column by 8 line screen, and DIP-DOS compatible with MS-DOS 2.11. It runs on three AA batteries, but the keyboard is tiny and you can't run most PC software.

q: Is the Cambridge Z88 worth buying?
a: If you mostly want to write, keep a diary and use a spreadsheet, yes. It's a small A4-size machine with a good keyboard that runs on four AA cells. It doesn't run PC software, so it's not a DOS replacement.

q: Is the Compaq SLT/286 worth the money over a Toshiba T3100?
a: The SLT/286 is lighter and has a VGA-compatible screen and a 286 at 12 MHz, so for travel it's nicer. The T3100 has a gas plasma screen that looks sharp but needs wall power. If you want battery operation, get the SLT.

q: Is the Macintosh Portable any good?
a: It has a very nice active-matrix screen and runs up to 10 hours on its lead-acid battery. But it weighs about 16 pounds and costs around $6,500, so many people find it too heavy and expensive for what it does.

q: Is the Toshiba T1000 a good first laptop for word processing?
a: For plain text it's fine. The T1000 has an 80C88 CPU, 512K RAM expandable to 1.2M, and a 3.5 inch drive, plus MS-DOS in ROM. The screen is a bit hard to read at some angles, and it's slow for anything fancy.

q: Should I buy a used laptop?
a: Only if it's cheap and you can test it first. Check the battery, the screen for dead lines, and the keyboard. Old NiCad packs often hold very little charge, and replacement packs can cost $100 or more.

q: Should I get a 286 or a 386SX laptop?
a: A 386SX costs more but runs 386 software like Windows 3.0 in enhanced mode, and can use extended memory well. If you only run plain DOS programs, a 286 at 12 MHz is much cheaper and plenty fast.

q: What can I do about a laptop screen that has lines through it?
a: Lines can be a loose ribbon cable between the screen and the main board, or failing LCD drivers. Reseating the cable sometimes helps. If it doesn't, you will probably need a service center to replace the panel.

q: What does 'CGA-compatible' mean on a laptop LCD?
a: It means the machine accepts the same video signals as an IBM Color Graphics Adapter, so 640x200 or 320x200 software runs. On a monochrome LCD the colors just get mapped to shades of gray or blue, which can make some programs hard to read.

q: What does 'supertwist' mean in an LCD?
a: Supertwist, or STN, means the liquid crystal molecules twist 180 to 270 degrees instead of 90. That gives much better contrast and viewing angle than older twisted nematic screens, which is why newer laptops read so much better.

q: What does 'suspend mode' do on a laptop?
a: Suspend saves the state of your RAM and shuts off most hardware, so you can stop work and come back to the same screen later. It sips battery, though it'll eventually run out if you leave it for days.

q: What does the Compaq LTE offer over older laptops?
a: The LTE is a smaller notebook-sized 286 that weighs about 6 pounds with a 20 or 40 meg hard disk and a VGA-compatible screen. It was one of the first real notebooks you could carry all day.

q: What is a docking station for a laptop?
a: It's a base unit that lets you connect the laptop to a full-size monitor, keyboard, and expansion cards at your desk. It saves unplugging cables, but each maker uses its own design, so it only fits one model.

q: What is a gas plasma display?
a: It's a flat panel that glows orange-red using neon gas, as on the Toshiba T3100 and the IBM PC Convertible's cousins. It's bright and sharp but draws a lot of power, so those laptops must be plugged in.

q: What is an LCD backlight and does it use a lot of power?
a: A backlight is a small fluorescent lamp behind the LCD that makes it readable in dim light. It can use a third of your power, so switch it off if you're working in good light to extend battery life.

q: What is the Grid Compass?
a: The Grid Compass was one of the first clamshell laptops, from 1982, with a magnesium case and an electroluminescent screen. It's expensive and doesn't run DOS programs without some tinkering, so it's mainly of interest to collectors and the military.

q: What is the NEC UltraLite?
a: The NEC UltraLite is a 4.4 pound notebook with a V30 CPU and no floppy or hard drive. It uses ROM cards for storage with MS-DOS built in, which is very light but pricey, and the memory card capacity is quite limited.

q: What is the Psion Organiser II?
a: It's a pocket computer with a 2-line LCD display, a small keyboard, and a built-in programming language called OPL. It's good for address books and small programs, and you can add storage with Datapak cartridges.

q: What is the Tandy 100 and is it still useful?
a: The Tandy 100 is a small notebook-sized machine with an 8 line LCD, built-in modem, and a basic word processor. It runs for days on four AA cells. It's great for taking notes or doing text and uploading by phone, but little else.

q: What is the Zenith SupersPort?
a: It's a well-regarded laptop from Zenith Data Systems, available with 8088, 286, or 386SX CPUs and a backlit supertwist LCD. It has a 3.5 inch drive and a small hard disk, and it's easy on the eyes.

q: What is the best way to protect a laptop in a briefcase?
a: Use a padded case, park the hard disk first, and take out any floppies from the drive. Don't toss it in the trunk of a car, and avoid putting heavy books on top of the screen.

q: What is the difference between a laptop and a luggable?
a: A luggable like the Compaq Portable III or Osborne weighs 20 pounds or more and needs wall power. A laptop runs on batteries and weighs maybe 10 pounds or less, so you can actually use it on your lap.

q: What's the difference between a 20 meg and a 40 meg laptop hard drive?
a: Mostly storage. 20 megabytes holds DOS and a few applications, while 40 holds a lot more, including Windows. The 40 is usually a bit faster and costs a few hundred more, and I'd go for it if you can afford it.

q: Which is better for a portable, a 3.5 inch or a 5.25 inch floppy?
a: The 3.5 inch, easily. It's smaller, tougher in its hard shell, and holds 720K or 1.44M. Just make sure the desktop machine you swap files with can read the same format, or you'll need a 5.25 inch drive for transfer.

q: Which laptop has the best screen for use in sunlight?
a: Reflective LCDs without a backlight work best in bright light, but the best ones are hard to find. Backlit supertwist screens on the Zenith SupersPort are fine indoors but wash out in direct sun.

q: Why does my laptop keyboard feel so mushy?
a: Many laptops use short-travel keys to keep the case thin. The IBM PC Convertible and Toshiba T3100 are better than most. If you type a lot, try the keyboard in a store before you buy.

q: Why does my laptop screen look washed out in the cold?
a: LCD fluid gets sluggish when it's cold, so contrast drops and the display ghosts. Let the machine warm up to room temperature for a while before you turn it on, and avoid leaving it in a car trunk in winter.

q: Why won't my laptop battery charge fully any more?
a: Your NiCad cells may have worn out after 300 to 500 cycles, or developed a memory effect. Try a couple of full discharge and recharge cycles. If capacity doesn't come back, you will need a new pack.

q: Can I mix IPX and TCP/IP on the same Ethernet cable?
a: Yes, since they are just different protocols sharing the wire, and Ethernet frames carry both. You need drivers that support multiple stacks, or software like Novell's LAN WorkPlace for DOS.

q: Can I print to a LaserWriter from a PC?
a: Yes, you need a PostScript driver in your application and an AppleTalk connection, such as a LocalTalk PC card or a gateway. Some people instead put the printer on a serial port using an adapter.

q: Can I run Ethernet over regular telephone wire?
a: Yes, with StarLAN at 1 Mbps for now, and the new 10BASE-T standard is just coming in at 10 Mbps. 10BASE-T needs a hub and decent twisted pair, preferably category 3 or better, not just any old phone cable.

q: Can I use a Mac as a NetWare client?
a: Yes. NetWare for Macintosh lets Macs log in over AppleTalk, so you don't need NetWare client software on the Mac, or you can use an Ethernet card and EtherTalk.

q: Can Macs and PCs share the same NetWare server?
a: Yes, with NetWare for Macintosh, which adds AppleTalk and AFP services on the server. Macs then see the server as a normal AppleShare volume, and files can be shared with the PCs.

q: Do I need to use shielded twisted pair for Ethernet?
a: Not for 10BASE-T, which runs fine on unshielded twisted pair if it's good quality, and you should keep it away from fluorescent lights and motors. Shielded is mostly used with IBM Token Ring.

q: How do I back up a NetWare server?
a: Use a tape drive with software such as Novell's NBACKUP or a third party like Cheyenne ARCserve or Palindrome. Run it on a schedule at night, and test restores now and then.

q: How do I configure IPX for my network card?
a: Run WSGEN or SHGEN from the Novell disks and choose your card driver with the correct IRQ, I/O base and DMA settings. It creates an IPX.COM file linked to that exact hardware setup.

q: How do I connect two Macs together so I can share files?
a: Plug a LocalTalk box (or PhoneNet connector) into each Mac's printer port and run cable between them. Then pick Chooser, turn AppleTalk on, and turn on File Sharing in the Sharing Setup control panel under System 7.

q: How do I log in to a NetWare server from DOS?
a: Load IPX and NETX, switch to the first network drive (usually F:), and type LOGIN servername/username. Then enter your password when prompted.

q: How do I map a drive in NetWare?
a: Use MAP, for example MAP G:=SYS:PUBLIC. MAP INS S1:=SYS:APPS adds a search drive, and MAP by itself lists all your current mappings.

q: How do I set up printing on a NetWare network?
a: Create a print queue and a print server with PCONSOLE, then attach your printer to the server's LPT port or run RPRINTER on a workstation. Users send jobs with CAPTURE, such as CAPTURE L=1 Q=laserq.

q: How do trustee rights work?
a: Rights such as Read, Write, Create, Erase, Modify, File Scan, Access Control, and Supervisory are assigned to users or groups on a directory. They flow down to subdirectories unless blocked by an inherited rights mask.

q: How fast is LocalTalk in real life?
a: The raw speed is 230.4 kbps, but with protocol overhead and busy nodes you might see around 10 to 20 KB per second. Copying a big file feels slow compared with Ethernet.

q: How many devices can I put on a LocalTalk network?
a: The spec allows 32 devices per segment, and in practice that is plenty slow already. Total cable length is meant to stay below 300 meters, and past that you need a router or bridge.

q: How much RAM does a NetWare 386 server need?
a: A minimum of about 4 MB, but disk caching and directory tables use the rest. A server with 8 MB or more is much happier, and more memory for a bigger disk is the best speedup.

q: How much does an Ethernet card cost these days?
a: A 3Com EtherLink or Novell NE2000 for a PC runs roughly $300 to $500, and Mac NuBus cards are a bit more, often $400 to $600. Prices are falling as clones come out.

q: Is PhoneNet really as good as the Apple LocalTalk connectors?
a: Yes, electrically they're about the same, and PhoneNet is much cheaper. It uses ordinary telephone wire, so you can daisy-chain it, but keep total cable under about 1000 feet and 32 devices per zone segment.

q: Is it worth getting a dedicated server, or can I use a peer-to-peer setup?
a: For a few users, peer-to-peer such as AppleShare on a Mac or Tops is fine and cheap. For more than five or six people or when you need backups and security, a dedicated server pays off.

q: My Ethernet card and my serial card both use IRQ 3. What do I do?
a: Move one of them. Most Ethernet cards let you set jumpers to IRQ 2, 3, 4, 5, and 5 is often free on XT-class machines unless you have a hard disk controller there. Match the change in IPX config.

q: What are IPX and NETX?
a: IPX is Novell's network protocol, a derivative of Xerox XNS, and NETX is the shell that redirects DOS calls to the server. Both are loaded in memory from AUTOEXEC.BAT or a batch file.

q: What does 'File server not found' mean when I run LOGIN?
a: Your shell can't see any server. Check that IPX loaded without errors, the cable is connected, and your IPX card settings (IRQ, I/O address) match what the driver was generated for.

q: What does 10BASE-T stand for?
a: 10 is 10 Mbps, BASE means baseband signalling, and T is twisted pair. It uses a star layout with a hub and runs up to 100 meters from the hub to each station.

q: What does AppleTalk actually mean? Is it the same as LocalTalk?
a: Not quite. AppleTalk is the protocol suite, LocalTalk is the cabling and hardware (230.4 kbps). You can run AppleTalk over LocalTalk, Ethernet (EtherTalk) or token ring (TokenTalk).

q: What does CSMA/CD mean?
a: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. A station listens before sending, and if two transmit at once they detect the collision, back off a random time, and retry.

q: What does EtherTalk do?
a: EtherTalk is Apple's driver that runs AppleTalk protocols on Ethernet. You install it with a NuBus Ethernet card, such as the Apple Ethernet NB Card, then choose Ethernet in the Network control panel.

q: What does Hot Fix do on NetWare?
a: When the server finds a bad block on write, it redirects the data to a reserved area, the Hot Fix Redirection Area, which is about 2 percent of the disk. It's automatic and transparent to users.

q: What does a bridge do and how is it different from a router?
a: A bridge joins two segments at the data link level and passes frames based on MAC address, without caring about protocols. A router works at the network level and looks at addresses like IPX or AppleTalk network numbers.

q: What is AppleShare?
a: AppleShare is Apple's file server software, running on a dedicated Mac. Clients see it in the Chooser, log in as registered users or guests, and mount server volumes on the desktop.

q: What is Novell NetWare?
a: NetWare is a network operating system that turns a PC into a dedicated file and print server. Workstations run DOS with a shell and see server volumes as ordinary drive letters.

q: What is SFT NetWare?
a: System Fault Tolerant NetWare adds features such as disk mirroring and duplexing, a Transaction Tracking System, and hot fix. Level III will even mirror whole servers, though that's not out yet.

q: What is TOPS?
a: TOPS is a peer-to-peer network from Sun's TOPS division that lets Macs and PCs share files and printers over AppleTalk or LocalTalk. Each user publishes folders, and other machines mount them as drives.

q: What is a MAC address?
a: It's the unique 48-bit hardware number built into each Ethernet card, written as six hex bytes. The first three identify the manufacturer; 3Com cards start with 02608C, for example.

q: What is a hub and do I need one?
a: A hub is the central box that twisted pair stations connect to, and it repeats frames to all ports. You need one for 10BASE-T or StarLAN, but not for a coax thinnet bus.

q: What is a login script?
a: It is a text file the server runs when you log in, set in SYSCON, and it maps drives, sets variables, and attaches printers. There is a system script plus one per user.

q: What is a network number, and why does NetWare ask for one?
a: It's an ID that identifies a cable segment so routers can find it. Every segment on a NetWare internet needs a unique network number in hex, and servers on the same cable must agree on it.

q: What is a repeater?
a: A repeater simply regenerates the signal to extend an Ethernet segment, passing everything through. It joins two segments into one collision domain, and you can use up to four between any two stations.

q: What is a search drive in NetWare?
a: A search drive acts like a PATH entry, mapped to a server directory so you can run programs from anywhere. They're numbered S1 to S16, and map to the next free drive letter starting at Z.

q: What is a zone in AppleTalk?
a: A zone is just a logical grouping of devices, shown in the Chooser's zone list. It makes finding printers and servers easier on big internetworks, and zones are set up on routers like the Kinetics FastPath or Shiva.

q: What is an NE2000 and why do people keep recommending it?
a: It's Novell's 16-bit Ethernet card based on the National Semiconductor 8390 chip. It's cheap, clones are everywhere, and nearly every driver and network OS supports it.

q: What is an NLM?
a: A NetWare Loadable Module is a program or driver you load on a NetWare 386 server with the LOAD command. Disk drivers, LAN drivers, and utilities such as MONITOR are NLMs.

q: What is the difference between Ethernet II and 802.3 frames?
a: They look nearly alike, but Ethernet II has a type field where 802.3 has a length field. NetWare defaults to 802.3 frames, and TCP/IP usually expects Ethernet II, so mixed networks need to set it correctly.

q: What is the difference between NetWare 286 and 386?
a: NetWare 286 runs in 286 protected mode and is limited to 256 users and 2 GB disk per volume. NetWare 386 (3.0 and up) uses 32-bit code, bigger volumes, NLMs and loads and unloads modules without rebooting.

q: What is the supervisor account in NetWare?
a: SUPERVISOR is the all-powerful user on the server, created at install. Set its password straight away, and use SYSCON to add users, groups, trustee rights and login scripts.

q: What is thin Ethernet and how long can a segment be?
a: Thin Ethernet is 10BASE2, using RG-58 coax with BNC T connectors and 50 ohm terminators at each end. A segment can be 185 meters with up to 30 nodes, and the T goes right on the card.

q: What's the difference between thinnet and thicknet?
a: Thicknet (10BASE5) is the yellow cable, up to 500 meters per segment and 100 nodes, with vampire taps and AUI transceivers. Thinnet is cheaper and easier to install, but shorter in range.

q: Which is better for a small office, AppleTalk or Ethernet?
a: For a few Macs and a LaserWriter, LocalTalk is cheap and works fine. If you move big files or have PCs too, Ethernet is about 40 times faster at 10 Mbps and worth the card cost.

q: Why do I get the error 'Network error on server: Error sending on network'?
a: Usually a cable or connector problem, or a bad card or terminator. Check the BNC T on your PC, then try another card; the error means your NETX could not talk to the server.

q: Why does my LaserWriter not show up in the Chooser?
a: Check that AppleTalk is set to Active, the cable is seated at both ends, and the printer has finished warming up. A bad terminator or a break in the daisy chain will also make it vanish.

q: Why does my whole thinnet Ethernet go down when one PC is unplugged?
a: Because the coax bus needs to be continuous and terminated at both ends. Pulling the cable off a T-connector breaks the bus and leaves it unterminated, so everyone drops. Leave the T in place and remove only the stub.

q: Why is my network so slow all of a sudden?
a: Check for a flaky card flooding the cable with garbage, a loose BNC, or someone running big transfers. On NetWare, load MONITOR to check utilization and cache buffers, since low cache will slow everything.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Are used 9-pin dot matrix printers still worth buying over a laser?
a: Yes, if you're on a budget. A laser printer like the HP LaserJet II costs around $1800 new, while a used dot matrix is $100. Letter quality needs a daisy wheel or 24-pin printer, such as the Panasonic KX-P1124.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Can I put a hard disk in a used PC XT that doesn't have one?
a: Yes. A 20 meg Seagate ST-225 with a controller card runs about $250 to $300 new. Make sure the power supply is at least 130 watts, as the original 63 watt one may struggle.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Can I run Lotus 1-2-3 on a used PC with 256K?
a: Version 1A will run in 192K, but 2.0 needs 256K and 2.01 does better with 320K or more. Larger spreadsheets need more RAM, so budget for a memory upgrade if you plan to build big models.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Can I use my old Apple II disks on a used Macintosh?
a: Not directly, since the Mac uses 3.5 inch disks and the Apple II 5.25. You'd need the Apple IIe card for the Mac LC or a serial transfer using a communications program such as MacTerminal.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How can I check that a used 5.25 inch drive works properly?
a: Format a blank disk, copy a few files to it, and read them back on a different machine if you can. Drives out of alignment may read their own disks but fail on others.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How can I tell if a used hard drive is about to die?
a: Listen for grinding or clicking at boot, and run Norton Utilities or SpinRite to check for bad sectors. If the bad-sector list is long or growing, walk away. Ask the seller to let you run a test.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How do I clean a used keyboard that has sticky keys?
a: Pop the keycaps off with a small screwdriver and wash them in warm soapy water. Wipe the board with isopropyl alcohol on a swab. Take a photo or sketch the layout first so you can put them back correctly.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How do I find out what DOS version is on a used PC?
a: Type VER at the prompt. It will say something like MS-DOS Version 3.30. Anything 3.0 or above supports hard disks over 10 meg reasonably, and 3.3 handles larger partitions with extended DOS partitions.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How do I know if a used monitor is worn out?
a: Check for burn-in ghosts, dim or blurry text, and color that bleeds. A monochrome monitor should be crisp when you turn up the brightness. Shake-test for sound, no rattling, and check it warms up within a minute.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How do I test the memory in a used PC?
a: Run a diagnostic like Checkit, PC-Tools, or the IBM Advanced Diagnostics disk. Also watch the boot-time memory count, which should reach the full amount without errors. A parity error message means bad RAM.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How much does a 1200 baud modem cost used?
a: A Hayes-compatible 1200 baud external modem is about $50 to $80 used in 1989. New ones are around $100. Make sure it's Hayes AT-command compatible so the software works with it.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How much does it cost to replace a floppy drive on an old PC?
a: A new 360K 5.25 inch drive is about $60 to $80 and a 1.2 meg drive is around $80 to $100. A 3.5 inch 720K runs about $90. Used ones are cheaper but test them first.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How much is a used Atari 520ST worth?
a: A 520ST with a monitor usually goes for $300 to $450 used. The built-in MIDI ports make it popular with musicians. Check that the single-sided drive works, since those are the usual failure.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How much is a used Commodore 128 worth?
a: Roughly $100 to $150 for the computer alone, and $50 or so for a 1571 drive. It runs C64 software and CP/M, and has an 80-column mode. The 1541 drives are slow, so the 1571 is nicer.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How much should I pay for a used Hercules graphics card?
a: About $50 to $70. It gives 720x348 monochrome graphics and works with Lotus and many other programs. Clone Hercules-compatible cards are cheaper and work fine for most things.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: How much should I pay for a used IBM PC XT with a hard disk?
a: Around $400 to $600 if it has 640K, a 10 or 20 meg drive, and a monitor. Less if it's the monochrome card only. Check that the drive spins up cold and the keyboard is the original, since those are costly to replace.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is a used Amiga 1000 worth it compared to a new 500?
a: A used 1000 goes for about $500 with a monitor. The 500 is cheaper new, around $600 with more built in. The 1000 has the nicer case and a RAM expansion slot in front, but the 500 runs the same software.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is a used Amstrad PC1512 any good?
a: For around $400 it's a decent XT-speed machine with an 8086 CPU at 8 MHz and a color monitor option. The proprietary mouse and keyboard connectors can make upgrades awkward, but it runs most DOS software.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is a used Commodore 64 still worth buying in 1988?
a: For about $75 to $100 with a 1541 drive, yes, if you mainly want games and cheap fun. The software library is huge and cheap. For word processing or serious work, an XT clone is a better use of money.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is a used Osborne or Kaypro worth buying?
a: Only for under $100 and only if you already know CP/M. The software is still around but the small screens and 4 MHz Z80 chips are limiting. An old PC clone gives you much more software choice.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is a used Tandy 1000 a good buy?
a: For $300 to $500 used, yes, especially the EX or SX. They run most PC software and have good 16-color graphics and sound. Watch for the odd proprietary expansion slots that limit which cards work.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is it safe to buy a used computer without a manual?
a: Mostly, yes. DOS manuals are easy to buy, and the Peter Norton guides are better anyway. You do want the original disks or at least the DOS version, so ask the seller what version is installed.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is it worth getting a used 2400 baud modem or should I buy new?
a: New 2400 baud modems run about $120 to $200 now, and used ones are only a little cheaper. Buying new gets you a warranty. Used is fine if it is a Hayes or US Robotics and the seller shows it dialing.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is it worth upgrading a used XT to a 286 with a motherboard swap?
a: Often yes, if the case and power supply are sturdy. A 286 board costs about $250 to $400 and you can keep the drives and cards. You may need a new keyboard that works in AT mode.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Is the IBM PCjr worth anything used?
a: Not much. Maybe $100 to $200 with the monitor. The chiclet keyboard is awful, expansion is limited, and it doesn't run all PC software. Cartridge games are the main attraction.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Should I buy a used 8088 or save for a new 286?
a: A 286 clone is now about $1000 to $1500 new, and used XTs are $400 or so. If you plan to use Windows or big spreadsheets, save for the 286. For text and BBS use, the XT is plenty.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Should I buy a used computer with a bad power supply and replace it?
a: Yes if the price reflects it. A replacement 150 or 200 watt supply for an XT or AT costs $50 to $90. Just check that the motherboard and drives weren't fried when it failed.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Should I pay for a used machine with a cashier's check or cash?
a: Cash in person is simplest, after you've tested the machine. Avoid mailing money to strangers for equipment you haven't seen. If shipping is unavoidable, use COD so you can look before paying.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What does 'IBM compatible' really mean?
a: It means the machine runs the same software and takes the same expansion cards, with a BIOS that behaves like IBM's. Compaq, AST and Dell are quite solid. Cheap clones may fail on some programs like Flight Simulator.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What does 'turbo' mean on a clone XT?
a: It means the machine can switch the 8088 from 4.77 MHz to something like 8 or 10 MHz, usually by a button or keystroke. Some timing-dependent games run too fast in turbo, so you'll want to switch back.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What does 'wait states' mean when buying an AT clone?
a: It means the CPU pauses a cycle while it waits for slower RAM. A 12 MHz 286 with one wait state is still faster than an 8 MHz with zero. Zero wait state boards cost more and run quicker.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What does 640K of RAM cost to add to an old PC?
a: Memory chips are around $2 to $3 each for 256K DRAMs, so filling a multifunction card to 640K costs about $60 to $100 in 1989. Prices bounced up in 1988 but have been falling back.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What does MFM versus RLL mean on a hard disk?
a: They're two ways of encoding data. RLL packs about 50 percent more onto the same disk, so a 20 meg MFM drive can become 30 meg with an RLL controller. Not every drive handles it reliably, though.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What does a used Compaq Portable cost?
a: The original Compaq Portable with two floppies goes for around $400 to $600. They're well built but heavy at about 28 pounds. The Portable II or III with a hard disk is closer to $1000 or more.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What does a used Macintosh SE cost?
a: A Mac SE with 1 meg and two floppy drives goes for around $1000 to $1400 used. With an internal 20 meg hard disk expect $1500 or so. Prices are held up quite well because of the strong software.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What is a fair price for a used Apple IIe in 1987?
a: A complete IIe with 128K, an 80-column card, two disk drives and a monitor runs about $400 to $550. A bare unit with no drives should be under $250. Software is easy to find at user groups.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What is a fair price for a used Epson FX-80 printer?
a: About $100 to $150 in good shape. The FX-80 is a solid 9-pin dot matrix and it is Epson-compatible with nearly everything. Look at a test printout to make sure no pins are dead.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What is a good used laptop for a student in 1990?
a: A Toshiba T1000 or Zenith SupersPort goes for around $500 to $800 used. The T1000 is light and runs 8088 DOS programs for hours. Don't expect color or a hard disk at that price.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What is a math coprocessor and do I need one in a used machine?
a: It's an 8087 for XTs, 80287 for ATs, that does floating point math quickly. You only need one for CAD, some spreadsheets, or scientific programs. It costs $100 to $300 depending on speed.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What is the difference between CGA, EGA and VGA?
a: CGA gives 4 colors at 320x200. EGA gives 16 colors at 640x350. VGA, which came with IBM's PS/2 in 1987, gives 16 colors at 640x480 or 256 colors at 320x200. A used machine with EGA is a good deal.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What should I ask a seller before buying a used computer?
a: Ask how old it is, whether it was ever repaired, and what the hard drive size and DOS version are. Request a demo with a real program, not only the power-on screen. Ask if you can return it within a week.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What should I look for when buying a used Macintosh?
a: Check that the 3.5 inch drive reads disks and the screen is bright and sharp. A Mac Plus with 1 meg and an external drive goes for about $700 to $900 used. The 128K and 512K Macs are much less useful today.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: What's the best place to find used computers?
a: Check newspaper classifieds, local user group swap meets, and bulletin boards. Computer Shopper has plenty of ads too. College bulletin boards often post machines when labs upgrade, and they tend to be cheap.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Which is better for a used machine, an AT clone or an XT clone?
a: The AT with a 286 is much faster, roughly three to five times an XT, and runs OS/2 if you ever want it. Used ATs cost about $400 more. If you only run WordStar and Lotus, an XT is fine.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Why are used IBM PCs so heavy and expensive compared to clones?
a: IBM used solid steel cases, good keyboards, and strong power supplies. You also pay for the name. A clone with the same parts often sells for half the price and will run the same programs.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Why does my used PC say 'Non-system disk or disk error' on boot?
a: It's looking for DOS on drive A and finding a disk without it. Take the floppy out, or put in a bootable DOS disk. If it has a hard drive and still complains, the drive may not be partitioned or the boot sector is bad.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Why does my used computer lose the date every time I turn it off?
a: The battery for the clock chip is dead. On ATs it's a 6 volt battery or a lithium cell on the motherboard, about $5 to $10. XTs usually need a clock card, so DOS asks for the date at boot.

topic: buying a used computer and what things cost
q: Why won't my used hard drive boot after I moved it to another computer?
a: The drive probably has a different controller or geometry than the new machine expects. An MFM drive must be low-level formatted by the same type of controller, so back up first and reformat with FDISK and FORMAT.

q: Can I put a 286 board in my 8088 XT clone?
a: Yes, cards like the Orchid Tiny Turbo 286 plug into an XT slot and take over from the 8088. Expect about three times the speed, but the 8-bit bus and slow hard disk will still hold you back.

q: Can I run a 386 motherboard in my old AT case?
a: Usually yes, if it is a baby AT board with matching mounting holes. You will have to move your keyboard connector and the power supply connections, but it is a common upgrade and costs less than a whole new machine.

q: Can I upgrade my Apple IIGS with an accelerator?
a: Yes, the Applied Engineering TransWarp GS and the Zip GS both replace the 2.8 MHz speed with 7 to 10 MHz. Most software works fine, but some copy-protected disks and timing-sensitive games need the board turned off.

q: Can I use a 5.25 inch 1.2 MB drive and still read my old 360K disks?
a: Mostly yes, but a 1.2 MB drive writes narrower tracks, so a 360K disk written in it may not read reliably on a real 360K drive. Reading is generally fine. Format 360K disks on a 360K drive.

q: Can a PC use a 5 MB or larger RAM disk to speed up compiles?
a: Yes, with a 286 or 386 and extended memory, a VDISK or RAMDRIVE.SYS disk puts your compiler and temp files in memory. Turbo Pascal and Microsoft C builds can run many times faster, but save your work to a real disk.

q: Can the original IBM PC power supply handle a hard disk and extra cards?
a: The 63.5 watt supply in the PC is marginal. A hard drive, a multifunction card and a graphics card can overload it, and you'll see random resets. A 130 watt replacement from a clone vendor is cheap and fixes it.

q: Do I need an 8087 for my PC XT?
a: Only if your software uses it. AutoCAD, some spreadsheets and Fortran programs can, but word processors and most games gain nothing. Check the program's manual before spending around a hundred and fifty dollars.

q: Do I need to change my jumpers when I add memory to my AT?
a: Often yes, or you must run the setup program. Many clones set the RAM size with a DIP switch on the motherboard, while IBM ATs need the SETUP disk. Without that, the system will not see the new memory.

q: Does a faster CPU make my dot-matrix printer print faster?
a: No, the printer's mechanism is the limit. What can help is a print spooler or a buffer card that frees the computer sooner. Programs like PrintCache or a hardware buffer return control while it prints.

q: How can I add more memory to my Amiga 500?
a: Plug a trapdoor expansion board into the slot under the machine. A 512K board adds a clock, and 1 MB boards from Commodore and others are common. Use "Chip RAM" only if your Agnus supports it.

q: How do I add a math coprocessor to my 386?
a: Power off, find the empty 80387 socket beside the CPU, and match the notched corner. Buy the right speed grade, 16 or 20 MHz, for your machine. Software must support it, such as AutoCAD, Lotus 1-2-3 or Excel.

q: How do I get a Mac SE/30 to use more than 8 MB?
a: You need Connectix MODE32, or a ROM patch that makes the system 32-bit clean, plus 4 MB SIMMs in the machine. Then the SE/30 can address up to 128 MB in theory, and you will run into the SIMM price first.

q: How do I install a hard card in my XT?
a: Set it to the lowest free slot, plug it in, run the low-level format if it needs one, then use FDISK and FORMAT from DOS. Make sure your power supply can handle the extra 10 to 15 watts.

q: How do I know which IRQ is free for my new card?
a: On an AT, IRQ 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 are the common ones. COM1 uses 4, COM2 uses 3, and LPT1 uses 7. Pick an unused one and set the jumper. Utilities such as MSD can show you which are in use.

q: How do I set the SCSI ID on an external drive?
a: Look for a switch or dial on the back of the drive. Each device in the chain needs a different number from 0 to 6, because the Mac itself uses 7. On a startup disk, the Mac prefers the lowest ID.

q: How do I tell if my Mac has a 68881 socket?
a: Open the case and look for an empty PGA socket near the CPU. The Mac II, SE/30 and IIx have one, while the Plus and SE need an accelerator with a coprocessor. The 68882 is a pin-compatible replacement.

q: How do I use extended memory on a 286 under DOS?
a: DOS itself can't use it, but you can make a RAM disk with VDISK.SYS in your CONFIG.SYS, or use programs written for it such as Windows 3.0 in standard mode. Some utilities can also turn it into expanded memory.

q: How many MHz do I need to run Windows 3.0 well?
a: A 286 at 12 MHz works in real or standard mode, but a 386 at 20 MHz or more is much nicer for 386 enhanced mode. Aim for 2 MB of RAM at least, and 4 MB if you multitask DOS programs.

q: How much RAM can a Mac II take?
a: Eight slots of 1 MB SIMMs gives you 8 MB in the Mac II as shipped, and the ROM limit with 32-bit clean upgrades is higher. Without a 32-bit clean ROM, System 6 tops out at 8 MB of usable memory.

q: How much faster is a 68020 than a 68000 at the same clock?
a: With its 32-bit bus and instruction cache, a 68020 is roughly 1.5 to 2 times faster than a 68000 at the same MHz. A 68030 adds data cache and an MMU and gains a bit more, particularly in loops.

q: Is a 68030 accelerator for my Mac SE worth the money?
a: If you do spreadsheets, page layout or heavy graphics, yes. A Novy or Radius 030 board makes an SE feel like an SE/30 for much less. If you only run MacWrite, skip it.

q: Is an SX upgrade chip available for my 286 AT?
a: Yes, products like the Kingston SX Now and Cyrix upgrade boards replace the 286 with a 386SX-style processor. You get 386 instructions and a modest speedup, but the AT bus still limits things and the gain varies by board.

q: Is it better to buy a new 386 or upgrade my AT with a 386 board?
a: If your case, power supply and disk are decent, a board like the Intel Inboard 386/AT is cheaper. But a new 386 machine gets you 32-bit memory and a better bus, and most upgraded ATs still run their old 16-bit RAM.

q: Is it better to get a 40 MB drive or two 20 MB drives?
a: One 40 MB drive is cheaper per megabyte, uses one slot and one power connection, and is usually faster. Two drives give you a backup option if one dies, but most people are better off buying a tape drive for that.

q: Is it safe to overclock my 8088 by changing the crystal?
a: Many people swap the 14.318 MHz crystal for a faster one to get 8 or 10 MHz. It often works, but the floppy controller, serial timing and the system clock will all go off. A real turbo board is cleaner.

q: Is it worth getting a 14.4 MHz or 16 MHz upgrade for my Atari ST?
a: Not generally. A 68000 accelerator board for the ST is rare and fiddly to install, and it can break compatibility with games. The Mega STE-like speedups just aren't big enough compared with a better hard drive.

q: Is the Intel 486 worth waiting for or should I buy a 386 now?
a: The 486 runs about twice as fast as a 386 at the same clock, but 486 systems cost thousands more. If you need a machine now for DOS and Windows, a fast 386 with cache is the sensible buy at current prices.

q: Should I buy a hard disk with MFM or RLL controller?
a: RLL stores about 50 percent more data on the same disk, so a 20 MB MFM drive becomes about 30 MB. But the drive must be rated for it, and some will give errors. ESDI or SCSI drives are even better if you can afford them.

q: What does 32-bit clean mean on a Mac?
a: It means the ROM and software use all 32 address bits instead of only the low 24. Older Macs like the II and SE/30 are not clean, so they can't use more than 8 MB without a patch like Connectix MODE32.

q: What does MMU mean and do I need one?
a: It stands for memory management unit, which translates addresses and protects memory. The 68030 and 386 have it built in. You need it only for virtual memory or multitasking Unix, such as A/UX on a Mac.

q: What does a turbo switch really do on my 386?
a: It switches the clock between full speed and a slower mode, like 8 MHz, that simulates an older machine. Use the slow setting for timing-sensitive games or copy-protected disks and the fast one for everything else.

q: What does an accelerator card actually do for my Mac Plus?
a: It replaces the 68000 with a faster CPU, usually a 68020 or 68030 at 16 to 25 MHz, and often adds its own RAM and cache. CPU-bound work gets two to five times quicker, but disk and screen speed stay about the same.

q: What does the 8087 actually speed up in Lotus 1-2-3?
a: Only the math-heavy recalcs, such as big spreadsheets with trig or financial functions. A normal budget sheet barely changes. Lotus 1-2-3 Release 2 and later do detect and use an 8087 when present.

q: What is a DMA channel and why do cards fight over them?
a: DMA lets a device move data to memory without the CPU. The AT has seven channels and some are used by the floppy and others. Two cards claiming the same channel or IRQ will lock up the machine, so set jumpers carefully.

q: What is a Radius Accelerator?
a: It is a 16 MHz 68020 board for the Mac Plus and SE sold by Radius. It plugs under the CPU and can be combined with their full-page display. It gives roughly twice the speed of a stock machine.

q: What is a cache and does it help much?
a: A cache is a small block of very fast memory that holds recently used data so the CPU skips slow RAM. On a 25 MHz 386 a 32K or 64K cache can give a noticeable speedup, often 20 percent or more.

q: What is an SCSI interface and why do Mac people care?
a: It is a standard bus for connecting hard drives, scanners and CD-ROMs. Every Mac since the Plus has one built in. You can chain up to seven devices, each with its own ID, and must end the chain with a terminator.

q: What is interleave and how do I set it?
a: It is how many sectors the disk skips between logically consecutive ones so the controller can keep up. On an XT it is often 6 or 3. Tools like SpinRite and Disk Technician let you test and change it.

q: What is the difference between 68881 and 68882?
a: The 68882 is a faster, pipelined version of the 68881 and does the same job. It is pin-compatible, so you can drop it into a socket. At the same clock it's up to about 1.5 times faster on some operations.

q: What is the difference between a 386SX and a 386DX?
a: The SX has a 16-bit external data bus and 24-bit addressing, while the DX is 32 bits throughout. The SX runs the same software and costs less, but it is noticeably slower than a DX at the same clock.

q: Which gives more speed for my Mac IIcx, a faster CPU card or more RAM?
a: If you are running out of memory and System swaps, more RAM wins. Otherwise a 68030 clock or cache card helps. With only 2 MB, go to 4 or 5 MB first, since MultiFinder eats a lot.

q: Which is better for an Amiga 2000, a GVP A2000-030 or a Commodore A2630?
a: The GVP is usually cheaper and can carry a SCSI controller and RAM on the same board. The A2630 is a 25 MHz 68030 with 68882 support and very compatible. Either is a big jump over the stock 7 MHz 68000.

q: Why does my computer beep and not start after I add RAM?
a: Likely a bad or misseated chip, or mismatched speeds. Power off, reseat the SIMMs or DIPs, check they are the right type, and make sure parity chips are included if the board needs them. Count the beeps for a clue.

q: Why does my old game run too fast after I installed a turbo board?
a: Many games time themselves by counting CPU cycles instead of reading a clock. Most turbo cards have a hardware switch or a key combo like Ctrl-Alt-minus to drop back to 4.77 MHz. Check your manual.

q: Will a faster video card speed up Windows 3.0?
a: Yes, quite a bit. A card with 16-bit bus, like a Paradise or Tseng ET4000 based board, makes screen redraws much faster than a plain 8-bit VGA. A CPU upgrade helps less than people expect.

q: Will an accelerator void my Apple warranty?
a: Possibly. Apple dealers may refuse service if opening the machine damages anything, and the SE and Plus require removing the case. Many upgrades are installed by authorized dealers, so ask first before voiding it yourself.

q: Can I connect an IBM PC joystick to a sound card game port?
a: Yes, the Sound Blaster has a 15-pin game port and works with standard analog PC joysticks. If you also have a game card, only one should be enabled, or they will conflict at port 201 hex. Disable one before using both.

q: Can I hook up two mice to one computer?
a: Not usually. Most mouse drivers only handle one at a time. You can have a serial mouse on COM1 and a bus mouse on a card, but the driver will pick one. Check your mouse documentation for multiple-device support.

q: Can I plug an Atari joystick into my Commodore 64?
a: Yes. The C64 uses the same 9-pin Atari-style joystick connector, so Atari 2600 joysticks work fine in either control port. Port 2 is the one most games use. Just power off before plugging in to be safe.

q: Can I use a PS/2 mouse on an older AT clone?
a: Not directly. The PS/2 mouse uses a mini-DIN connector and needs the matching port on the motherboard, which most ATs lack. You would need a serial mouse instead. Some adapters exist, but they only work with mice made for both.

q: Can I use a keyboard cleaner spray on my keys?
a: Compressed air is fine for dust. For sticky keys, use isopropyl alcohol on a swab. Don't pour liquids into the board. If you spill coffee, unplug it, flip it upside down, and rinse it with distilled water, and let it dry thoroughly for a few days.

q: Do I need a special keyboard for the Apple IIgs?
a: Yes, the IIgs uses the Apple Desktop Bus keyboard, which plugs into the ADB port. Older Apple II keyboards won't work. You can chain a mouse into the keyboard's second ADB port. The ADB bus also works on Macs.

q: How can I use a mouse in a program that doesn't support one?
a: Some mouse drivers can emulate cursor keys. Use a program that maps mouse movement to arrow keys, like the one shipped with Logitech's mouse software. Results vary, and it works best with menus or text editors.

q: How do I change the repeat rate on my AT keyboard?
a: On an AT, use the MODE command in DOS 3.3: MODE CON RATE=32 DELAY=1 sets the fastest rate. This works on AT-class machines, and the setting resets at power off, so put it in AUTOEXEC.BAT.

q: How do I clean a mouse ball?
a: Twist the retaining ring, take out the ball, and wash it with warm water or alcohol and dry it. Then scrape the lint off the little rollers inside with a fingernail or toothpick. Do this every few months if you use it daily.

q: How do I get a joystick to work on a Tandy 1000?
a: The Tandy 1000 has two built-in joystick ports for Tandy digital-style sticks. They are not the same as standard analog IBM PC sticks, so buy a Tandy-compatible one. Most Tandy games support them directly.

q: How do I get a keyboard to work on a PCjr?
a: The PCjr keyboard connects by a cord or an infrared link, and its layout has no numeric keypad. Use Fn with other keys to get F-keys, Break, and Pause. Old XT keyboards don't plug in, so you need a PCjr model.

q: How do I install a Microsoft Mouse under DOS?
a: Run MOUSE.COM from the install disk, or put it in AUTOEXEC.BAT so it loads every boot. Or add DEVICE=MOUSE.SYS to CONFIG.SYS. Programs like Windows or Word will then find the mouse by themselves. Use /1 or /2 for the COM port if needed.

q: How do I remap keys on my PC?
a: Use a resident utility like ProKey or SmartKey, or the Norton Utilities' keyboard tools. They load as TSRs from AUTOEXEC.BAT. You can swap Caps Lock with Control or define macros. Beware of conflicts with other TSRs.

q: How do I switch between a mouse and keyboard in Lotus 1-2-3?
a: Lotus 1-2-3 release 2 doesn't support a mouse natively. You use the slash menu and cursor keys. A few third-party drivers add mouse support, but most users stick to the keyboard, which is faster once you know the commands.

q: How do I tell if my PC keyboard is an XT or AT type?
a: Look at the plug and the back of the board. Both use a 5-pin DIN, but XT and AT signaling differ. Many boards like the Keytronic have an XT/AT switch underneath. Plugging an AT board into an XT usually gives nothing or a keyboard error at boot.

q: How do I use my Mac mouse for double clicking more easily?
a: Open the Control Panel and use the Mouse settings to set the double-click speed to slow. That gives you more time between clicks. You can also change the tracking speed there to make the pointer move faster or slower.

q: How long do keyboards generally last?
a: A quality board like the Model M is rated for tens of millions of keystrokes and can last a decade or more. Cheap boards might start failing in a couple of years. Dirt and spills are the usual cause of trouble.

q: Is a Kensington Expert Mouse a good buy?
a: For Mac users, it's a good trackball. It has a big ball and four buttons. It's pricey at about $100, but it's very comfortable and accurate. Dirt can build up under the ball, so clean it from time to time.

q: Is a mouse pad really necessary?
a: Not strictly, but it helps a lot. A pad gives the ball good grip and keeps dust off the desk surface from getting into the mouse. On a slick desk the pointer will skip. Optical mice must use their special pad.

q: Is it worth getting a two-button mouse for the Macintosh?
a: Not for stock software. The Mac is designed around a single button, and no program expects a second one. Third-party multi-button mice exist, but they just emulate clicks with extra buttons. Stay with the Apple mouse unless you need the extra buttons.

q: Is the Amiga mouse compatible with the Atari ST?
a: Mostly yes. They use the same 9-pin connector and similar quadrature signals, so an Amiga mouse often works on an ST. Some people report slightly different tracking or button behavior, but it generally works fine.

q: Is the IBM Model M worth the money over a cheap clone keyboard?
a: Yes, if you type a lot. The Model M has buckling spring keys with a solid click and lasts for years. Cheap clones use mushy foam-and-foil switches that wear out. It's heavy, but you'll notice the difference in a day.

q: What are function keys on a PC keyboard for?
a: They're programmable keys that applications define. Typical examples are F1 for help and F10 for the menu bar. The original PC had 10 along the left side, while the enhanced keyboard has 12 across the top.

q: What does 'Caps Lock' versus 'Control' placement matter on keyboards?
a: On the original PC and AT boards, Control sits below Shift and Caps Lock is in a wasteful spot for editing. Unix users and Emacs fans prefer Control next to A, as on the Model M's rivals and Sun keyboards. Some utilities can swap them.

q: What does 'N-key rollover' mean?
a: It means the keyboard can register many keys held down at once without dropping or misreading any. Fast typists overlap keystrokes, and a board with poor rollover will lose letters. Most decent boards handle at least 2-key rollover, better ones handle more.

q: What does DPI mean for a mouse?
a: It means dots per inch, the number of counts the mouse reports for each inch you move it. Typical mice run around 200 DPI. Higher resolution makes the pointer move farther per inch of travel, which helps on high-res screens.

q: What does a 'quadrature' mouse mean?
a: Quadrature refers to the two signals, offset by a quarter cycle, produced by the mouse's sensors. By comparing which one changes first, the computer can tell which direction you moved. Amiga, Atari ST and bus mice all use it.

q: What does a keyboard 'Alt-numeric keypad' trick do in DOS?
a: Hold Alt, type a decimal ASCII code on the numeric keypad, then release Alt, and the character appears. For example, Alt-1-7-8 gives a graphics block character. It works with the number keys on the keypad only, with Num Lock on.

q: What does a keyboard's 'dead key' mean on European layouts?
a: A dead key puts an accent like ^ or ` on the screen without moving the cursor. The next letter you press gets the accent. It lets you type characters like é or ü on a European keyboard. Press the accent then space for the mark alone.

q: What is a ball mouse versus the Mac's ADB mouse?
a: The ADB mouse, introduced with the Mac SE and Mac II in 1987, uses the Apple Desktop Bus instead of the old 9-pin connector on the original Mac. It plugs into the keyboard or the ADB port and is generally interchangeable on new machines.

q: What is a good keyboard for programming?
a: One with a solid feel and a good layout. Many programmers like the Model M or the Northgate OmniKey, with Control next to A and a row of function keys on the left. The Northgate costs more, but it is very popular among serious typists.

q: What is a serial mouse versus a bus mouse on a PC?
a: A serial mouse plugs into a COM port and uses no extra card. A bus mouse, like Microsoft's, uses its own interface card and doesn't tie up a serial port. Bus mice need a free slot and an IRQ, usually IRQ 2 or 3.

q: What is a trackball and is it better than a mouse?
a: A trackball is like an upside-down mouse. You roll the ball with your fingers while the unit stays put. It's great where desk space is tight, and many find it easier on the wrist. Precision work takes some getting used to.

q: What is the 'enhanced' keyboard IBM introduced?
a: It's the 101-key layout from 1986 with 12 function keys across the top, a separate cursor keypad, and Control keys on both sides of the space bar. It works on newer ATs and PS/2s. Older XTs may not recognize some of its keys.

q: What is the Sun keyboard layout like for Unix users?
a: The Sun Type 4 puts Control next to A, with Escape in the top-left and function keys on the left side for the L-keys. Many Unix people prefer it for vi and Emacs. The extra Meta keys are on either side of the space bar.

q: What is the best way to keep a joystick from wearing out?
a: Don't slam it. Cheap sticks with microswitches handle abuse better than rubber-dome ones. Wipe off dust and don't eat over it. For heavy arcade games, a stick like the Wico Bat Handle is built to take a beating.

q: What is the difference between capacitive and mechanical keyboard switches?
a: Mechanical switches make contact with metal, while capacitive ones sense a change in capacitance when a key is pressed, with no contact. Capacitive boards, like the old IBM 3277 and Key Tronic types, tend to last a long time. Mechanical switches can get dirty.

q: What is the difference between optical and mechanical mice?
a: A mechanical mouse uses a rubber ball turning rollers. An optical mouse, like Mouse Systems', needs a special metal pad with a printed grid and senses the lines with reflected light. Optical ones have no ball to clog but you must use the pad.

q: What's the difference between a Logitech C7 and a Microsoft mouse?
a: Both are serial mice with similar hardware. The Logitech C7 has three buttons and works in Microsoft mode or Mouse Systems mode with a switch. Microsoft's has two buttons and fewer options. Logitech is usually a bit cheaper.

q: Which Apple II mouse card do I need?
a: The Apple Mouse Interface Card works in the Apple IIe and II+ slots, with MousePaint and other programs that support it. The IIc has a mouse port built in. Put the card in slot 4 unless the software says otherwise.

q: Which is better for flight sims, a joystick or the keyboard?
a: A joystick, no question. Keyboard control is all or nothing, so you can't make small corrections. Get an analog stick like the CH Products Mach I or the Gravis. Calibrate it in the game, since most PC sticks drift.

q: Which joystick is best for an Atari ST?
a: The Atari ST uses the same 9-pin connectors as the Amiga. The Competition Pro is a popular choice, with its microswitches and solid build. Quickshot sticks are cheaper but feel sloppy. Port 1 is also used for the mouse.

q: Why do some programs ignore my Num Lock setting?
a: Programs read the keyboard directly and ignore the BIOS flag, or the lock state isn't set at boot. You can turn on Num Lock at startup with a small utility in AUTOEXEC.BAT, or set it by modifying the byte at 0040:0017 using DEBUG.

q: Why does my Amiga mouse pointer jump around?
a: Usually the mouse ball rollers are dirty. Open it, clean the two small rollers with a cotton swab and a little alcohol, and wipe off the ball. If it still jumps, check that the plug is firmly in port 1 and not loose.

q: Why does my Commodore 64 keyboard type wrong characters?
a: Check the shift lock key and make sure you're in the right mode, since SHIFT with the Commodore key toggles upper/lowercase. If keys are actually dead, the keyboard contacts may be dirty, or the CIA chip could be bad.

q: Why does my PC joystick only work in one direction?
a: Likely it needs centering. PC sticks are analog and read pot resistance, so they vary. Run the game's calibration option and move the stick to each corner when asked. If it still fails, the pots may be dirty or worn.

q: Why does my keyboard beep at me when I type fast?
a: The keyboard buffer is full. The BIOS holds only about 15 keystrokes, and if the program isn't reading them quickly, it beeps and drops the rest. It happens during disk access or in slow programs. Just slow down or use a keyboard buffer utility.

q: Why does my mouse cursor freeze in Windows 2.x?
a: It could be an IRQ conflict. If the mouse is on COM1 and another card, like a modem, shares IRQ 4, the mouse will lock up. Move the modem to COM2 or set the mouse to another port. Check driver settings in SETUP.

q: Why won't my keyboard work after I plugged it in with the computer on?
a: The AT and XT keyboard ports are not designed for hot plugging. You can blow a fuse on the motherboard or damage the keyboard controller. Power off, plug in, and reboot. If it still fails, check the fuse and the keyboard cable.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Are there online games on GEnie?
a: Yes. Air Warrior is a multiplayer flight combat game, and there are others like Stellar Emperor and Federation. They cost extra beyond the base rates, so check which hourly price applies.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Can I get Usenet newsgroups through CompuServe or GEnie?
a: Not really. Neither one carries Usenet itself. They have their own forums with similar topics, so for real Usenet you will need a university or company account, or a UUCP site.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Can I get stock quotes online, and which service is best?
a: Yes. CompuServe and The Source both have delayed stock quotes, and CompuServe's stock and portfolio tools are the most complete. Prodigy has quotes with a small fee, and GEnie's financial area is more basic.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Can I send e-mail from CompuServe to someone on Usenet?
a: Yes, there is now a gateway to the Internet. In CompuServe Mail you address the message as >INTERNET:user@host, and it will go out. Replies come back in your CompuServe mailbox with your user ID.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Can I use Prodigy with my regular terminal program like Procomm?
a: No. Prodigy only works with its own front-end software, because it sends graphics, not plain ASCII text. So you can't capture sessions or run scripts the way you can on CompuServe.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Can I use a 9600 baud modem on any of these services?
a: Not generally. In the late eighties most of them are just 300, 1200, and 2400, though 9600 is starting to turn up on a few CompuServe nodes in big cities. Check with your local node before buying a modem.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Do I need a Hayes-compatible modem for these services?
a: It is not mandatory, but almost all terminal software assumes Hayes AT commands, such as ATDT for dialing. If you buy a modem that isn't Hayes-compatible, you may have to set it up by hand.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How can I cut down my CompuServe bill?
a: Use an offline reader like TAPCIS, stay out of the pricey services, download at 2400 instead of 300, and log on evenings or weekends. Also watch for extended-service charges in the menus.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How do I download a file from a CompuServe forum library?
a: Go to the forum's library with the DL section, browse or use the keyword search, then pick DOWNLOAD and the file name. Choose a protocol your terminal program supports, such as CIS B+ or XMODEM, and start the receive on your end.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How do I find a local access number for CompuServe?
a: Call CompuServe's customer service at their 800 number and ask for the nearest CompuServe Network node for your area code. You can also use the online listing at GO PHONES once you have a node that works.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How do I log on to CompuServe for the first time with my modem?
a: Set your terminal to 7 bits, even parity, 1 stop bit, dial your local CompuServe Packet Network number, and hit Control-C when you connect. At Host Name: type CIS, then enter your ID like 71234,567 and your password.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How do I see all the messages I haven't read on GEnie?
a: In a RoundTable bulletin board, use SET to choose categories and topics, then ask for new messages with the NEW command. Most people also do it with an offline reader to save connect time.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How do I sign up for GEnie?
a: Set your modem to 300 or 1200 baud, half duplex, dial a GEnie number, and type HHH after you connect. At the U#= prompt enter JOINGENIE and follow the questions. Have your credit card or checking account number ready.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How many e-mail messages can I send on Prodigy each month?
a: The basic flat fee covers about 30 messages a month. After that each additional message costs a quarter or so. People who write lots of mail get hit with extra charges, so check your plan.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: How safe is it to give my credit card number to CompuServe or GEnie?
a: It is about as safe as giving it to any company by phone. They are established services, and the number goes only to their billing. Just keep your password private and do not share it in a message.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Is CIM better than just using a terminal program?
a: It is easier for beginners, but costs the same connect time and is slower than a command line if you know the GO pages. Experienced users still prefer TAPCIS or a plain terminal with a script.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Is CompuServe worth it for someone with an IBM clone?
a: Yes, if you want help. The IBM forums and the vendor support sections often get you answers from the actual authors, and the file libraries are big. Just watch the hourly charges and use an offline reader.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Is Prodigy a real online service or just a toy?
a: It is real, and for the flat monthly fee it is easy to use, with news, shopping, and bulletin boards. The ads on every screen are annoying though, and you cannot download files or use your own terminal program.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Is The Source still around, or did it go away?
a: CompuServe bought The Source in 1989, and the accounts were moved over. If you were a Source user, CompuServe has been taking in the members. Check your mail for how to switch.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Is it better to join one big service or several small ones?
a: For most folks one main service plus a local BBS is plenty. CompuServe has the widest range, GEnie is cheap for evenings, and a local BBS costs nothing. More accounts just means more bills.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Is there good Amiga support on CompuServe?
a: Yes, the Amiga forums, which you reach with GO AMIGA, are busy. Commodore people post there, and the libraries have lots of public domain programs, including many from Fred Fish disks.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What are Prodigy's bulletin boards like?
a: They are busy and friendly, with topics like computers, pets, and money. You can't attach files to your posts, and the service keeps an eye on what you post, so rough talk can get you in trouble.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What baud rate should I use for CompuServe?
a: At 1200 baud you can read comfortably, and 2400 is better if your modem and local node support it. CompuServe's 300 baud rate is cheaper per hour but painfully slow for anything but mail.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What do I need to run Prodigy?
a: On a PC you need an IBM-compatible with at least 512K of RAM, a graphics display like CGA, EGA or VGA, and a 1200 or 2400 baud Hayes-compatible modem. The Prodigy starter kit has the software and a local access number.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What do the CompuServe user IDs with the comma mean?
a: The ID is two numbers split by a comma, like 76543,210. Early accounts started with 7 for the consumer group. The comma is part of the address, so for Internet mail you need to change it to a period.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What does 7E1 mean in my modem settings?
a: It means 7 data bits, even parity, and 1 stop bit. CompuServe uses it for the login. Many BBSes use 8N1, which is 8 bits, no parity, and 1 stop bit, and you need it for binary file transfers.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What does GO mean on CompuServe?
a: GO is how you jump straight to a service by its page name, like GO IBMNET or GO PCS. It beats walking through the menus, and it saves connect time, which is money.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What does connect time mean?
a: Connect time is the total time you are logged on to the service, billed by the minute or hour. Reading mail, downloading, and sitting idle all count, so it pays to log off when you are done.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is CIM on CompuServe?
a: CIM is the CompuServe Information Manager, a front-end program for the PC and Mac that came out in 1989. It gives you menus and icons in place of GO commands, and it handles downloads for you.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is TAPCIS and do I need it?
a: TAPCIS is a shareware program by Howard Benner that logs on, grabs your mail and forum messages, and logs off so you can read them offline. If you pay by the hour, it pays for itself in a month or two.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is The Source?
a: The Source is one of the oldest consumer online services, run out of McLean, Virginia. It offers e-mail, news, stock quotes, chat, and bulletin boards. It was a pricey service, and a bit text-heavy compared to newer ones.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is a RoundTable on GEnie?
a: A RoundTable is GEnie's name for a special interest area, much like a CompuServe forum. Each has a bulletin board, a software library, and a real-time conference room. The Apple II and IBM ones are very busy.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is a node on a packet network like Telenet or Tymnet?
a: A node is a local dial-in point that connects your call to a bigger packet network. It lets you reach a distant service like GEnie or CompuServe for a small hourly surcharge, without making a long-distance call.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is a sign-on kit for Prodigy?
a: It is a boxed set of software on floppy disks with instructions, sold at stores like Sears. It includes your first month and a starting ID. You install it on your hard disk, then dial a local number.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is the Apple II area like on GEnie?
a: It is one of the best places to find Apple II help, with a large software library, lots of active users, and some of the better-known developers. A8 and A2 RoundTable files are what many Apple people use.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is the CB Simulator on CompuServe?
a: CB is the real-time chat area, with numbered channels like on a citizens band radio. You pick a handle and talk with whoever is on the channel. It's popular in the evening, but the hourly charge adds up fast.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is the CompuServe B protocol?
a: CIS B is CompuServe's own file transfer protocol, which supports error checking and lets you resume or pick up where you left off. B Plus is the improved version. Many terminal programs support it, and XMODEM is the fallback.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is the CompuServe standard pricing plan?
a: The basic plan is a flat monthly fee, around eight dollars, that covers a core group of services like news, weather, and shopping. Forums and other premium services still cost by the hour.
