topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is the QuickLink or Aladdin kind of program for GEnie?
a: Aladdin is a GEnie offline reader that logs on, picks up your mail and RoundTable messages, and sends your replies. It works like TAPCIS does on CompuServe, and it is worth it for saving time.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: What is the best terminal program for dialing into these services?
a: On a PC, Procomm and Telix are favorites, and Qmodem is another good one. On a Mac, Red Ryder and MacTerminal are common. All can do XMODEM, and most do some CompuServe B protocol.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Which is better for a Mac user, CompuServe or GEnie?
a: CompuServe has the bigger Mac forums and the vendor support, with Apple people on board. GEnie is cheaper, and its Mac RoundTable is decent, so it comes down to whether support or price matters more.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Which is cheaper, CompuServe or GEnie?
a: GEnie, as long as you stay on evenings and weekends, where they charged about five dollars an hour at 300 or 1200 baud. CompuServe costs more per hour, but it has more users and more files.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Why do I get garbage characters when I connect to CompuServe?
a: Most likely your word format or baud rate does not match. Try 7 bits, even parity, 1 stop bit, then 8-N-1 only when you start a binary download. A noisy phone line can also cause it, so redial.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Why does CompuServe keep dropping me in the middle of a download?
a: Line noise or call waiting is the usual cause. Turn off call waiting with *70 before dialing, and if you can, use CIS B+ since it handles errors better than XMODEM when the line is bad.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Why does Prodigy have those ads at the bottom of the screen?
a: The ads are how Prodigy, owned by IBM and Sears, pays for the flat rate. They are sent along with each screen, and that is why the screens use a graphics system rather than plain text.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Why does it cost extra to use the CompuServe forums?
a: Forums are marked as extended services, so they are charged at the full hourly rate. The basic ones, like news and weather, are included in the flat fee and cost nothing extra.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Why does my GEnie text show doubled characters?
a: Your terminal program is set to half duplex, so it echoes what you type and GEnie echoes it back. Switch to full duplex. GEnie wants half duplex only for the initial HHH signup at the start.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Why is Prodigy unhappy about people sending lots of mail?
a: Prodigy sells itself on a flat monthly fee, and mail heavy users cost more than they pay. That's why the monthly limit on messages exists, and why they have been in an argument with members who mass mail.

topic: online services: CompuServe, GEnie, Prodigy, The Source
q: Why is The Source more expensive than CompuServe?
a: It started as a business-oriented service and priced itself that way, with higher hourly rates in prime time. CompuServe and GEnie went after home users with cheaper evening rates, and The Source never really matched them.

q: Can I give copies of shareware to my friends?
a: Yes, as long as you pass it along unmodified with all the original files and documentation. That's the whole idea of shareware. Just tell your friends they need to register if they keep using it.

q: Can I run shareware on CP/M?
a: Yes, there is a big library of public domain CP/M software. The SIG/M and CP/M User Group disks have hundreds of volumes. Programs like NSWP, WordStar-compatible editors, and Kermit are common.

q: Can I sell a disk of shareware programs?
a: Yes, many disk vendors do. You can charge a copying fee but not the price of the software, and you must make clear the buyer still has to register. Some authors ban sale of their program, so check the license.

q: Can I use Macintosh shareware on my Mac Plus?
a: Mostly yes, but check the documentation for system requirements, since some programs need System 6 or more RAM. Files usually come as StuffIt or .sit archives, so get StuffIt or the free UnStuffIt to unpack them.

q: Can shareware programs have viruses?
a: Yes, any file from a BBS could. There have been trojan horse programs, like a fake version of ARC and a hard disk wiper called EGABTR. Download from well-run boards that scan uploads, and check programs with something like VIRUSCAN or FLU_SHOT+ if you can.

q: How do I compile a program from source posted on Usenet?
a: Unpack the shar files with sh, read the README, and edit the Makefile for your system. Then type make. If you get errors it's usually a missing header or a system difference, so check the config options.

q: How do I download a file with XMODEM from a BBS?
a: Pick the file on the BBS, choose XMODEM when asked for a protocol, then start the receive command in your terminal program, such as Procomm or Telix. Give it a filename if prompted. Transfers at 2400 baud take a few minutes per 100K.

q: How do I find out which version of a shareware program is newest?
a: Check the version number in the program and the date on the files, then compare with what's on big BBSes or CompuServe's IBM forums. Registering usually gets you update notices from the author.

q: How do I get rid of the Stoned virus?
a: Boot from a clean, write-protected DOS floppy, then use a scanner like SCAN or a cleaning program to fix the boot sector. On a floppy, copy your files to a clean disk and reformat the infected one. Use FDISK /MBR only on later DOS versions.

q: How do I make a self-extracting archive?
a: With PKZIP, use ZIP2EXE filename.ZIP, which creates an EXE that unpacks itself when run. ARC users can use the older ARC utilities. Self-extractors are good for newcomers who don't have an unpacker.

q: How do I open a .SIT file on my Mac?
a: You need StuffIt, either Raymond Lau's shareware StuffIt or the free UnStuffIt program. Also, files often come in BinHex .hqx format, so you must convert those with BinHex 4.0 or StuffIt first.

q: How do I send my registration fee to a shareware author?
a: Look for the REGISTER.DOC or ORDER.FRM file in the archive. Print the form, fill it in, and mail it with a check or money order to the address listed. Some authors also take credit cards by phone.

q: How do I unpack a file ending in .ARC on my PC?
a: You need the ARC program from System Enhancement Associates, or the shareware PKXARC. Type PKXARC filename.ARC and it extracts everything to the current directory. PKARC makes new archives.

q: How much should shareware cost?
a: Most programs ask $10 to $50, and word processors or databases may go to $75 or more. Some authors have a suggested donation, so read the docs. Registered users often get extras that make the price worthwhile.

q: Is Sidekick public domain?
a: No. Sidekick is a commercial product from Borland. If you want a free pop-up utility, try shareware like Metz Software's pop-ups or other TSR notepads available on BBSes.

q: Is freeware the same as public domain?
a: No. Freeware is free to use but the author keeps the copyright and may limit what you can do, like selling it or changing it. Public domain has no such restrictions.

q: Is it legal to copy a shareware disk if the author said 'copy freely'?
a: Yes, the license in the docs gives you that right. Just keep the files intact and don't charge for the software. If you keep using it past the trial period, you're expected to register.

q: Is it worth paying the shareware fee if I already have the program working?
a: Yes, if you use it regularly. Registration usually gets you the latest version, a printed manual, and support, and it keeps the author writing. Most fees are $20 to $40, which is cheap next to commercial packages.

q: Is the Amiga PD library really any good?
a: Yes. Fred Fish disks and the Amicus disks have good utilities, games, and demos. Some stuff is rough, but there's lots of quality like PowerPacker, Virus checkers, and many editors. Join a user group for the cheapest copies.

q: What are the Fred Fish disks?
a: Fred Fish collects Amiga public domain and freely distributable programs and sells them on numbered disks. There are over 300 now. Each one has source code for many programs, and user groups copy them cheaply.

q: What are the best shareware games for the PC?
a: Commander Keen from Apogee and id is great fun, as is Scorched Earth for later, but for 1990 try Kroz, Jill of the Jungle, and Hugo. Also, NetHack and Rogue-likes are free. Many use EGA graphics.

q: What does .ZIP mean and why is everybody switching to it?
a: ZIP is Phil Katz's PKZIP archive format. It compresses better and faster than ARC, and PKZIP 1.10 is the standard on most BBSes now. Use PKUNZIP filename.ZIP to extract.

q: What does PC-File do?
a: PC-File is a shareware database program by Jim Button. It's easy to learn, handles mailing lists and inventories nicely, and is cheap to register. Newer versions come as PC-File+ with more features.

q: What does PKZIP -v do?
a: It lists the contents of a ZIP file, showing file names, sizes, compression ratios, and dates, without extracting anything. Run PKUNZIP -v filename.ZIP. It's handy for seeing what's in an archive before you unpack it.

q: What is 'user-supported software'?
a: It's another term for shareware, used by Jim Button and others. The author lets you try the program for free and asks for a voluntary payment if you like it. Some say 'honor system software' as well.

q: What is BinHex?
a: BinHex is a way to turn Macintosh files into plain text so they can travel through mail and Usenet. The file ends in .hqx. Decode it with BinHex 4.0 or StuffIt to get the original file back.

q: What is Kroz?
a: Kroz is a shareware game by Scott Miller of Apogee, a maze and treasure game using text graphics. The first episode is free and you can order further episodes by registering. It runs even on monochrome systems.

q: What is LHARC?
a: LHARC is a compression utility by Haruyasu Yoshizaki that makes .LZH files. It often compresses a little better than PKZIP, though it is slower. Many Amiga and Atari ST files use it, and it's free.

q: What is NetHack?
a: NetHack is a free dungeon-exploring game descended from Hack and Rogue, with source code you can compile on Unix, Amiga, Atari ST, and PCs. It's constantly updated by volunteers. Expect to die a lot.

q: What is PC-Write and is it any good?
a: PC-Write is a shareware word processor by Bob Wallace of Quicksoft. It's fast, has a good editor and spell checker, and registration is $75. Many people use it instead of WordPerfect.

q: What is a nagware screen?
a: It's the reminder that pops up when you start or exit a shareware program, asking you to register. Registering usually removes it. Some versions also delay startup for a few seconds to encourage you.

q: What is a shar file?
a: A shar, or shell archive, is a text file with Unix shell commands that recreate the files when you run it with sh. It's the common way to post source code to Usenet. Always read it before you run it.

q: What is an ASP and why does it matter?
a: ASP is the Association of Shareware Professionals, formed in 1987. Members agree to a code of ethics and offer a way to settle disputes with users. A program from an ASP member is a good sign.

q: What is the GNU project?
a: GNU is Richard Stallman's Free Software Foundation project to build a free Unix-like system. Programs like GNU Emacs and GCC are already available and widely used. The GNU General Public License lets you copy and modify them but requires you to share your changes.

q: What is the best free terminal program for the PC?
a: Procomm is popular and the shareware version is solid, with Telix and Qmodem close behind. All support Zmodem and have dialing directories. Try each one and see which feels best.

q: What is the best shareware anti-virus program for DOS?
a: VIRUSCAN from McAfee Associates is the one most people use. It scans for known viruses like Brain, Stoned, and Jerusalem. Update often because new viruses come out regularly, and use FLU_SHOT+ to watch for changes.

q: What is the difference between shareware and public domain software?
a: Public domain means the author gave up all rights, so you can do anything with it. Shareware is still copyrighted. You can copy it and try it freely, but if you keep using it you're expected to send the author the registration fee.

q: What is uuencode and how do I decode a file?
a: Uuencode turns binary files into text so they can be posted on Usenet. Save the articles in order, strip the headers, and run uudecode filename on Unix. On a PC use UUDECODE.EXE or similar.

q: Where can I find good public domain software for my Atari ST?
a: Check the ST section on GEnie or CompuServe, and local ST user groups. The Fred Fish disks are for the Amiga, but the ST has similar PD libraries from groups like Public Domain Software Library. Many BBSes carry them too.

q: Where do I find programs posted on Usenet?
a: Look in comp.sources.misc, comp.sources.unix, and comp.binaries.ibm.pc. The sources groups are moderated and have source code, and binaries groups have uuencoded executables. Watch for multi-part postings.

q: Which is better for a PC BBS, PCBoard or Wildcat?
a: Both are solid shareware. PCBoard has a bigger user base and lots of add-ons, while Wildcat is easier to set up. For a first board, I'd try Wildcat. If you expect many users and doors, go with PCBoard.

q: Which is the best shareware spreadsheet for the PC?
a: As-Easy-As by TRIUS is the one to try. It reads and writes Lotus 1-2-3 files and has most of the commands. Registration is $50 or so. It's a solid replacement if you can't afford Lotus.

q: Who invented shareware?
a: The idea grew from Andrew Fluegelman's PC-Talk, which he called Freeware, and Jim Button's PC-File, both in 1982. Bob Wallace then used the name shareware for PC-Write. Fluegelman died in 1985.

q: Why do some shareware programs have a time limit?
a: Authors do it to encourage people to register instead of using the program forever for free. Others disable features like saving or printing in the unregistered version. Registering gets you a full version or a key.

q: Why does PKUNZIP say 'Error in ZIP file'?
a: Usually the file was damaged in the download or is truncated. Try downloading it again, preferably using Zmodem. Use PKUNZIP -t to test the archive before extracting.

q: Why does my downloaded program say 'Bad command or file name'?
a: Either you aren't in the right directory, the file isn't an EXE, COM, or BAT, or it's not in your PATH. If it's still an archive you must extract it first. Type DIR to see the files.

q: Can I open a store that rents software?
a: Not anymore. A law passed in late 1990 forbids renting out commercial software without the copyright holder's permission. Before that, rental shops were common, mostly for games, and publishers complained that renters just copied the disks.

q: Can I put my one copy on both my work and home computer?
a: Strictly, most licenses cover one machine, and the law only gives you a backup. Some publishers allow home and office if only one is used at a time, so read the license agreement in the box or call the vendor.

q: Can I see copy protection on a floppy by looking at it?
a: Sometimes. A few publishers burn a tiny hole in the media with a laser, which you can see as a pinprick when you hold the disk up to the light. The program then checks that this spot reads bad.

q: Can I trust the SPA's numbers on how much piracy costs?
a: Take them with salt. They claim that for each legitimate copy sold, at least one is copied illegally, and they count every copy as a lost sale. Plenty of copied software would never have been bought at full price.

q: Can a BBS sysop really get in trouble for pirated programs on the board?
a: Yes. If copyrighted commercial programs sit on the board and people download them, the sysop can be held liable. The SPA has threatened sysops, and in some cases police have seized the computer and modems.

q: Can a dongle on the parallel port mess up my printer?
a: Sometimes. Cheap keys can garble data or break handshaking, especially if you stack two of them. Put the key closest to the computer, try a shorter cable, and ask the vendor for a newer revision if it keeps happening.

q: Did Lotus ever take the copy protection off 1-2-3?
a: Yes, Lotus dropped it in 1986 after a lot of complaints from customers. You can now install the 2.x releases straight to a hard disk without hunting for the key disk every time you start it.

q: Do I have to send in the registration card?
a: Not to own the software legally, since your receipt is your proof. But sending it in gets you on the mailing list for upgrades and bug fixes, and some publishers won't give phone support without it.

q: Does Macintosh software use copy protection much?
a: Less than it used to. Many publishers dropped it by the late eighties, since hard disks are common and customers complained a lot. Some programs still use a key disk or a serial number that gets checked at startup.

q: How can I check my disks for viruses?
a: On a PC, run a scanner such as McAfee's SCAN or use Flu-Shot to watch for suspicious writes. Mac owners can get Disinfectant, which is free. Also keep write protect tabs on any disk you don't need to write to.

q: How do I replace a protected disk that went bad?
a: Call the publisher and tell them. Many will replace a damaged original if you mail back the bad disk with a handling fee, often around ten to twenty dollars. Keep your receipt or registration card handy.

q: How do I write protect a floppy?
a: On a 5.25 inch disk, cover the square notch on the edge with a sticker or tape. On a 3.5 inch disk, slide the little plastic tab so the hole is open. Then the drive can't write on it.

q: How long does it take to download a 360K disk at 2400 baud?
a: At 2400 baud you get about 240 characters per second, so 360K takes around 25 minutes if it isn't compressed. Zipped, it might be half that. At 1200 baud, double all of it.

q: Is WordPerfect copy protected?
a: No, WordPerfect 4.2 and 5.0 are not copy protected, so you can copy the files to your hard drive and use them normally. The company makes its money on support, and the toll-free phone line is a big reason people buy it.

q: Is a shrink-wrap license binding?
a: That's the agreement printed on the package saying that opening the wrapper means you accept its terms. Whether a court would enforce it is unsettled, and the Vault versus Quaid decision went against a law that tried to back it up.

q: Is it legal to make a backup copy of software I bought?
a: In the US, section 117 of the copyright law lets you make an archival copy of a program you own, for backup only. It doesn't cover handing copies to friends, and the backup should go with the original if you sell it.

q: Is it worth registering shareware if the program works fine anyway?
a: Yes, since registering usually gets you a printed manual, the latest version and support. It also keeps the author in business. Most authors of programs like PC-Write and PC-File depend on those checks from people who tried it.

q: Is pirated software really more likely to have a virus?
a: Yes. Disks swapped between friends and files from pirate boards are how Brain, Stoned and Jerusalem spread around. If you only use sealed originals and your own write protected backups, your risk is a lot lower.

q: What are weak bits in copy protection?
a: A weak bit is a spot on the disk written so that it reads back differently each time. The program reads it several times and expects inconsistent results. A bit-for-bit copy gives the same result every time, so the check fails.

q: What do half tracks have to do with Apple II copy protection?
a: Apple II drives can move the head in half-track steps. Some programs write data between the normal tracks, and standard copy programs only see the whole tracks, so they miss it. A nibble copier with the right parameters can follow it.

q: What does an Action Replay cartridge do on the Commodore 64?
a: Datel's Action Replay plugs into the expansion port and has a freeze button. Press it and it saves whatever is in memory to disk or tape, which also gives you a fast loading backup of your own games.

q: What does cracked mean when people talk about a program on a BBS?
a: A cracked program has had its protection check patched out so it runs without the original disk or key. The cracker often adds a title screen with a group name, and these copies are what travel around the boards.

q: What does it mean when a program is copy protected?
a: It means the disk is made so ordinary commands like COPY or DISKCOPY won't give you a working duplicate. The publisher puts odd formatting or damaged spots on the floppy that the program checks for at startup.

q: What does the ad mean when it says now unprotected?
a: It means the publisher took out the copy protection in that version. You can copy it to your hard disk and make backups with plain DOS commands. The license still applies, so it's not a license to give it to your friends.

q: What exactly is shareware?
a: It's copyrighted software the author lets you copy and pass around so you can try it first. If you keep using it, you're asked to send money to the author. PC-Write, PC-File and ProComm are well-known examples.

q: What if my hard drive dies before I uninstall a protected program?
a: Run the vendor's uninstall before reformatting or moving it. If the drive already crashed, call the publisher and send in your original disk, since most will give you another install if you can show you own the program.

q: What is Copy II PC?
a: It's a utility from Central Point Software that copies many protected IBM PC floppies. They also sell the Option Board, a card that plugs into your PC and reads disk formats the regular controller can't handle.

q: What is Lenslok?
a: It's a plastic gadget with two small prisms that came packed with some ZX Spectrum games, such as Elite. The game shows scrambled bars on screen, and you read a two letter code through the lens to start playing.

q: What is a boot block virus on the Amiga?
a: It's code hiding in the first two sectors of a floppy. When you boot with that disk, it copies itself into memory and then writes itself onto every disk you insert. The SCA virus from 1987 is the famous one.

q: What is a copy party?
a: It's a get-together where users bring computers and disks and swap or duplicate each other's software, popular among Apple II and Commodore owners. It's piracy, no matter how friendly it feels, and the SPA says so too.

q: What is a dongle?
a: It's a little hardware key that plugs into your parallel or serial port. The program looks for it at startup and refuses to run without it. You see them on expensive packages like CAD software, mostly Rainbow's Sentinel or Aladdin's HASP.

q: What is a fast loader for the C64?
a: It's a cartridge or program that replaces the very slow 1541 disk routines with quicker ones. Epyx FastLoad is a popular cartridge and loads some programs five to ten times faster, although certain protected games won't work with it.

q: What is a key disk?
a: It's the original floppy you must put in drive A at startup to prove you own the program, even when everything else is installed on your hard drive. Lotus 1-2-3 used one for a while.

q: What is a nibble copier?
a: On the Apple II it's a copy program like Locksmith or Copy II Plus that reads the disk as raw nibbles instead of normal sectors. That lets it duplicate disks with nonstandard formatting that the regular DOS COPYA can't handle.

q: What is a pirate BBS?
a: It's a bulletin board where users trade cracked commercial programs. Most use upload and download ratios, such as one upload for every ten downloads, so people keep adding new software. Sysops running them are exactly who the SPA looks for.

q: What is a site license?
a: It's an agreement where a company or school pays for the right to use a program on a set number of machines, or all machines at one location. It usually costs much less per seat than buying boxed copies one at a time.

q: What is the SPA?
a: The Software Publishers Association is a trade group of software companies, based in Washington DC. They run anti-piracy campaigns and, from about 1988, have gone after companies and bulletin boards that use or distribute unlicensed copies.

q: What was the Vault versus Quaid court case about?
a: Vault sold the Prolok protection, and Quaid Software sold RamKey, which could copy Prolok disks. In 1988 the Fifth Circuit ruled that Louisiana's law backing shrink-wrap license restrictions was overridden by federal copyright law, so Quaid won.

q: What's the difference between freeware, public domain and shareware?
a: Public domain means no copyright at all, so anyone can do anything with it. Freeware is still copyrighted, but free to use. Shareware is copyrighted and free to try, but you're expected to pay if you keep it.

q: Which is better for the Apple II, Copy II Plus or Locksmith?
a: Both handle most titles. Copy II Plus is the more popular, and Central Point keeps releasing new versions with updated parameter lists for specific programs. Locksmith has a good name too, so whichever one has the newest version for the titles you own.

q: Why can't I copy my Amiga game with the Workbench DiskCopy?
a: Many Amiga games boot from the boot block and use custom track layouts instead of AmigaDOS. Workbench DiskCopy only handles standard tracks, so you need something like X-Copy, which can read nonstandard formats.

q: Why do all the files on pirate boards end in .ZIP?
a: PKZIP by Phil Katz packs many files into one archive and usually shrinks them by around half. That saves download time at 1200 or 2400 baud. It replaced the older ARC format, which many boards also use.

q: Why do games get more copy protection than business software?
a: Business buyers want to install on a hard disk and they complained loudly, so most major business packages dropped protection by about 1987. Games get swapped among friends, so the publishers worry more about them and keep it.

q: Why do some games ask me to type a word from the manual?
a: That's manual lookup protection. The game asks for something like the fourth word on line 6 of page 22, and a plain disk copy won't help you without the book. Photocopying a whole manual is a nuisance, which is the idea.

q: Why does my drive make a loud grinding noise when some games start?
a: The program is moving the head to a track beyond the normal range, or slamming it back to track zero, to test for its protection. It's ugly but usually harmless, though it's hard on an old drive if it happens a lot.

q: Why does my protected game work on my XT but not on my AT?
a: A 1.2MB drive in an AT spins at 360 rpm, while an XT's 360K drive runs at 300, and it writes narrower tracks. Protection schemes that depend on exact timing or format can fail with that drive, so you may need a second 360K drive.

q: Why doesn't Borland copy protect Turbo Pascal?
a: Borland sells under what they call a no-nonsense license: treat the software like a book. One person can use it at a time, you can move it between machines, but you can't have two people using it at once. That keeps the price low too.

q: Why won't DISKCOPY make a working copy of my game disk?
a: DISKCOPY only reproduces standard sectors in the normal DOS format. Protected disks hide nonstandard tracks or deliberately bad sectors that it skips, so the copy loads but the program notices the missing pieces and quits.

q: Will copy protected programs run from my hard drive?
a: Many come with an install program that puts one copy on your hard disk and counts how many installs you've made. Others still want the original in drive A. Don't just copy the files by hand, because it won't work.

q: Are the Microsoft Press books better than the third-party ones?
a: They're accurate and complete, and the Programmer's Guides and Encyclopedia are reliable, but they can be dry. Third-party books are often easier to read. For reference on Microsoft products, I'd pick Microsoft Press.

q: Are the O'Reilly Nutshell books any good?
a: Yes, they're compact references for Unix tools, like the Nutshell handbooks for sed and awk, and for X Window System. They're not tutorials, but they're a better buy than the vendor manuals.

q: Can I legally scan or post a magazine article on the net?
a: Not without permission. The copyright belongs to the publisher or author, and posting the whole text is infringement. A short quote with credit is usually fine, and you can also post a summary and the issue reference.

q: Can I still get back issues of Byte from 1984?
a: Call BYTE's back-issue desk in Peterborough, New Hampshire, though some issues sell out. Libraries often keep bound volumes, and used bookstores or other readers on the net might sell them. Check the ad pages in the latest issue for the address.

q: Can I type in a program from Compute! on a different computer?
a: Usually not directly. BASIC dialects differ, so PEEK, POKE, graphics and sound commands will break on another machine. Simple programs may port with some changes, but machine-language DATA is specific to the CPU.

q: How can a library help me find computer books and magazines?
a: Ask for the Computer Literature Index or the Business Periodicals Index to look up articles by subject. If your library lacks an issue, interlibrary loan can get a copy. University libraries usually carry more technical journals.

q: How do I find out which magazine issue reviewed a product?
a: Check the annual index published in the December issue of many magazines, or look in the Computer Literature Index at a library. Some magazines also publish a yearly index you can order by mail.

q: How do I learn Turbo Pascal quickly?
a: Read the Turbo Pascal manual's tutorial, then get Tom Swan's Mastering Turbo Pascal. Type in small programs and use the built-in editor and compiler. The compile speed is so fast that experimenting is easy.

q: Is BYTE still worth reading now that it's all 80386 stuff?
a: Yes, BYTE is still the best for technical depth. It covers the Mac, Amiga, Unix and the PC, and the articles are long enough to teach you something. Steve Ciarcia's Circuit Cellar column is great if you like building hardware.

q: Is Computer Gaming World worth reading for adventure game fans?
a: Yes, it has in-depth reviews, strategy tips and news on titles like Ultima, Wizardry and Sierra's games. It's more serious than most game magazines. Scorpia's adventure column is good if you're stuck.

q: Is The C Programming Language by Kernighan and Ritchie good for a beginner?
a: It's the definitive book, but terse. If you've never programmed, start with something gentler like Kelley and Pohl's A Book on C, then use K&R as your reference. The second edition for ANSI C came out in 1988, so get that one.

q: Is Turbo C or Microsoft C better, according to the magazines?
a: Reviews tend to say Turbo C is faster to compile and easier to use, while Microsoft C usually produces better optimized code and has CodeView for debugging. Beginners like Turbo C, and professionals often use Microsoft C.

q: Is Van Wolverton's Running MS-DOS worth getting?
a: Yes, it's one of the clearest DOS books around. It covers batch files, ANSI.SYS, CONFIG.SYS, and more, and each edition follows the DOS version. Get the edition matching your DOS version, 3.3 or 4.0.

q: Is it a good idea to buy a used computer book from the 1970s?
a: For theory, like Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming, sure. For anything about specific machines or software, probably not, since the information is dated. Check the copyright page and avoid anything older than about 1980 for PC topics.

q: Is it safe to buy hardware from the ads in a magazine?
a: Mostly, if you use a credit card and check the seller's warranty, return policy and restocking fee. Look for an established company with a street address. Avoid anything that sounds too cheap, and be wary of vendors who add big shipping fees.

q: Is it worth getting a subscription to Compute! for my Commodore 64?
a: If you still use the 64, yes. Compute! and Compute!'s Gazette have type-in programs and games, and the magazines print checksum programs like The Automatic Proofreader so you can catch typos. They have more 64 content than most other magazines now.

q: Is the Mac Bible worth the money?
a: If you're new to the Mac, yes. It covers the Finder, System files, fonts and many programs with plenty of tips, and it's an easy read. Experienced users may find it basic, but it's a solid desk reference.

q: Is the Waite Group's Microsoft C Bible any good?
a: Yes, it's a handy function reference for Microsoft C with examples and notes on portability and compatibility. Use it with the compiler manuals. It doesn't teach C, so you'll want a tutorial book first.

q: Should I buy Inside Macintosh for programming?
a: If you'll write Mac programs, you can't do without it. It's several volumes now, with Volume V covering the Mac II, and it's dense reading. Beginners should start with Kernighan and Ritchie-style tutorials like Dave Mark's Macintosh Programming books before diving in.

q: Should I buy the manual or a third-party book for WordPerfect 5.0?
a: WordPerfect's manual is OK for basics but poor on tips. A third-party book like Alan Simpson's or Mastering WordPerfect from Sybex is easier to follow. Keep the reference card from WordPerfect next to your keyboard.

q: What are Abacus Software books?
a: Abacus publishes books and software for Atari ST, Amiga, and Commodore machines. Their Internals and Tricks & Tips books give detailed hardware and programming info. They're good value if you own one of those machines.

q: What does 'Norton SI 14.2' mean in a review?
a: It's the Norton System Information index, comparing the CPU speed with a 4.77 MHz IBM PC/XT set at 1.0. So 14.2 means the machine is about fourteen times faster at that test. It doesn't measure disk or video speed.

q: What does 'Part 1 of 3' mean in a Usenet posting of a magazine article?
a: The article was too long for one posting, so it was split into parts. Collect all parts and join them in order, removing the headers. Some groups ask people to post only short quotes because of copyright.

q: What does 'RTFM' mean and why does everyone say it?
a: It means Read The Fine Manual, though people sometimes use a stronger word than Fine. It's the standard reply when someone asks a question that the manual answers directly. Check the index before posting.

q: What does 'beta' mean in a magazine preview of software?
a: It means the program is still being tested and isn't finished, so bugs and missing features are likely. Reviewers often say a beta copy was used. Wait for the final release review before buying.

q: What does 'type-in program' mean in a magazine?
a: It means the magazine prints the full source code, usually BASIC or machine-code DATA statements, and you type it in yourself. Most come with checksums so you can find typing errors. Save to disk often, because one wrong digit can crash the machine.

q: What does the 'Jerry Pournelle' column in BYTE do?
a: Chaos Manor is Pournelle's monthly diary of what he's using, from computers to software, as he sets up his home office. It's opinionated and chatty rather than a formal review, but many readers enjoy it.

q: What does the Peter Norton Programmer's Guide to the IBM PC actually cover?
a: It covers the PC's hardware and the BIOS and DOS interrupts, memory layout, video modes and disk structure. It's a solid first reference if you want to write assembly or understand the machine. It stops short of being a full interrupt list.

q: What is Computer Shopper?
a: A huge monthly tabloid, often well over 600 pages, packed with ads for clones, drives, memory chips and software from mail-order dealers. It also has columns and reviews. It's best for comparing prices before you buy.

q: What is Dr. Dobb's Journal good for these days?
a: DDJ is for programmers: source listings, algorithms, and C, Forth and assembly articles. It started with Tiny BASIC and the CP/M crowd. If you want code to read and type in, it's one of the best things on the newsstand.

q: What is Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming and should I read it?
a: It's a multi-volume set on algorithms: Fundamental Algorithms, Seminumerical Algorithms, and Sorting and Searching. It's heavy on math, but it's the classic. Get it for reference, and read it slowly if you're serious about programming.

q: What is MacUser's focus compared to Macworld?
a: Macworld is the older, more general magazine with big feature stories. MacUser is livelier and more critical, with lots of product comparisons and rated reviews using mice ratings. Many Mac users subscribe to both.

q: What is a 'Sams book' and are they reliable?
a: Howard W. Sams publishes hands-on guides and technical references like the Waite Group titles. They are mostly reliable, and I find the hardware repair and programming manuals useful. Check the date and edition, since some are outdated.

q: What is a 'shareware' magazine disk, and is it safe?
a: Many magazines now offer disks with shareware and public domain programs. Usually they're checked for viruses and bugs, but run a scanner anyway. If you keep using a program, register it with the author.

q: What is the best book for learning Unix?
a: The UNIX System by Stephen Bourne, or The UNIX Programming Environment by Kernighan and Pike. For a gentler start, try Unix for People or Learning the vi Editor from O'Reilly. Practice on a real system as you read.

q: What is the difference between Dr. Dobb's and Micro Cornucopia?
a: Dr. Dobb's is larger and covers many systems. Micro Cornucopia is a small magazine for hobbyists, especially Kaypro and other CP/M users, with hardware hacks and plenty of reader letters. It's friendlier and cheaper.

q: What is the difference between InfoWorld and PC Week?
a: Both are weekly newspapers about the business PC market. PC Week is aimed at corporate buyers and managers and gets news first, while InfoWorld has more reviews and opinions, like Robert X. Cringely's column. Both are free to qualified readers.

q: What is the difference between a magazine review and a lab test?
a: A review is one writer's opinion after using the product, while a lab test runs the same set of benchmarks on a group of products. Labs are better for comparing speed, and reviews are better for ease of use and quirks.

q: What's a good book for someone buying their first PC?
a: Try Peter Norton's Inside the IBM PC for the machine, or something like Running MS-DOS by Van Wolverton for DOS. Also read a couple of magazines before buying. Know what you want to do first, and then pick hardware.

q: What's the best magazine for Atari ST users?
a: ST-Log and Antic's Atari ST coverage were good, and Atari Explorer is a newer one. Check ST Informer too, a tabloid with news. For programming, the Atari ST Internals book from Abacus is very helpful.

q: Where can I find a list of all the DOS interrupts and BIOS calls?
a: Get Ralf Brown's interrupt list if you can find it on a BBS, or buy Microsoft's MS-DOS Encyclopedia. The Norton guide and the Waite Group's books cover the common INT 10h, INT 13h and INT 21h calls.

q: Which book explains how to write device drivers for DOS?
a: Look at Writing MS-DOS Device Drivers by Robert Lai, or the technical reference sections of the MS-DOS Encyclopedia. Drivers are loaded from CONFIG.SYS with DEVICE=, so you'll need to know the header and strategy/interrupt routines.

q: Which is better for an IBM PC owner, PC Magazine or PC World?
a: PC Magazine is thicker and heavier on utilities, reviews and lab benchmarks, and Jim Seymour and John Dvorak are worth reading. PC World is a bit friendlier for newer users. If you program or manage machines, get PC Magazine.

q: Which is the best book for learning assembly language on the 8086?
a: Try Peter Abel's IBM PC Assembly Language and Programming, or Leo Scanlon's 8086/8088 Assembly Language Programming. Both teach with DEBUG and MASM examples. Intel's own 8086 manual is the reference once you get going.

q: Which magazine covers OS/2 well?
a: PC Magazine, PC Week and InfoWorld cover OS/2 regularly, and BYTE has technical pieces. Version 1.1 added Presentation Manager in late 1988. The Microsoft OS/2 Programmer's Reference is the key book for developers.

q: Which magazine is best for Amiga owners?
a: AmigaWorld is the glossy general one, and Amazing Computing has more technical and programming content. Info magazine is also good. For programming, the Amiga ROM Kernel Manuals from Commodore are what you need.

q: Why are computer magazines so full of ads?
a: Ads pay for most of the magazine, so a monthly issue like PC World can be over 400 pages with half ads. The ads are useful for mail-order prices, though. Compare vendors in Computer Shopper to find the best deals.

q: Why are there so many different editions of the Norton Utilities books?
a: The books follow versions of the software and DOS. Newer editions cover new features such as the Norton Utilities 4.5 and Advanced Edition. Match the book to the version you own so the commands and screens agree.

q: Why do the magazine benchmarks show different speeds for the same 286 machine?
a: Labs use different tests. Some run Norton SI, which mostly measures CPU speed relative to the original PC, others use real application timings. Wait states, cache and disk controllers also change the numbers, so compare tests from the same magazine.

q: Why does my type-in checksum not match the magazine's?
a: You've mistyped a line. Look at the line number the checksum program flagged and compare each number carefully. Also check that you used the right version of the checker for your machine and magazine issue.

q: Can I run Emacs in its own X window?
a: Yes, in GNU Emacs 18 you can use the emacstool or xterm-based setup, and with the X patches you can start emacs -d host:0 to get a window of its own, depending on the patch level you have.

q: Can I run X on a PC with an 80386?
a: Yes, but you need Unix on it, such as SCO Xenix or Interactive 386/ix with X11, or a version of Minix or 386BSD-like system if you can find one. 4MB of RAM is the minimum, and 8MB is much better.

q: Can I run X over a serial line or modem?
a: Not very well. X expects Ethernet speed, and at 9600 baud even a basic xterm is painful. Some people run it over SLIP at 19.2k for a few simple clients, but it's slow.

q: Can I use X to log in to a remote machine from an X terminal?
a: Yes. Many X terminals can use XDMCP to ask a host running xdm for a login screen, or you can configure a telnet window to start an xterm on the terminal itself.

q: Can two people share an X display?
a: Not easily, but you can use xhost to let a coworker's client open windows on your screen. For a true shared view, you would need something beyond plain X; the standard doesn't have that.

q: How can I change the background color of the root window?
a: Use xsetroot, for example xsetroot -solid steelblue. You can also use -gray, or -bitmap with a bitmap file for a pattern. Put it in your .xinitrc to make it stick.

q: How can I tell what X server and version I am running?
a: Run xdpyinfo. It shows the vendor string, the release number, screen size, depth, visuals, and extensions. xdpyinfo is part of the standard MIT distribution from X11R3 on.

q: How do I compile X11 from source on my Sun?
a: Edit mit/config/site.def and your machine's .macros file, then run make World from the top directory. It uses imake to build the Makefiles. Expect it to take several hours and plenty of disk space, around 100MB.

q: How do I configure the twm menus?
a: Edit .twmrc in your home directory. You define menus with a Menu block, with entries and functions like f.exec for running programs. Copy system.twmrc as your starting point.

q: How do I cut and paste between xterm windows?
a: Hold the left button and drag to select text, then click the middle button in another xterm to paste it at the cursor. The selection gets copied just by highlighting it, no menu needed.

q: How do I find the keycode of a key?
a: Run xev in a window and press the key. It prints the keycode and keysym in the output for each event. Then you can use that with xmodmap.

q: How do I find the name of a font to use in xterm?
a: Run xlsfonts to list what the server has, and xfontsel if you have X11R5 style tools. Then use xterm -fn with the name, like -fn 9x15 or -fn fixed. xfd will show you what a font looks like.

q: How do I get a scrollbar in xterm?
a: Start it with xterm -sb, or put XTerm*scrollBar: true in your .Xdefaults. You can set the saved lines with -sl, for example xterm -sb -sl 500.

q: How do I get a second xterm on another machine displayed on my screen?
a: Set the DISPLAY variable on the remote machine to yourhost:0, like setenv DISPLAY myhost:0, then run xterm. You'll also need to allow the remote host with xhost +remotehost on your own machine.

q: How do I iconify a window in twm?
a: Click the little dot on the left of the title bar. Click the icon to bring it back. You can also use the twm root menu with the left or middle mouse button on the background.

q: How do I print an X window?
a: Dump it with xwd, then pipe it through xpr to produce output for your printer. For a PostScript printer use xpr -device ps. Something like xwd | xpr -device ps | lpr works.

q: How do I set the size and position of a window when I start it?
a: Use the -geometry option, like xterm -geometry 80x24+100+50. That means 80 columns by 24 lines, 100 pixels from the left and 50 from the top. A minus sign measures from the right or bottom.

q: How do I start X on my Sun workstation?
a: Type xinit or startx if your site has a script for it. On Suns running OpenWindows or MIT X11 you usually start the server, then an xterm, then a window manager like twm from your .xinitrc.

q: How do I take a screenshot in X?
a: Use xwd to dump a window to a file, such as xwd > shot.xwd and then click the window. View it with xwud, or convert it to PostScript or a printer format with xpr.

q: How much memory do I need to run X comfortably?
a: Plan on 8MB for a workstation running a window manager and a few xterms. 4MB works but swaps a lot. Color servers and big clients like emacs under X eat more.

q: Is X the same thing as Sunview or NeWS?
a: No. SunView and NeWS are Sun's own window systems. X is a network protocol from MIT that works across vendors. Sun is now pushing X11 with OpenWindows, which can even run NeWS in the same server.

q: Is X11R4 a big improvement over R3?
a: Yes, for most people. R4 added twm, the new xdm, better fonts, and more contributed clients. It also fixed many bugs. If you can get a vendor release based on it, upgrade.

q: Is it worth getting an X terminal instead of a workstation?
a: If you already have a big timesharing host, yes. An NCD or HP X terminal costs much less than a Sun workstation and gives you the same X display. But you'll load your server and the Ethernet heavily.

q: Is there a decent X based text editor?
a: GNU Emacs 18.5x has X support through the xterm interface, and version 19 is in the works. There's also xedit from MIT, which is rather limited, and the commercial editors that come with vendor desktops.

q: Is there a good book on X programming?
a: Look at Oliver Jones' Introduction to the X Window System, and the Xlib Programming Manual from O'Reilly, which is Volume One of their series. Volume Two is the reference manual, and you'll want both.

q: What do the three mouse buttons do in xterm with ctrl held down?
a: Ctrl plus left gives the main options menu, ctrl plus middle gives the VT options with things like scrollbar and reverse video, and ctrl plus right gives the font menu.

q: What does the X in X Window System stand for?
a: Nothing much. It's just the letter after W, since X came out of MIT's Project Athena as a successor to the W window system at Stanford. Nobody means anything deeper by it.

q: What does the xclock command do and why would I run it?
a: It draws a clock, either analog or digital with -digital. Try xclock -update 1 for a second hand. It's mainly handy as a simple test that your server connection is working.

q: What does xhost do?
a: It controls which machines may open windows on your X server. Run xhost +hostname to allow one, xhost -hostname to remove it. Be careful with plain xhost +, since that lets anybody on the network in.

q: What does xmodmap do?
a: It changes the keyboard mapping and pointer buttons. You can swap Caps Lock and Control with a short script, like xmodmap -e 'remove Lock = Caps_Lock'. Use xev to find the keycodes.

q: What does xrdb do?
a: It loads resource settings into the X server so every client on any machine sees them. Run xrdb -load .Xresources or xrdb .Xdefaults. It beats keeping separate .Xdefaults files on every host you log into.

q: What is Motif and how is it different from Open Look?
a: They're both toolkits and look-and-feel standards on top of X. Motif comes from OSF and is backed by DEC, HP, and IBM. Open Look comes from Sun and AT&T. They're not compatible, so applications are built for one or the other.

q: What is PEX?
a: It's the PHIGS Extension to X, which adds 3D graphics to the server. It's still being worked out by the MIT X Consortium, so don't expect to find it on many machines yet.

q: What is a client and what is a server in X?
a: The server is the program running on your display, handling the screen, keyboard, and mouse. Clients are applications like xterm that ask it to draw. It seems backwards, but the server serves the display.

q: What is a colormap in X?
a: It's a table that turns pixel values into actual RGB colors on an 8-bit display. Only 256 entries are available, so every client shares them. Clients that grab too many can leave others with wrong colors.

q: What is an X display name like unix:0.0 mean?
a: It's host:display.screen. The host is the machine, the first number is the display on that machine, and the second is the screen if it has more than one monitor. Most single-screen setups use :0 or :0.0.

q: What is imake?
a: It's a tool that builds Makefiles for you from an Imakefile and a set of machine-specific config files, using the C preprocessor. It lets the same X source build on many different Unix systems.

q: What is the .Xdefaults file for?
a: It holds your resource settings for X applications, such as xterm*background: black or XTerm*scrollBar: true. Put it in your home directory. Under X11R4 you can also load settings with xrdb.

q: What is the Athena widget set?
a: It's the toolkit that comes with the MIT X distribution, used by xterm, xclock and others. It's simple and a bit plain, but it's free, and it works everywhere X runs.

q: What is the Xt Intrinsics?
a: It's the toolkit foundation library that sits on top of Xlib. It provides widgets, resource handling, and event dispatch. The Athena and Motif widget sets are both built on top of it.

q: What is the best X terminal emulator for a beginner?
a: Stick with xterm. It emulates a VT102 and Tektronix 4014, comes with every X distribution, and the man page documents all the options. Once you're used to it, you can look at alternatives like cmdtool on Suns.

q: What is the difference between X10 and X11?
a: X11 is a complete redesign with a different protocol, so X10 clients won't talk to X11 servers without a translator. X11 added better graphics, color handling, and extensibility. Use X11, since X10 is basically dead.

q: What is the difference between xterm and a Sun console window?
a: A Sun shelltool or cmdtool runs inside SunView and only works on that display. xterm is a standard X client, so it also works across the network and on every other vendor's X server.

q: What is xdm?
a: It's the X display manager. It puts up a login window on the screen and starts your session after you log in, like getty and login do for text terminals. Mostly useful for X terminals and workstations that always run X.

q: Where can I ask for help with X problems?
a: Try comp.windows.x on Usenet. It's busy and the regulars know the MIT source well. Read the FAQ-like postings and the man pages first, and say what machine and X release you're running.

q: Where can I get the X11R4 sources?
a: Anonymous FTP to expo.lcs.mit.edu has the full MIT distribution, including contrib clients. If you have no net access, you can order a tape from the MIT X Consortium for a small fee.

q: Which window manager is better, twm or uwm?
a: twm is the better choice. It comes with X11R4, has title bars, icons, and a decent config file in .twmrc. uwm is older, menu-driven, and has no title bars. Most people moved to twm.

q: Why are my colors wrong in X?
a: Color names come from rgb.txt in the X lib directory. If you ask for a color the server can't allocate, or run out of colormap cells, you get black or white. Check your colormap with xcmap-like tools and close color hogs.

q: Why do I get 'Error: Can't open display' when I run xterm?
a: Your DISPLAY variable isn't set, or points at a server that won't accept you. Check echo $DISPLAY, make sure it looks like host:0, and that xhost on the server permits your machine.

q: Why does the X server take over my whole screen and mouse?
a: The server owns the display, keyboard, and mouse by design. On a workstation, you can't use the console as before. Use xterm for your commands, and exit the window manager or kill the server to get back.

q: Why is my xterm so slow over the network?
a: Usually it's the Ethernet being busy or the remote host being loaded. Jump scroll helps, so try xterm -j or use the scrollbar less. Also avoid heavy graphics clients running over a slow serial or Internet link.

q: Can I change the section heading style in LaTeX?
a: Yes, but not easily in the standard styles. Look at the \@startsection command in article.sty, which sets the indentation, spacing and font. Copy it into your own style file and tweak the arguments.

q: Can I use TeX on an IBM PC?
a: Yes. PCTeX and MicroTeX are commercial versions, and emTeX is a good free one by Eberhard Mattes that runs under DOS. You'll want a hard disk and at least 640K, and the fonts take a fair bit of space.

q: Can TeX do hyphenation in other languages?
a: TeX's hyphenation patterns are loaded when the format is built, and US English is the default. Patterns for German, French, Dutch and others exist, and you can make a format with them using INITEX. Ask your site admin.

q: How can I get two columns in LaTeX?
a: Use the twocolumn option, as in \documentstyle[twocolumn]{article}. You can also switch in the middle with \twocolumn and \onecolumn, which start a new page. Floats and wide tables may need some fiddling.

q: How do I change the font size in LaTeX?
a: Give the size as an option to the document style, for example \documentstyle[12pt]{article}. The standard sizes are 10pt, 11pt and 12pt. For local changes use declarations like \large or \small.

q: How do I change the margins in LaTeX?
a: Set parameters such as \oddsidemargin, \evensidemargin, \textwidth, \topmargin and \textheight in the preamble, using \setlength. Remember the default offset is one inch, so \oddsidemargin 0pt gives you a 1 inch margin.

q: How do I do a fraction in TeX?
a: In LaTeX use \frac{a}{b} in math mode. In plain TeX you write {a \over b}. For smaller inline fractions, the result is shrunk automatically, and \displaystyle can force full size.

q: How do I get a DVI file onto my printer?
a: You need a DVI driver for your printer, such as dvips for PostScript printers or dvilj for HP LaserJets. Run something like dvips file to produce PostScript, then send that to the printer. Your site admin should know what's installed.

q: How do I get a real quotation mark in TeX?
a: Type two backquotes to open and two apostrophes to close, like ``this''. The plain double quote character " gives you a closing quote either way, which looks wrong at the start of a phrase.

q: How do I include a PostScript picture in a TeX document?
a: Use a driver that supports \special, such as dvips, and a macro package like psfig or epsf to include the encapsulated PostScript file. TeX only reserves the space, and the driver inserts the picture at print time.

q: How do I make a footnote?
a: Type \footnote{text} right after the word where you want the mark. TeX numbers it and puts the text at the bottom of the page. In plain TeX the command is \footnote{mark}{text}.

q: How do I make a letter in LaTeX?
a: Use \documentstyle{letter} and the commands \address, \signature, then \begin{letter}{Recipient address} with \opening{Dear Sir,} and \closing{Yours,}. It handles the layout. Lamport's book has a good example.

q: How do I make a table in LaTeX?
a: Use the tabular environment, such as \begin{tabular}{lcr}, where the letters set left, centered or right columns. Separate cells with & and end rows with \\. Put a | in the argument for vertical rules and \hline for horizontal ones.

q: How do I make a table of contents in LaTeX?
a: Put \tableofcontents after \begin{document} and run LaTeX twice. The first run writes the .toc file and the second run reads it back in and prints the table. Same trick applies to cross references.

q: How do I preview my document on screen?
a: Use a DVI previewer: xdvi or dviapollo on workstations, and the preview programs that come with emTeX or PCTeX on a PC. On a Mac, Textures shows the typeset page right away. It saves a lot of paper.

q: How do I print a backslash in LaTeX?
a: Typing \\ is a line break, so use $\backslash$ in math mode. In plain TeX, $\backslash$ works as well. For lots of literal code, put it in a verbatim environment and everything is printed as typed.

q: How do I put a figure in my paper with a caption?
a: Use the figure environment, with \begin{figure}, your content, \caption{text}, and \end{figure}. LaTeX floats it to a good place, and the position options like [htb] tell it where to try. Use \label after the caption to refer to it.

q: How do I put in a mathematical equation in LaTeX?
a: For inline math put it between dollar signs, like $x^2 + y^2$. For a displayed equation use \begin{equation} ... \end{equation}, which numbers it, or \[ ... \] if you don't want a number.

q: How do I split a large document into several files?
a: Put each chapter in its own file and use \include{chap1} in the main file. With \includeonly{chap1} in the preamble you can process just one while keeping page and reference numbers from earlier runs.

q: How do I start a new paragraph in LaTeX?
a: Leave a blank line in the source. One newline is just a space to TeX, but a blank line ends the paragraph. Don't use \\ for paragraphs, that only forces a line break and leaves you with ugly spacing.

q: How do I type an underscore in LaTeX?
a: Use \_ in ordinary text. A bare underscore means subscript and is only allowed in math mode, so TeX complains with a Missing $ error otherwise. This bites everyone with filenames and variable names.

q: Is it worth learning TeX if I only write a few papers a year?
a: If you write any math, yes. The output is far better than a word processor gives you and the equations are easy once you learn the basics. LaTeX will get you going in an afternoon with a template from a colleague.

q: Is there a TeX for the Macintosh?
a: Yes, OzTeX and Textures are both available. Textures from Blue Sky Research is commercial and nicely integrated with the Mac, while OzTeX is cheaper shareware. Either one handles LaTeX if you load the macros.

q: Is there a way to check my spelling in a TeX file?
a: On Unix, run spell on the source or use detex to strip the commands first, then pipe it to spell. On a PC, some editors and tools like Word Perfect's speller work on plain text. Many people also use ispell.

q: What are .tfm files?
a: TFM files are TeX font metric files holding the width, height and depth of each character, plus kerning and ligature info. TeX only needs these to typeset. The driver needs the actual bitmaps, usually .pk or .gf files, to print.

q: What are the Computer Modern fonts?
a: Computer Modern is the family of typefaces Knuth designed with METAFONT for TeX, including roman, italic, bold, typewriter and math symbols. They're the defaults in TeX and LaTeX, so most papers look the same unless you change them.

q: What does 'Missing $ inserted' mean?
a: You used a math-only character or command, like ^, _ or \alpha, outside math mode. Wrap it in dollar signs. It can also mean a dollar sign is missing at the end of a math expression, so check your pairs.

q: What does 'Overfull \hbox' mean?
a: TeX couldn't break a line without making it wider than the column, so something sticks out into the margin. Rewrite the sentence, add \hyphenation hints, or put \sloppy in effect. The warning tells you the points of overflow and the line number.

q: What does \documentstyle do?
a: It is the first line of a LaTeX 2.09 document and picks the overall layout, such as article, report, book or letter. Options in square brackets, like 11pt or twoside, go before the style name in braces.

q: What does \newpage do versus \clearpage?
a: \newpage ends the current page and starts a new one. \clearpage does that too, but first flushes out any pending figures and tables, which would otherwise float to later pages. Use \clearpage before a new chapter.

q: What does the % character do in TeX?
a: It starts a comment, and TeX ignores everything from the % to the end of the line, including the newline. If you actually want a percent sign in your text, type \% instead.

q: What does the tilde do in TeX?
a: The ~ is a tie, a space where TeX won't break the line. Use it in things like Figure~3 or Dr.~Smith so the reference isn't split between lines. It keeps the two words together.

q: What is BibTeX?
a: BibTeX is a program by Oren Patashnik that builds bibliographies for LaTeX from a database file of references. You cite with \cite, name a style with \bibliographystyle, and run LaTeX, BibTeX, then LaTeX twice more.

q: What is INITEX?
a: INITEX is the form of TeX used to build format files. It starts with no macros loaded, reads in plain.tex or lplain.tex, and dumps a fast format file, so later runs don't have to read all that again.

q: What is METAFONT?
a: METAFONT is Knuth's companion program for designing fonts. You describe letter shapes with equations and pens in a program, and it makes bitmap fonts for a specific printer resolution. Computer Modern, the standard TeX font, was made with it.

q: What is TeX and who wrote it?
a: TeX is a typesetting system written by Donald Knuth at Stanford, mainly to get math and books looking right. You feed it a plain text file with commands and it produces a DVI file, which you then print through a driver.

q: What is a .aux file?
a: LaTeX writes the .aux file to remember label and citation info between runs. On the next run it reads it back and fills in the reference numbers. If it gets corrupted by an error, just delete it and run again.

q: What is a document that I can use to get a thesis formatted in TeX?
a: Many universities have their own thesis style file, so ask your graduate office or other students first. Otherwise start with the report or book style and adjust margins by setting \oddsidemargin and \textwidth.

q: What is a ligature in TeX?
a: It is a combined character such as fi, fl or ff that TeX substitutes automatically from the font so the letters don't collide. You don't have to do anything. The font's TFM file defines which ones exist.

q: What is the \verb command?
a: \verb|text| prints the text exactly as typed, in typewriter font, with any delimiter character you pick. It's good for short bits of code inline. It can't be used inside another command's argument, such as a footnote.

q: What is the best book for learning TeX?
a: The TeXbook by Knuth is the real reference and it's fun, but it's dense. For LaTeX, get Leslie Lamport's LaTeX: A Document Preparation System. Most people find that one easier to start with.

q: What is the difference between TeX and LaTeX?
a: LaTeX is a set of macros written on top of TeX by Leslie Lamport. It gives you things like \documentclass-style structure, sections, cross references and automatic numbering, so you don't have to build all that yourself in plain TeX.

q: What is the difference between \def and \newcommand?
a: \def is the plain TeX primitive and silently redefines whatever was there. LaTeX's \newcommand complains if the command already exists, which saves you from clobbering something by accident. Use \renewcommand when you mean to redefine.

q: What is the difference between a .dvi and a .ps file?
a: A DVI file is device independent output from TeX, with no fonts embedded. A .ps file is PostScript produced from the DVI by a driver like dvips for a specific printer. DVI files are small, while PostScript ones tend to be large.

q: Where can I get TeX for free?
a: TeX is in the public domain, so you can ftp the source from labrea.stanford.edu or from sites like the Aston archive in England. Many Unix vendors ship it too. Tom Rokicki's web2c port is common on Unix.

q: Which is better, TeX or troff?
a: For equations TeX is generally considered better, with nicer line breaking and spacing. troff is on every Unix box and has eqn, tbl and pic that people already know. If you need heavy math or good looking books, I'd go with TeX.

q: Why do my references show up as ?? in LaTeX?
a: LaTeX hasn't yet seen the label info from a previous run. Run it a second time so the .aux file gets read. If you still see ??, check that your \label is spelled the same as the \ref.

q: Why does TeX ignore multiple spaces in my text?
a: TeX treats any run of spaces as a single space, and the same for a newline. If you really need extra space, use \ (backslash space), ~ for a tie, or \hspace{1in} in LaTeX. For verbatim text use the verbatim environment.

q: Why does TeX say 'Undefined control sequence'?
a: You used a command TeX doesn't know, usually a typo or a missing macro package. The error message shows the offending command just before the line where it stopped. Check spelling and that you loaded the right style file.

q: Why is my LaTeX run so slow?
a: A big part is loading the format and fonts, and on a PC the disk speed matters a lot. Make sure you use a preloaded format file instead of reading lplain.tex each time. Also use \includeonly to skip chapters you aren't working on.
